RACGP: Trans and gender diverse health

subtopic_detail: Low mood and tearfulness clearly tied to a recent redundancy with retained enjoyment and fleeting thoughts that life is not worth living
stem: A 42-year-old man was made redundant seven weeks ago. He feels flattened and tearful, worries about the mortgage and lies awake after going to bed. He still enjoys his daughter's netball; appetite, weight and waking time are unchanged. Once or twice he has thought his family would be better off without him, which frightens him, and he has no plan. He asks for antidepressants.

data_table.Examination: Tearful about work but brightens describing his daughter, no psychomotor change

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Safety planning with psychological therapy and early planned review
options.rationale: Symptoms proportionate to an identifiable stressor within three months, with preserved enjoyment, intact appetite and weight and no early morning waking, describe an adjustment disorder rather than a major depressive episode, and psychological therapy with practical problem solving is the evidence-based treatment. Passive thoughts of being a burden still require an explicit safety plan and early review, because adjustment disorder carries a real suicide risk despite not meeting depressive criteria. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start an antidepressant today as he asks and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Acceding to a clear patient request has value and antidepressants would be appropriate if he met criteria for a depressive episode. Evidence does not support antidepressants for adjustment disorder, and prescribing here exposes him to adverse effects, discontinuation problems and a diagnostic label that may affect insurance, without expected benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer him urgently to the acute mental health team for same day review
options.rationale: Urgent assessment is indicated for active suicidal intent, a formed plan, access to means with expressed intent, or psychotic depression. Fleeting ego dystonic thoughts that frighten him, with strong protective factors and no plan or intent, do not meet that threshold and an emergency response may deter future disclosure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a hypnotic and review in one month
options.rationale: His sleep onset difficulty is real and hypnotics would shorten it in the short term. They do not address the worry driving the insomnia, carry dependence risk, and are specifically discouraged where suicidal thoughts are present because of overdose potential. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure him this is a normal reaction and review only if it worsens
options.rationale: Normalising his reaction is a reasonable and important part of the conversation, since distress after redundancy is expected. Symptoms that have persisted seven weeks with impairment and passive suicidal thoughts warrant active treatment and scheduled follow up rather than open ended watchful waiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Adjustment disorder is an emotional or behavioural response to an identifiable stressor beginning within three months of it, causing distress out of proportion to what would be expected or significant functional impairment, and not meeting criteria for another disorder. The distinction from a major depressive episode rests on the biological features and on pervasiveness, since preserved reactivity of mood, normal appetite and weight and absence of early morning waking all argue against a depressive episode. This distinction matters because treatment differs: psychological therapy and practical problem solving have evidence in adjustment disorder while antidepressants do not, and prescribing them conveys risk without expected benefit. Suicide risk is nonetheless substantial in adjustment disorder and is not proportional to the diagnostic label, so safety planning and scheduled review are required whenever thoughts of death are disclosed.
key_points: Onset is within three months of an identifiable stressor
Preserved enjoyment, appetite and sleep pattern argue against a depressive episode
Psychological therapy and problem solving are the evidence-based treatment
Antidepressants lack evidence for adjustment disorder specifically
Suicide risk is real and requires safety planning regardless of the label
explanation.pearls: Adjustment disorder is over represented among people who die by suicide relative to how mild the diagnosis sounds, with the act often occurring impulsively and close to the stressor, which is why means restriction and a written safety plan belong in the first consultation.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Older man with rooms impassable from accumulated possessions who feels distress only when others try to discard them and has no intrusive contamination thoughts
stem:
You are the general practitioner doing a home visit on a 68-year-old man after his daughter rang the practice. Newspapers, containers and unopened purchases are stacked to shoulder height through the hallway and only a narrow path remains to the kitchen, where the stove cannot be reached.

He tells you calmly that everything has a use and he will sort it when he has time, and he becomes visibly distressed only when his daughter suggests a skip bin. He describes no repetitive washing, checking or counting, and no intrusive thoughts he is trying to neutralise. His mood is reactive and he denies anhedonia. He scores 28 out of 30 on cognitive screening and manages his own finances and medications accurately.

data_table.Examination: Well kempt and oriented, speech normal in rate and form, mood reactive with no psychomotor slowing, no delusional explanation offered for the accumulation, insight limited regarding the safety risk, Mini Mental State Examination 28 out of 30, gait steady
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a high dose and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: High dose serotonergic medication is the pharmacological approach to obsessive compulsive disorder, but response rates in hoarding disorder are considerably lower. Medication is added when depression or anxiety coexists rather than as the primary treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy specifically adapted for difficulty discarding
options.rationale: Persistent difficulty parting with possessions, distress at the thought of discarding, and clutter that prevents rooms from being used as intended defines a condition in its own right, and the treatment with the best evidence is a structured cognitive behavioural program covering motivation, sorting skills and graded discarding. It outperforms generic therapy and is delivered over months. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Arrange a forced clean out by council officers with family present to remove the risk
options.rationale: Involuntary clearance reliably produces rapid re-accumulation and a rupture in the therapeutic relationship, and it is reserved for imminent and otherwise unmanageable danger. Even then it is coordinated with treatment rather than used instead of it. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer for comprehensive neuropsychological assessment for a frontal lobe syndrome
options.rationale: Accumulation that begins abruptly in later life, especially with disinhibition, apathy or personality change, does warrant assessment for a frontotemporal process. His cognition screens normally and he continues to manage complex daily tasks. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hoarding disorder)

options.text: Refer to the aged care assessment team for placement in supported residential care
options.rationale: Residential placement addresses functional decline from cognitive or physical impairment, neither of which he has, and it does not treat the behaviour that produced the clutter. He manages his medications and finances independently. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Difficulty discarding possessions became a separate diagnosis because it differs from obsessive compulsive disorder in phenomenology, treatment response and course. The accumulation is driven by beliefs about usefulness, waste and emotional attachment rather than by intrusive thoughts that the person is trying to neutralise, and distress arises at the prospect of discarding rather than from the clutter itself. Insight is characteristically poor, which is why referral usually comes from family, neighbours or council rather than the person. Prevalence rises with age and the associated risks are substantial, including falls, fire, structural damage, infestation and eviction. Treatment is a specifically adapted cognitive behavioural program, often combined with practical in home support, and medication addresses comorbid depression or anxiety rather than the behaviour itself.
key_points: Distress arises at discarding, not from the clutter or from intrusive thoughts
Clutter must prevent rooms being used for their intended purpose
Insight is typically poor and referral usually comes from others
Adapted cognitive behavioural therapy is the primary treatment
Late onset accumulation with personality change suggests a frontal process
explanation.pearls: Forced clearance without concurrent psychological treatment is followed by re-accumulation to the previous level in the majority of cases within two years, so a skip bin arranged without therapy is a temporary fix that also destroys the working relationship needed for the real one.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Adolescent girl with a widening area of missing scalp hair pulled out when studying, with relief afterwards and no scaling or broken hair of varying length on the rest of the scalp
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old girl brought by her mother because of a bald patch at the crown that has widened over six months. Her mother has noticed hair on the desk when she is studying for exams.

When you see her alone she tells you she pulls hairs out one at a time while she is concentrating or lying in bed, feels a build up of tension first and a sense of relief afterwards, and has tried to stop several times. She denies eating the hair. She is embarrassed and now wears her hair up to hide it. She is doing well at school, has friends, sleeps normally and denies low mood or thoughts of self-harm. There are no intrusive thoughts and no rituals.

data_table.Examination: Irregular patch of hair loss at the crown measuring about 5 cm with hairs of varying lengths within it, no scaling, erythema, scarring or broken hair beyond the patch, eyebrows and eyelashes intact, no palpable abdominal mass, mood euthymic with reactive affect, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a low dose and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants have repeatedly failed to outperform placebo for pulling behaviours, unlike in obsessive compulsive disorder where they are central. They are reserved for coexisting depression or anxiety, neither of which she has. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid scalp lotion and review the patch in eight weeks
options.rationale: Topical corticosteroid treats an autoimmune patch of hair loss, which produces a smooth bald area with exclamation mark hairs at the margin rather than hairs of differing lengths within it. Her varying hair lengths indicate mechanical removal at different times. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Alopecia)

options.text: Prescribe oral terbinafine for four weeks after sending scalp scrapings for fungal culture
options.rationale: Fungal scalp infection also produces patchy loss in a young person, but with scaling, broken hairs close to the skin and often occipital lymphadenopathy. Her scalp skin is entirely normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric surgeon for assessment of a possible gastric hair mass
options.rationale: Surgical referral is warranted when hair is swallowed, which produces abdominal pain, vomiting, a palpable mass or iron deficiency. She denies eating hair, her abdomen is normal and her iron studies are unremarkable. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Trichotillomania)

options.text: Refer for habit reversal training delivered by a trained psychologist over several sessions
options.rationale: Repetitive pulling with rising tension beforehand and relief afterwards, plus repeated failed attempts to stop, identifies a body focused repetitive behaviour, and habit reversal training combining awareness training with a competing response has the strongest evidence of any intervention. It is first line ahead of any medication in adolescents. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Recurrent hair pulling typically begins around puberty, affects girls more often than boys in clinical samples, and is frequently concealed for years by hairstyle changes. The diagnosis rests on the behavioural account rather than on the appearance of the scalp, though hairs of varying length within an irregular patch with normal underlying skin is the characteristic finding and separates it from autoimmune and infective causes. It sits with skin picking among the body focused repetitive behaviours, which differ from obsessive compulsive disorder in that the behaviour is preceded by tension or an urge rather than by an intrusive thought, and it responds to behavioural rather than serotonergic treatment. Swallowing the pulled hair occurs in a minority and carries a real risk of a gastric hair mass, so it must be asked about directly.
key_points: An urge with tension before and relief after defines the behaviour
Hairs of varying length within the patch indicate mechanical pulling
Normal scalp skin excludes fungal and autoimmune causes
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms medication
Ask directly about swallowing hair because of gastric mass risk
explanation.pearls: Around a fifth of people who pull also swallow the hair, and the resulting gastric mass can extend into the small bowel as a tail, so persistent abdominal pain with unexplained iron deficiency in a puller is a surgical presentation rather than a psychiatric one.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Adolescent unable to fall asleep before three in the morning on school nights who sleeps soundly until midday on holidays with normal total sleep time
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16-year-old boy whose mother is worried that he is depressed because he cannot get out of bed for school and has been late eleven times this term. He lies awake until about three in the morning however early he goes to bed, then has to be dragged out at seven.

During the recent two week school holidays he went to sleep at about three and woke spontaneously at about eleven, felt refreshed and had no difficulty. His mood is good on weekends and in the holidays, he enjoys skateboarding and his appetite is normal. He drinks no caffeine after midday and does not use cannabis. His sleep diary shows a consistent sleep period of eight hours whenever he is allowed to choose the timing.

data_table.Examination: Alert with reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, no anhedonia described on direct questioning, no suicidal ideation, weight stable, general physical examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin all within normal limits, two week sleep diary showing sleep onset between 2:45 and 3:15 am with an eight hour sleep period when the wake time is unconstrained

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start low dose melatonin timed several hours before his current sleep onset with morning light
options.rationale: A stable eight hour sleep period that is simply shifted later, with normal quality and refreshed waking when the timing is unconstrained, is a circadian phase problem rather than an inability to sleep. Small doses of melatonin given in the early evening shift the body clock earlier, and timed bright light after waking consolidates the shift. (Source: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people

options.text: Start a sedating antidepressant at night and review his mood symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressant treatment addresses a depressive episode, which would show low mood and loss of interest across weekends and holidays as well as school days. His mood and enjoyment are intact whenever the timing constraint is removed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start temazepam at night for two weeks and taper it once his sleep pattern has settled
options.rationale: A hypnotic forces sleep onset without moving the underlying clock, so the pattern returns as soon as it is stopped, and benzodiazepines are not recommended for adolescents. His problem is the timing of the sleep period rather than an inability to sleep at all. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start a high dose of melatonin at his usual bedtime and continue it for at least three months
options.rationale: Melatonin shifts the clock through its timing rather than its sedative effect, so a large dose given at the current late bedtime acts as a hypnotic and can even delay the phase further. The drug is appropriate; the dose and timing are not. (Source: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people)
source_refs: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography before deciding on any specific treatment approach
options.rationale: A sleep study answers questions about breathing, limb movements or unusual events during sleep, none of which are suggested here. His diary already demonstrates normal sleep duration and consolidation once the timing is free. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder

explanation.summary: The circadian clock runs later during adolescence for biological reasons, and in a minority the shift is severe enough that sleep onset cannot be achieved before the early hours despite adequate opportunity. The diagnostic signature is a normal duration and quality of sleep whenever the timing is unconstrained, contrasted with severe difficulty on school days, which is why holidays and weekends are the most informative part of the history. The pattern is regularly misread as depression, school refusal or laziness, and it does frequently produce secondary low mood, so the direction of causation must be teased out. Treatment combines evening melatonin at a low dose given well before current sleep onset, bright light exposure on waking, avoidance of evening screens and light, and gradual advancement of the schedule, with weekend consistency the hardest and most important element.
key_points: Normal sleep when timing is unconstrained separates this from insomnia
Holidays and weekends are the most informative part of the history
Melatonin works by shifting phase, so timing matters more than dose
Morning bright light consolidates the advance in phase
Secondary low mood is common and resolves as the schedule corrects
explanation.pearls: Melatonin advances the body clock when taken about five hours before habitual sleep onset, so in an adolescent falling asleep at three in the morning the first dose belongs around ten at night, and giving it at the current bedtime wastes the phase shifting effect entirely.

sources.label: RANZCP: Sleep disorders in young people
Australasian Sleep Association: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder

subtopic_detail: Older woman with two years of difficulty maintaining sleep requesting a repeat hypnotic after four weeks of temazepam with a normal screening for depression and sleep apnoea
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71-year-old woman who has come in asking for another script for the sleeping tablet another doctor started a month ago. She wakes at about two each morning and lies there for two hours, and this has been going on for two years.

She says the tablet worked well for the first fortnight and now she needs it just to get the same sleep she had before. She is not low in mood, still plays bridge twice a week and gardens most days. Her husband says she does not snore and has never stopped breathing at night. She drinks one glass of wine with dinner and no coffee after lunch. She naps for an hour most afternoons in her armchair and is in bed by nine each night.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg per square metre, neck circumference 33 cm, Geriatric Depression Scale 2 out of 15, Mini Mental State Examination 29 out of 30, no postural drop, gait steady with no aid
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function and ferritin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the current hypnotic at the same dose and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Benzodiazepine hypnotics are recommended for no more than two to four weeks, and continued use in an older person roughly doubles the risk of falls and hip fracture while the hypnotic effect fades. She has already reached the recommended limit. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia and plan a gradual hypnotic taper
options.rationale: Structured behavioural therapy including stimulus control, sleep restriction and cognitive work is first line for persistent insomnia at every age and produces benefits that persist after treatment ends, unlike hypnotics. Her rising dose requirement after two weeks is tolerance, which is the signal to plan withdrawal rather than to repeat the script. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines

options.text: Switch to a sedating antihistamine at night and review her sleep pattern in four weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antihistamines carry a substantial anticholinergic burden that contributes to confusion, urinary retention and falls in older people, and tolerance to the sedation develops within days. Substituting one hypnotic for a worse one does not address the maintaining factors. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start mirtazapine at night for its sedating effect and review her sleep again in six weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antidepressants have a role when insomnia accompanies a depressive episode, but they are not indicated for insomnia without depression. Her depression screen is negative and she remains engaged and active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography before making any change to her current medication
options.rationale: A sleep study is indicated when obstructive breathing, limb movements or parasomnia is suspected, signalled by snoring, witnessed apnoea, a large neck or unrefreshing sleep despite adequate duration. Her partner reports none of these and her neck circumference is small. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Insomnia)

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia is defined by difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep on at least three nights a week for three months with daytime consequences, and it is maintained by behaviours that develop in response to poor sleep rather than by whatever started it. Excessive time in bed, daytime napping and clock watching are the usual culprits, and they are precisely what behavioural therapy targets through stimulus control and sleep restriction. Australian guidance is unambiguous that psychological treatment is first line at all ages and that hypnotics are limited to short courses, because tolerance develops within weeks while the harms of falls, fracture, cognitive impairment and daytime sedation accumulate. Digital and telephone delivered programs have made the therapy accessible outside metropolitan areas, which removes the commonest practical excuse for a repeat script.
key_points: Behavioural therapy is first line for chronic insomnia at any age
Benefits of therapy persist after treatment ends, unlike hypnotics
Hypnotics are limited to two to four weeks because of tolerance
Eleven hours in bed with an afternoon nap dilutes sleep pressure
Benzodiazepines roughly double fall and fracture risk in older people
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction that sets the time in bed to match actual sleep time, in her case about six hours with a fixed rise time, is the single most effective component of the therapy, and it usually worsens daytime sleepiness in the first fortnight before the improvement appears.

sources.label: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence, benzodiazepines

subtopic_detail: Residual nightly trauma related nightmares with waking in a sweat after completing an adequate course of trauma focused psychological therapy that resolved the daytime symptoms
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41-year-old former soldier who completed sixteen sessions of trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy with an experienced psychologist four months ago. His avoidance, hypervigilance and intrusive daytime memories have largely resolved and he has returned to work full time.

What has not changed is that five or six nights a week he wakes at about two in the morning from a dream replaying a specific incident, drenched in sweat and with his heart racing, then stays awake. His partner says he shouts but does not get out of bed or act out the dreams. He drinks two standard drinks on a Friday and no more. He takes no regular medication and his physical examination and screening bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic with reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no current suicidal ideation, no postural blood pressure drop, cardiovascular and respiratory examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his treatment?

options.text: Start quetiapine at night and titrate the dose slowly against his nightmare frequency
options.rationale: Low dose antipsychotics are widely prescribed for sleep in this population but Australian guidance does not support them as adjuncts, and they bring weight gain, metabolic change and sedation. They are considered only for treatment resistant illness under specialist supervision. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.text: Start temazepam at night and review his nightmare frequency again in four weeks' time
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are specifically discouraged in this condition because they suppress the emotional processing that psychological treatment depends on, worsen outcomes in several trials and carry dependence risk in a group with high comorbid substance use. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.text: Repeat a second full course of trauma-focused psychological therapy with a new therapist
options.rationale: A further course is reasonable when the daytime symptoms have failed to respond, whereas his avoidance and hypervigilance have largely resolved and only the nocturnal symptom persists. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.text: Start prazosin at night and titrate the dose slowly against his nightmare frequency
options.rationale: Persisting trauma related nightmares after an adequate course of trauma-focused psychological therapy are the recognised indication for adjunctive prazosin, which reduces noradrenergic activity during sleep and is titrated upward from a small night time dose. Postural blood pressure is checked as the dose rises. (Source: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health)
source_refs: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

options.text: Arrange polysomnography to look for a disorder of rapid eye movement sleep behaviour
options.rationale: A sleep study is indicated when the person physically enacts dreams, leaves the bed or injures a partner, which raises a parasomnia of later life. His partner reports shouting only, with no motor enactment. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Parasomnias)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance places trauma-focused psychological therapy ahead of medication for posttraumatic stress disorder, and most people who complete an adequate course improve substantially. Residual symptoms are common and it is worth identifying which domain persists, because the answer differs for daytime intrusions, avoidance, mood and sleep. Trauma related nightmares are among the most persistent symptoms and respond poorly to antidepressants alone, which is why an adjunctive noradrenergic blocker occupies a specific niche and imagery rehearsal therapy is offered where it is available. The evidence for prazosin is mixed, with a large negative trial in stable veterans alongside several positive studies, so it is used as a trial with a clear review point rather than as an open ended prescription, and blood pressure is monitored during titration.
key_points: Trauma-focused psychological therapy is first line, ahead of medication
Identify which symptom domain persists before adding anything
Nightmares respond poorly to antidepressant monotherapy
Benzodiazepines worsen outcomes and are specifically discouraged
Dream enactment with movement suggests a parasomnia, not nightmares
explanation.pearls: Prazosin is started at 1 mg at night because of first dose hypotension, and the postural blood pressure should be rechecked at each increase, with most responders settling between 3 mg and 10 mg nightly over several weeks of titration.

sources.label: Phoenix Australia: Australian guidelines for posttraumatic mental health

subtopic_detail: Man presenting with debt and marital crisis after escalating sports betting with chasing of losses, no alcohol or drug use and no manic features
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 36-year-old man who says his wife has told him to get help or leave. Over three years his sports betting has grown from a weekly bet to daily in play betting, and he has taken out a personal loan of 40000 dollars and borrowed from his brother without telling her.

He describes needing larger stakes for the same excitement, returning the next day to win back what he lost, and lying about how much he bets. He has tried to stop four times and lasted at most a fortnight. He drinks two standard drinks a week and uses no other substances. He has never had a period of reduced sleep with elevated mood or overspending outside gambling. He denies current suicidal thoughts but says he has felt hopeless about the debt.

data_table.Examination: Appears tired but well kempt, speech normal in rate and volume, mood described as flat with reactive affect, no grandiosity or pressured speech, no perceptual disturbance, cognition intact, no signs of chronic liver disease or intravenous drug use
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function and urine drug screen all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start naltrexone at 50 mg daily and review his gambling and his mood in eight weeks
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists have modest evidence in this condition and are considered when psychological therapy has failed or when there is a strong family history of alcohol use disorder. Medication is not the first intervention when structured therapy has not yet been tried. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start a mood stabiliser for an underlying bipolar disorder and review his mood in eight weeks
options.rationale: Excessive gambling occurring only during periods of elevated mood, reduced sleep and other disinhibited spending would point to a mood disorder, which can also cause financial harm. His gambling has been continuous for three years with no elevated episodes. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for gambling with financial counselling alongside
options.rationale: Tolerance to stake size, chasing losses, concealment and repeated failed attempts to stop define a behavioural addiction, and structured cognitive behavioural therapy targeting gambling related cognitions has the strongest evidence, delivered alongside financial counselling because unresolved debt is a powerful driver of relapse. Both are available free through Australian gambling help services. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

options.text: Refer to a residential withdrawal unit for supervised abstinence over the next two weeks
options.rationale: Inpatient withdrawal exists to manage the physiological consequences of stopping a substance, and there is no physical withdrawal syndrome from gambling. Removing him from home for a fortnight does not address the cognitions or the debt that will greet him on return. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Advise him to self exclude from venues and review his gambling again in three months' time
options.rationale: Self exclusion and blocking software are useful harm reduction measures and should be part of the plan, but used alone they leave the underlying cognitions untreated and online accounts are easily reopened. It is an adjunct rather than a treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Gambling disorder)

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is classified with the substance use disorders because it shares tolerance, loss of control, preoccupation, concealment and continuation despite harm, and Australians lose more per adult to gambling than any other population. Chasing losses is the most specific feature and distinguishes problem gambling from recreational betting more reliably than the amount wagered. Screening matters because affected people rarely raise it themselves and present instead with depression, anxiety, relationship breakdown, workplace theft or suicidal thinking, and suicide risk in this group is several times the background rate. Treatment centres on cognitive behavioural therapy addressing beliefs about luck, skill and near misses, combined with practical measures including self exclusion, account blocking and financial counselling, with family involvement where the person agrees.
key_points: Chasing losses is the most specific feature of disordered gambling
Screen for it when depression, debt or relationship crisis presents
Suicide risk is several times higher than in the general population
Cognitive behavioural therapy for gambling is the primary treatment
Financial counselling and self exclusion are adjuncts, not substitutes
explanation.pearls: Continuous forms such as in play sports betting and electronic gaming machines cause disproportionate harm compared with weekly lottery products, because the short interval between stake and outcome allows chasing within a single sitting.

subtopic_detail: Choice of relapse prevention pharmacotherapy after alcohol withdrawal in a man with compensated cirrhosis and normal renal function
stem: A 54-year-old man has completed a five-day inpatient alcohol withdrawal with no withdrawal signs for 48 hours. He drank 15 standard drinks daily for a decade and wants to stay abstinent. He has cirrhosis without ascites or encephalopathy, takes no opioids and is booked with the drug and alcohol counsellor.

data_table.Examination: Spider naevi, palmar erythema, firm liver edge, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 22 micromol/L, albumin 37 g/L, INR 1.2, creatinine 74 micromol/L, eGFR above 90 mL/min/1.73m2, platelets 118 x10^9/L

lead_in: Which relapse prevention medication should you start?

options.text: Oral naltrexone daily for at least six months
options.rationale: Naltrexone is at least as effective for reducing heavy drinking days but undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism and is avoided in significant liver disease, whereas acamprosate is renally cleared and both are otherwise first line. Liver function must also be monitored if it is ever used. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Oral disulfiram with supervised daily administration
options.rationale: Disulfiram carries a risk of severe hepatotoxicity and depends on a supervised aversive reaction, making it unsuitable in established cirrhosis. It is reserved for highly motivated people with normal liver function and a supervising partner. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Oral baclofen at low dose titrated upwards
options.rationale: Baclofen is renally cleared and is sometimes used in advanced liver disease, but the evidence base is weaker and the Australian position places it as a second line option after the established agents. It also carries sedation and a withdrawal syndrome of its own. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Oral diazepam tapered over a further month
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines treat the withdrawal syndrome and are stopped once it has resolved, which happened 48 hours ago, and continuing them creates dependence while raising encephalopathy risk in cirrhosis. They have no relapse prevention role. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

options.text: Oral acamprosate for at least six months
options.rationale: Acamprosate is not metabolised by the liver and is cleared renally, so preserved synthetic function with normal creatinine makes it the appropriate choice in cirrhosis, and it is started immediately after withdrawal is complete. It reduces the risk of returning to any drinking. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction)

explanation.summary: Relapse prevention pharmacotherapy is offered to everyone with moderate to severe alcohol use disorder alongside psychosocial treatment, yet it remains substantially underprescribed in Australian practice. The two first line agents work differently, with acamprosate stabilising glutamatergic transmission to support ongoing abstinence and naltrexone blunting the rewarding effect of alcohol to reduce heavy drinking. The choice between them turns on organ function and on concurrent medication, since acamprosate is renally cleared and contraindicated in severe renal impairment, while naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and is also incompatible with any opioid analgesia. Disulfiram remains an option for motivated people with supervision and normal liver function, and in all cases the medication is a support for counselling rather than a replacement for it.
key_points: Acamprosate is renally cleared and suits significant liver disease
Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and blocked by opioid use
Disulfiram risks hepatotoxicity and needs supervised administration
Start relapse prevention as soon as withdrawal has resolved
Medication supplements rather than replaces psychosocial treatment
explanation.pearls: Acamprosate is contraindicated once the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below 30 mL per minute per 1.73 square metres, so the practical rule is that the kidney decides for acamprosate and the liver decides for naltrexone.

subtopic_detail: Restarting a mood stabiliser after eleven days without any doses in a woman whose maintenance dose was previously well tolerated
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman with bipolar II disorder maintained on lamotrigine 200 mg daily for three years without any rash or other problem. She went interstate for a funeral, left her tablets at home and has taken none for eleven days.

She feels her mood starting to drop and wants to restart today. She takes no other medication, in particular no sodium valproate and no oral contraceptive. She has had no rash, no fever and no mouth ulceration at any time. She has no intercurrent illness and her renal and liver function were normal three months ago. She asks whether she can simply take her usual 200 mg tonight and carry on as before.

data_table.Examination: Skin entirely clear with no rash anywhere including the mucous membranes, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, mood mildly low with reactive affect, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function all within normal limits three months ago

lead_in: What should you advise about restarting her medication?

options.text: Restart at her previous maintenance dose tonight because she tolerated it for three years
options.rationale: Resuming the full dose after a gap of this length is the specific prescribing error associated with severe cutaneous reactions, since the risk relates to the rate of dose escalation rather than to cumulative past exposure. Three years of tolerance offers no protection once the drug has washed out. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Restart at half her previous maintenance dose and increase to the full dose in one week
options.rationale: Halving the dose still starts far above the recommended initial step and compresses the escalation into a week, which is the pattern the slow schedule exists to prevent. After this gap, re-titration begins at the original starting dose and follows the original rate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Restart at the original starting dose and follow the full titration schedule again
options.rationale: Tolerance to the rash risk is lost after an interruption of about five days or more, so a gap of eleven days means the escalation must begin again from the initial dose with the same slow steps used at first prescription. Previous tolerance of the maintenance dose does not carry over. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Switch to sodium valproate at an equivalent mood stabilising dose to avoid re-titration
options.rationale: Valproate is a recognised mood stabiliser but carries substantial teratogenic risk in a woman of childbearing potential and is subject to pregnancy prevention requirements. Changing agents to avoid a four to six week titration is a disproportionate trade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Restart at her previous maintenance dose with a short course of prophylactic corticosteroid
options.rationale: There is no evidence that corticosteroid cover prevents the cutaneous reaction, and premedicating implies that a fast restart is otherwise acceptable. It also risks masking early rash while the reaction progresses. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Lamotrigine is effective for maintenance in bipolar disorder, particularly for preventing depressive episodes, and its main hazard is a serious cutaneous reaction that occurs in roughly one in a thousand adults. That risk is driven by how fast the dose is escalated, which is why the initial schedule takes several weeks and why the rate is halved again when the drug is combined with valproate, since valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine concentrations. Enzyme inducers including carbamazepine and oestrogen containing contraception have the opposite effect and require higher doses, so starting or stopping the pill changes the level substantially. After any interruption of about five days or more the person is treated as new to the drug and the full titration is repeated, and every patient should be told to stop the drug and seek review immediately if a rash appears.
key_points: The cutaneous risk tracks the rate of escalation, not the cumulative exposure
An interruption of five days or more resets the titration requirement
Valproate doubles lamotrigine levels and halves the starting dose
Oestrogen containing contraception lowers lamotrigine levels
Any rash means stopping the drug and seeking review the same day
explanation.pearls: Starting a combined oral contraceptive can halve the lamotrigine concentration and precipitate relapse, while stopping it can double the level and cause toxicity, so the contraceptive decision and the mood stabiliser dose must be made in the same consultation.

subtopic_detail: Confusion and unsteadiness three weeks after a dose increase of an enzyme inducing mood stabiliser in an older woman with a low serum sodium and concentrated urine
stem: A 74-year-old woman has been muddled and unsteady for three days. Her carbamazepine was increased from 400 mg to 600 mg daily three weeks ago. She takes no diuretic and has not vomited.

data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic, no postural drop or oedema; oriented to place but not date, no seizures
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 252 mmol/kg, urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L, thyroid and adrenal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the carbamazepine, restrict fluid and substitute another mood stabiliser
options.rationale: Withdrawing the agent and restricting fluid is the correct direction, but stopping an anticonvulsant mood stabiliser abruptly in a woman whose illness has been stable for years risks both seizure and relapse, so the dose is reduced with a planned substitution rather than ceased outright. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reduce the carbamazepine dose, restrict fluid and recheck sodium daily
options.rationale: A concentrated urine with urine sodium above 40 mmol/L in a euvolaemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function defines inappropriate antidiuresis, and carbamazepine is among the commonest drug causes with the risk rising after a dose increase and with age. Reducing the dose with fluid restriction corrects it while avoiding abrupt withdrawal, and daily sodium prevents overcorrection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give a 500 mL bolus of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride and reassess
options.rationale: Isotonic saline is the treatment for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, which shows dry mucous membranes, a postural drop, a raised urea and a urine sodium below 20 mmol/L. Given in this setting it is excreted while the free water is retained, and the sodium can fall further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give 100 mL of 3 per cent hypertonic saline, repeated twice if needed
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures, coma or other severe neurological manifestations, and she is oriented to place with no focal deficit. Used without that indication it risks correcting the sodium faster than the 8 to 10 mmol/L daily ceiling. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start oral tolvaptan and continue the carbamazepine unchanged
options.rationale: A vasopressin receptor antagonist is a specialist option for persistent inappropriate antidiuresis where the cause cannot be removed, and it requires close monitoring because of rapid correction. Leaving the responsible drug unchanged treats the consequence while the cause continues. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Carbamazepine causes hyponatraemia in a substantial minority of users through a direct antidiuretic effect, and the incidence rises with age, with higher doses and with concurrent diuretics or antidepressants. The biochemical picture is that of inappropriate antidiuresis, with a low serum osmolality, a urine osmolality that is inappropriately high and a urine sodium above 30 to 40 mmol/L in a clinically euvolaemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function. Symptoms are non-specific and in older people are commonly attributed to dementia or to the psychiatric illness itself, so a sodium level belongs in the work up of any confusion or fall in someone taking the drug. Management removes or reduces the cause, restricts fluid, and above all corrects slowly, because raising the sodium faster than 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours risks osmotic demyelination.
key_points: Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are common drug causes of low sodium
Euvolaemia with concentrated urine and urine sodium above 40 defines the syndrome
Exclude thyroid and adrenal insufficiency before accepting the diagnosis
Hypertonic saline is only for seizures, coma or severe neurological signs
Correction faster than 8 to 10 mmol/L per day risks osmotic demyelination
explanation.pearls: Check the sodium two to four weeks after starting or increasing carbamazepine in anyone over 65, because the fall is usually asymptomatic at first and is the single most common reason the drug has to be abandoned in older patients.

subtopic_detail: Constipation, fatigue and renal colic in a woman on long term lithium with a raised corrected calcium and a parathyroid hormone that is not suppressed
stem: A 52-year-old woman has taken lithium for bipolar I disorder for 18 years and has been well for a decade. She passed a kidney stone six weeks ago and has been tired and constipated for months. She takes no thiazide, calcium or vitamin D, and has no tremor or ataxia.

data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.82 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), parathyroid hormone 8.4 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L, lithium 0.7 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for her biochemistry?

options.text: Lithium associated overactivity of the parathyroid glands after years of use
options.rationale: Lithium raises the set point at which calcium suppresses parathyroid hormone, so the hormone remains inappropriately unsuppressed in the face of a high calcium, and the effect accumulates over years of treatment. The low phosphate and the renal stone fit the same mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Lithium toxicity from accumulation as her renal function has declined
options.rationale: Toxicity presents with a raised level alongside coarse tremor, vomiting, ataxia and confusion, and her level is squarely within range with none of those signs. Lithium associated hyperparathyroidism, unlike toxicity, is not concentration dependent and occurs with levels in range. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Malignancy related hypercalcaemia from a parathyroid hormone related peptide
options.rationale: Tumour related hypercalcaemia suppresses parathyroid hormone to the bottom of the range because the peptide acts on the same receptor. An unsuppressed hormone excludes that mechanism, and she has no weight loss or other features of malignancy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hypercalcaemia)

options.text: Excess vitamin D increasing intestinal absorption of dietary calcium
options.rationale: Vitamin D excess raises calcium and phosphate together while suppressing parathyroid hormone, and her phosphate is low with the hormone raised. She also takes no supplement and her vitamin D level is unremarkable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Familial benign hypercalcaemia unmasked by biochemistry taken after the stone
options.rationale: The familial condition gives lifelong mild hypercalcaemia with a characteristically low urinary calcium excretion and rarely causes stones. Her hypercalcaemia is new against previously normal results and it has already produced a stone. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Hypercalcaemia)

explanation.summary: Long term lithium requires structured monitoring precisely because its important complications develop slowly and silently. Renal function, thyroid function and calcium are checked every six to twelve months, alongside the lithium level itself, and each one detects a different problem. The calcium abnormality arises because lithium shifts the calcium sensing receptor set point upward, so the parathyroid glands behave as though the calcium is lower than it is, and prevalence rises with duration of treatment to affect a meaningful minority of long term users. Symptoms overlap with both depression and lithium side effects, so fatigue, constipation and low mood in a long term user should prompt a calcium rather than a dose change. Management ranges from observation with monitoring in mild asymptomatic cases through to parathyroid surgery when there is stone disease, bone loss or a substantially elevated calcium, and lithium can often be continued if it remains the only effective treatment.
key_points: Lithium raises the parathyroid set point so the hormone stays unsuppressed
Prevalence increases with duration of treatment over years
Malignant and vitamin D related hypercalcaemia suppress the hormone
Symptoms mimic both depression and lithium side effects
Stone disease or bone loss shifts management towards parathyroid surgery
explanation.pearls: Thiazide diuretics also raise calcium and reduce lithium clearance simultaneously, so adding one to a long term lithium user can produce hypercalcaemia and lithium toxicity in the same fortnight, and the combination needs level and calcium checks within a week of starting.

subtopic_detail: Persistent tongue and jaw movements emerging after years of an antipsychotic in a man already taking benzatropine, with no restlessness or subjective urge to move
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man with schizophrenia who has taken haloperidol for 22 years and benzatropine alongside it for most of that time. Over the last eight months his wife has noticed his tongue pushing against his cheek and a chewing movement of his jaw when he is watching television.

He is not distressed by the movements and does not feel any urge to move, and he describes no inner restlessness. The movements stop while he is speaking and are absent in sleep. His psychotic symptoms have been in remission for six years on the current dose. He takes no other medication, has no tremor and no cogwheel rigidity. There are no chorea elsewhere and no family history of a movement disorder.

data_table.Examination: Repetitive lateral tongue movements and chewing jaw movements at rest that cease during speech, occasional lip pursing, no truncal or limb chorea, no rigidity or bradykinesia, no tremor, gait normal, Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale score 12, no restlessness observed or reported
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and copper studies all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Increase the anticholinergic dose and review his involuntary movements in six weeks
options.rationale: Raising the anticholinergic dose is the treatment for drug induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia, but it measurably aggravates tardive movements. His examination shows no rigidity or bradykinesia to treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the antipsychotic dose because the movements reflect inadequate symptom control
options.rationale: A dose increase suppresses the movements briefly by further blocking the same receptors and then worsens the underlying disorder, which is why it is described as masking. His psychosis has been in remission for six years, so there is nothing to treat. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Start propranolol and titrate the dose against the severity of his involuntary movements
options.rationale: Beta blockade is the treatment for the subjective inner restlessness with an urge to move that can accompany antipsychotic treatment, a condition he explicitly does not have. His movements are unaccompanied by any urge and stop during speech. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease the anticholinergic and discuss switching to an antipsychotic with lower risk
options.rationale: Anticholinergics worsen this movement disorder rather than helping it, unlike drug induced parkinsonism where they are used, so withdrawing benzatropine is the first step and costs nothing. Switching from a high potency first generation agent to one with lower liability, most evidence favouring clozapine, is the next consideration. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Stop the antipsychotic abruptly and monitor his movements over the following three months
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation frequently unmasks or transiently worsens the movements and carries a high risk of psychotic relapse after 22 years of treatment. Any change to the antipsychotic is made gradually and with a plan for maintaining remission. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

explanation.summary: Involuntary orofacial movements emerging after prolonged dopamine blockade affect a meaningful proportion of long term antipsychotic users, with risk rising with age, duration of exposure, female sex, diabetes and the use of first generation high potency agents. The movements are choreoathetoid, typically begin in the tongue, lips and jaw, are absent in sleep and often suppress during speech or voluntary tongue protrusion, and they are frequently more distressing to family than to the patient. They must be separated from drug induced parkinsonism, which is rigid and bradykinetic and improves with anticholinergics, and from the restlessness syndrome, which carries a subjective urge to move and responds to beta blockade or dose reduction. Management withdraws anticholinergics, reduces or switches the antipsychotic where psychiatric stability allows, and considers a vesicular monoamine transporter inhibitor where one is available, with regular standardised rating to track change.
key_points: Anticholinergics aggravate these movements and are withdrawn first
Absence of any urge to move separates this from the restlessness syndrome
Increasing the antipsychotic masks the movements and worsens the disorder
Clozapine carries the lowest liability of the available antipsychotics
Standardised rating at each review documents change objectively
explanation.pearls: Standardised rating with the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale every six months is recommended for anyone on long term antipsychotic treatment, because the movements are often unnoticed by the patient and a documented baseline is what allows a later change to be attributed correctly.

subtopic_detail: Severe irritability and low mood confined to the week before menstruation with complete resolution within days of onset, documented prospectively over two cycles
stem: A 33-year-old woman describes a week each month of irritability, tearfulness and feeling unable to cope that lifts within two days of her period starting, with complete wellbeing in between. She has never been depressed outside this pattern.

data_table.Symptom charting: Two cycles of daily ratings: symptoms begin five to seven days before bleeding and clear by day 3
data_table.Examination: Euthymic on day 9 of her cycle
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and full blood count normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken only in the luteal phase
options.rationale: Prospectively confirmed symptoms confined to the luteal phase with complete resolution after menstruation respond to serotonergic treatment within a day or two rather than over weeks, which is why dosing restricted to the second half of the cycle works as well as continuous dosing. It also limits total exposure and side effects. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken continuously
options.rationale: Continuous dosing is equally effective and is preferred when symptoms spill beyond the luteal phase or when cycles are irregular. Her charted symptoms are strictly confined to the luteal phase, which makes intermittent dosing the more economical choice. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: A combined oral contraceptive taken in an extended regimen
options.rationale: Suppressing ovulation helps some women and is a reasonable option for those who also want contraception, but the evidence is weaker than for serotonergic treatment and she is not seeking a hormonal method. It is generally second line for the mood symptoms themselves. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: Micronised progesterone through the second half of each cycle
options.rationale: Progesterone supplementation has repeatedly failed to outperform placebo for these symptoms and can aggravate them in sensitive women. It persists in practice despite the evidence, which is why it appears here. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

options.text: A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add-back therapy
options.rationale: Medical suppression of the ovarian cycle is highly effective but is reserved for severe symptoms that have failed serotonergic and hormonal treatment, because of bone loss and menopausal symptoms. It is a specialist step, not a starting point. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)

explanation.summary: Severe premenstrual mood symptoms are distinguished from ordinary premenstrual discomfort by the degree of functional impairment and from an underlying mood or anxiety disorder by the symptom-free interval in the follicular phase. Diagnosis requires prospective daily ratings over at least two cycles rather than retrospective recall, because retrospective report agrees poorly with charted symptoms and a substantial proportion of women who describe this pattern turn out to have premenstrual worsening of a continuous disorder instead. That distinction matters because premenstrual exacerbation of an existing depressive or anxiety disorder is treated by optimising treatment of that disorder rather than by intermittent dosing. Serotonergic antidepressants are first line and uniquely act within days in this condition, which allows luteal phase only dosing, and non-pharmacological measures including exercise and cognitive behavioural therapy have supporting evidence.
key_points: Two cycles of prospective daily ratings are required for the diagnosis
A symptom-free follicular phase separates it from a continuous disorder
Serotonergic response occurs within days rather than over weeks
Luteal phase dosing is as effective as continuous dosing here
Progesterone supplementation does not outperform placebo
explanation.pearls: If the charted ratings show symptoms that improve but never fully remit after menstruation, the diagnosis is premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying disorder, and intermittent dosing will fail because the baseline condition needs continuous treatment.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Young man requesting a fourth cosmetic procedure for a nose he believes is deformed, with hours of daily mirror checking and an unremarkable appearance on examination
stem: A 24-year-old man wants a referral to a fourth surgeon about his nose, after two rhinoplasties and a revision, each leaving him briefly relieved then convinced the result was worse. He spends three or four hours a day checking his profile in reflective surfaces, leaves the house only after dark and has lost his apprenticeship through absences.

data_table.Examination: Nose appears unremarkable; belief held with absolute conviction; passive thoughts that life is not worth living

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide the referral, assess suicide risk and refer for psychological therapy
options.rationale: Adding therapy alongside a fourth procedure still endorses the belief that the nose is the problem and repeats a cycle that has already failed three times. The therapy and risk assessment are appropriate, but providing the referral is not. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Start an antipsychotic alone because his belief is held with full conviction
options.rationale: Absolute conviction occurs in about a third of people with this disorder and is graded as poor insight rather than reclassified as a psychotic illness, so serotonergic treatment and therapy remain the approach. Antipsychotics are used only as augmentation when response is inadequate. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Reassure him that his nose looks normal and review him in a month
options.rationale: Reassurance functions in the same way as his mirror checking, giving momentary relief and reinforcing the preoccupation, and it is one of the behaviours the therapy explicitly targets. It also leaves the suicide risk unassessed for a month. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder

options.text: Refer for assessment of an eating disorder given his appearance concerns
options.rationale: Appearance preoccupation in an eating disorder centres on weight and body shape and is accompanied by dietary restriction, compensatory behaviours or binge eating. His concern is confined to a single facial feature with no disordered eating described. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders)

options.text: Decline the referral, assess suicide risk and refer for psychological therapy
options.rationale: Preoccupation with a flaw not observable to others, repetitive checking, avoidance and marked functional loss identifies the disorder, and further surgery predictably fails to relieve it while the risk of suicide in this group is among the highest in psychiatry. Tailored cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention is the primary treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

explanation.summary: Body dysmorphic disorder affects around two per cent of the population and is markedly overrepresented in cosmetic surgery and dermatology clinics, where it is rarely recognised because the presenting request looks ordinary. The diagnosis requires preoccupation with a perceived defect that is not observable or appears slight to others, repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking or reassurance seeking, and clinically significant distress or impairment. Insight is frequently absent, and delusional conviction is now treated as a specifier rather than as a separate psychotic disorder, which keeps the treatment pathway the same. Cosmetic procedures almost never help, with most patients reporting the same or worse concern afterwards and many transferring the preoccupation to a new feature. Rates of suicidal ideation and attempts are very high, so risk assessment is part of every consultation.
key_points: The perceived defect is not observable or appears slight to others
Repetitive checking, grooming or reassurance seeking is required
Delusional conviction is a specifier, not a separate psychotic disorder
Cosmetic procedures rarely help and often shift the preoccupation
Suicidal ideation and attempts are substantially more common than average
explanation.pearls: Asking how many hours a day the person spends thinking about the feature separates this from ordinary appearance concern, since an hour or more daily is the working threshold, and most people presenting for repeat cosmetic procedures with this disorder report three hours or more.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders
BMJ Best Practice: Body dysmorphic disorder

subtopic_detail: Daytime sleep attacks with knee buckling on laughter in a nineteen year old whose sleep diary shows eight hours nightly
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old apprentice who has fallen asleep at his workbench three times in the past month and was nearly stood down after dozing off during a safety briefing. He says the sleepiness comes on suddenly and that a ten minute nap leaves him refreshed for a couple of hours.

He has twice felt his knees give way while laughing with his friends, staying fully aware throughout and recovering within a minute. He sometimes cannot move for a few seconds as he wakes. A two week sleep diary shows a consistent bedtime with eight hours of sleep each night, and his partner reports no snoring and no witnessed pauses in breathing. He scores 3 on a depression screening questionnaire and describes his mood as good.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg per square metre, Mallampati class 1 oropharynx, no goitre, normal cranial nerve and peripheral neurological examination, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, ferritin 88 micrograms/L (30 to 300), Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19 out of 24, two week actigraphy confirms eight hours of sleep nightly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Hypersomnia does occur in depression, but he screens negative, describes his mood as good and wakes refreshed from naps, whereas depressive hypersomnia is typically unrefreshing. Serotonergic agents are used in this condition for cataplexy rather than as an initial empirical trial. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Start modafinil now and arrange a sleep study if there is no response
options.rationale: Starting a wake promoting agent before the sleep study contaminates the multiple sleep latency test, which must be performed off stimulants, and in Australia subsidised access depends on a confirmed diagnosis. Treating first also leaves the driving and workplace safety assessment without a diagnosis to rest on. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.text: Arrange thyroid function and iron studies, then review in four weeks
options.rationale: These are reasonable screening tests for fatigue, but they have already been done and are normal, and neither explains sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion. Repeating normal investigations delays the study that establishes the diagnosis. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.text: Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
options.rationale: Sudden emotionally triggered loss of muscle tone with preserved awareness, refreshing naps, sleep paralysis and severe daytime sleepiness despite adequate nocturnal sleep is the pattern of narcolepsy with cataplexy, and the diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography to exclude other causes followed by a multiple sleep latency test. A mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods confirms it. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

options.text: Advise sleep hygiene measures and review him again in eight weeks
options.rationale: Sleep hygiene advice addresses insufficient or irregular sleep, which the diary and actigraphy have already excluded by documenting eight consistent hours nightly. Insufficient sleep syndrome is far commoner in this age group but does not produce cataplexy. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management

explanation.summary: Excessive daytime sleepiness in a young adult is most often caused by insufficient or irregular sleep, and a sleep diary with actigraphy is what separates that from a primary hypersomnia. Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of hypocretin producing neurons in the hypothalamus and is defined clinically by sleepiness with cataplexy, a sudden partial or complete loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most often laughter, during which the person remains fully conscious. Sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations and disrupted nocturnal sleep complete the tetrad but are individually non-specific, and cataplexy is the feature that carries real diagnostic weight. Diagnosis in Australia requires overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test performed off stimulants and antidepressants, which is why treatment is not started first.
key_points: Cataplexy with preserved awareness is the most specific clinical feature
Refreshing short naps distinguish this from depressive hypersomnia
A sleep diary excludes insufficient sleep as the explanation
The multiple sleep latency test must be performed off stimulants
Diagnosis precedes treatment because access and driving advice both depend on it
explanation.pearls: Cataplexy is frequently misread as syncope or as a seizure, and what separates them at the bedside is that consciousness is fully retained throughout the attack, so a patient who can recount what was said while they were slumped on the floor has had cataplexy rather than a faint.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy diagnosis and management
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Four consecutive winters of low mood with hypersomnia and carbohydrate craving that remit each spring in a woman living in Hobart
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who has come in each of the last four Junes with the same complaint. She describes flat mood, sleeping ten to eleven hours and still feeling leaden, craving bread and sweet food, and gaining four or five kilograms over the winter that she loses again by December.

She moved to Hobart five years ago from Cairns. Her mood and energy are entirely normal from about October to April, and she has never had a period of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or increased activity. She works indoors and leaves for work and returns home in the dark through winter. She is not suicidal, functions at work with effort, and her weight and sleep are the symptoms she most wants addressed.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg per square metre, no goitre, no tremor, affect reactive during the consultation, no psychomotor retardation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone and free thyroxine within normal limits, ferritin 65 micrograms/L (30 to 200), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 46 nmol/L (greater than 50), Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 14 out of 27

lead_in: What would you first recommend for her current episode?

options.text: Start lithium as a mood stabiliser and arrange monitoring of the levels
options.rationale: Lithium is used where there is a bipolar diathesis, and she has never had an episode of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or increased goal directed activity. A seasonal pattern alone does not make a depressive illness bipolar. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Start high dose oral colecalciferol and review her mood in eight weeks
options.rationale: Her vitamin D level is only marginally below the target and supplementation has not been shown to treat depressive episodes, seasonal or otherwise. Correcting the level is reasonable for bone health but is not a treatment for the presenting problem. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer for electroconvulsive therapy assessment at the local mental health unit
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is reserved for severe, treatment resistant, psychotic or life threatening depression, and she is working, eating and not suicidal with a moderate symptom score. Offering it at this stage is disproportionate to the severity. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Advise increased outdoor exercise alone and review her again in three months
options.rationale: Exercise and daylight exposure are worth encouraging but a three month review takes her to the end of winter, by which time the episode would have remitted regardless of what was done. Morning outdoor light is genuinely useful, but as an adjunct rather than as the whole plan. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Start bright light therapy each morning and review her again in four weeks
options.rationale: Depressive episodes with a seasonal pattern and the atypical features of hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and weight gain respond to bright light of about 10000 lux for 30 minutes soon after waking, with benefit usually apparent within one to two weeks. It is recommended first for moderate seasonal episodes because it works quickly, is well tolerated, and can be started before the winter in subsequent years to prevent recurrence. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
