explanation.summary: A seasonal pattern is a specifier applied to recurrent major depressive episodes rather than a separate diagnosis, and it requires episodes that begin and remit at characteristic times of year across at least two consecutive years with no non seasonal episodes in between. The symptom profile is characteristically atypical, with hypersomnia, increased appetite with carbohydrate craving, weight gain and leaden heaviness, in contrast to the insomnia and weight loss of melancholic depression. Prevalence rises with latitude, so the pattern is far more common in Tasmania than in northern Queensland, and a recent move south is a genuinely relevant piece of history. Bright light therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for the seasonal pattern, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors all have evidence, and treatment can be started prophylactically in early autumn once the pattern is established.
key_points: The seasonal specifier requires at least two consecutive years of the same pattern
Hypersomnia with carbohydrate craving and weight gain is the typical profile
Absence of any elevated mood episode argues against a bipolar diathesis
Bright light of about 10000 lux for 30 minutes after waking is the usual regimen
Prophylactic treatment can be started before the season in later years
explanation.pearls: Bright light therapy should be given within an hour of waking rather than in the evening, because evening exposure delays the circadian phase and can worsen the hypersomnia the treatment is meant to relieve.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal affective disorder

subtopic_detail: Emotional exhaustion and cynicism in a surgical registrar whose symptoms lift entirely on annual leave and who has no impairment at work
stem: A 31-year-old surgical registrar consults you with eight months of dreading work, nothing left to give her patients and uncharacteristic impatience at handover. Two weeks of leave restored her by day five and the dread returned within a week of going back. She sleeps and eats normally, still enjoys netball, and would step back if a patient were at risk.

data_table.Examination: Affect reactive, no thoughts of self-harm
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 8/27, GAD-7 6/21, AUDIT-C 3

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Structured review with workload focused counselling and no notification
options.rationale: Her symptoms are work bound, remit fully on leave and are accompanied by preserved enjoyment, sleep and appetite elsewhere, which describes occupational burnout rather than a major depressive episode, and the intervention that works is directed at workload, recovery and role rather than at the person alone. The mandatory notification threshold requires that a practitioner is placing the public at substantial risk of harm through an impairment, and a registrar who is functioning safely, has insight and is engaging in treatment does not meet it. (Source: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners)
source_refs: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners

options.text: Mandatory notification to the regulator, with review arranged
options.rationale: Mandatory notification is triggered by impairment, intoxication, significant departure from accepted standards or sexual misconduct placing the public at substantial risk, none of which is present in a practitioner who is working safely and seeking help. Notifying in these circumstances deters doctors from disclosing distress, which is the harm the threshold is set to avoid. (Source: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners)
source_refs: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressant treatment is directed at a depressive episode, and her symptoms remit completely on leave with preserved anhedonia free enjoyment, sleep and appetite, which is not that illness. Medicating a workload problem leaves the cause untouched and can delay the changes that would help. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Certify her unfit for work for three months and review after that
options.rationale: Prolonged certified absence without a formal diagnosis or a plan to change the work conditions usually leads to the same symptoms recurring on return, as her own two week experience demonstrates. Time away helps only when it is paired with a change in the demands she returns to. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer to the employee assistance program and take no further action
options.rationale: An employee assistance program is a useful adjunct but a single referral without continuing review leaves no one tracking whether she deteriorates into a depressive episode. Adequate care requires ongoing review by her own general practitioner alongside any referral. (Source: RACGP: Keeping the doctor alive, a self care guidebook for medical practitioners)
source_refs: RACGP: Keeping the doctor alive, a self care guidebook for medical practitioners

explanation.summary: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon characterised by emotional exhaustion, cynicism or depersonalisation, and reduced professional efficacy, and it is classified as a factor influencing health status rather than as a mental disorder. The clinical task is to separate it from a major depressive episode, because the treatments differ, and context dependence separates them most reliably, since burnout remits away from the workplace while a depressive episode follows the person everywhere. The two overlap and burnout is a risk factor for depression, so a doctor presenting this way needs ongoing review rather than a single assessment. Doctors seeking care for their own mental health face a specific additional barrier in the fear of mandatory notification, and Australian guidance is explicit that treating practitioners notify only where there is substantial risk of harm to the public from impairment, not merely because a colleague is unwell.
key_points: Burnout remits away from work whereas a depressive episode does not
Preserved enjoyment, sleep and appetite argue against major depression
Effective intervention targets workload and role, not only the individual
Mandatory notification requires substantial risk of harm from impairment
Burnout is a risk factor for depression, so continuing review is required
explanation.pearls: Every practitioner should have their own general practitioner and should not self prescribe or be treated by a colleague informally, because self treatment is associated with delayed presentation and with the under recognition of deterioration that turns burnout into a depressive episode.

sources.label: AHPRA: Guidelines for mandatory notifications about registered health practitioners
RACGP: Keeping the doctor alive, a self care guidebook for medical practitioners
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Weight loss in a twelve year old boy restricting by food texture since toddlerhood with no body image concern or fear of weight gain
stem: A 12-year-old boy has lost 4 kg in six months, falling from the 25th to below the 3rd centile. Since age three he has eaten only about eight dry beige foods and gags on anything wet or lumpy. He has no fear of gaining weight.

data_table.Examination: Weight below the 3rd centile, height on the 25th, Tanner stage 1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents this is ordinary fussy eating and review in a year
options.rationale: Ordinary selective eating does not cause a fall across centiles, weight loss and bradycardia, and this presentation meets the threshold for a feeding and eating disorder. A year of observation would allow further growth failure and pubertal delay. (Source: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards)
source_refs: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards

options.text: Start family based treatment for anorexia nervosa with weekly weighing
options.rationale: Family based treatment is the evidence-based approach for anorexia nervosa, which requires a fear of weight gain or behaviour that interferes with it, and he wants to gain weight and has no body image disturbance. Applying a treatment built around challenging a drive for thinness to a sensory and choking based avoidance misses the mechanism. (Source: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards)
source_refs: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards

options.text: Refer to a paediatric eating disorder service with dietitian involvement
options.rationale: Restriction driven by sensory characteristics of food and by fear of choking, without body image disturbance or fear of weight gain, and producing weight loss with nutritional deficiency, is avoidant restrictive food intake disorder, which is managed by a multidisciplinary eating disorder service with dietetic and psychological input. Treatment uses graded exposure to new textures alongside nutritional restoration rather than the approaches designed for weight and shape concerns. (Source: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards)
source_refs: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards

options.text: Refer for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to exclude an organic cause
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated where there is dysphagia, food impaction, reflux symptoms or suspicion of eosinophilic disease, and his symptoms are texture aversion from toddlerhood rather than difficulty with swallowing itself. Coeliac serology and inflammatory markers are already normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder

options.text: Start fluoxetine for restrictive eating and review him in four weeks
options.rationale: No medication has an established role as primary treatment for this disorder, and antidepressants in underweight children carry particular monitoring requirements without addressing the avoidance. Fluoxetine does have a role in bulimia nervosa in adults, which is a different disorder entirely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder is defined by a persistent failure to meet nutritional or energy needs leading to weight loss, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements or marked psychosocial interference, in the absence of body image disturbance or a drive for thinness. Three patterns are described, namely sensory sensitivity to the appearance, smell or texture of food, lack of interest in eating, and fear of an aversive consequence such as choking or vomiting, and children commonly show more than one, as this boy does. It is distinguished from ordinary selective eating by the presence of that nutritional or functional impact, and from anorexia nervosa by the absence of weight and shape concerns, which is why the specific questions about fear of weight gain and body checking matter. Medical instability is assessed exactly as it would be in any restrictive eating disorder, since bradycardia, hypotension and electrolyte disturbance carry the same significance whatever the motivation for the restriction.
key_points: The disorder is defined by nutritional impact without weight or shape concern
Sensory, low appetite and aversive consequence patterns often coexist
Bradycardia in an underweight child signals medical instability regardless of diagnosis
Family based treatment for anorexia nervosa is not the correct model here
Treatment combines graded texture exposure with nutritional restoration
explanation.pearls: A resting heart rate below 50 beats per minute, a postural blood pressure drop of more than 20 mmHg, or a temperature below 35.5 degrees Celsius in a child with restrictive eating are indications for medical admission regardless of which eating disorder is causing the restriction.

sources.label: ANZAED: Australia and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders practice standards
BMJ Best Practice: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder

subtopic_detail: Eight months of not speaking at school in a six year old who talks fluently at home and passed school hearing screening
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old girl whose teacher has written a letter because she has not spoken a word at school since she started in February. Her parents bring a phone video in which she is chatting and singing at home with her younger brother, using full sentences and a wide vocabulary.

At school she nods, points and writes answers on a whiteboard, and she will speak to no one, including other children. She played normally in the waiting room but has not spoken to you during the consultation, standing close to her mother and answering by nodding. Her school hearing screening in March was normal. Her parents describe her as shy with strangers since she was a toddler but say she has always spoken freely with family.

data_table.Examination: Well grown child, alert and engaged with toys, makes intermittent eye contact and uses gesture and pointing appropriately, no speech during consultation, no dysmorphic features, normal gait and coordination
data_table.Investigations: School hearing screening normal, growth and development otherwise age appropriate, no formal language assessment yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for formal audiology assessment before considering any other referral
options.rationale: Hearing loss is a reasonable consideration for a child who does not speak, but she has passed screening and, more decisively, speaks fluently and sings at home, which requires intact hearing. Repeating the hearing assessment delays the referral that addresses the anxiety. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Refer to a speech pathologist for assessment of a developmental language disorder
options.rationale: A developmental language disorder affects language in every setting, whereas her vocabulary and sentence structure are age appropriate at home on the video her parents have brought. Speech pathology may join the team later, but the primary problem is situational anxiety rather than language competence. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is shyness and review her again in twelve months
options.rationale: Eight months of complete absence of speech in a whole setting is well beyond situational shyness and beyond the one month threshold that defines the disorder. Untreated, the pattern becomes entrenched and predicts later social anxiety disorder and academic underachievement. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy with a graded school based program
options.rationale: Consistent failure to speak in a specific setting for more than a month, with fluent speech elsewhere, is selective mutism, an anxiety disorder for which behavioural treatment using graded exposure and stimulus fading delivered in the school environment is first line. Involving the teacher matters because progress depends on changing how adults in the setting respond, and pressuring the child to speak reliably makes it worse. (Source: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

options.text: Start a low dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Medication is considered when a structured behavioural program has been tried and has not produced progress, or where impairment is severe, and it is an adjunct rather than a first step in a 6-year-old. Fluoxetine does have evidence in selective mutism, but after behavioural treatment rather than instead of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is an anxiety disorder in which a child who speaks normally in some settings consistently fails to speak in specific social situations where speech is expected, most often school, for at least one month beyond the first month of attendance. It is frequently misread as oppositional behaviour, as shyness or as a language or hearing problem, and the demonstration that the child speaks fluently somewhere is what settles those questions. Comorbid social anxiety disorder is present in the majority, and a minority have a coexisting language or communication difficulty, so assessment includes both. Treatment is behavioural, using graded exposure, stimulus fading and shaping delivered largely in the setting where the child is mute, with the adults around the child coached not to pressure or to speak for them, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors reserved for cases that do not respond.
key_points: Fluent speech in one setting excludes hearing loss and language disorder
The diagnostic threshold is one month beyond the first month of school
Comorbid social anxiety disorder is present in most affected children
Treatment is delivered in the setting where the child does not speak
Pressuring the child to speak reliably worsens the avoidance
explanation.pearls: Stimulus fading is the core technique, in which the child first speaks to a trusted person in the empty classroom and a peer or teacher is then gradually introduced into the room, because the aim is to transfer existing speech into the feared setting rather than to teach speech the child already has.

sources.label: RANZCP: Child and adolescent anxiety disorders

subtopic_detail: An evening urge to move the legs relieved by walking in a man on risperidone whose ferritin is 22 micrograms per litre
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 46-year-old man with schizophrenia who has been on the same dose of risperidone for three years without change. He complains of a crawling discomfort deep in both calves that builds while he is watching television after dinner and is worst when he first gets into bed.

Walking around the flat relieves it completely within a minute, and it returns when he sits back down. He has no symptoms in the morning or at work, and he is no more restless in the waiting room now than at any previous review. His partner says his legs jerk repeatedly in the first hours of sleep. He has had heavy nosebleeds this year and his diet is limited.

data_table.Examination: No akathisic pacing or inability to remain seated during a 20 minute interview, no cogwheel rigidity, no tremor, no abnormal involuntary movements of the face or tongue, normal power and reflexes in both legs with intact pinprick and vibration sense
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (130 to 180), ferritin 22 micrograms/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 14 per cent (16 to 45), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, fasting glucose within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Add propranolol for akathisia and review his symptoms in two weeks
options.rationale: Akathisia is a subjective restlessness of the whole body that is present throughout the day, is not confined to the legs, is not relieved by brief walking and typically follows a dose increase or a recent start. He has been on an unchanged dose for three years and sits still throughout the interview. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start oral iron replacement and investigate the cause of the iron loss
options.rationale: An urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations that worsen at rest in the evening, are relieved by movement and are accompanied by periodic limb movements describes restless legs syndrome, and iron deficiency is the commonest reversible cause with replacement indicated when ferritin is below about 75 micrograms per litre. The nosebleeds and restricted diet need their own assessment, since treating the deficiency without finding its source leaves the cause unaddressed. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome

options.text: Add benzatropine at night and review his symptoms again in two weeks
options.rationale: Anticholinergic agents treat drug induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia, neither of which is present on examination, and they are ineffective for this circadian urge to move. They also worsen cognition and carry a risk of aggravating tardive movements. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start a dopamine agonist at night and review his symptoms in two weeks
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists do treat the syndrome but are no longer first line because of augmentation, in which symptoms intensify and spread over months of treatment, and they should not be started before reversible causes are corrected. They remain an option once iron is replete and symptoms persist. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome

options.text: Reduce the risperidone dose and review his symptoms again in two weeks
options.rationale: Reducing an effective antipsychotic that has maintained him for three years risks relapse of psychosis, and the symptom pattern here is not the dose related akathisia that a reduction would target. Antipsychotics can aggravate the syndrome, but iron correction is tried before destabilising treatment that is working. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is diagnosed clinically on five features, namely an urge to move the legs usually with uncomfortable sensations, worsening at rest, relief with movement, a circadian pattern worst in the evening or at night, and the absence of a better explanation such as cramp or positional discomfort. It is commonly confused with akathisia in psychiatric patients, and the distinguishing features are that akathisia is generalised rather than confined to the legs, lacks the evening predominance, is not relieved by brief walking, and is temporally linked to starting or increasing a dopamine blocking drug. Periodic limb movements of sleep, described by a bed partner as repeated leg jerks, accompany the syndrome in most patients and support the diagnosis. Iron deficiency, chronic kidney disease, pregnancy and dopamine blocking or serotonergic drugs are the secondary causes to look for, and iron status should be checked in every patient because replacement can abolish symptoms entirely.
key_points: The five clinical criteria include a circadian pattern and relief with movement
Akathisia is generalised and follows a dose change, unlike this pattern
Periodic limb movements reported by a partner support the diagnosis
Replacement is indicated at a ferritin below about 75 micrograms per litre
Reversible causes are corrected before starting symptomatic drug therapy
explanation.pearls: The ferritin threshold for iron replacement in restless legs syndrome is around 75 micrograms per litre, which is well above the level at which iron deficiency anaemia is diagnosed, so a normal haemoglobin with a ferritin in the 20s is still an indication to treat.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome
BMJ Best Practice: Restless legs syndrome

subtopic_detail: A fourth relapse within two years each time oral antipsychotic is stopped, in an improving involuntary inpatient with no insight into the need for treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar preparing the discharge plan for a 27-year-old man with schizophrenia who was admitted involuntarily six weeks ago after a relapse. This is his fourth admission in two years, and on each occasion he stopped his oral medication within a month of discharge and was readmitted within three months.

His symptoms have responded well to the current oral antipsychotic and he is now settled on the ward, sleeping, eating and attending groups. He remains convinced that he has never been unwell and that the tablets are only to keep staff happy, and he says plainly that he will not take them once he is home. He has a supportive sister and stable public housing. He has no history of violence, and there is no substance use.

data_table.Examination: Settled and cooperative, speech normal in rate and form, no thought disorder, no current hallucinations, persistent belief that he has never had a mental illness, no suicidal or homicidal ideation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, fasting lipids and glucose within normal limits, electrocardiogram QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate discharge plan?

options.text: Discharge on the oral antipsychotic with weekly community team review
options.rationale: This is precisely the plan that has failed on three previous occasions, because supervision does not resolve a stated intention not to take the medication. Repeating an intervention with a documented pattern of failure is not a neutral choice given the harm each relapse causes. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Keep him in hospital as an involuntary inpatient until his insight improves
options.rationale: Insight often does not return even with full symptomatic remission, so this plan has no endpoint, and continued detention is not the least restrictive option once treatment can be delivered in the community. Mental health legislation across Australia requires the least restrictive setting consistent with safe treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Discharge him with no order and ask his sister to supervise the medication
options.rationale: Placing the responsibility for enforcing treatment on a family member damages the relationship he depends on and gives her no authority to act when he declines. Carer involvement is valuable as support rather than as a substitute for a treatment framework. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Discharge on clozapine and arrange the required haematological monitoring
options.rationale: Clozapine is indicated for illness that has failed to respond to adequate trials of two antipsychotics, whereas his symptoms respond well whenever he takes medication, so the problem is adherence rather than resistance. Relapse despite taking medication would instead point to treatment resistance. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

options.text: Apply for a community treatment order with a long-acting injectable antipsychotic
options.rationale: A repeated pattern of relapse on cessation, a stated intention not to continue, and preserved response when treated is the situation community treatment orders exist for, and a long-acting injectable removes the daily decision that adherence otherwise depends on. It is also the least restrictive option that can deliver effective treatment, since the alternative that reliably prevents relapse is continued detention. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Community treatment orders exist in every Australian state and territory, with differing names and criteria, but all share a requirement that the person has a mental illness requiring treatment, that treatment can be provided in the community, that they are unable or unwilling to consent, and that the order is the least restrictive option available. A documented pattern of relapse following cessation is the evidence base on which such an order is usually justified, and the order authorises treatment rather than detention. Long-acting injectable antipsychotics pair naturally with these orders because non-adherence becomes visible immediately as a missed appointment rather than silently over weeks of untreated illness, and evidence supports their use earlier than has traditionally been the practice. Recovery oriented care still applies under an order, so the plan should include carer involvement, psychosocial supports, regular review and a clear intention to revoke the order when it is no longer needed.
key_points: An order requires that treatment can be safely delivered in the community
Persistent lack of insight is common and does not justify indefinite detention
A pattern of relapse on cessation is the usual evidential basis for an order
Long-acting injectables make non-adherence immediately visible
Treatment resistance and non-adherence are different problems with different answers
explanation.pearls: A community treatment order authorises treatment but not detention, so a person who refuses the injection while on an order is brought in for the medication to be given rather than admitted, and each order carries a statutory review date and a right of appeal to an independent tribunal.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for the management of schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Reported seizures in a toddler that occur only when the mother is present and stop during a period of covert nursing observation
stem: A 3-year-old girl is admitted for the fourth time this year for collapses. Her mother, an enrolled nurse, describes episodes of stiffening, perioral cyanosis and unresponsiveness lasting two minutes, none ever witnessed by a clinician. Nursing staff recorded seven episodes, all when the mother was alone with her, and none on the four nights she went home.

data_table.Examination: Thriving, developmentally normal, plays freely on the ward
data_table.Investigations: Two electroencephalograms, cardiac monitoring, brain MRI and metabolic screen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a third electroencephalogram with ambulatory recording
options.rationale: Two normal studies and normal imaging in a developmentally normal child whose episodes have never been witnessed by a clinician make a third study very unlikely to change anything. Continuing to investigate also escalates the very process that is harming the child. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.text: Start an antiepileptic drug empirically and review in a month
options.rationale: Treating unwitnessed episodes with normal investigations exposes a well child to the adverse effects of a drug she does not need and appears to validate the reported illness. Empirical treatment in this situation has been shown to prolong the harm rather than resolve the uncertainty. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.text: Convene a multidisciplinary meeting and make a child protection notification
options.rationale: Episodes occurring only in one person's presence, ceasing entirely in their absence, in a thriving child with repeatedly normal investigations, is the pattern of illness fabricated or induced by a carer, which is a form of child abuse and is notifiable on reasonable suspicion. A multidisciplinary meeting that assembles the whole medical record is essential first, because the diagnosis rests on the pattern across admissions rather than on any single episode, and no single clinician holds that view. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.text: Discharge her with an ambulance call plan and review in a month
options.rationale: Discharging without addressing the pattern returns the child to the situation generating the episodes and the invasive investigations that follow them. A call plan increases rather than reduces the medical contact that is the mechanism of harm. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

options.text: Tell the mother you suspect she is causing the episodes and gauge her reaction
options.rationale: Direct confrontation before the protective process is in place risks flight from the hospital, escalation of the behaviour, or a move to another health service where the history begins again. The family is told, but by the protective and medical teams together as part of a planned process rather than by a single clinician on the ward. (Source: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness

explanation.summary: Fabricated or induced illness, also described as factitious disorder imposed on another, is a form of child abuse in which a carer exaggerates, fabricates or induces symptoms, resulting in unnecessary investigation and treatment. The recognised warning signs are symptoms witnessed only by one carer, a history that does not fit any recognisable illness, repeatedly normal investigations, symptoms that resolve when the carer is absent, a carer with health care knowledge or unusual familiarity with medical terminology, and a child who remains well between reported events. Harm arises from the investigations and treatments themselves, from school absence and from the child internalising the identity of being ill, so continuing to investigate is not a neutral holding position. Because the diagnosis lives in the pattern across multiple presentations rather than in any one event, the essential step is to assemble the complete record in a multidisciplinary meeting including the treating teams, child protection and often hospital legal advice, before anything is said to the family.
key_points: Symptoms witnessed only by one carer and absent in their absence is the key pattern
Repeatedly normal investigations in a thriving child is a warning sign, not reassurance
Further investigation is itself a source of harm rather than a neutral option
The diagnosis rests on the pattern across the whole record
Confrontation before protective planning risks flight and escalation
explanation.pearls: Covert video surveillance is used in only a small number of Australian centres and never on a clinician's own initiative, because it requires hospital executive approval, legal advice and coordination with police and child protection before any recording begins.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Fabricated or induced illness
RACGP: Abuse and violence, working with our patients in general practice
BMJ Best Practice: Fabricated or induced illness by carers

subtopic_detail: Escalating pregabalin use obtained from several prescribers by a man stable on methadone who reports it gives him a lift
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 38-year-old man who has been stable on methadone through your practice for two years, with negative urine drug screens and steady employment. He was prescribed pregabalin for sciatica by a locum eight months ago.

Today he asks for an early script, saying the pain is worse. When you ask how he takes it, he tells you he now uses about 900 mg in the evening rather than the prescribed 150 mg twice daily, because it gives him a lift and helps him sleep, and that he has been getting extra from two other practices. He has had two falls at home in the past month and his partner says he has been slurring his words in the evenings. His sciatica has otherwise settled and his straight leg raise is full and painless today.

data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented with no slurred speech at this morning appointment, no nystagmus, gait steady, straight leg raise full and painless bilaterally, no focal neurological deficit, no injection sites
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for methadone with no other substances detected, full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Check the real time prescription monitoring record and plan a supervised taper
options.rationale: Obtaining supplies from several prescribers is exactly what real time prescription monitoring is designed to reveal, and reviewing it establishes the true total dose before any plan is made. Abrupt cessation of high dose pregabalin risks a withdrawal syndrome with agitation, insomnia and seizures, so the dose is reduced gradually under supervision with the original pain indication reassessed at the same time. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Stop the pregabalin immediately today and review him again in four weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after months of high dose use can precipitate withdrawal with agitation, sweating, insomnia and seizures, and a four week gap leaves him without support through that period. The drug needs to stop, but by taper rather than by sudden cessation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue the current prescription and add a benzodiazepine for his sleep
options.rationale: Adding a second sedative to a combination of methadone and high dose pregabalin substantially increases the risk of respiratory depression and death. His falls and evening slurring already indicate excessive sedation on the current combination. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Increase the prescribed pregabalin to match what he is currently taking
options.rationale: Prescribing to the level of misuse legitimises a dose that is causing falls and slurred speech and does not address the mechanism, which is the sedative effect rather than uncontrolled neuropathic pain. His straight leg raise is now full and painless, so the original indication has resolved. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Cease the methadone program and refer him to a residential detoxification unit
options.rationale: Removing effective opioid agonist treatment from a man who has been stable on it for two years markedly increases his risk of relapse to injecting and of overdose death. Residential withdrawal has a role for a pregabalin taper that fails in the community, but never at the cost of the opioid treatment that is working. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

explanation.summary: Pregabalin was once regarded as having low misuse potential, but it is now a recognised drug of dependence, particularly among people with a history of opioid or other substance use, in whom it produces euphoria and sedation at supratherapeutic doses. The most serious hazard is the combination with opioids, since both depress respiration and the combination is disproportionately represented in Australian overdose deaths. Real time prescription monitoring is operational across Australian jurisdictions and gives a prescriber an immediate view of all monitored medicines dispensed to a patient, which converts a suspicion of multiple prescribers into documented fact before a conversation takes place. The management principles are to establish the true dose, keep the opioid agonist treatment intact, taper the pregabalin gradually because abrupt cessation causes a withdrawal syndrome including seizures, and treat the underlying pain and sleep problems by other means.
key_points: Pregabalin misuse is concentrated among people with a substance use history
The combination with opioids markedly raises the risk of respiratory depression
Real time prescription monitoring documents supply from multiple prescribers
Abrupt cessation causes a withdrawal syndrome that can include seizures
Opioid agonist treatment is preserved rather than withdrawn as a sanction
explanation.pearls: Pregabalin is renally cleared, so the same dose produces much higher concentrations as kidney function falls, and an older patient or one with chronic kidney disease can develop sedation, ataxia and falls on a dose that was previously well tolerated.

sources.label: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

subtopic_detail: Repetitive unwanted images of harming her baby in a woman six weeks postpartum who avoids bathing him and finds the thoughts abhorrent
stem: A 29-year-old woman six weeks after her first baby's birth discloses that she keeps getting sudden images of holding him under the bath water. She finds them horrifying and has never wanted to act on them. She has stopped bathing him, put the kitchen knives away and checks him repeatedly at night.

data_table.Examination: Fully oriented, no delusions about the infant, insight preserved, infant thriving
data_table.Screening: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 11, self-harm item zero

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent admission to a mother and baby unit for assessment
options.rationale: Admission is the right response to postpartum psychosis or to severe depression with risk, both of which involve altered reality testing or an intention to act, and neither is present in a woman with intact insight who finds the thoughts abhorrent. Admitting her would confirm the fear that disclosure leads to separation, which is the main reason these symptoms go unreported. (Source: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Make a child protection notification and review her in one week
options.rationale: Egodystonic intrusive thoughts are not associated with an increased risk of harm to the infant, and the baby here is thriving and well cared for. Notifying in the absence of any risk indicator penalises honest disclosure and does not protect the child. (Source: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Start an antipsychotic and arrange psychiatric review within a week
options.rationale: Antipsychotic treatment is directed at psychotic symptoms, and she has no delusions, no hallucinations and no disturbance of reality testing. Antipsychotics would be indicated for postpartum psychosis, which typically begins in the first two weeks with a fluctuating confusional picture and delusional beliefs about the infant, and which is a psychiatric emergency. (Source: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Explain the nature of the thoughts and refer for exposure based therapy
options.rationale: Unwanted, repugnant intrusive images of harm that the mother recognises as her own and resists, with avoidance and checking as the resulting compulsions, is perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder, and telling her explicitly that these thoughts are common, are not a sign that she will act, and are treatable is itself therapeutic. Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention targeting the avoidance and checking is first line, with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor compatible with breastfeeding added if symptoms are severe or therapy is not available. (Source: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.text: Reassure her this is normal after birth and review in three months
options.rationale: Intrusive thoughts of harm are indeed reported by a majority of new parents, but hers have produced avoidance of care tasks, night long checking and considerable distress, which is the point at which the phenomenon becomes a disorder. A three month review leaves treatable and worsening symptoms unaddressed. (Source: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

explanation.summary: Intrusive thoughts of accidental or deliberate harm to the infant are reported by most new parents, and they become perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder when they are persistent and distressing enough to drive avoidance, checking, reassurance seeking or other compulsions. The decisive clinical distinction is between egodystonic thoughts, which the mother experiences as unwanted, senseless and contrary to her wishes and which are not associated with an increased risk of harm, and the egosyntonic delusional beliefs of postpartum psychosis, in which the infant may be seen as abnormal, possessed or better off dead and the risk is real and urgent. The two are separated by reality testing, insight, the presence of confusion or perceptual disturbance, and the timing, since psychosis characteristically begins abruptly within the first two weeks. Women very commonly conceal these thoughts for fear that their baby will be removed, so naming the phenomenon, normalising it and explaining that it is treatable is both diagnostic and the first step of treatment.
key_points: Egodystonic intrusive thoughts are not associated with increased risk to the infant
Avoidance and checking are the compulsions that mark the transition to disorder
Preserved insight and reality testing exclude postpartum psychosis
Psychosis usually begins within two weeks with fluctuating confusion
Fear of infant removal is the main barrier to disclosure
explanation.pearls: Sertraline is the usual first choice when a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is needed in a breastfeeding mother, because it has the lowest relative infant dose of the class and is the best studied, and obsessive compulsive symptoms typically require higher doses and a longer trial of eight to twelve weeks than depressive symptoms do.

sources.label: COPE: Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

subtopic_detail: Irritability and fidgety movements at forty two in a man whose father died in a nursing home at fifty five after a movement disorder
stem: A 42-year-old man is referred with two years of irritability, apathy and difficulty organising himself at work. While talking he makes brief finger flicks and facial grimaces he seems unaware of. His father died in a nursing home at 55 after an undiscussed movement disorder. His well 19-year-old daughter asks to be tested too.

data_table.Examination: Involuntary movements flowing into voluntary ones, milkmaid grip, MoCA 24/30
data_table.Investigations: Caeruloplasmin normal, MRI shows mild caudate atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start an antidepressant and review the movements in six months
options.rationale: His mood symptoms do warrant treatment, but deferring the diagnosis leaves the executive decline, the chorea and the family implications unaddressed for months. Depression here is part of the illness rather than an alternative explanation for it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Refer to a neurogenetics service for diagnostic testing with counselling
options.rationale: He has neurological signs and cognitive change, so testing him is diagnostic rather than predictive, and it can proceed once he is counselled about the implications for him and for his relatives. Establishing his result is also the necessary first step before his daughter's request can be addressed at all, since her risk cannot be defined until his status is known. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Predictive testing for adult onset genetic disorders)
source_refs: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Predictive testing for adult onset genetic disorders

options.text: Arrange genetic testing for him and his daughter at one appointment
options.rationale: Predictive testing of an at risk asymptomatic adult is done through a separate multi session protocol with counselling before and after the result, never as an add on to a relative's diagnostic test. Testing them together also removes her ability to decline or to defer, which is central to the protocol. (Source: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Predictive testing for adult onset genetic disorders)
source_refs: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Predictive testing for adult onset genetic disorders

options.text: Start tetrabenazine for the movements and review him in six weeks
options.rationale: Tetrabenazine suppresses chorea but carries a substantial risk of worsening depression and suicidality, which is hazardous in a man already depressed and undiagnosed. His movements are mild and are not causing functional difficulty, so treating them is not the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Repeat neuroimaging in twelve months and review him at that point
options.rationale: Imaging is supportive rather than diagnostic here, and caudate atrophy is already present, so repeating it adds a year of uncertainty without resolving the question. Imaging would be the right next step if the presentation suggested a structural or vascular cause rather than a familial one. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Huntington disease)

explanation.summary: Huntington disease commonly declares itself psychiatrically before it declares itself neurologically, with irritability, apathy, depression and executive dysfunction preceding chorea by years, so a psychiatrist is often the first doctor to see it. The family history is frequently obscured, because the previous generation may have been given a vague label, died before the diagnosis was clear, or deliberately withheld it, which means an unexplained neurodegenerative death in a parent before 60 deserves specific enquiry. Testing a symptomatic person is diagnostic and can be arranged through a neurology or neurogenetics service with counselling, whereas testing an asymptomatic at risk relative is predictive and follows a separate protocol with structured pre test counselling over several sessions, a waiting period, and support at disclosure, because of the documented psychological risk. Predictive testing is not performed on asymptomatic minors, since the result confers no medical benefit in childhood and removes the person's future right to choose not to know.
key_points: Psychiatric and executive symptoms often precede chorea by several years
An unexplained neurodegenerative death in a parent warrants specific enquiry
Testing a symptomatic person is diagnostic, not predictive
Predictive testing of asymptomatic relatives follows a separate counselling protocol
A relative's risk cannot be defined until the symptomatic person is tested
explanation.pearls: Suicide risk in Huntington disease peaks twice, at the point just before a formal diagnosis is made and again when independence starts to be lost, so those two moments rather than the late stage are when risk assessment matters most.

sources.label: Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Predictive testing for adult onset genetic disorders
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Agitation with a hydrocarbon smell and a perioral rash in a fifteen year old brought in after inhaling from a paint tin
stem: A 15-year-old boy is brought in by police, found behind a shopping centre with a tin of spray paint. He is agitated and shouting that the walls are moving. He smells of solvent and has a glazed silver rash around his mouth.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 /min, BP 128/74 mmHg, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Slurred speech, ataxic gait, no focal deficit, no head injury
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.4 mmol/L, ECG sinus tachycardia, normal QRS, QTc 430 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of his agitation?

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline if he becomes more agitated and combative
options.rationale: Catecholamines are specifically hazardous after hydrocarbon inhalation because the myocardium is sensitised to them and ventricular arrhythmia can follow, which is the mechanism of sudden death in this setting. There is also no indication for adrenaline in agitation of any cause. (Source: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use

options.text: Give intramuscular droperidol and apply physical restraint until he settles
options.rationale: Physical struggle generates a surge of endogenous catecholamines, which carries the same arrhythmia risk as giving them exogenously, and restraint here is the intervention most likely to precipitate collapse. Sedation may become necessary but restraint as the opening move inverts the priorities. (Source: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate and admit for cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate treats sodium channel blockade, identified by a broad QRS, and his QRS is normal with no acidosis on the blood gas. It is used in tricyclic or local anaesthetic toxicity when the QRS is broad. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give activated charcoal and observe in the short stay unit for four hours
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind inhaled hydrocarbons and cannot be safely given to an agitated adolescent with a reduced level of alertness. Attempting it introduces an aspiration risk with no possible benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Nurse him in a quiet low stimulus area with continuous cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Intoxication from inhaled solvents is short lived and usually resolves within a few hours, so a calm low stimulus environment with verbal de-escalation and continuous cardiac monitoring manages the agitation while avoiding the catecholamine surge that physical struggle or sympathomimetic drugs would produce. If sedation does become necessary for safety, a benzodiazepine is preferred because it does not sensitise the myocardium. (Source: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use)
source_refs: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use

explanation.summary: Volatile substance use, including spray paint, petrol, glue and aerosol propellants, produces rapid onset intoxication with euphoria, disinhibition, ataxia, slurred speech and sometimes hallucinations, and it resolves over one to a few hours as the hydrocarbon is exhaled. The characteristic examination findings are a solvent odour and a perioral or perinasal rash, sometimes with paint residue, and chronic use causes cerebellar, cognitive and peripheral nerve damage as well as renal and hepatic injury. The immediate danger is sudden sniffing death, in which hydrocarbons sensitise the myocardium to catecholamines so that a surge from fright, exertion or a struggle precipitates ventricular fibrillation, which is why calm handling rather than restraint is the governing principle of acute care. Australian responses to volatile substance use have focused on supply measures alongside youth and community programs, and every acute presentation is an opportunity to engage the young person with youth health and drug and alcohol services once they are sober.
key_points: Hydrocarbons sensitise the myocardium to catecholamines
Physical struggle produces the same catecholamine surge as giving a sympathomimetic
Intoxication is short lived and usually resolves within a few hours
A perioral rash with a solvent odour is the characteristic examination finding
Benzodiazepines are preferred if pharmacological sedation becomes necessary
explanation.pearls: Chronic petrol sniffing where leaded fuel is still available causes an encephalopathy with tremor, ataxia and seizures from lead toxicity, so a chronic user with neurological signs needs a blood lead level as well as assessment of the solvent exposure itself.

sources.label: NSW Health: Management of people with volatile substance use
BMJ Best Practice: Inhalant use disorder

subtopic_detail: A sixteen year old who cannot fall asleep until the early hours and cannot be woken for school but sleeps normally through the holidays
stem: A 16-year-old boy has missed 14 days of school this term because he cannot be woken. He lies awake until about 3 am whatever time he goes to bed, then sleeps until midday if left alone. Through the recent holiday he slept 3 am to 11 am with good mood and energy.

data_table.Investigations: Sleep diary: onset 2.30 to 3.30 am, waking 11 am to midday on free days; thyroid function and ferritin normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe an antidepressant and arrange psychology review
options.rationale: A depressive episode requires persistent low mood or loss of interest, and his mood and energy were good throughout a holiday during which he slept the same total hours at his own preferred times. Treating the mislabelled diagnosis exposes him to medication while leaving the timing problem untouched. (Source: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents

options.text: Advise a fixed earlier bedtime with no phone in the bedroom
options.rationale: Removing screens and setting a consistent schedule are worthwhile components but on their own they simply lengthen the time he lies awake, because the underlying circadian phase has not been shifted. Sleep hygiene alone is appropriate where the difficulty is behavioural rather than a delayed body clock. (Source: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography before treatment
options.rationale: A sleep study measures sleep architecture and breathing and is indicated when obstructive sleep apnoea, a parasomnia or narcolepsy is suspected, none of which fits a boy who sleeps soundly and unbroken for eight or nine hours once asleep. The diagnosis here is made from the sleep diary rather than from laboratory monitoring. (Source: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents

options.text: Give low dose melatonin early evening with morning bright light
options.rationale: Preserved sleep quality and duration with a consistently shifted timing that normalises on free days identifies a delayed circadian phase, and treatment combines a small melatonin dose several hours before his current sleep onset to advance the clock with timed bright light on waking to consolidate the shift. Sleep scheduling and screen advice are added alongside rather than instead of this. (Source: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents)
source_refs: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents

options.text: Start a sedative hypnotic nightly and review in two weeks
options.rationale: Hypnotics have no role in a circadian timing disorder and do not advance the phase, so waking remains as difficult while dependence and next day sedation become new problems. They are not recommended for adolescent insomnia in Australian practice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder is the commonest circadian rhythm disorder of adolescence and reflects a genuine biological shift in the timing of the sleep-wake cycle at puberty, amplified by evening light exposure and social schedules. It is routinely mistaken for depression, school refusal or laziness, and the distinguishing feature is that sleep itself is normal in quality and duration whenever the young person is allowed to sleep at their preferred times, which is why performance during school holidays is such a useful piece of history. The consequences of missing the diagnosis are substantial, since chronic sleep restriction on school days produces irritability, poor concentration and low mood that can then be treated as a primary mood disorder. Treatment advances the circadian phase using small doses of melatonin timed several hours before habitual sleep onset for its chronobiotic rather than hypnotic effect, combined with bright light on waking, gradual advancement of the schedule and reduced evening light, and relapse is common when holidays allow the phase to drift back.
key_points: Normal sleep quality and duration at preferred times is the diagnostic clue
Performance during school holidays separates this from a depressive episode
Melatonin is used for its phase advancing effect, not as a hypnotic
Timed morning bright light consolidates the shift
Relapse after holidays is common and warrants a maintenance plan
explanation.pearls: Melatonin advances the clock only when given several hours before habitual sleep onset, so a dose taken at the current 3 am bedtime is useless and a dose of around 0.5 to 1 mg taken in the early evening is what shifts the phase; larger doses act as sedatives without improving the phase advance.

sources.label: RACGP: Assessment and management of sleep disorders in adolescents
Australasian Sleep Association: Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders

subtopic_detail: Writhing tongue and lip movements developing after years of haloperidol in a man already taking benzatropine for stiffness
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 54-year-old man with schizophrenia who has taken haloperidol 10 mg daily for nine years. Benzatropine 2 mg daily was added six years ago for muscle stiffness and has been continued since.

Over the past four months his wife has noticed continuous movements of his tongue and lips. He is largely unaware of them. His psychotic symptoms have been well controlled for several years and he takes his medication reliably. On examination there are continuous writhing movements of the tongue with lip smacking and intermittent grimacing, plus occasional choreiform movements of the fingers. The movements lessen briefly when you ask him to open his mouth and hold his tongue still, and increase when he is distracted by mental arithmetic. There is no cogwheel rigidity, no tremor and no subjective inner restlessness.

data_table.Examination: Continuous choreoathetoid movements of the tongue with lip smacking and intermittent grimacing, occasional choreiform finger movements, movements briefly suppressible on request and worse with distraction, no cogwheel rigidity, no resting tremor, no akathisia on questioning or observation
data_table.Investigations: Urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Increase the benzatropine dose to control the abnormal movements
options.rationale: Anticholinergic medication reliably worsens these movements rather than relieving them, so increasing it aggravates the very problem being treated. Benzatropine is effective for acute dystonia and drug induced parkinsonism, which are different movement disorders with a different mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add propranolol and continue his current medications unchanged
options.rationale: A beta blocker is a treatment for akathisia, and he specifically denies inner restlessness and shows none on observation. Choosing a treatment for the wrong drug induced movement disorder leaves the causative regimen untouched. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Withdraw the benzatropine and switch him to a different antipsychotic
options.rationale: Anticholinergics unmask and worsen tardive movements so benzatropine is withdrawn slowly, and the causative high potency first generation antipsychotic is switched to an agent with lower tardive liability, with clozapine carrying the strongest evidence where the movements are severe or the illness has been difficult to treat. Abrupt cessation of the antipsychotic is avoided because withdrawal can transiently worsen the movements and destabilise the psychosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop the haloperidol abruptly today and review him again next week
options.rationale: Sudden withdrawal risks relapse of a psychotic illness that has been stable for years and can transiently worsen the movements through withdrawal emergent dyskinesia. A planned cross taper to a lower liability agent achieves the same aim safely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange genetic testing and brain imaging for an inherited chorea
options.rationale: Huntington disease would be considered where there is a family history, cognitive decline or a progressive chorea without a plausible drug cause, and here nine years of a high potency antipsychotic provides that cause. Investigation is reserved for atypical features rather than a classic orofacial drug induced picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Tardive dyskinesia is a delayed onset movement disorder characterised by choreoathetoid movements that favour the orofacial region, and it emerges after months to years of dopamine receptor blockade with a higher incidence for first generation agents, in older patients and in those with longer cumulative exposure. It must be separated from the other drug induced movement disorders because the treatments diverge sharply: acute dystonia and parkinsonism respond to anticholinergics, akathisia to dose reduction with propranolol or a benzodiazepine, while anticholinergics actively worsen tardive movements. The mainstays of management are recognition and dose review, withdrawal of anticholinergic medication, and a switch to an antipsychotic with lower tardive liability, with clozapine having the best evidence for improvement in established cases. Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors such as valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are effective and are used internationally, although Australian access is limited, and tetrabenazine is an alternative that carries a risk of depression. Movements can be irreversible, which is why routine surveillance with a structured examination is recommended for anyone on long term antipsychotic treatment.
key_points: Orofacial choreoathetosis after prolonged dopamine blockade defines the syndrome
Anticholinergics worsen tardive movements and must be withdrawn
Propranolol treats akathisia, a different drug induced movement disorder
Switch to a lower liability agent; clozapine has the best evidence in established cases
Abrupt antipsychotic withdrawal risks relapse and withdrawal emergent dyskinesia
explanation.pearls: At the bedside, the effect of distraction separates them: tardive movements increase when the patient performs mental arithmetic and can be briefly suppressed voluntarily, whereas drug induced parkinsonian tremor lessens with distraction and increases with sustained posture.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: A fifteen year old playing online until dawn with falling grades and rage when the console is removed, whose parents want the internet cut off
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 15-year-old boy with his parents, who are exhausted and want the home internet disconnected. Over the past year he has played online games for eight to ten hours most days, often until dawn, and his school reports have fallen from solid passes to failures.

He has stopped attending football and no longer sees the friends he used to. He becomes verbally abusive and once punched a door when his father removed the console. He denies low mood and says he would be fine if everyone left him alone, though he admits he has tried to cut back several times and could not. He has lost 3 kg and often skips breakfast to keep playing. He uses no alcohol or other drugs and there is no history of gambling or in-game purchasing.

data_table.Examination: Slim, tired looking, engaged and articulate when discussing gaming, reactive affect with no psychomotor change, no evidence of intoxication or withdrawal, no self-harm marks
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 48 micrograms/L (30 to 300), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, HbA1c within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.text: Support the parents to disconnect the internet at home immediately
options.rationale: Abrupt unilateral removal of access commonly escalates conflict and aggression without building the self regulation the young person needs, and it forfeits his engagement in treatment. Negotiated graded limits achieve better adherence than a unilateral cut off. (Source: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people)
source_refs: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people

options.text: Refer for family based behavioural therapy with a structured sleep and school plan
options.rationale: Management of problematic gaming in an adolescent is psychosocial and family centred, combining negotiated graded reduction in screen time, restoration of sleep and school attendance, reintroduction of the activities and friendships he has dropped, and work with the parents on consistent limits. Screening for a co-occurring mood, anxiety or attention disorder happens alongside this because those conditions are frequently present and change the plan. (Source: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people)
source_refs: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in four weeks
options.rationale: There is no evidence base for pharmacotherapy of gaming behaviour itself, and he does not describe a depressive or anxiety syndrome that would independently warrant an antidepressant. Medication becomes relevant if a treatable comorbid disorder is identified on assessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is a normal phase of adolescent development
options.rationale: Heavy gaming is common in adolescence and usually needs no intervention, but functional collapse across school, sleep, nutrition, friendships and family relationships is what distinguishes a disorder from a hobby. Normalising this level of impairment delays effective help. (Source: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people)
source_refs: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people

options.text: Refer him to a residential drug and alcohol withdrawal service for admission
options.rationale: He uses no substances, so a withdrawal service has nothing to treat and the model of care does not match the problem. Residential treatment is considered for severe refractory cases within specialist mental health services rather than as an initial step. (Source: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people)
source_refs: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people

explanation.summary: Gaming disorder is recognised in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases and is defined by impaired control over gaming, escalating priority given to gaming over other activities, and continuation despite negative consequences, with significant functional impairment over at least twelve months in most cases. Prevalence estimates in Australian adolescents are low, in the order of a few per cent, which means most heavy gaming is not disorder and the assessment hinges on functional impact rather than hours played. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, depression, anxiety and social difficulties all over-represented, and gaming frequently serves as avoidance of an underlying problem such as bullying, social anxiety or undiagnosed learning difficulty. Treatment is psychological and family based, and the evidence favours graded negotiated reduction with restoration of sleep, education and offline social contact over abrupt prohibition, which tends to escalate conflict.
key_points: Functional impairment, not hours played, defines the disorder
Comorbid attention, mood and anxiety disorders are common and must be sought
Gaming often functions as avoidance of an underlying difficulty
Treatment is family based and psychosocial, not pharmacological
Graded negotiated reduction works better than abrupt removal of access
explanation.pearls: Sleep is the most productive first target, because restoring a consistent sleep window forces a reduction in overnight gaming while giving a visible early win, and the daytime irritability that parents attribute to withdrawal from gaming usually improves within two weeks of the sleep schedule holding.

sources.label: RACGP: Problematic internet and gaming use in young people
World Health Organization: International Classification of Diseases eleventh revision, gaming disorder

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of tearfulness and poor sleep after being made redundant in a man who still enjoys his weekends and has no diurnal variation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 47-year-old man three weeks after he was made redundant from a job he had held for eighteen years. He asks for antidepressants because he feels he is not coping.

He describes tearfulness when he thinks about telling his extended family, difficulty getting to sleep as he worries about the mortgage, and a preoccupation with how unfairly the process was handled. He still enjoys cycling at the weekend and went to a friend's birthday dinner last week and had a good time. He denies any diurnal variation in mood, no loss of appetite and no weight change, and his concentration is intact when he is doing something he chooses. He has no thoughts of self-harm, no previous episodes of depression and no family history of mood disorder. He drinks two standard drinks most evenings, up from one.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when describing the redundancy but settles quickly and engages, affect reactive with preserved humour, no psychomotor retardation, speech and thought form normal, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, HbA1c within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start sertraline at 50 mg daily and review him again in two weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants have limited benefit in adjustment reactions where the symptoms are proportionate to a current stressor and anhedonia is absent, and starting one here medicalises a normal response while exposing him to side effects. An antidepressant becomes appropriate if he develops persistent anhedonia, diurnal variation or other features of a depressive episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine for his initial insomnia
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines risk dependence and are particularly unwise alongside increasing alcohol intake, and they do not address the financial worry keeping him awake. Their limited role is short term use for severe agitation or insomnia where non-drug measures have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure him that no intervention is required and review in three months
options.rationale: His distress is genuine and is affecting sleep and family relationships, and his alcohol intake has risen, so leaving him without support for three months misses a chance to intervene early. Watchful waiting is reasonable for milder distress with intact sleep and no change in substance use. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer urgently to the acute mental health team for same day assessment
options.rationale: Urgent referral is driven by risk of harm to self or others, psychotic symptoms or severe functional collapse, and he has none of these with no suicidal ideation on direct questioning. Escalating care to this level would be disproportionate and would consume an acute service place. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Refer for structured problem solving therapy with review of his alcohol use
options.rationale: A distressing but proportionate reaction to an identifiable stressor with preserved capacity for enjoyment and no biological features of a depressive episode is best treated with structured psychological intervention aimed at the practical problems driving the distress, alongside brief intervention for his rising alcohol intake. Review is arranged so that an evolving depressive episode is picked up if the pattern changes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Distinguishing an adjustment disorder from a major depressive episode is one of the commonest and most consequential judgements in primary care mental health, because the treatments differ and antidepressants perform poorly when the diagnosis is wrong. The features that point towards a depressive episode are pervasive anhedonia, diurnal mood variation, early morning waking, appetite and weight change, psychomotor change, guilt and worthlessness beyond the circumstances, and suicidal ideation; the features that point towards adjustment are a clear temporal link to a stressor, distress that fluctuates with reminders of it, preserved capacity for pleasure, and symptoms that are understandable in proportion to the event.
