The correct management of adjustment reactions is psychological and practical, with structured problem solving and, where relevant, financial, legal or employment supports, since the stressor itself is often modifiable. Escalating alcohol use is a common and under-asked complication that predicts a worse trajectory and warrants brief intervention at the first visit, and follow up is scheduled because a proportion of adjustment presentations evolve into a depressive episode.
key_points: Preserved capacity for pleasure argues against a depressive episode
Diurnal variation, early morning waking and weight change point to depression
Antidepressants have limited benefit in proportionate reactions to a stressor
Structured problem solving targets the modifiable stressor
Rising alcohol use is common, predicts a worse course and warrants brief intervention
explanation.pearls: Asking specifically whether the person still enjoys the things they chose to do last weekend separates adjustment from a depressive episode more reliably than asking about mood, because anhedonia is the symptom that does not remit when the person is distracted from the stressor.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

subtopic_detail: A new father screening above threshold at the six week check with irritability and withdrawal while his partner is being treated for postnatal depression
stem: A 33-year-old man attends his baby's six week check. His partner is being treated for postnatal depression. For a month he has felt flat and irritable, wakes at 4 am and enjoys nothing. He drinks four or five beers most nights, up from two on weekends.

data_table.Screening: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 14, self-harm item negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Explain the scale is not validated in men and take no further action
options.rationale: The scale has been studied in fathers and performs acceptably, although a lower cut off is generally applied in men because they score lower for equivalent severity. Dismissing the result on validity grounds would leave a father with clear depressive symptoms untreated. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline

options.text: Arrange his own assessment and care plan, addressing his alcohol use
options.rationale: A father with persistent low mood, anhedonia, early morning waking and rising alcohol use scoring above the male threshold has a depressive episode in his own right and needs a full assessment with a management plan in his name, including psychological therapy, consideration of an antidepressant and brief intervention for alcohol. Paternal depression independently affects infant development and the mother's recovery, so treating him is part of caring for the family rather than an aside. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline

options.text: Advise his symptoms will settle once his partner's treatment works
options.rationale: Paternal depression is not simply a reaction to maternal illness and does not reliably remit when the mother improves, so deferring his care to her treatment response leaves him untreated for months. His anhedonia and early morning waking indicate an independent episode. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline

options.text: Refer the couple for relationship counselling as the main intervention
options.rationale: Relationship support is a valuable addition when conflict is prominent but it does not treat a depressive episode with biological features, and offering it alone frames a clinical illness as a couple problem. Couple focused therapy is best considered once both partners' individual treatment is under way. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline

options.text: Notify child protection services because of his reported irritability
options.rationale: Irritability and snapping at family members in the context of a treatable depressive illness does not meet a threshold for statutory notification, and reporting at this point would damage the therapeutic relationship without protecting anyone. A notification obligation arises if there is a reasonable belief that a child is at risk of significant harm. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline

explanation.summary: Perinatal depression in fathers affects roughly 5 to 10 per cent of new fathers and peaks in the first six months after birth, yet it is screened for far less consistently than maternal depression and presents differently, with irritability, anger, withdrawal into work, risk taking and increased alcohol use often more prominent than expressed sadness. Australian guidance now recommends considering the mental health of both parents across the perinatal period, and the Edinburgh scale can be used with fathers although a lower cut off is applied because men score lower at equivalent severity. The strongest single risk factor is depression in the mother, which means a mother diagnosed with postnatal depression should prompt an enquiry about her partner rather than the reverse. Treating the father matters for outcomes beyond his own wellbeing, since paternal depression is independently associated with child emotional and behavioural difficulties and with a slower maternal recovery.
key_points: Paternal perinatal depression affects around 5 to 10 per cent of new fathers
Presentation skews towards irritability, withdrawal and increased alcohol use
The Edinburgh scale can be used in men with a lower cut off
Maternal depression is the strongest risk factor and should prompt enquiry
Paternal depression independently affects child outcomes and maternal recovery
explanation.pearls: A cut off of around 10 to 12 is generally used for fathers on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale rather than the 13 applied to mothers, so a father scoring 11 who would be dismissed as subthreshold on the maternal cut off warrants a full assessment.

sources.label: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: National perinatal mental health guideline
BMJ Best Practice: Paternal perinatal depression

subtopic_detail: A wife who has lost 6 kg and sleeps in a chair by the door because her husband with dementia wanders at night, presenting about her own back pain
stem: A 74-year-old woman attends with low back pain. Her husband has moderate Alzheimer disease and tries to leave the house at night, so she sleeps in an armchair by the door. She has lost 6 kg in eight months, stopped her swimming class, cries most days and feels guilty. She refuses residential care.

data_table.Mental state: Tearful; denies suicidal ideation; no psychotic features
data_table.Examination: Lumbar paraspinal tenderness, no neurological deficit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Treat the back pain and arrange a carer assessment with respite
options.rationale: Her back pain is the presenting complaint but the sleep deprivation, weight loss, social withdrawal and persistent low mood identify carer strain with a probable depressive episode, so management pairs analgesia with a formal carer assessment, referral for in home and overnight respite, a dementia service review of the night time wandering, and her own mental health follow up. Naming her as a patient in her own right is what unlocks the carer support services she is eligible for. (Source: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia

options.text: Treat the back pain and review her in three months as planned
options.rationale: Addressing only the presenting complaint misses the reason she has lost 6 kg and stopped everything she used to enjoy, and carers commonly present with somatic problems rather than naming their distress. Routine review alone would be appropriate if her mood, weight and social engagement were intact. (Source: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia

options.text: Prescribe a sedative for her husband so she can sleep at night
options.rationale: Sedating a person with dementia to manage a carer's sleep carries a recognised risk of falls, further confusion and increased mortality, and non-pharmacological approaches to night time wandering such as environmental modification, door alarms and daytime activity should come first. Medication for behavioural symptoms is a last resort after a structured behavioural assessment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange urgent permanent residential placement for her husband
options.rationale: She has clearly declined residential care and forcing the issue at a first conversation risks her disengaging from services altogether, when respite and in home support may keep the arrangement viable. Permanent placement is a decision reached over time with the family once supports have been trialled, or urgently if the situation becomes unsafe. (Source: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia

options.text: Refer her for urgent psychiatric admission for guilt and crying
options.rationale: She has no suicidal ideation, no psychotic features and retains function despite considerable strain, so inpatient admission is disproportionate and would remove the only carer her husband has. Admission would be indicated by active suicidal intent, psychosis or an inability to care for herself. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

explanation.summary: Around a million Australians provide unpaid care and carers of people with dementia carry among the highest burden, with rates of depression and anxiety substantially above those of the general population of the same age. Carers characteristically present with somatic complaints rather than psychological ones, and their distress surfaces only if the clinician asks directly about sleep, weight, social contact and how they are coping, which is why the opportunistic enquiry during an unrelated consultation is so productive. Night time behavioural symptoms are one of the strongest predictors of both carer breakdown and transition to residential care, so addressing wandering with environmental measures, daytime activity, review of medications and overnight respite is often the most effective single intervention. In Australia, practical supports are accessed through My Aged Care assessment, Carer Gateway and dementia specific services, and eligibility hinges on the carer being identified as such in the record. The statement that her husband would be better off without her requires careful exploration, since expressions of being a burden in a distressed carer can carry suicidal intent that is easily missed.
key_points: Carers present with somatic complaints; distress emerges only on direct enquiry
Sleep deprivation, weight loss and social withdrawal quantify the strain
Night time behavioural symptoms strongly predict carer breakdown and placement
Sedating the person with dementia to protect carer sleep carries real harms
Identifying her as a carer in the record unlocks assessment and respite
explanation.pearls: Statements such as he would be better off without me should always be explored explicitly for suicidal intent rather than accepted as self criticism, because older carers who express feeling a burden carry a suicide risk well above that of their age peers and the phrasing is easily heard as guilt alone.

sources.label: RACGP: Supporting carers of people with dementia
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guidelines

subtopic_detail: Episodes of watching himself from outside his body with the world looking flat and two dimensional, while knowing the experience is not real
stem: A 24-year-old man has eight months of episodes, several times a week, of watching himself from behind his own head while the world looks flat and artificial. Episodes last twenty minutes to several hours and throughout them he knows the experience is not real. There is no palpitation, breathlessness or fear of dying. He has never used drugs.

data_table.Examination: Insight fully retained, no hallucinations, no memory gaps
data_table.Investigations: Brain imaging and electroencephalogram normal, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start an antipsychotic, as the experiences indicate psychosis
options.rationale: Psychosis involves loss of insight into the unreality of the experience, and he consistently knows that what he describes is not real, which is the defining distinction. Antipsychotics are not an established treatment for this condition and expose him to metabolic and movement adverse effects. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for psychological therapy with psychoeducation about the symptoms
options.rationale: Persistent experiences of detachment from self and surroundings with intact insight, in the absence of substance use, seizures or a panic syndrome, identify depersonalisation-derealisation disorder, and the evidence supports psychoeducation with cognitive behavioural approaches that reduce symptom monitoring and catastrophic interpretation, alongside treatment of comorbid anxiety or depression. Explaining that the symptom is a recognised dissociative phenomenon rather than a sign of impending madness is itself therapeutic, because fear of the symptom perpetuates it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start an antiepileptic after repeating the electroencephalogram
options.rationale: Temporal lobe seizures can produce derealisation but characteristically last seconds to a couple of minutes, often with an olfactory or gustatory aura, automatisms or postictal confusion, none of which he describes during episodes lasting hours. His imaging and sleep deprived recording were both normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Depersonalisation-derealisation disorder)

options.text: Treat him for panic disorder with an antidepressant and exposure
options.rationale: Depersonalisation commonly occurs during panic attacks, but panic requires a crescendo of autonomic symptoms with fear of catastrophe, and he has no palpitation, breathlessness or fear of dying and the episodes last hours rather than peaking within ten minutes. Where the two coexist, treating the panic does resolve the dissociation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange assessment for dissociative identity disorder with a specialist
options.rationale: That diagnosis requires distinct identity states with associated amnesia, and he reports no memory gaps or lost time despite a history of childhood adversity. Both are dissociative disorders, but he has no identity disruption or amnesia. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Depersonalisation-derealisation disorder)

explanation.summary: Transient depersonalisation is extremely common, reported by up to half of the population at some point and particularly during sleep deprivation, acute stress or cannabis use, but as a persistent distressing disorder it affects roughly 1 to 2 per cent and is substantially under-recognised. The cardinal feature that separates it from psychosis is preserved reality testing: the person knows the experience is not real, which is why the as if quality of their description matters so much diagnostically. The differential requires exclusion of substance effects, particularly cannabis and ketamine, temporal lobe epilepsy where episodes are brief and stereotyped with other ictal features, panic disorder where dissociation rides on an autonomic surge, and post-traumatic and other dissociative disorders. Childhood emotional neglect and abuse are the strongest developmental risk factors. Treatment is psychological rather than pharmacological, and a substantial part of the benefit comes from explanation, because patients commonly fear they are going mad and that fear drives the symptom monitoring which perpetuates the condition.
key_points: Preserved insight into unreality separates this from psychosis
Exclude cannabis and ketamine use, temporal lobe seizures and panic disorder
Ictal derealisation lasts seconds to minutes, not hours
Childhood emotional neglect is the strongest developmental risk factor
Treatment is psychological; explanation alone reduces symptom perpetuation
explanation.pearls: Patients almost always describe the experience with an 'as if' construction, such as 'as if I am watching myself', and that grammatical hedge is the clinical marker of retained reality testing; a patient who states without qualification that they genuinely are outside their body has crossed into psychosis and the diagnosis changes.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Trauma and dissociation resources

subtopic_detail: Prolonged thrashing episodes with eyes squeezed shut and preserved awareness afterwards in a woman already on two antiepileptic drugs
stem: A 29-year-old woman diagnosed with epilepsy four years ago takes levetiracetam and lamotrigine at therapeutic doses. Three episodes this week lasted eight to fifteen minutes, with asymmetric limb thrashing, pelvic movement and eyes squeezed shut against attempts to open them. Afterwards she is tearful and can recount what staff said during the episode.

data_table.Examination: No tongue biting, incontinence or postictal confusion
data_table.Investigations: Video electroencephalography captured two typical episodes with no epileptiform change; drug levels therapeutic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange a saline injection to provoke an event and confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Deceptive provocation damages the therapeutic relationship that the explanation of the diagnosis depends upon, and it is not required when typical events have already been captured on video. Provocation, if used at all, is performed openly with consent using suggestion rather than a sham injection. (Source: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement)
source_refs: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement

options.text: Tell her the tests are normal and discharge her to her general practitioner
options.rationale: Communicating only that tests are normal leaves her without a diagnosis to make sense of real and disabling symptoms, and this pattern of communication predicts repeat presentations and poorer outcomes. A positive diagnostic label delivered with an explanation of mechanism is what changes the trajectory. (Source: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement)
source_refs: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement

options.text: Treat her for factitious disorder and notify the driving licence authority
options.rationale: Functional seizures are not consciously produced and labelling them as feigned is both inaccurate and harmful to engagement. Driving restrictions do still apply to unexplained loss of control of a vehicle and are discussed openly with her, but that is a separate matter from a diagnosis of deliberate deception. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)

options.text: Add a third antiepileptic drug and refer for epilepsy surgery assessment
options.rationale: Escalating antiepileptic treatment for events that are not epileptic adds side effects without benefit and reinforces an incorrect diagnosis. Surgical assessment is for drug resistant focal epilepsy with a demonstrated epileptogenic zone, which the video recording specifically excludes here. (Source: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement)
source_refs: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement

options.text: Explain the diagnosis positively and plan supervised antiepileptic withdrawal
options.rationale: Typical events captured on video electroencephalography without any electrographic correlate establish functional seizures, and the single most important therapeutic step is a clear positive explanation of the diagnosis, framed as a recognised condition that is real and treatable rather than as an absence of disease, followed by planned withdrawal of unnecessary antiepileptic drugs and referral for psychological therapy. A significant minority stop having events after the explanation alone. (Source: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement)
source_refs: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement

explanation.summary: Functional seizures, also called dissociative or psychogenic non-epileptic seizures, account for roughly 20 to 30 per cent of patients referred to specialist epilepsy services and are frequently misdiagnosed as drug resistant epilepsy, with the average delay to correct diagnosis measured in years and considerable iatrogenic harm from antiepileptic drugs and intensive care admissions for apparent status. Semiological features that favour a functional mechanism include prolonged duration beyond two minutes, asynchronous or thrashing limb movements, pelvic thrusting, side to side head rolling, eye closure with resistance to opening, preserved awareness or recall of the event, absence of postictal confusion, and a lactate that fails to rise after an apparently generalised convulsion. None of these is individually diagnostic, which is why video electroencephalography capturing a typical event remains the reference standard. Management begins with how the diagnosis is delivered, since a positive explanation that validates the reality of the symptoms while naming the mechanism is associated with better outcomes than a statement that investigations are normal, and it is followed by withdrawal of unnecessary antiepileptic drugs and psychological therapy, with cognitive behavioural approaches having the best evidence.
key_points: Functional seizures account for a fifth to a third of specialist epilepsy referrals
Prolonged asynchronous events with forced eye closure and preserved recall are suggestive
A lactate that does not rise after an apparent convulsion argues against epilepsy
Video electroencephalography capturing a typical event is the reference standard
How the diagnosis is delivered is itself a determinant of outcome
explanation.pearls: Serum lactate rises within minutes after a genuine generalised tonic-clonic seizure and typically normalises by about an hour, so a sample taken within 10 to 15 minutes of an apparent convulsion that shows a normal lactate is strong evidence against a generalised epileptic event; a sample taken two hours later proves nothing.

sources.label: Epilepsy Society of Australia: Functional seizures position statement

subtopic_detail: A man convinced he has motor neurone disease after eleven months of normal investigations who examines his own tongue daily and requests another neurology opinion
stem: A 41-year-old man has been preoccupied for eleven months with the conviction that he has motor neurone disease. He examines his tongue several times daily and reads patient forums for hours each evening. He accepts that two specialist assessments were normal but says they were done too early, and requests a third opinion.

data_table.Examination: Normal bulk, tone and power, no fasciculation, reflexes normal
data_table.Investigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography normal twice, most recently six weeks ago; creatine kinase 118 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Arrange the third neurology opinion he requests to provide reassurance
options.rationale: Repeated specialist opinions provide only transient relief and then strengthen the belief that something remains undetected, so each one entrenches the illness behaviour. A further opinion is warranted only if new objective signs emerge on examination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Repeat the electromyography now to settle the question definitively
options.rationale: Repeating a normal test in the absence of new clinical findings cannot settle the question, because the concern is not about the result but about the possibility that disease is not yet detectable. Reinvestigation also validates the checking behaviour that maintains the disorder. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Consolidate his care with one clinician and refer for psychological therapy
options.rationale: Persistent disease preoccupation with checking and reassurance seeking despite appropriate normal investigation is illness anxiety disorder, and management consolidates care with a single clinician offering regular scheduled appointments not contingent on symptoms, sets an explicit agreement to stop further investigation without new signs, and refers for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the checking and catastrophic interpretation. The reality of his distress is acknowledged explicitly while the focus shifts from finding disease to reducing preoccupation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Tell him firmly that nothing is wrong and decline further appointments
options.rationale: Blunt dismissal with withdrawal of care typically drives the person to other providers and further investigation elsewhere, fragmenting their care and increasing iatrogenic risk. The therapeutic move is regular scheduled contact with one clinician rather than reduced access. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start an antipsychotic, since his belief about the diagnosis is fixed
options.rationale: A delusion is held with unshakeable conviction despite contrary evidence, whereas he accepts the tests were normal and worries that disease may not yet be detectable, which is anxious doubt rather than fixed false belief. That distinction is what separates illness anxiety disorder from a somatic delusional disorder, where antipsychotic treatment would be appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Illness anxiety disorder is characterised by preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness, with either minimal somatic symptoms or symptoms grossly disproportionate to the concern, persisting for at least six months and accompanied by either excessive health related behaviours or maladaptive avoidance. It is distinguished from somatic symptom disorder, in which distressing physical symptoms are prominent, and from a somatic delusional disorder, in which the belief is held with delusional conviction rather than anxious uncertainty. The therapeutic paradox at the centre of management is that reassurance and reinvestigation reduce anxiety for hours to days and then increase it, so each cycle of testing makes the disorder worse while appearing kind in the moment. Effective management consolidates care with one clinician using regular appointments scheduled by time rather than triggered by symptoms, agrees explicit criteria for further investigation, and refers for cognitive behavioural therapy, which has the strongest evidence; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors help where there is comorbid depression or where therapy alone is insufficient. Clinicians must also remain alert to genuine disease developing, which is why the agreement is framed around new objective findings rather than a blanket refusal ever to investigate again.
key_points: Preoccupation with illness for six months or more with checking or avoidance defines it
Reassurance and repeat testing worsen the disorder over time
One coordinating clinician with time based appointments is the structural intervention
Cognitive behavioural therapy has the strongest evidence; antidepressants help if comorbid
Anxious doubt distinguishes this from a somatic delusional disorder
explanation.pearls: Scheduling appointments by the calendar rather than by symptoms is the specific manoeuvre that breaks the cycle, because a fortnightly appointment that happens regardless of how he feels removes the incentive for symptom escalation as the route to being seen.

sources.label: RACGP: Managing medically unexplained symptoms in general practice
BMJ Best Practice: Illness anxiety disorder

subtopic_detail: Elation, pressured speech and reduced need for sleep starting five days after prednisolone was increased for a vasculitis flare
stem: A 52-year-old woman admitted five days ago with a vasculitis flare had her prednisolone increased from 10 mg to 75 mg daily. For three nights she has slept two hours without tiring, telephoned relatives at 3 am planning to sell her house, and speaks uninterruptibly.

data_table.Examination: Elated and irritable, flight of ideas, attention intact, MMSE 29/30, no fluctuating conscious level; no past mood disorder
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L, glucose 11.4 mmol/L, CRP 18 down from 96 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat as hyperactive delirium and search for occult infection
options.rationale: Delirium requires disturbance of attention and awareness with a fluctuating course, and she is fully oriented with intact attention on digit span and no fluctuation in conscious level. Her inflammatory markers are falling and her urine culture is negative, so an occult infection is unlikely to be driving this. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start an antidepressant, as grandiosity reflects agitated depression
options.rationale: Elation with reduced need for sleep, pressured speech and grandiosity is an elevated mood state, and an antidepressant would be expected to worsen it. Corticosteroids can also precipitate depression, but that presents with low mood and psychomotor slowing rather than this picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give regular diazepam alone and review her in seventy two hours
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine may be a useful adjunct for sedation and sleep but does not treat the manic syndrome itself, and using it alone for three days leaves her making high risk financial decisions. Benzodiazepine monotherapy is reasonable for short term management of anxiety or agitation without an affective syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Discuss steroid dose reduction with the renal team and start an antipsychotic
options.rationale: A first manic episode beginning days after high dose corticosteroid with no personal or family history of mood disorder indicates a corticosteroid induced mood disorder, and management combines review of the steroid dose with the treating team, reducing to the lowest dose that controls the vasculitis, with a short course of an antipsychotic such as olanzapine or quetiapine for symptom control. The steroid cannot simply be stopped because the underlying vasculitis is being actively treated, which is why this is a negotiation with the renal team rather than a unilateral decision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start lithium as maintenance for a first episode of bipolar disorder
options.rationale: Lithium is a treatment for primary bipolar disorder and long term maintenance is not indicated for an episode precipitated by an identified and removable cause. Her impaired renal function also makes lithium a poor choice on safety grounds. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid induced psychiatric disturbance is common, affecting a substantial minority of patients on high dose treatment, and the risk rises steeply above the equivalent of about 40 mg of prednisolone daily. Elevated mood, insomnia and irritability dominate in the first weeks while depression is more characteristic of prolonged treatment or of dose reduction, and frank psychosis and delirium also occur. The syndrome is usually dose related and reversible, and the most important step is to review the steroid dose with the team treating the underlying disease, since abrupt cessation is often unsafe and the right answer is the lowest dose that controls the primary condition. Symptomatic treatment with a second generation antipsychotic is preferred to lithium or valproate for a drug induced episode, particularly where renal or hepatic function is impaired, and prophylaxis should be considered in someone who has previously reacted to corticosteroids and needs a further course. Practical protection also matters, because patients in this state can make irreversible financial and interpersonal decisions during an episode that lasts only days.
key_points: Risk rises above the equivalent of about 40 mg prednisolone daily
Elevated mood and insomnia dominate early; depression is later or on withdrawal
Intact attention and no fluctuation separate this from hyperactive delirium
Review the dose with the treating team rather than stopping the steroid
A second generation antipsychotic is preferred to lithium, especially in renal impairment
explanation.pearls: A patient who has had a corticosteroid induced mood episode has roughly a 50 per cent chance of recurrence with a subsequent high dose course, so the episode is documented prominently and prophylactic olanzapine or quetiapine is considered from day one of any future pulse rather than waiting for symptoms.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Corticosteroid induced psychiatric disorders

subtopic_detail: Small figures seen at the end of the bed in a man with a four year tremor and shuffling gait whose levodopa was increased last month
stem: A 76-year-old man has had a resting tremor and shuffling gait for four years, and his levodopa with carbidopa was increased four weeks ago. He now sees small figures of children at the end of his bed and a cat crossing the lounge room, is frightened, and accuses his wife of letting people into the house.

data_table.History: Alertness varies through the day
data_table.Examination: Resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, Mini Mental State Examination 24 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative; electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and make no other change
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors do have a genuine role in the cognitive and psychotic symptoms of Lewy body and Parkinson disease dementia and are worth considering, but leaving a recently increased dopaminergic dose unchanged ignores the most likely precipitant. Reviewing the temporally related drug change comes first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Treat empirically for a urinary tract infection and reassess
options.rationale: Infection is always worth excluding as a precipitant of psychosis in an older person, but his urinalysis is bland, his inflammatory markers are normal and his culture has shown no growth. Empirical antibiotics would treat nothing while the dopaminergic precipitant continued. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose and review him in one week
options.rationale: Risperidone has substantial dopamine D2 blocking activity and reliably worsens parkinsonian motor features, and in this population it also carries the risk of severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions. It is a reasonable choice for psychosis in someone without a parkinsonian syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give haloperidol as required for the frightening hallucinations
options.rationale: A high potency first generation antipsychotic is the most hazardous option here, capable of precipitating marked rigidity, immobility and neuroleptic malignant syndrome in a patient with a parkinsonian disorder. Haloperidol retains a limited role in hyperactive delirium in patients without parkinsonism or Lewy body pathology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Review his antiparkinsonian medications and reduce the dopaminergic load
options.rationale: Visual hallucinations beginning four weeks after a dopaminergic dose increase point first to the medication, so the initial step is a systematic review that withdraws adjuncts with a poor ratio of benefit to psychiatric risk such as anticholinergics, amantadine and dopamine agonists, then reduces levodopa to the lowest dose giving acceptable mobility. Where psychosis persists after that, quetiapine or clozapine are the antipsychotics used because they have the least effect on motor function. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Psychosis affects a large proportion of people with Parkinson disease over the course of their illness and is one of the strongest predictors of nursing home placement and carer breakdown. Visual hallucinations are the characteristic symptom, often beginning as well formed images of people or animals with insight preserved, and progressing to loss of insight with delusions, most commonly of infidelity or of intruders. Contributors are both the disease itself, with Lewy body pathology and cholinergic deficit, and dopaminergic treatment, so the assessment always begins by excluding an intercurrent illness and then reviewing the drug chart, withdrawing agents in order of psychiatric risk relative to motor benefit before reducing levodopa. Where an antipsychotic is needed, the choice is constrained to quetiapine or clozapine, since all agents with meaningful D2 blockade worsen motor function and people with Lewy body pathology can suffer severe sensitivity reactions with marked rigidity and a mortality risk. The overlap with dementia with Lewy bodies is considerable, and fluctuating alertness with early visual hallucinations and parkinsonism should prompt consideration of that diagnosis, for which cholinesterase inhibitors are particularly useful.
key_points: Visual hallucinations of people or animals are the characteristic symptom
Exclude intercurrent illness, then review the drug chart before adding anything
Withdraw anticholinergics, amantadine and agonists before reducing levodopa
Only quetiapine and clozapine are acceptable antipsychotics in this population
Fluctuating alertness with early hallucinations suggests dementia with Lewy bodies
explanation.pearls: Severe antipsychotic sensitivity occurs in roughly half of people with Lewy body pathology given a D2 blocking agent and carries a two to threefold increase in mortality, so a single dose of haloperidol given overnight for agitation can leave a previously mobile patient rigid and bedbound.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Parkinson disease psychosis

subtopic_detail: Crying that starts and stops abruptly without sadness between episodes in a man eight weeks after a left hemisphere stroke
stem: A 68-year-old man is in rehabilitation eight weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct. His wife reports he bursts into tears several times a day, often when greeted or during a television advertisement, and the crying stops as abruptly as it starts. He says he is not sad. Between episodes he engages in therapy and sleeps and eats well.

data_table.Examination: Abrupt onset and offset crying with rapid return to baseline, no anhedonia
data_table.Investigations: Screening bloods and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Explain the symptom and start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
options.rationale: Abrupt stereotyped crying triggered by minor stimuli with no sustained low mood or anhedonia between episodes is emotionalism after stroke rather than a depressive episode, and it responds to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors at lower doses and within days rather than the weeks needed for depression. Explanation to the patient and family is a substantial part of treatment because the symptom is distressing largely through being misread as uncontrollable grief. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Start an antidepressant at full dose for a post-stroke depressive episode
options.rationale: Post-stroke depression is common and would require persistent low mood or anhedonia, and he specifically denies sadness and remains engaged, eating, sleeping and looking forward to visits. The distinction matters because emotionalism responds to lower doses and much more quickly. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Refer for grief focused psychological therapy to process his disability
options.rationale: Adjustment to disability after stroke is real and therapy can help with it, but this symptom has a neurological mechanism and does not resolve with psychological processing of loss. His expressive dysphasia would also limit a purely verbal therapy as the primary approach. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Reassure the team that the crying needs no treatment and will settle
options.rationale: Although emotionalism does improve over months in many patients, it causes significant embarrassment and social withdrawal and interferes with rehabilitation participation, and effective treatment is available. Watchful waiting is reasonable only for mild infrequent episodes that the patient and family find tolerable once explained. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.text: Start a low dose antipsychotic to control the emotional lability
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have no role in this symptom and add sedation, falls risk and extrapyramidal effects in an older patient in active rehabilitation. They would be considered for psychotic symptoms or severe agitation, neither of which is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Three distinct emotional syndromes follow stroke and are routinely conflated: post-stroke depression, which affects roughly a third of survivors and requires sustained low mood or anhedonia with the usual biological features; emotionalism, a disorder of the expression rather than the experience of emotion, with abrupt episodes triggered by trivial stimuli, little corresponding subjective feeling and rapid return to baseline; and apathy, with reduced initiation and motivation in the absence of sadness, which families frequently report as depression. The distinction is practical rather than academic, because emotionalism responds to serotonergic antidepressants at doses lower than those used for depression and within a few days to a fortnight, whereas depression needs full therapeutic dosing over weeks and apathy responds poorly to antidepressants. Screening for mood after stroke is recommended in Australian guidelines, and dysphasia complicates it, requiring observer rated tools and collateral history rather than self report questionnaires alone. Left untreated, emotionalism restricts social contact and rehabilitation participation because patients avoid situations in which they expect to cry.
key_points: Emotionalism affects expression rather than experience of emotion
Abrupt onset and offset with no sustained sadness is the discriminating pattern
It responds to serotonergic antidepressants at lower doses and within days
Apathy after stroke is a third syndrome commonly mislabelled as depression
Dysphasia mandates observer rated tools and collateral history for mood screening
explanation.pearls: The response of emotionalism to a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is typically apparent within 3 to 7 days, so a lack of any change in crying frequency after two weeks should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis rather than the dose escalation that would be appropriate in depression.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management
Cochrane Review: Interventions for emotionalism after stroke

subtopic_detail: Choosing analgesia for a fractured ankle in a man taking an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor whose last dose was this morning
stem: A 44-year-old man has a closed displaced ankle fracture needing operative fixation today and severe pain. He has taken tranylcypromine 30 mg daily for eight months for treatment resistant depression, after four failed trials, with the best response of his life. His last dose was this morning.

data_table.Examination: Neurovascularly intact fracture, no clonus or hyperreflexia
data_table.Investigations: Bloods normal; ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What analgesia and antidepressant management is most appropriate?

options.text: Give fentanyl now and postpone surgery for two weeks after stopping it
options.rationale: Fentanyl is a reasonable non-serotonergic choice, but delaying fixation of a displaced ankle fracture for two weeks to wash out the antidepressant would cause malunion, prolonged pain and immobility for a theoretical anaesthetic convenience. The interaction is managed by drug selection rather than by deferring necessary surgery. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management scientific evidence)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management scientific evidence

options.text: Give pethidine now and stop the antidepressant until after surgery
options.rationale: Pethidine is the single most dangerous opioid in this setting because it inhibits serotonin reuptake and has precipitated fatal excitatory reactions with irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Abruptly stopping the antidepressant also achieves nothing useful within today's timeframe because enzyme inhibition is irreversible and persists for about two weeks. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors

options.text: Give tramadol now and continue the antidepressant perioperatively
options.rationale: Continuing the antidepressant is correct but tramadol is contraindicated, since it inhibits serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake and lowers the seizure threshold, making it as hazardous as pethidine in this combination. The right decision about the antidepressant does not rescue the wrong choice of analgesic. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors

options.text: Give titrated morphine now, continue the antidepressant, and alert the anaesthetist
options.rationale: Morphine and the other pure mu agonists without serotonergic activity are the opioids of choice and are given in reduced initial doses with close monitoring because responses can be exaggerated, while the irreversible enzyme inhibition means stopping the drug today confers no protection and would risk relapse of a severe illness that has responded to nothing else. The essential action is to flag the interaction to the anaesthetist, who must avoid pethidine and indirect sympathomimetics such as ephedrine and metaraminol and use a direct acting vasopressor in reduced dose if hypotension occurs. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors

options.text: Withhold all opioids, give a regional block and stop the antidepressant
options.rationale: Regional anaesthesia is genuinely valuable here and reduces opioid requirement, but withholding all opioids leaves severe pain undertreated when safe options exist, and stopping the drug today provides no benefit while risking relapse. Regional technique is an addition to safe systemic analgesia rather than a substitute for it. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management scientific evidence)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management scientific evidence

explanation.summary: Irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitors such as tranylcypromine and phenelzine remain in use for treatment resistant depression, where they can be strikingly effective after multiple failed trials, so the clinical task is to manage their interactions rather than to avoid the drugs. Two distinct reactions must be prevented: serotonin toxicity, driven by any agent that increases synaptic serotonin, which makes pethidine and tramadol contraindicated while morphine, oxycodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl and buprenorphine are acceptable in reduced initial doses; and hypertensive crisis from indirectly acting sympathomimetics, which release stored noradrenaline that can no longer be metabolised, so ephedrine and metaraminol are avoided in favour of a direct acting agent at reduced dose. Because the enzyme inhibition is irreversible and recovery depends on synthesis of new enzyme over roughly two weeks, stopping the drug on the day of surgery offers no protection at all, and current anaesthetic practice is to continue it and adapt the technique. The same logic covers the tyramine reaction, which is a dietary rather than a perioperative problem unless enteral feeds or particular foods are introduced.
key_points: Pethidine and tramadol are contraindicated; pure mu agonists are acceptable
Irreversible inhibition persists about two weeks, so stopping on the day is futile
Indirect sympathomimetics such as ephedrine and metaraminol risk hypertensive crisis
Use a direct acting vasopressor at reduced dose if pressure support is needed
Continue the antidepressant and adapt the anaesthetic rather than deferring surgery
explanation.pearls: The mechanism explains the drug list: indirect sympathomimetics such as ephedrine displace stored noradrenaline that monoamine oxidase can no longer degrade, so the pressor response is exaggerated and unpredictable, whereas phenylephrine acts directly on the receptor and is safe at a reduced starting dose of roughly a third to a half of usual.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors
Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management scientific evidence

subtopic_detail: A six year old who speaks freely at home but has not spoken at school for eighteen months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old girl whose teacher has asked her parents to seek help. She has not spoken a word at school since she started, although she nods, points and will write answers on a whiteboard.

At home she chatters constantly, argues with her brother and tells long stories to her grandmother. At the shops she goes silent if a stranger speaks to her and hides behind her mother. Her parents say she was a cautious toddler who took a long time to warm to new people, and her hearing was tested last year and was normal.

data_table.Examination: Sits close to her mother and does not speak during the consultation, makes brief eye contact, nods and shakes her head appropriately to questions, completes a drawing task and hands it over, no repetitive movements or unusual mannerisms, plays reciprocally with a doll offered to her, articulate speech heard on a video recorded at home showing age-appropriate sentences and pretend play

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for behavioural therapy delivered with the school, using graded exposure to speaking situations
options.rationale: Selective mutism responds to behavioural treatment that uses stimulus fading and shaping to extend the child's speaking from a comfortable setting into the classroom, and it works only when the school is part of the plan. Early intervention matters because prolonged non speaking entrenches avoidance and limits academic and social participation. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Commence a low dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review her speech at school in six weeks
options.rationale: Medication is an adjunct considered when a well delivered behavioural program has not produced progress, or when the anxiety is so severe that the child cannot engage with it. Starting it before any behavioural intervention reverses the accepted order of treatment. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Refer for a multidisciplinary autism assessment before any anxiety focused intervention is commenced
options.rationale: Autism is the differential when social communication differences persist across all settings, whereas this girl converses fluently and plays reciprocally at home and the silence is situational. Her selective pattern is the finding that distinguishes the two conditions. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Advise the school to require a spoken answer before she is allowed to move on to the next activity
options.rationale: Pressuring a child to speak raises anxiety at the exact moment speech is being attempted and reliably increases avoidance, which is why behavioural programs begin below the threshold at which she freezes. Communication through writing or gesture is accepted while speaking is being shaped. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Arrange repeat audiology and a speech pathology assessment before considering any psychological treatment
options.rationale: Hearing and language assessment is warranted when speech is abnormal or absent in every setting, and her hearing was formally tested last year with normal age-appropriate speech documented at home. Repeating those tests delays the treatment that addresses the anxiety. (Source: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on selective mutism)
source_refs: Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on selective mutism

explanation.summary: Selective mutism is an anxiety disorder in which a child consistently fails to speak in specific social situations, usually school, despite speaking normally in others, and it must have lasted at least one month beyond the first month of school to meet criteria. It commonly begins in early childhood in children with behavioural inhibition and a family history of anxiety, and it is frequently mislabelled as shyness, oppositionality or a language disorder. Treatment is behavioural, using graded exposure with stimulus fading, in which the child speaks first to a trusted person and gradually in the presence of others, and shaping, in which any communication is reinforced and progressively moved towards speech. School collaboration is essential because the classroom is where the avoidance lives, and pressure to speak is explicitly avoided. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, most often fluoxetine or sertraline, are added for children who do not respond to an adequate behavioural program or whose anxiety is too severe to engage with one.
key_points: The defining feature is consistent failure to speak in specific settings with normal speech in others, lasting beyond one month of school.
Normal reciprocal social communication and language at home separate it from autism and from language disorder.
Graded exposure with stimulus fading and shaping, delivered in partnership with the school, is first line.
Demanding speech increases anxiety and avoidance and is counterproductive.
Medication is reserved for severe cases or non response to an adequate behavioural program.
explanation.pearls: A short video of the child speaking freely at home, brought to the consultation by the parents, is the single most efficient way to establish that speech and language are age appropriate and to avoid an unnecessary developmental referral.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children
Speech Pathology Australia: Clinical guideline on selective mutism

subtopic_detail: Defiance and explosive tantrums at home and school in a seven year old with normal development and no aggression to others
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing the mother of a 7-year-old boy who has had a year of daily arguments, refusal to follow instructions and tantrums lasting up to forty minutes when asked to turn off the television.

His teacher reports the same pattern at school with peers but no fighting or bullying, and his academic progress is on track. His mother says she spends most of the evening shouting and has begun to give in to stop the noise. He is well, sleeps through the night, and has no history of fire setting, cruelty to animals or stealing.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative and chatty during the consultation, normal vocabulary and comprehension for age, no motor overactivity or impulsivity observed across a twenty minute consultation, no low mood or anhedonia on direct questioning, reciprocal social interaction with normal eye contact and shared attention, growth parameters on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Teacher report scale showing elevated oppositional and defiant items with inattention and hyperactivity items in the normal range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence a trial of a stimulant medication and arrange review of his behaviour at home and school in four weeks
options.rationale: Stimulants treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, which frequently coexists with oppositional behaviour, but his teacher rated inattention and hyperactivity items in the normal range and no overactivity was observed. Treating the wrong target exposes him to appetite and sleep effects without addressing the behaviour. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children

options.text: Refer the family to a structured parenting program that teaches consistent limits and positive reinforcement
options.rationale: Parent management training programs are the first line treatment for oppositional behaviour in primary school-aged children and have the strongest evidence of any intervention, working by re-establishing predictable consequences and increasing positive attention for wanted behaviour. They also directly target the coercive cycle in which giving in to end a tantrum reinforces it. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children

options.text: Prescribe low dose risperidone for the tantrums and arrange metabolic monitoring at baseline and twelve weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are considered only for severe aggression that persists after an adequate psychosocial intervention, and they carry weight gain, metabolic and prolactin effects in children. Tantrums without aggression towards people or property do not meet that threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer him for individual play therapy weekly and review his progress with the therapist after three months
options.rationale: Individual therapy for the child alone performs less well than parent focused intervention at this age, because the behaviour is maintained by interaction patterns at home and in the classroom. Individual work is added for older children and for comorbid anxiety or trauma. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children

options.text: Arrange a paediatric review for a formal neurodevelopmental assessment before offering any behavioural intervention
options.rationale: Developmental assessment is indicated where language, learning or social communication concerns exist, and this boy has age-appropriate language, on track academic progress and reciprocal social interaction. Waiting for an assessment delays an intervention that can start now. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children

explanation.summary: Oppositional defiant disorder is defined by a persistent pattern of angry or irritable mood, argumentative and defiant behaviour and vindictiveness that exceeds what is developmentally expected and causes impairment, and it is distinguished from conduct disorder by the absence of aggression towards people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness and serious rule violation. Assessment gathers information from home and school, screens for the disorders that commonly coexist or mimic it, particularly attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, learning disorder, anxiety, depression, trauma and language disorder, and asks about parental mental health, family violence and alcohol use, all of which shape the response. Parent management training is first line and works by interrupting the coercive cycle in which escalation is rewarded by the parent withdrawing a demand. Australian programs with good evidence include group based parenting interventions delivered through community child health services. Medication has no first line role, and antipsychotics are reserved for severe persistent aggression after psychosocial treatment, with baseline and ongoing metabolic monitoring.
key_points: Oppositional defiant disorder lacks the aggression, property destruction and serious rule breaking that define conduct disorder.
Assessment requires collateral from school and screening for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, learning, mood, anxiety and trauma.
Parent management training is the first line intervention at primary school age.
Giving in to end a tantrum reinforces it, which is the specific pattern these programs target.
Antipsychotic medication is reserved for severe persistent aggression after psychosocial treatment has been tried.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the behaviour occurs with every adult or only with one: defiance confined to a single caregiver points to the interaction pattern and predicts a strong response to parent training, whereas behaviour that is identical across all settings and adults raises the likelihood of a coexisting neurodevelopmental disorder.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Disruptive behaviour disorders in children
BMJ Best Practice: Oppositional defiant disorder

subtopic_detail: Discharge planning after inpatient opioid withdrawal in a man whose tolerance has fallen
stem:
You are the registrar discharging a 34-year-old man from a six day inpatient withdrawal admission for heroin dependence. He has used intravenously for eight years and has had two previous non fatal overdoses.

He has declined opioid agonist treatment for now and plans to stay with his sister, who is in the room and asks what she should do if she finds him unresponsive. He says he intends to stay off heroin but acknowledges he has relapsed after previous admissions.

data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented with no withdrawal features, pupils 3 mm and equal, no track marks with surrounding cellulitis, chest clear, no oedema, gait steady
data_table.Investigations: Liver function tests within normal limits, hepatitis C antibody positive with undetectable viral load after treatment, electrocardiogram with a corrected QT interval of 420 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate step to take before he leaves the ward?

options.text: Give him written overdose prevention information and a follow up appointment with the community drug service
options.rationale: Written information and follow up are worthwhile but neither reverses an overdose in the minutes that matter, and the first weeks after withdrawal are when the risk is highest. Information supplements the antidote rather than substituting for it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)

options.text: Arrange a naltrexone implant before discharge to block the effect of any opioid he uses in the coming months
options.rationale: Naltrexone implants are not registered or routinely funded in Australia and available depot preparations are used in limited settings with specialist oversight, and blocking treatment in someone who may resume use carries its own overdose risk when the blockade wanes. It is not the step that protects him in the first weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)

options.text: Supply take home naloxone and train both him and his sister to recognise an overdose and give it
options.rationale: Opioid tolerance falls substantially within days of abstinence, so the period immediately after withdrawal treatment or release from custody carries the highest overdose mortality, and take home naloxone supplied with training to the person and to those around them reduces deaths. In Australia naloxone is available free without a prescription through the take home naloxone program at participating pharmacies and services. (Source: Australian Government Department of Health: Take home naloxone program)
source_refs: Australian Government Department of Health: Take home naloxone program

options.text: Prescribe a short course of diazepam to manage the anxiety and insomnia that commonly follow withdrawal treatment
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines combined with opioids are a leading contributor to fatal respiratory depression, so supplying them to a person at high risk of resuming opioid use increases the danger. Post withdrawal insomnia is managed with non drug measures and review. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)

options.text: Defer naloxone supply until he has decided about opioid agonist treatment at his community appointment next week
options.rationale: Supply is not conditional on accepting agonist treatment, and the week between discharge and that appointment is precisely the window of greatest risk. Naloxone is offered to everyone at risk of witnessing or experiencing an opioid overdose. (Source: Australian Government Department of Health: Take home naloxone program)
source_refs: Australian Government Department of Health: Take home naloxone program

explanation.summary: Loss of tolerance is the central mechanism behind overdose deaths after any period of abstinence, and the days and weeks following inpatient withdrawal, hospital discharge or release from custody carry a mortality risk many times higher than continued use. Take home naloxone addresses this directly: the Australian program supplies naloxone as a prefilled syringe or nasal spray free of charge and without a prescription to people at risk and to their family, friends and support workers. Training covers recognising overdose through unresponsiveness, slow or absent breathing and blue lips, calling for an ambulance, giving naloxone, and repeating the dose because naloxone has a shorter duration of action than most opioids. Supply is offered alongside, not instead of, the interventions with the strongest evidence for reducing mortality in opioid dependence, which are methadone and buprenorphine maintenance. Co-prescribed benzodiazepines and alcohol substantially increase overdose risk and are avoided in this population.
key_points: Tolerance falls within days of abstinence, making the post withdrawal period the highest risk window for fatal overdose.
Take home naloxone is free and prescription free in Australia and is supplied with brief training.
Training includes giving repeat doses because naloxone wears off before most opioids do.
Supply is offered regardless of whether the person accepts opioid agonist treatment.
Benzodiazepines and alcohol markedly increase the risk of fatal respiratory depression with opioids.
explanation.pearls: Naloxone has a duration of action of roughly 30 to 90 minutes while heroin lasts longer and methadone far longer, so anyone who is revived must still go to hospital and the person giving naloxone is taught to expect to repeat the dose after a few minutes if breathing does not return.

sources.label: Australian Government Department of Health: Take home naloxone program

subtopic_detail: Subacute cognitive complaints with prominent self reported memory failure and poor effort on testing in a seventy four year old
stem: A 74-year-old man says his memory has gone, dating the onset to four months ago, shortly after his wife died. He lists in detail what he has forgotten. He has stopped going to bowls, wakes at 4 am and has lost 6 kg. His daughter says he manages his medications and banking without error.

data_table.Examination: Psychomotor slowing; answers I do not know to most questions; Montreal Cognitive Assessment 21 out of 30, recall improving with cueing
data_table.Investigations: Screening bloods normal; imaging shows age-appropriate atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Refer to a memory clinic for amyloid positron emission tomography
options.rationale: Molecular imaging is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty in specialist settings after reversible contributors have been treated, and it is not funded for routine use in Australia. Performing it while an untreated depressive episode is driving the presentation risks an incorrect and irreversible diagnostic label. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor and repeat testing in three months
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors are indicated once a diagnosis of Alzheimer disease or a related dementia is established, and they carry gastrointestinal and bradycardic effects. Starting one here treats a diagnosis that has not been made and leaves the depressive episode untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for driving assessment and notify the licensing authority
options.rationale: Notification and formal driving assessment follow a diagnosis of a progressive cognitive disorder or clear evidence of unsafe driving, neither of which is established here. Acting on a provisional label has serious consequences for independence and for the therapeutic relationship. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)

options.text: Treat the depression and repeat cognitive testing once mood responds
options.rationale: A dateable subacute onset, prominent self reported memory failure, do not know responses with recall that improves on cueing, and preserved instrumental function point to cognitive impairment driven by depression, which improves as mood is treated. Repeating cognitive assessment after treatment is what separates a reversible depressive picture from a neurodegenerative one, and a proportion will still prove to have an underlying dementia. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Assessment and management of people with dementia)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Assessment and management of people with dementia

options.text: Reassure him that grief explains this and review in six months
options.rationale: Bereavement is the trigger but early morning waking, six kilograms of unintentional weight loss and withdrawal from valued activities describe a depressive episode rather than uncomplicated grief. Six months of untreated depression in an older man carries substantial suicide risk. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Depression in older adults frequently presents with cognitive impairment, historically called pseudodementia, and distinguishing it from early neurodegenerative disease is one of the commonest diagnostic problems in old age psychiatry. Several features favour a depressive cause: a relatively abrupt onset that the person can date, prominent complaints about memory rather than the minimisation typical of Alzheimer disease, do not know answers rather than confabulated or near miss responses, recall that improves substantially with cueing, and preserved performance of complex instrumental tasks at home. Biological depressive features such as early morning waking, weight loss and anhedonia support the diagnosis, and a reversible medical screen and structural imaging are still performed. Treating the depression, with an antidepressant and psychological therapy and with electroconvulsive therapy where the episode is severe or psychotic, and then repeating cognitive assessment once mood has improved, is the definitive diagnostic step. Follow up remains important because a substantial proportion of older people with depression related cognitive impairment are later diagnosed with dementia, so cognitive review continues even after a good response.
key_points: Dateable subacute onset with prominent memory complaints favours depression over neurodegenerative disease.
Do not know responses and recall that improves with cueing contrast with the impaired encoding of Alzheimer disease.
Preserved instrumental function at home is strong evidence against established dementia.
Treating the depression and repeating cognitive assessment afterwards is the diagnostic manoeuvre.
A significant proportion of these patients later develop dementia, so cognitive follow up continues.
explanation.pearls: Cued recall is the discriminating bedside test: in depression related impairment the information was stored but not retrieved, so a category cue restores it, whereas in Alzheimer disease the information was never encoded and cueing does not help.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Assessment and management of people with dementia
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Six weeks of morning abdominal pain with school non attendance in a thirteen year old who is well on weekends
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 13-year-old girl who has attended school four days in the last six weeks. Each school morning she has stomach pain and nausea from about seven o'clock and cries when her mother insists she gets in the car.

On weekends and during the recent school holidays she was symptom free and went to a sleepover without difficulty. Her mother works from home and has been letting her stay in her room on the laptop. She has no truancy history, wants to keep up with her friends and says she feels sick at the thought of walking through the school gate.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with no organomegaly or masses, growth tracking along the 50th centile with no weight loss, no pallor, no mouth ulcers, no joint swelling, mood reactive with normal affect during the consultation, no thoughts of self-harm on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), coeliac serology negative with normal immunoglobulin A, faecal calprotectin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Certify her as medically unfit for school for four weeks and arrange educational materials to be sent home
options.rationale: Formalising absence removes the anxiety in the short term and reinforces avoidance, making return progressively harder as the time away lengthens. Medical certification for anxiety based non attendance is one of the commonest iatrogenic contributors to entrenched school refusal. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Refer her for an abdominal ultrasound and gastroenterology review before addressing the school attendance pattern
options.rationale: Her symptoms occur only on school mornings and resolve entirely at weekends and in school holidays, and her inflammatory markers, coeliac serology and calprotectin are unremarkable, so further gastrointestinal investigation is very unlikely to yield a diagnosis. Continued investigation also communicates to the family that a physical cause is still being sought. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on functional abdominal pain)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on functional abdominal pain

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review her attendance and side effects in four weeks
options.rationale: Medication is added when anxiety is severe or when a graded return program has not succeeded, and it does not by itself restore attendance. Beginning with medication also risks leaving the avoidance cycle and the school arrangements untouched. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Recommend enrolment in distance education so that she can continue learning without the distress of attending
options.rationale: Distance education removes the exposure that treatment depends on and isolates her from the peer contact she values, and it is considered only after an adequate graded return has failed or where there is a specific safety issue such as bullying. Choosing it now forecloses the treatment with the best evidence. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
