source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

options.text: Arrange a graded return to school plan with the school wellbeing team and cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Anxiety based school refusal is treated with early graded exposure that returns the young person to school in planned steps, coordinated with the school so that arrival, a safe place and a staff contact are organised, alongside cognitive behavioural therapy for the anxiety. The longer the absence continues the harder return becomes, so this is arranged promptly rather than after further investigation. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Anxiety disorders in children

explanation.summary: School refusal is anxiety driven non attendance in a young person who wants to succeed at school, and it is distinguished from truancy, in which the young person conceals the absence and shows no distress, and from withdrawal driven by depression, bullying or an undiagnosed learning disorder. The diagnostic signature is somatic symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea or headache that occur on school mornings and resolve on weekends and holidays, with a normal examination and unremarkable screening investigations. Management is prompt and collaborative: a graded return plan negotiated with the school, cognitive behavioural therapy for the young person, and coaching for parents on maintaining expectation of attendance while validating distress. Duration of absence is the strongest predictor of difficulty in returning, which is why certification of unfitness and early transfer to distance education are avoided. Screening for coexisting anxiety and mood disorders, bullying, learning difficulties and family stressors is part of assessment, and medication is added for severe anxiety or when a well delivered return program stalls.
key_points: Symptoms confined to school mornings with complete resolution on weekends and holidays is the defining pattern.
School refusal differs from truancy in that the young person is distressed and the parents know where they are.
Prompt graded return coordinated with the school plus cognitive behavioural therapy is first line.
Certifying unfitness or moving to distance education reinforces avoidance and worsens prognosis.
Screen for bullying, learning difficulty, depression and family factors as maintaining contributors.
explanation.pearls: The length of time out of school is the single best predictor of the difficulty of return, so a young person missing school for six weeks needs a return plan started within days rather than after a further round of investigations.

subtopic_detail: Excessive water drinking with a large diurnal weight gain and a falling sodium in a man with chronic schizophrenia
stem: A 41-year-old man with long-standing schizophrenia drinks from bathroom taps and carries a two litre bottle. He is more confused in the late afternoon than the morning and vomited twice last night. He takes no diuretic.

data_table.Weights: 78.4 kg at 7 am, 82.1 kg at 4 pm
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 124 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg, urine osmolality 88 mmol/kg, urine sodium 12 mmol/L, urea 2.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restrict fluid with a supervised plan and monitor twice daily weights
options.rationale: Dilute urine with a low urine osmolality and low urine sodium in the setting of documented excessive intake identifies primary polydipsia, in which the kidney is appropriately excreting free water and the problem is the volume consumed. Supervised fluid restriction with diurnal weight monitoring is the treatment, and weight is used because it tracks water load hour by hour while sodium lags behind. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Start a 3 per cent sodium chloride infusion with hourly levels
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures, obtundation or respiratory compromise, and he has only mild afternoon disorientation. Actively raising the sodium in a patient who will correct rapidly once drinking stops risks overcorrection and osmotic demyelination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start demeclocycline and repeat his electrolytes in three days
options.rationale: Demeclocycline is used in chronic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion where water restriction alone fails, and it is inappropriate when the kidney is already maximally diluting the urine. His urine osmolality of 88 mmol per kilogram excludes inappropriate antidiuresis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease olanzapine and substitute an antipsychotic less linked to hyponatraemia
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can contribute to inappropriate antidiuresis, but that produces concentrated urine rather than the maximally dilute urine seen here, and abruptly changing an agent that has maintained stability for three years risks relapse. Medication review is reasonable later if the drinking persists despite behavioural measures. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

options.text: Give intravenous 0.9 per cent sodium chloride and recheck in six hours
options.rationale: Isotonic saline is the treatment for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, and he has moist mucous membranes, no postural drop and a low urea, all indicating water excess rather than volume depletion. Giving saline to a water overloaded patient adds to the load the kidney must excrete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Primary polydipsia affects a substantial minority of people with long standing schizophrenia and can progress to water intoxication with hyponatraemia, seizures, rhabdomyolysis and death. The biochemical signature separates it from other causes of hyponatraemia: serum osmolality is low, urine osmolality is maximally dilute at well under 100 mmol per kilogram, and urea is low, indicating that the kidney is handling a large water load appropriately, whereas the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion produces inappropriately concentrated urine with urine sodium above about 30 mmol per litre. Symptoms characteristically worsen through the day as water accumulates, which is why diurnal weight monitoring against a target weight is the practical monitoring tool on inpatient units. Management is behavioural, with supervised fluid restriction, restricted access to water sources, weight based escalation protocols and treatment of the underlying psychotic illness, and severe symptomatic hyponatraemia is managed with hypertonic saline in a monitored setting. Overcorrection is a real hazard in this group because the sodium can rise very quickly once drinking stops.
key_points: Maximally dilute urine with low urine sodium and low urea distinguishes primary polydipsia from inappropriate antidiuresis.
Symptoms worsen through the day as water accumulates, so afternoon confusion with morning clarity is characteristic.
Diurnal weight change against a target weight is the practical bedside monitor of water load.
Supervised fluid restriction is the treatment; hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or obtundation.
Sodium can rise rapidly once drinking stops, so overcorrection and osmotic demyelination are genuine risks.
explanation.pearls: A rise of more than about three to four per cent of body weight between morning and late afternoon is the practical threshold used on inpatient units to trigger fluid restriction and urgent electrolyte measurement, because it identifies dangerous water loading before the sodium has fallen far.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Longstanding sensory based food restriction with faltering growth in a thirteen year old with no body image concern
stem: A 13-year-old boy has dropped from the 50th to below the 10th centile for weight over two years. He eats six foods, all beige and dry, and gags at the smell of cooked vegetables. He has eaten this way since he was three. He wants to be bigger for football and has never felt fat.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index on the 5th centile, no lanugo or dental erosion
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 14 micrograms/L (30-200), zinc low, sinus bradycardia 52 /min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence family based treatment focused on parental control of eating
options.rationale: Family based treatment is the first line for anorexia nervosa in adolescents and its central task, externalising an illness that drives weight and shape concern, does not map onto restriction driven by sensory aversion. Elements of parental support for intake are used, but the treatment model and the exposure work differ. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Prescribe an appetite stimulant and review his weight in three months
options.rationale: Appetite is not the limiting factor when food is refused because of its smell, texture or appearance, and pharmacological appetite stimulation has little evidence in this disorder. Three months of monitoring without intervention would allow further growth faltering. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Refer for dietetic nutritional rehabilitation with graded sensory exposure
options.rationale: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder driven by sensory sensitivity is treated by combining dietetic work to correct energy and micronutrient deficits with graded exposure that systematically introduces new foods, alongside parent coaching and screening for coexisting autism and anxiety. Weight restoration and exposure proceed together because nutritional repletion alone does not broaden the diet. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Admit for nasogastric feeding and cardiac monitoring for his bradycardia
options.rationale: Admission is driven by medical instability such as a heart rate under about 40 beats per minute, postural instability, hypothermia, electrolyte derangement or a prolonged corrected QT interval, none of which he has. Admitting a stable adolescent forfeits the outpatient exposure work that his disorder requires. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines

options.text: Arrange gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies to exclude an organic cause
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated for dysphagia, odynophagia, vomiting, abdominal pain or positive coeliac serology, and his serology is negative with normal immunoglobulin A and his restriction is clearly sensory in character. Investigating further reinforces the search for a physical explanation and delays treatment. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on faltering growth)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on faltering growth

explanation.summary: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder is characterised by failure to meet nutritional or energy needs through avoidance driven by sensory characteristics of food, lack of interest in eating, or fear of an aversive consequence such as choking or vomiting, and it is defined by the absence of the weight and shape concerns that drive anorexia nervosa. It commonly begins in early childhood, persists for years before referral, and is strongly associated with autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and anxiety disorders. Consequences include growth faltering, micronutrient deficiencies such as iron, zinc and vitamins A, C and D, dependence on supplements, and marked psychosocial impairment around shared meals. Treatment is multidisciplinary, pairing dietetic rehabilitation with graded exposure to new foods and parent coaching, with cognitive behavioural approaches adapted for the fear based subtype and with medical admission reserved for genuine instability. Assessment includes measuring the micronutrients that a narrow diet predictably depletes, which are frequently abnormal even when the full blood count and electrolytes are normal.
key_points: Restriction is driven by sensory aversion, low interest or fear of aversive consequences, without weight or shape concern.
Coexisting autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and anxiety are common and shape treatment.
Micronutrient deficiencies such as iron and zinc occur even when routine bloods are normal.
Treatment combines dietetic nutritional rehabilitation with graded sensory exposure and parent coaching.
Admission is decided on medical instability, not on the diagnosis itself.
explanation.pearls: Asking directly whether the young person wants to be thinner is the quickest bedside test: a boy who says he wants to gain weight to play football but gags at the texture of vegetables has sensory based avoidance, and treating him with an anorexia nervosa model wastes months.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Academy for Eating Disorders: Clinical practice guidelines
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Clinical practice guideline on faltering growth
BMJ Best Practice: Avoidant restrictive food intake disorder

subtopic_detail: Persistent dense amnesia with confabulation four weeks after treated Wernicke encephalopathy in a man who has stopped drinking
stem: A 58-year-old man is four weeks past an admission with confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia treated with parenteral thiamine. Those signs have resolved and he has not drunk alcohol since. He describes a fishing trip yesterday that did not happen.

data_table.Examination: Alert with normal digit span, no recall at five minutes despite cueing, disoriented to date
data_table.Investigations: Mean cell volume 104 fL, B12 and thyroid function normal, brain computed tomography shows atrophy only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and review in the cognitive clinic
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors have no established benefit in alcohol related amnestic syndromes, in which the lesion is in the mammillary bodies and thalamic nuclei rather than in cholinergic projections. Their use here exposes him to adverse effects without benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue thiamine and arrange neuropsychological assessment after abstinence
options.rationale: Cognitive impairment after alcohol related brain injury continues to improve for months with sustained abstinence and nutritional repletion, so formal assessment is deferred until that trajectory has been allowed to run before any permanent conclusion about capacity or accommodation is reached. Ongoing thiamine is continued because deficiency frequently persists and further episodes cause additional damage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)

options.text: Correct each confabulated account as it occurs to reorient him
options.rationale: Confabulation in this syndrome reflects a failure to retrieve and monitor memory rather than deliberate fabrication, and repeated confrontation produces distress without improving accuracy. Consistent orientation cues and a structured environment help more than correction. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Wernicke Korsakoff syndrome)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Wernicke Korsakoff syndrome

options.text: Apply for a guardianship order now to arrange supported accommodation
options.rationale: Substitute decision making may ultimately be required, but applying before the extent of recovery is known risks imposing a permanent arrangement on a man whose cognition may improve substantially over the coming months. Interim supported discharge with review is the proportionate step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)

options.text: Give a further three days of high dose parenteral thiamine
options.rationale: Parenteral thiamine is given for acute Wernicke encephalopathy and for high risk drinkers entering withdrawal, and he completed that treatment with resolution of his eye signs and ataxia. Repeating a parenteral course will not reverse established amnestic damage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction medicine)

explanation.summary: Korsakoff syndrome is the chronic amnestic state that follows thiamine deficiency, classically after Wernicke encephalopathy, and is characterised by dense anterograde amnesia with variable retrograde loss, disorientation and confabulation, in the setting of preserved alertness, attention and immediate memory. The preservation of attention distinguishes it from delirium, and the isolated memory deficit with relatively intact other domains distinguishes it from a global dementia. Recovery is possible and often substantial: with sustained abstinence and nutritional repletion, cognition continues to improve over many months, so definitive statements about capacity, driving and long term accommodation are deferred rather than made at the point of medical stability. Management is continued thiamine, treatment of the alcohol use disorder, a structured environment with consistent routines and external memory aids, and formal neuropsychological assessment timed after a meaningful period of abstinence. Confabulation is best managed by orientation cues and redirection rather than confrontation, and families benefit from an explanation that the person is not lying.
key_points: Preserved attention with dense anterograde amnesia separates Korsakoff syndrome from delirium.
Confabulation reflects retrieval and monitoring failure, not deliberate deception, and confrontation is unhelpful.
Cognition improves for many months with abstinence and nutrition, so formal assessment is deferred.
Thiamine replacement continues because deficiency often persists and further episodes cause further damage.
Decisions about guardianship, driving and accommodation wait until the recovery trajectory is known.
explanation.pearls: Around a quarter of people with alcohol related brain injury recover substantially and a further half improve partially with sustained abstinence, which is why formal neuropsychological assessment is timed at several months rather than at the point of discharge.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Wernicke Korsakoff syndrome

subtopic_detail: Repugnant intrusive thoughts of harming her baby with avoidance of bathing in a woman with intact reality testing
stem: Six weeks after the birth of her first baby, a 30-year-old woman discloses that images of drowning the baby come to her when she runs the bath, so her husband now does all the bathing. She calls the thoughts horrible and not like her, checks the baby's breathing twenty times a night and has hidden the knives. She delights in the baby.

data_table.Examination: Thoughts unwanted and repugnant, no delusional beliefs about the baby, insight intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit urgently to a mother and baby unit with supervised contact
options.rationale: Admission of this kind is for postpartum psychosis or severe depression with command phenomena or delusional beliefs about the infant, in which risk to the baby is genuine. Applying it to ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts confirms the woman's worst fear and deters other mothers from disclosing. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period

options.text: Advise another adult be present at all times and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Formalising avoidance and supervision reinforces the belief that the thoughts signal danger, which is the maintaining mechanism of the disorder. A four week gap also leaves a distressed woman without treatment while her checking and avoidance consolidate. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period

options.text: Explain the nature of intrusive thoughts and refer for exposure therapy
options.rationale: Ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts with compulsive checking and avoidance, in a woman with intact reality testing who is appalled by the content, describe perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder, and exposure with response prevention is the treatment with the best evidence. Normalising the experience is therapeutic in itself, because the distress is driven by the meaning she attaches to the thoughts rather than by the thoughts themselves. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period

options.text: Commence a low dose antipsychotic and arrange psychiatric review this week
options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis presents with delusions, hallucinations, a fluctuating confusional picture or beliefs that the baby is in danger or evil, and it typically begins within the first two weeks with reduced need for sleep. Her thoughts are recognised as her own, unwanted and senseless, which is the opposite of a delusion. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period

options.text: Report to child protection on the basis of her disclosure
options.rationale: Reporting obligations arise where a child is at risk of significant harm, and ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts in a mother who is avoiding the feared situation and seeking help are associated with very low risk of acting on them. Reflexive reporting in this situation causes lasting harm to engagement with perinatal services. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period)
source_refs: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period

explanation.summary: Intrusive thoughts of harm coming to the infant are reported by a large majority of new parents, and in a minority they become frequent, distressing and accompanied by compulsions such as checking and by avoidance of the feared situation, meeting criteria for perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder. The clinical task is to separate these ego-dystonic thoughts from the ego-syntonic beliefs of postpartum psychosis and from the ruminations of severe depression, because the management diverges completely. Ego-dystonic thoughts are unwanted, recognised as senseless, experienced with horror, and lead the mother to avoid the baby in the feared context, and the risk of acting on them is very low. Treatment is psychoeducation that normalises the phenomenon, cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention, and a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor such as sertraline, which is compatible with breastfeeding, when symptoms are moderate to severe. Disclosure carries great shame and fear of child protection involvement, so an explicit explanation of what the thoughts mean and what will happen next is part of the treatment.
key_points: Intrusive thoughts about harm to the infant are near universal and become a disorder when accompanied by compulsions and avoidance.
Ego-dystonic thoughts with intact insight and preserved reality testing are the signature of perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder.
Postpartum psychosis is distinguished by delusions, hallucinations, fluctuating confusion and reduced need for sleep.
Exposure and response prevention is first line, with sertraline added for moderate to severe symptoms.
Reflexive child protection reporting or enforced supervision confirms the woman's fears and deters disclosure.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the thought is wanted: a woman who describes the image as horrible and who has asked someone else to bathe the baby is avoiding the feared stimulus, whereas a woman who believes the baby must be saved from something is describing a delusion and needs urgent psychiatric assessment.

sources.label: Centre of Perinatal Excellence: Mental health care in the perinatal period
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Perinatal mental health
BMJ Best Practice: Obsessive compulsive disorder

subtopic_detail: Choosing an antipsychotic for a first psychotic episode in a man with focal epilepsy taking carbamazepine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 26-year-old man with focal epilepsy since childhood, controlled on carbamazepine with his last seizure two years ago. Over three months he has developed the belief that his neighbours are broadcasting his thoughts, and he now hears two voices discussing him.

The symptoms are present every day and are unrelated to his seizures, and there has been no change in seizure frequency or aura. He uses no substances, and a urine drug screen is negative. His neurologist has confirmed that his antiepileptic dose is unchanged and his last electroencephalogram was stable.

data_table.Examination: Guarded with persecutory delusions of thought broadcasting and third person auditory hallucinations, no clouding of consciousness, fully oriented with intact attention, no postictal confusion, no focal neurological deficit, no tremor or rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, sodium 137 mmol/L (135 to 145), liver function tests within normal limits, carbamazepine level within the therapeutic range, electrocardiogram with a corrected QT interval of 408 milliseconds, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showing left mesial temporal sclerosis unchanged from previous imaging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence clozapine now, given that psychosis arising with epilepsy is typically refractory to other antipsychotic agents
options.rationale: Clozapine lowers the seizure threshold more than any other antipsychotic, with a dose related risk that becomes substantial above about 600 mg daily, and it is reserved for treatment resistant psychosis after two adequate trials. Choosing it first in a man with established epilepsy inverts the risk calculation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Withhold antipsychotic treatment and ask the neurologist to increase the carbamazepine dose to suppress the psychosis
options.rationale: Interictal psychosis is not abolished by increasing antiepileptic doses, and his seizures are already controlled with a level in the therapeutic range. Some antiepileptic drugs can themselves contribute to psychiatric adverse effects, so escalating without indication risks harm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence chlorpromazine at night, titrating the dose upwards according to his response over the next two weeks
options.rationale: Chlorpromazine has one of the highest seizure risks among antipsychotics, along with clozapine, and it also carries marked sedation and postural hypotension. Safer alternatives with a lower seizure risk exist and are preferred in epilepsy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence risperidone at a low dose and titrate slowly, anticipating that carbamazepine will lower its plasma concentration
options.rationale: Risperidone and aripiprazole carry a comparatively low seizure risk and are preferred when psychosis coexists with epilepsy, and starting low with slow titration further reduces that risk. Carbamazepine is a potent enzyme inducer that substantially reduces the concentration of risperidone and of its active metabolite, so a higher than usual dose is often needed and the response is monitored with this interaction in mind. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Treat this as a postictal phenomenon and observe him without antipsychotic treatment for a further two weeks
options.rationale: Postictal psychosis follows a cluster of seizures after a lucid interval of hours to days and remits within days to weeks, whereas his symptoms have been continuous for three months with no change in seizure frequency. Observation would leave a chronic interictal psychosis untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Psychosis occurs in people with epilepsy several times more often than in the general population, and temporal lobe epilepsy with mesial temporal sclerosis carries a particular association. The first task is to classify the psychosis in relation to seizures: ictal and postictal psychoses are temporally linked to seizure activity and are managed largely by optimising seizure control, whereas interictal psychosis is continuous, unrelated to seizure timing, and requires antipsychotic treatment in its own right. All antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold to some degree, but the risk is highest with clozapine and chlorpromazine and lowest with agents such as risperidone, aripiprazole and haloperidol, so choice is guided by that gradient combined with starting low and titrating slowly. Pharmacokinetic interactions matter as much as seizure risk: carbamazepine, phenytoin and phenobarbital are enzyme inducers that markedly reduce antipsychotic concentrations, while valproate can raise the concentration of some agents. Care is shared with neurology so that antiepileptic choice, which can itself contribute to psychiatric adverse effects, is reviewed alongside the antipsychotic.
key_points: Classify the psychosis as ictal, postictal or interictal, because management differs fundamentally.
Interictal psychosis is continuous, unrelated to seizure timing, and requires antipsychotic treatment.
Clozapine and chlorpromazine carry the highest seizure risk; risperidone and aripiprazole are preferred in epilepsy.
Carbamazepine is a potent enzyme inducer that lowers antipsychotic plasma concentrations substantially.
Starting low and titrating slowly further reduces the seizure risk of any antipsychotic.
explanation.pearls: Postictal psychosis has a characteristic lucid interval of about twelve to seventy two hours between a seizure cluster and the onset of symptoms, and recognising that gap prevents a self-limiting episode from being treated as a chronic psychotic illness.

subtopic_detail: Agitation with tremor and autonomic arousal on day three after surgery in a patient whose long term night sedation was omitted
stem: A 72-year-old woman is agitated and climbing out of bed on the third night after a total hip replacement, having been oriented and calm for two days. Her daughter mentions she has taken a tablet for her nerves nightly for twenty five years, never asked about on admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 /min, BP 168/94 mmHg, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Restless, coarse tremor, diaphoretic, disoriented, attention impaired
data_table.Investigations: CRP 42 mg/L falling from 88, urine and chest radiograph clear
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol, as required oxycodone; no benzodiazepine charted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Recommence a benzodiazepine at an equivalent dose with a slow supervised taper
options.rationale: Autonomic arousal with tremor, insomnia and delirium appearing around day two to three of an unplanned interruption to twenty five years of nightly benzodiazepine use is withdrawal, and reinstating an equivalent dose treats the cause rather than the symptom. A gradual taper is then planned, ideally after discharge, because abrupt cessation in hospital is how the problem arose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe regular haloperidol for the agitation with daily liaison review
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are used for distressing agitation in delirium when non drug measures fail, but they do not treat benzodiazepine withdrawal and can lower the seizure threshold in a patient already at risk of withdrawal seizures. Treating the agitation while the withdrawal continues allows progression to seizures and to a delirium tremens like state. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Stop the oxycodone and treat her pain with regular paracetamol alone
options.rationale: Opioids contribute to postoperative delirium and a review of the dose is sensible, but opioid effects cause sedation and miosis rather than the tremor, sweating, hypertension and tachycardia seen here. Leaving her in pain also worsens delirium. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on delirium)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on delirium

options.text: Start empirical intravenous antibiotics for presumed postoperative sepsis
options.rationale: Infection is always considered in postoperative delirium, but her C reactive protein is falling from its day one peak, her white cell count is normal, and her wound, chest and urine give no source. Empirical antibiotics would not address the withdrawal that explains her autonomic signs. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on delirium)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on delirium

options.text: Arrange urgent CT of the brain and withhold sedating medication
options.rationale: Brain imaging is indicated for a fall with head strike, focal neurological signs, anticoagulation with new deficit, or delirium that does not resolve with treatment of the identified cause, none of which apply. Delaying treatment of an evolving withdrawal syndrome while awaiting a scan risks seizures. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on delirium)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on delirium

explanation.summary: Benzodiazepine withdrawal is a frequently missed cause of postoperative delirium because long term night sedation is often not disclosed at admission and is not reconciled onto the drug chart. Symptoms begin one to two days after stopping a short-acting agent and later with longer acting ones, and consist of anxiety, insomnia, tremor, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, perceptual disturbance and, in severe cases, seizures and a delirium resembling delirium tremens. The diagnostic clue is the combination of autonomic arousal with delirium and a lucid interval of a day or two after admission, in a patient in whom the usual delirium precipitants have been excluded or are improving. Treatment is reinstatement of an equivalent benzodiazepine dose, with conversion to a long-acting agent such as diazepam where a taper is planned, and the taper itself is conducted slowly over weeks to months in a planned outpatient setting rather than opportunistically during an acute admission. Medication reconciliation at admission, including specific questions about sleeping tablets and tablets for nerves, prevents the problem entirely.
key_points: Unrecognised long term benzodiazepine use is a common and reversible cause of postoperative delirium.
Withdrawal produces autonomic arousal with tremor and sweating alongside the delirium, unlike opioid or metabolic causes.
A lucid interval of one to three days after admission fits the pharmacokinetics of the omitted drug.
Reinstating an equivalent dose is the treatment, with a slow planned taper arranged later.
Antipsychotics treat agitation but not withdrawal, and do not prevent withdrawal seizures.
explanation.pearls: Asking specifically about tablets for nerves or for sleep, rather than about benzodiazepines by name, is what uncovers decades of use in an older person who does not think of the tablet as a real medication and did not bring it in with her other boxes.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine: Position statement on delirium

subtopic_detail: Fever with rigidity and a very high creatine kinase two days after antiparkinsonian medication was withheld before surgery
stem: A 71-year-old man with nine years of Parkinson disease was admitted two days ago with small bowel obstruction and kept nil by mouth; his levodopa with carbidopa and entacapone have not been given since. He has never taken an antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 126 /min, BP swinging between 165/95 and 105/60 mmHg, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Severe generalised lead-pipe rigidity, sweating, fluctuating conscious state, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 6800 U/L (<200), white cell count 15.8 x10^9/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L, brain imaging normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous dantrolene and transfer to intensive care for cooling
options.rationale: Dantrolene, along with cooling and intensive supportive care, is used adjunctively in severe hyperthermic rigidity, and intensive care involvement is appropriate, but it does not correct the dopaminergic deficit that is generating the syndrome. Supportive measures run alongside dopaminergic replacement rather than in place of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Give intramuscular olanzapine for his agitation and reassess the rigidity
options.rationale: Any dopamine blocking agent will deepen the dopaminergic deficit and can convert a severe episode into a fatal one, and people with Parkinson disease are additionally prone to marked sensitivity to antipsychotics. Agitation here is a symptom of the syndrome rather than an indication for a dopamine antagonist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start empirical intravenous antibiotics for presumed sepsis and continue nil by mouth
options.rationale: Cultures and empirical antibiotics are reasonable while sepsis remains in the differential, but continuing to withhold dopaminergic therapy perpetuates the cause, and nil by mouth status is not a reason to omit these drugs when a nasogastric tube or a transdermal agonist is available. The rigidity, the creatine kinase of nearly 7000 and the temporal link to drug omission are not explained by infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Give a benzodiazepine and restart his usual medication when bowel function returns
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are useful adjuncts for agitation and for catatonic features but do not reverse the underlying dopaminergic withdrawal, and waiting for bowel function may mean days more without treatment. Delay in this syndrome is associated with renal failure, aspiration and death. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Reinstate his dopaminergic therapy now by nasogastric tube or transdermal patch
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy causes parkinsonism hyperpyrexia syndrome, which is clinically indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome but is caused by loss of dopaminergic stimulation rather than by receptor blockade, so the treatment is urgent replacement of the missing drug. A nasogastric tube already in situ allows levodopa to be given, and a rotigotine patch is used when enteral absorption is unreliable, with supportive care and intensive care review in parallel. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Parkinsonism hyperpyrexia syndrome, also called the neuroleptic malignant like syndrome of Parkinson disease, follows abrupt withdrawal or substantial dose reduction of dopaminergic therapy, and hospital admission is the commonest setting because patients are made nil by mouth, doses are missed around theatre, or drug charts are not reconciled. It presents within one to three days with hyperthermia, severe rigidity, autonomic instability, altered conscious state and a greatly raised creatine kinase, and it is complicated by rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury, aspiration pneumonia and venous thromboembolism, with mortality reported around ten to twenty per cent. The differential includes sepsis, serotonin toxicity, which is distinguished by clonus, hyperreflexia and mydriasis, and malignant catatonia. Treatment is immediate reinstatement of dopaminergic therapy by any available route, most often levodopa through a nasogastric tube or a rotigotine transdermal patch when the gut is unreliable, together with aggressive fluid resuscitation for rhabdomyolysis, cooling and intensive care support, with dantrolene and bromocriptine as adjuncts in severe cases. Prevention is straightforward and is the real lesson: Parkinson medication is time critical, is charted at the patient's usual times, and is given by an alternative route rather than omitted.
key_points: Abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy produces a syndrome clinically identical to neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Onset is typically one to three days after the last dose, most often during hospital admission or perioperatively.
Immediate reinstatement of dopaminergic therapy by nasogastric tube or transdermal patch is the definitive treatment.
Dopamine blocking drugs, including antipsychotics and metoclopramide, will worsen the syndrome and are avoided.
Clonus, hyperreflexia and mydriasis point instead to serotonin toxicity, which has different management.
explanation.pearls: A rotigotine patch is the practical rescue when the gut cannot be used, and an approximate conversion of total daily levodopa to transdermal rotigotine is calculated with neurology or pharmacy input so that replacement begins within hours rather than waiting for bowel function to return.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

subtopic_detail: Prolonged episodes with closed eyes and side to side head movement captured on video telemetry with a normal trace
stem: A 24-year-old woman has two years of episodes in which she falls, shakes and is unresponsive, unchanged on levetiracetam. Video electroencephalogram telemetry captured three typical episodes, each about eight minutes with eyes held closed, side to side head movement and asynchronous waxing and waning limb shaking, with a normal awake rhythm throughout.

data_table.Examination: No tongue biting or incontinence during any event
data_table.Investigations: Brain magnetic resonance imaging normal, postictal prolactin normal, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Increase levetiracetam, add lamotrigine and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Escalating antiseizure medication treats a condition that the telemetry has excluded and exposes her to adverse effects including irritability and rash for no benefit. Escalation would be correct if the recorded events had shown an ictal electrographic correlate. (Source: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder)

options.text: Tell her the episodes are not genuine seizures and discharge her
options.rationale: Framing the diagnosis as an absence of real illness is the single commonest reason these patients disengage, and it is both inaccurate and therapeutically destructive. The explanation must convey a positive diagnosis of a recognised disorder with an evidence-based treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder)

options.text: Explain the positive diagnosis, refer for therapy and plan drug withdrawal
options.rationale: Delivering the diagnosis well, showing the patient the recorded events and the normal trace, and referring for cognitive behavioural therapy adapted to functional seizures is the treatment with the best evidence, and withdrawing an ineffective antiseizure drug is part of that plan. A substantial proportion of patients improve on the explanation alone. (Source: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder)

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor as primary treatment
options.rationale: Antidepressants have a role where there is comorbid depression or anxiety but they are not a primary treatment for functional seizures, in which psychological therapy has the stronger evidence. Medication as monotherapy here would leave the central treatment undelivered. (Source: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder)

options.text: Repeat the imaging with an epilepsy protocol and further telemetry
options.rationale: Repeating investigations that have already given a clear positive answer reinforces the belief that something has been missed and delays treatment. Further imaging would be justified only if new focal signs or a new event semiology appeared. (Source: RANZCP: Functional neurological disorder)

explanation.summary: Functional seizures, also called psychogenic non epileptic seizures or dissociative seizures, account for around a fifth of patients referred to specialist epilepsy services and a similar proportion of apparent status epilepticus presentations. Video electroencephalogram telemetry capturing a typical event with a normal trace is the reference standard, and supportive semiological features include eye closure during the event, side to side head movement, asynchronous and waxing and waning limb movements, prolonged duration, absence of tongue biting or incontinence, and a normal post event prolactin. The diagnosis is positive rather than one of exclusion, and how it is communicated strongly predicts outcome, so the explanation should name the condition, affirm that the episodes are involuntary and real, use the recorded evidence, and immediately offer treatment. Cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for functional seizures is the intervention with the strongest randomised evidence. Around one in ten patients also has epilepsy, so antiseizure medication is withdrawn thoughtfully rather than abruptly stopped.
key_points: Video telemetry capturing a typical event with a normal trace is the reference standard.
Eye closure, asynchronous waxing and waning movements and prolonged duration support the diagnosis.
The diagnosis is positive and must be communicated as a real, involuntary and treatable condition.
Cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for functional seizures has the strongest evidence.
Around ten per cent of patients have coexisting epilepsy, so drug withdrawal is planned carefully.
explanation.pearls: Serum prolactin rises to at least twice baseline within 10 to 20 minutes of a generalised tonic clonic seizure and returns to normal by an hour, so a normal level taken in that window supports a functional event, but a normal level is meaningless if the sample is taken later or if the event was focal.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Non epileptic seizures

subtopic_detail: Sudden uncontrollable crying spells months after a stroke in a man whose sleep, appetite and interests are unchanged
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 68-year-old man in a stroke follow up clinic four months after a right hemisphere infarct. His wife reports that he bursts into tears several times a day, often triggered by something trivial like a television advertisement, and that the crying stops as abruptly as it starts.

He is embarrassed by it and says he does not feel sad when it happens. He has returned to lawn bowls twice a week and enjoys it, sleeps through the night and eats normally. His wife says his weight has been steady and he has not spoken about wanting to die.

data_table.Examination: Mild residual left sided weakness with independent mobility, speech fluent, euthymic affect between episodes with reactive expression, no psychomotor retardation, mini mental state examination 28 out of 30, no anhedonia elicited on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, sodium 139 mmol/L (135 to 145), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a low dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and explain that it reduces the frequency of the episodes
options.rationale: Preserved mood, sleep, appetite and enjoyment alongside abrupt stereotyped crying that does not match the inner emotional state identifies pseudobulbar affect, which responds to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors at doses lower and with a latency shorter than those needed for depression. Explaining the mechanism to the couple relieves much of the embarrassment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a full antidepressant dose for post stroke depression and review his mood using a structured rating scale in six weeks
options.rationale: Post stroke depression is worth excluding, but it causes sustained low mood with anhedonia and disturbance of sleep and appetite, and this man retains enjoyment of bowls and sleeps and eats normally. Full antidepressant dosing would be the right approach if those features were present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a low dose atypical antipsychotic to reduce the emotional lability and review his response in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics carry a raised risk of stroke and death in older people with cerebrovascular disease and have no evidence base in this condition. They are reserved for psychosis or for severe behavioural disturbance in dementia where other measures have failed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer him for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the depressive cognitions underlying his frequent episodes of crying
options.rationale: There are no depressive cognitions to target, since he does not feel sad during the episodes and his mood is otherwise normal. Psychological therapy is valuable for genuine post stroke depression and for adjustment difficulties after stroke. (Source: RANZCP: Depression in older people)

options.text: Reassure his wife that the crying is a normal grief reaction to his stroke and review him again in the clinic in three months
options.rationale: Adjustment distress after stroke produces sadness that is congruent with the situation and builds and fades gradually, rather than abrupt stereotyped episodes triggered by trivial stimuli. Leaving a treatable and socially disabling symptom untreated for three months is not justified when an effective option exists. (Source: RANZCP: Depression in older people)

explanation.summary: Pseudobulbar affect describes involuntary, stereotyped outbursts of crying or laughing that are disproportionate to, or incongruent with, the person's inner emotional state, and it arises when lesions disconnect cortical and cerebellar inhibition of brainstem centres for emotional expression. It complicates stroke, motor neurone disease, multiple sclerosis, traumatic brain injury and dementia, and is commonly mislabelled as depression because relatives describe frequent crying. The distinguishing features are the abruptness and stereotypy of the episodes, their trivial or absent triggers, the mismatch between the display and the felt emotion, and the preservation of sleep, appetite, interest and mood between episodes. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and tricyclics both reduce episode frequency, typically at lower doses and with a faster onset than in depression, which supports a distinct mechanism. Recognition matters because the symptom is profoundly socially isolating and patients often withdraw from public activities out of embarrassment.
key_points: Episodes are abrupt, stereotyped and incongruent with the person's inner emotional state.
Sleep, appetite, interest and between episode mood are preserved, unlike in depression.
The mechanism is disconnection of cortical inhibition of brainstem emotional expression.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors work at lower doses and faster than in depression.
The symptom is socially disabling and frequently misattributed to post stroke depression.
explanation.pearls: Expect a response to a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor in pseudobulbar affect within one to two weeks rather than the four to six weeks required for depression, so a lack of any change by three weeks should prompt a review of the diagnosis rather than simply waiting longer.

subtopic_detail: Four days of reduced sleep need with overspending and pressured speech six weeks into treatment for a depressive episode
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man who was started on sertraline six weeks ago by his general practitioner for a moderate depressive episode. His partner brought him in today because for the past four days he has been sleeping about three hours a night and waking full of energy.

He has spent 14000 dollars on recording equipment he does not need, is talking so fast that his partner cannot interrupt, and has emailed his manager a plan to restructure the company. He says he has never felt better. His mother was admitted to a psychiatric hospital in her thirties for something his family never discussed.

data_table.Examination: Elevated and expansive mood with pressured speech and flight of ideas, grandiose but not delusional content, no hallucinations, insight absent, orientated with intact attention, no tremor, no clonus and no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60 to 110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the sertraline at the current dose and add a short course of a hypnotic to restore his sleep while his mood is monitored
options.rationale: Continuing the antidepressant leaves the likely driver of the switch in place, and treating only the insomnia addresses a symptom while the manic episode escalates. Hypnotics may be used as an adjunct, but never in place of ceasing the precipitant and starting antimanic treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Halve the sertraline dose, arrange review in two weeks and advise his partner to bring him back sooner if his behaviour worsens
options.rationale: A partial dose reduction with a two week interval underestimates both the speed at which mania escalates and the financial and occupational harm already occurring. Dose reduction with close review is a reasonable approach to mild hypomanic symptoms in a patient with insight and a supportive environment. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Add lithium to the sertraline as an augmentation strategy and arrange measurement of his serum level in one week
options.rationale: Lithium is an effective antimanic agent but works too slowly for an acute episode used alone, and adding it while continuing the antidepressant leaves the precipitant in place. Augmenting an antidepressant with lithium is a strategy for treatment resistant unipolar depression, not for an emergent manic episode. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Cease the sertraline and commence an atypical antipsychotic with antimanic efficacy, arranging urgent specialist psychiatric review
options.rationale: Antidepressant emergent mania is managed by stopping the antidepressant and starting an agent with established antimanic efficacy such as olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone, with urgent review because insight is absent and the financial and occupational risk is active. The family history and the switch itself both point to an underlying bipolar diathesis that changes long term management. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

options.text: Switch him from sertraline to a different class of antidepressant such as mirtazapine and review his sleep and mood in two weeks
options.rationale: Every antidepressant class can precipitate a switch in a person with bipolar diathesis, so exchanging one for another perpetuates the risk rather than removing it. Switching antidepressant class is a strategy for inadequate response or intolerable adverse effects in unipolar depression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Antidepressant emergent mania is one of the clearest signals that an apparently unipolar depressive episode is part of a bipolar illness, and it typically appears within the first weeks to months of starting treatment. Risk factors include a family history of bipolar disorder, early onset depression, psychotic features, a rapid response to antidepressants and previous subthreshold hypomanic periods, and a careful collateral history often uncovers these before the switch occurs. Management requires ceasing the antidepressant and treating the manic episode in its own right with an antipsychotic with antimanic efficacy, lithium or valproate, with the choice shaped by the acuity, the patient's sex and reproductive plans, and any previous response. Reduced need for sleep rather than simple insomnia is the most discriminating single symptom of mania, because the person wakes energised rather than tired. Long term, the diagnosis shifts towards bipolar disorder, mood stabilisation becomes the foundation of treatment and future antidepressant use requires mood stabiliser cover.
key_points: A switch to mania on an antidepressant is a strong marker of underlying bipolar disorder.
Reduced need for sleep with preserved energy discriminates mania from simple insomnia.
Cease the antidepressant rather than reducing it or switching class.
Treat the episode with an agent of established antimanic efficacy and arrange urgent review.
Absent insight with active financial or occupational harm raises the urgency of assessment.
explanation.pearls: Valproate must not be used as the antimanic agent in any person who could become pregnant unless the conditions of a pregnancy prevention program are met, because first trimester exposure carries a roughly 10 per cent risk of major congenital malformation and a 30 to 40 per cent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Severe pain from a fractured tibia in a man maintained on sublingual buprenorphine with naloxone for opioid dependence
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar providing addiction medicine liaison to the orthopaedic ward. A 34-year-old man was admitted overnight with a tibial shaft fracture after falling from a ladder and is awaiting internal fixation this afternoon.

He takes sublingual buprenorphine with naloxone 16 mg daily, dispensed daily at his community pharmacy, and has been abstinent from other opioids for two years. He rates his pain 9 out of 10 despite regular paracetamol, and the orthopaedic intern has telephoned you because he is reluctant to prescribe opioids to a patient on an opioid treatment program.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Distressed by pain with the right leg in a backslab, no sedation with a normal level of alertness, pupils mid position, no withdrawal signs, no track marks, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, urine drug screen positive for buprenorphine only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to his analgesia?

options.text: Withhold all opioid analgesia and manage his pain with regular paracetamol, an anti-inflammatory and a regional nerve block alone
options.rationale: Denying opioids to a patient with a fractured tibia because of a history of dependence is a well described inequity that leaves severe acute pain untreated and destabilises recovery. Non opioid and regional techniques are valuable adjuncts but will not cover the pain of a tibial shaft fracture on their own. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management

options.text: Cease the buprenorphine immediately and transfer him to methadone so that full agonist analgesia can work without receptor competition
options.rationale: Switching maintenance agents during an acute admission is destabilising, takes days to achieve and is unnecessary because effective analgesia is achievable alongside continued buprenorphine. A planned transfer is a decision for his community prescriber in the outpatient setting. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management

options.text: Halve his buprenorphine dose today so that receptor occupancy falls and any full agonist opioid given afterwards becomes more effective
options.rationale: Reducing the maintenance dose risks precipitating withdrawal, which worsens pain perception, and the analgesic benefit does not offset that harm. Dose reduction is considered only in complex cases in discussion with an addiction medicine specialist and a pain service. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management

options.text: Continue his usual buprenorphine dose and add titrated short-acting full agonist opioid analgesia with multimodal and regional adjuncts
options.rationale: Continuing maintenance buprenorphine and adding a titrated full agonist alongside paracetamol, an anti-inflammatory and regional techniques is the Australian standard, and higher than usual full agonist doses are often required because buprenorphine occupies a high proportion of receptors. Stopping the maintenance dose is what causes problems, not continuing it. (Source: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management

options.text: Prescribe regular tramadol as the sole opioid agent because its partial mechanism is considered safer in a person with opioid dependence
options.rationale: Tramadol is a weak opioid with an unreliable analgesic effect that depends on cytochrome P450 2D6 metabolism, and it adds a seizure and serotonin toxicity risk without providing adequate analgesia for a long bone fracture. Choosing it out of caution provides the appearance of treatment rather than treatment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Patients maintained on buprenorphine frequently receive inadequate analgesia after injury or surgery because clinicians fear precipitating relapse, causing respiratory depression or interfering with the treatment program, and each of those fears is largely unfounded. Buprenorphine is a high affinity partial agonist that occupies a large fraction of mu receptors at therapeutic doses, so full agonists still work but often require higher doses and closer titration, and the safest course is to continue the maintenance dose rather than to withhold or reduce it. Multimodal analgesia with paracetamol, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory where not contraindicated, regional blockade and ketamine reduces the full agonist requirement substantially. Untreated acute pain is itself a potent trigger for relapse, so effective analgesia is part of addiction treatment rather than a threat to it. The community prescriber and the dispensing pharmacy must be contacted so that the maintenance dose continues accurately and the discharge plan is coordinated.
key_points: Continue the usual maintenance buprenorphine dose through the acute admission.
Full agonist opioids remain effective but often require higher doses and closer titration.
Multimodal and regional techniques substantially reduce the full agonist requirement.
Untreated acute pain is itself a major trigger for relapse.
Contact the community prescriber and pharmacy to coordinate dosing and discharge.
explanation.pearls: Naloxone in the sublingual combination product has negligible bioavailability by that route and exists only to deter injection, so it neither blocks the buprenorphine nor blocks the added full agonist and is not a reason to withhold analgesia.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists: Acute pain management

subtopic_detail: Private disclosure of a son withdrawing money without permission by a woman with intact cognition who asks for secrecy
stem: An 82-year-old woman attends for low mood with her son, who answers most questions. Seen alone, she says he takes money from her account without asking and shouts when she questions it. She is not afraid to go home and asks you to tell no one.

data_table.Examination: Mild reactive low mood; MoCA 27/30; weighs options and communicates a consistent choice; no injuries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Telephone the police today to report the financial abuse she describes
options.rationale: Acting against the expressed wishes of an adult with decision making capacity removes her control at the very moment she has entrusted you with the disclosure, and it frequently ends the therapeutic relationship and her access to help. Police involvement without consent is justified where there is an immediate risk of serious harm or where capacity is impaired. (Source: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse)
source_refs: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse

options.text: Raise the allegation with her son at the end of the consultation
options.rationale: Confronting the alleged perpetrator without her consent breaches confidentiality and can directly escalate the risk to her when they leave together. Any conversation with family occurs only with her agreement and after a safety plan is in place. (Source: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse)
source_refs: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse

options.text: Document, assess her safety and capacity, and refer to advocacy with consent
options.rationale: She has intact capacity, is not in immediate danger, and is entitled to decide what happens next, so the task is careful documentation, an explicit safety assessment, information about the national elder abuse helpline and advocacy services, and a follow up appointment that keeps the door open. Most older people disclose gradually, and maintaining the relationship is what eventually enables action. (Source: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse)
source_refs: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse

options.text: Apply to the civil and administrative tribunal for a financial management order
options.rationale: A financial management order removes a person's legal right to manage her own affairs and is available only where capacity to make financial decisions is impaired, which is not the case here. Her capacity is intact and the appropriate protective instrument is her own decision making, supported by advice. (Source: Australian Law Reform Commission: Elder abuse report)
source_refs: Australian Law Reform Commission: Elder abuse report

options.text: Accept her request for secrecy and treat the low mood with medication
options.rationale: Respecting her wishes does not mean doing nothing, because documentation, safety assessment and offering information all sit within her consent and are what make later action possible. Treating the mood symptom alone medicalises a situation whose cause is the abuse itself. (Source: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse)
source_refs: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse

explanation.summary: Elder abuse affects around one in six older Australians living in the community, with financial and psychological abuse the commonest forms and adult children the commonest perpetrators. Disclosure is often partial and hedged with requests for secrecy, driven by shame, fear of losing contact with family and fear of being moved into residential care, and how the clinician responds to that first disclosure largely determines whether the person ever discloses again. The governing principle is that an adult with decision making capacity has the right to make choices that others consider unwise, so the clinician's role is to assess capacity and immediate safety, document carefully and contemporaneously, offer information and referral, and arrange review. Seeing the person alone is essential and should be routine rather than exceptional, since a controlling relative who answers all questions is itself a warning sign. Overriding the person's wishes is reserved for impaired capacity or a serious and immediate risk of harm, and mandatory reporting obligations differ between jurisdictions and in residential aged care.
key_points: Financial abuse by an adult child is the commonest pattern of elder abuse in Australia.
Always interview the older person alone, particularly when a relative answers for them.
An adult with capacity has the right to decline intervention, including reporting.
Document contemporaneously, assess safety and capacity, and offer advocacy and helpline contacts.
Override the person's wishes only for impaired capacity or immediate serious risk.
explanation.pearls: An enduring power of attorney executed while the person had capacity does not entitle the attorney to use the money for their own benefit, and a relative who describes withdrawals as an early inheritance is describing a breach of fiduciary duty that the state tribunal can review and reverse.

sources.label: Australian Institute of Family Studies: Elder abuse
Australian Law Reform Commission: Elder abuse report

subtopic_detail: Foster child who does not seek comfort from carers but plays reciprocally with peers and uses imaginative play
stem: A 6-year-old boy has lived with the same foster carers since age three, after removal for severe neglect. His carer says he does not come to her when hurt or frightened, accepts comfort stiffly, seems flat and rarely shows pleasure at home. His teacher says he plays chasing games with two friends and spent last week running an elaborate pretend restaurant.

data_table.Examination: Good social reciprocity and spontaneous imaginative play in the interview, no overfamiliarity with strangers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for an autism spectrum assessment as the first step
options.rationale: Autism is the differential that matters most here, but it is argued against by his reciprocal peer play, spontaneous imaginative play, age-appropriate language and absence of restricted interests or sensory differences. Assessment would be the priority if the social difficulty extended across all relationships rather than being confined to attachment figures. (Source: RANZCP: Attachment disorders in children)

options.text: Refer the child and carer for attachment focused dyadic therapy
options.rationale: Persistent failure to seek or respond to comfort with limited positive affect in a child with a history of neglect, in the presence of normal peer social functioning, is reactive attachment disorder, and the treatment is a dyadic intervention that works with the child and carer together while supporting placement stability. No medication treats the disorder itself. (Source: RANZCP: Attachment disorders in children)

options.text: Commence low dose risperidone for his flat affect and withdrawal
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have no role in attachment disorders and carry metabolic and extrapyramidal risks that are particularly undesirable in a young child. Their use in this age group is limited to severe aggression or irritability in specific neurodevelopmental contexts after psychosocial measures have failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for individual play therapy without carer involvement
options.rationale: The disorder resides in the relationship rather than in the child alone, so an intervention that deliberately excludes the carer cannot address it and forgoes the mechanism of change. Individual therapy has a place for specific trauma symptoms alongside, not instead of, dyadic work. (Source: RANZCP: Attachment disorders in children)

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for his flat affect
options.rationale: The restricted positive affect here is a feature of the attachment disorder rather than a depressive episode, and there is no pervasive low mood, sleep or appetite disturbance to support antidepressant treatment. An antidepressant would be considered if a clear comorbid depressive disorder emerged. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Reactive attachment disorder arises when a young child experiences grossly insufficient care, such as severe neglect or repeated changes of primary caregiver, before the capacity for selective attachment has formed. The child shows a consistent pattern of not seeking and not responding to comfort from caregivers, together with limited positive affect and episodes of unexplained irritability, sadness or fearfulness even during non threatening interactions with the carer. It must be distinguished from autism spectrum disorder, where the social communication difficulty is pervasive across all relationships and is accompanied by restricted interests, repetitive behaviours and often language difference, none of which fit a child who plays imaginatively and reciprocally with peers. Its counterpart, disinhibited social engagement disorder, produces the opposite presentation of overfamiliarity with unfamiliar adults and persists even after placement improves. Treatment is psychosocial and focuses on the caregiving relationship, and placement stability is the strongest determinant of outcome, so supporting the foster carer is a therapeutic act in itself.
key_points: Reactive attachment disorder requires a history of grossly insufficient early care.
The child fails to seek or respond to comfort and shows limited positive affect with carers.
Normal reciprocal peer play and imaginative play argue strongly against autism.
Treatment is dyadic and psychosocial, and no medication treats the disorder itself.
Placement stability is the strongest single determinant of long term outcome.
explanation.pearls: Disinhibited social engagement disorder is the one attachment presentation that persists after the caregiving environment improves, so a child who continues to wander off with unfamiliar adults years into a stable placement needs ongoing supervision planning rather than reassurance that the placement has fixed the problem.

subtopic_detail: Eighteen months of aggression, fire setting and cruelty to a pet in a boy who concentrates well in class
stem: A 9-year-old boy is referred after a third school suspension this year. Over 18 months he has twice started fires in the shed, hit smaller children, and his mother found the family cat with its whiskers cut off. He says flatly that he does not care whether the children were hurt.

data_table.School: Sits still, attends a 40 minute lesson, completes written work; aggression is planned
data_table.Examination: Restricted affect, no remorse, no psychotic or depressive symptoms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Commence methylphenidate and titrate over four weeks with teacher ratings
options.rationale: Stimulant treatment is effective for aggression that is driven by impulsivity in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, but his attention ratings are normal, he sustains attention through a full lesson and the aggression is planned rather than impulsive. Treating conduct problems with stimulants in the absence of the disorder does not work. (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Commence low dose risperidone to reduce his aggression while awaiting therapy
options.rationale: Risperidone reduces aggression modestly but at the cost of substantial weight gain, metabolic disturbance and hyperprolactinaemia in a growing child, and it does not address the parenting and family factors that maintain the behaviour. It is reserved for severe aggression that persists despite an adequate trial of psychosocial treatment. (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Refer his mother to structured parent management training with a school plan
options.rationale: Structured parent management training combined with school liaison has the strongest evidence of any intervention for conduct disorder in this age group and directly addresses the collapse of consistent limit setting that his mother describes. It remains first line even when callous and unemotional traits are present, although the response is somewhat smaller. (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Refer him for individual anger management counselling for twelve sessions
options.rationale: Individual work with the child alone has a markedly weaker evidence base than family based treatment at this age, and anger management specifically targets impulsive rage rather than the planned instrumental aggression described here. Individual cognitive work has more to offer adolescents than primary school-aged children. (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents

options.text: Notify child protection because cruelty to animals indicates maltreatment
options.rationale: Cruelty to animals is a symptom of conduct disorder as well as a possible marker of maltreatment, and there are no injuries, no disclosure and no other indicators of harm in this assessment. A notification is required where there is a reasonable belief that the child is at risk of significant harm. (Source: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents)
source_refs: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents
