explanation.summary: Conduct disorder is defined by a repetitive and persistent pattern of behaviour that violates the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate social norms, spanning aggression to people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule violations. Distinguishing it from attention deficit hyperactivity disorder matters because the two frequently coexist and because aggression that is impulsive and driven by inattention responds to stimulants, whereas planned instrumental aggression in a child with normal attention does not. The specifier of limited prosocial emotions, sometimes described as callous and unemotional traits, identifies a subgroup with lack of remorse, shallow affect and indifference to performance, who have a worse trajectory and a somewhat reduced response to standard treatment but who still improve with it. Parent management training remains first line across the age range, with multisystemic therapy and functional family therapy used for adolescents with more entrenched difficulties. Medication is adjunctive and targets comorbidity or severe residual aggression rather than the disorder itself.
key_points: Planned instrumental aggression with normal attention ratings argues against attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
Parent management training with school liaison is first line and has the strongest evidence.
Limited prosocial emotions predict a worse trajectory but do not change the first line treatment.
Antipsychotics are adjunctive and reserved for severe aggression after psychosocial treatment fails.
Always screen for maltreatment, learning difficulty and substance use as maintaining factors.
explanation.pearls: Screen explicitly for a specific learning disorder in every child presenting with conduct problems, because undetected reading difficulty is present in around a third and the daily experience of failing in class is a powerful maintaining factor that no parenting program can undo on its own.

sources.label: RANZCP: Conduct disorder in children and adolescents
NICE: Antisocial behaviour and conduct disorders in children

subtopic_detail: New dyspepsia in an older man taking an anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation who has added an antidepressant and a self bought analgesic
stem: A 72-year-old man is reviewed six weeks after starting sertraline for depression, with his mood improved. For three weeks he has taken supermarket ibuprofen twice daily for knee pain, and for the past week has had burning epigastric discomfort after meals. He takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation, and has had no melaena or haematemesis.

data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness, no guarding, conjunctivae not pale
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 139 g/L (130 to 180), ferritin 96 micrograms/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the apixaban and substitute aspirin, continuing the other two medicines
options.rationale: Aspirin is inferior to a direct oral anticoagulant for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation and still carries gastrointestinal bleeding risk, so this trades a large stroke risk for a small change in bleeding risk. The anticoagulant is the one agent of the three with a clear mortality benefit that should be preserved. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Atrial fibrillation guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Atrial fibrillation guidelines

options.text: Cease the ibuprofen, review his knee pain with a safer analgesic and reassess
options.rationale: The non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug is the newest, most dispensable and most ulcerogenic element of a triple combination in which each agent independently raises gastrointestinal bleeding risk, and its removal addresses both the symptom and the risk. Paracetamol, topical therapy and exercise based management can cover the knee without the same hazard. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease the sertraline and substitute a different antidepressant class
options.rationale: Stopping an antidepressant that is working risks relapse of a depressive episode in an older man, and the serotonin reuptake inhibitor contributes far less to the bleeding risk than the non-steroidal drug does. Substituting the antidepressant would become reasonable if bleeding recurred after the analgesic had already been removed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Add a proton pump inhibitor and continue all three medicines
options.rationale: Gastroprotection reduces but does not abolish the bleeding risk of the combination, and it does nothing about the antiplatelet effect of the non-steroidal drug on the whole gastrointestinal tract below the stomach. Adding a proton pump inhibitor is the right move when the non-steroidal drug genuinely cannot be stopped. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Peptic ulcer disease)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Peptic ulcer disease

options.text: Switch the apixaban to warfarin with monitoring and continue the other two
options.rationale: Warfarin carries a higher rate of intracranial and overall major bleeding than apixaban in atrial fibrillation, so the switch increases rather than reduces harm. Warfarin remains preferred for mechanical heart valves and severe renal impairment, not for avoiding gastrointestinal bleeding. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Atrial fibrillation guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Atrial fibrillation guidelines

explanation.summary: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors deplete platelet serotonin, which is required for normal platelet aggregation, and so raise the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding by roughly one and a half times on their own. That modest effect becomes clinically important when it is combined with other agents acting on the same endpoint, and the combination of an anticoagulant, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug and a serotonergic antidepressant is one of the highest risk prescribing triads in general practice. The clinical skill is deciding which agent to remove: the anticoagulant carries a mortality benefit that should almost never be sacrificed, the antidepressant is treating an active illness and is working, and the non-steroidal drug is both the largest contributor to ulcer risk and the one with a ready alternative. Over the counter purchase is easily missed because patients do not consider supermarket analgesics to be medication and do not mention them unless asked directly. New dyspepsia in this setting is a warning shot that should prompt action before an overt bleed occurs.
key_points: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors impair platelet aggregation by depleting platelet serotonin.
Anticoagulant plus non-steroidal drug plus serotonergic antidepressant is a high risk triad.
Ask specifically about over the counter analgesics, which patients rarely volunteer.
Remove the non-steroidal drug first, since it carries the greatest ulcer risk and has alternatives.
Gastroprotection is for when the non-steroidal drug genuinely cannot be stopped.
explanation.pearls: If a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug is unavoidable in a patient on an anticoagulant, a proton pump inhibitor halves the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding but offers no protection against small bowel or colonic bleeding, which accounts for a substantial share of the excess events in this combination.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Atrial fibrillation guidelines
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Peptic ulcer disease

subtopic_detail: Choosing an antipsychotic for a man on high dose opioid substitution whose corrected QT interval is already 480 milliseconds
stem: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia, stable off antipsychotics for two years, has relapsed over the past month with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. He has taken methadone 120 mg daily for eight years and is abstinent from other drugs. He has no cardiac symptoms and no family history of sudden death.

data_table.Investigations: Corrected QT interval 480 ms, potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.7 to 1.1), corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the methadone dose over a week before starting any antipsychotic
options.rationale: Halving a long standing methadone dose precipitates withdrawal and greatly raises the risk of relapse to illicit opioid use and overdose, and it delays treatment of an acute psychotic episode. Gradual dose reduction in discussion with the opioid treatment prescriber is considered when the interval exceeds 500 milliseconds or after an arrhythmic event. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence intramuscular haloperidol and repeat the electrocardiogram afterwards
options.rationale: Haloperidol given parenterally carries the highest risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes of the commonly used antipsychotics, which is precisely the wrong property here. Parenteral haloperidol is reserved for acute behavioural emergencies in patients without a prolonged interval and with cardiac monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Correct his potassium and magnesium, then commence aripiprazole
options.rationale: Hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia are modifiable contributors to QT prolongation and should be corrected first, and aripiprazole has among the least effect on cardiac repolarisation of the available antipsychotics, making it the rational choice alongside high dose methadone. Repeating the electrocardiogram after establishing the dose confirms that the interval has not worsened. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence high dose quetiapine titrated rapidly, with weekly electrocardiograms
options.rationale: Quetiapine prolongs the QT interval in a dose-dependent way and rapid titration to a high dose in a man already at 480 milliseconds adds avoidable risk. Quetiapine is a reasonable choice in patients without baseline QT prolongation or concurrent QT prolonging drugs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Withhold antipsychotics and offer psychological therapy until the interval falls
options.rationale: Leaving an acute psychotic relapse untreated carries substantial risk to the patient and prolongs the duration of untreated psychosis, which worsens long term outcome. Psychological therapy is a valuable adjunct but is not a substitute for antipsychotic treatment in an acute relapse. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders)

explanation.summary: Methadone blocks the rapid delayed rectifier potassium current in a dose-dependent way and is the main reason that people on opioid substitution therapy carry an elevated baseline corrected QT interval, with the risk rising appreciably above doses of around 100 mg daily. When an antipsychotic is needed in this population the task is to add as little further repolarisation delay as possible while treating the psychosis effectively. Aripiprazole, and to a lesser extent olanzapine and lurasidone, have minimal effect on the QT interval, whereas haloperidol given parenterally, high dose quetiapine, ziprasidone and pimozide are the agents to avoid. Electrolyte disturbance is the most easily reversible contributor and should always be corrected, since hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia compound any drug effect. Thresholds worth knowing are a corrected interval above 500 milliseconds or an increase of more than 60 milliseconds from baseline, either of which demands reassessment of every contributing drug.
key_points: Methadone prolongs the QT interval in a dose-dependent manner, particularly above 100 mg daily.
Correct hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia before attributing the interval to drugs alone.
Aripiprazole has among the least effect on cardiac repolarisation of available antipsychotics.
Parenteral haloperidol, high dose quetiapine and ziprasidone should be avoided in this setting.
An interval above 500 milliseconds or a rise of more than 60 milliseconds demands drug review.
explanation.pearls: Check for a cytochrome P450 3A4 inhibitor whenever the corrected QT interval rises unexpectedly in a patient on methadone, because agents such as fluconazole, clarithromycin and some antiretrovirals raise methadone concentrations substantially and the interval falls again when the interacting drug is stopped.

subtopic_detail: Seeing people in the house three weeks after an increase in a dopamine agonist in a man with established Parkinson disease
stem: A 76-year-old man with nine years of Parkinson disease sees people standing in the hallway in the evenings. He describes them clearly, knows they are not real and is not frightened. His dopamine agonist dose was increased three weeks ago. There has been no fever, urinary symptom, fall or daytime drowsiness.

data_table.Examination: Oriented with sustained attention, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 25 of 30, unchanged from eight months ago
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, urine microscopy no organisms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Commence low dose risperidone, titrating to the hallucination frequency
options.rationale: Risperidone has high dopamine D2 receptor affinity and reliably worsens parkinsonian motor symptoms, sometimes severely and irreversibly in this population. It has no place in the treatment of hallucinations in Parkinson disease at any dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reduce and withdraw the dopamine agonist with his neurologist
options.rationale: Hallucinations that begin within weeks of increasing a dopaminergic drug, in a patient with preserved insight, stable cognition and no evidence of infection or metabolic disturbance, are drug induced until proven otherwise, and dopamine agonists are the most hallucinogenic of the Parkinson medications. Reducing the offending drug before adding another is the correct order of operations. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence low dose olanzapine at night and review him in four weeks
options.rationale: Olanzapine worsens motor function in Parkinson disease more than quetiapine or clozapine and is not recommended in this setting. If an antipsychotic is eventually required after dopaminergic reduction, quetiapine or clozapine are the agents with the least motor penalty. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence low dose quetiapine and keep the dopamine agonist unchanged
options.rationale: Quetiapine is the usual antipsychotic choice in Parkinson disease, but adding it while leaving the precipitating drug untouched treats the symptom and accepts the sedation and falls risk unnecessarily. It becomes appropriate when hallucinations persist or distress the patient after dopaminergic reduction has been attempted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor and neuropsychological assessment
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors help hallucinations in Parkinson disease dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies, but his cognitive score is unchanged over eight months and there is no fluctuating attention, so dementia does not explain this. That treatment becomes appropriate once a dementia has been established and the drug review has been completed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Visual hallucinations are common in Parkinson disease and have three broad drivers: dopaminergic medication, an emerging dementia, and an acute precipitant such as infection, metabolic disturbance or a new sedating drug. Sorting between them determines the treatment entirely, so the sequence is to exclude a delirium, review the cognitive trajectory and then scrutinise the medication timeline. Dopamine agonists carry a higher risk of hallucinations and of impulse control disorders than levodopa does, which is why they are the first drug to be reduced when psychotic symptoms emerge, followed if necessary by anticholinergics, amantadine and monoamine oxidase B inhibitors, with levodopa reduced last because motor function depends on it. Only when dopaminergic reduction is insufficient or motor deterioration makes it impossible is an antipsychotic added, and then quetiapine or clozapine are used because all other agents worsen parkinsonism. Preserved insight, as in this man, marks an earlier and more benign stage, whereas the loss of insight signals progression and a worse prognosis.
key_points: Exclude delirium and review the cognitive trajectory before attributing hallucinations to the disease.
Hallucinations starting within weeks of a dopaminergic increase are drug induced until proven otherwise.
Dopamine agonists are more hallucinogenic than levodopa and are reduced first.
Levodopa is reduced last because motor function depends on it.
Only quetiapine and clozapine are acceptable antipsychotics in Parkinson disease.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about new gambling, shopping, eating or sexual behaviour at every review of a patient on a dopamine agonist, because impulse control disorders affect around one in six of those treated, are almost never volunteered spontaneously and resolve when the agonist is withdrawn.

subtopic_detail: Persecutory beliefs emerging on week two of sight saving high dose steroid treatment that cannot be withdrawn
stem: A 71-year-old woman was started on prednisolone 60 mg daily twelve days ago for giant cell arteritis. Over four days she has become convinced that staff are recording her conversations and plotting against her, and last night she tried to leave the ward. The dose cannot be reduced for weeks without risking her sight.

data_table.Examination: Fully orientated, attention sustained, no fluctuation across three nursing shifts, fixed persecutory beliefs
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 8 mg/L (<5), sodium 137 mmol/L, glucose 9.8 mmol/L, brain computed tomography with atrophy only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the prednisolone and treat the arteritis with an anti-inflammatory
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of high dose corticosteroid after twelve days risks both irreversible visual loss from uncontrolled arteritis and adrenal insufficiency, and no anti-inflammatory substitutes for corticosteroid in giant cell arteritis. The steroid is sight saving and must continue while the psychiatric complication is treated alongside it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Giant cell arteritis)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Giant cell arteritis

options.text: Manage as a hyperactive delirium with orientation measures alone
options.rationale: Delirium is the key differential on a medical ward, but her attention is intact, her conscious state has not fluctuated across three shifts and her inflammatory markers and imaging are unremarkable, which is the combination that excludes it. Delirium management would be correct if attention were impaired and the picture waxed and waned. (Source: RANZCP: Delirium in older people)

options.text: Start a low dose atypical antipsychotic and continue the sight saving steroid
options.rationale: Corticosteroid induced psychosis responds well to low dose antipsychotic treatment, so where the steroid cannot be reduced the correct course is to continue it at the dose the underlying disease demands and treat the psychosis concurrently. The antipsychotic is then tapered as the steroid dose falls, rather than continued indefinitely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence lithium with level monitoring to prevent further disturbance
options.rationale: Lithium has been used prophylactically in patients with recurrent steroid induced mood disturbance requiring repeated courses, but it acts too slowly for an acute psychosis and carries significant toxicity risk in an older woman. It is a consideration for planned future courses, not for the episode in front of you. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Transfer to an acute psychiatric unit for management of the psychosis
options.rationale: Transferring a woman who needs daily titration of sight saving immunosuppression to a unit without that medical capability endangers her vision and fragments her care. Transfer would be appropriate if the psychiatric risk could not be managed on the medical ward once her arteritis was stable. (Source: RANZCP: Delirium in older people)

explanation.summary: Corticosteroid induced psychiatric disturbance is strongly dose dependent, affecting a few per cent of patients below 40 mg of prednisolone daily and close to a fifth of those above 80 mg, and it typically emerges within the first two weeks of treatment. Mood elevation and irritability are the commonest presentations, but frank psychosis with persecutory delusions occurs and is more likely at higher doses and in older patients. The essential differential on a medical ward is delirium, and attention and fluctuation separate them: a steroid psychosis has a clear sensorium and a stable conscious state, whereas delirium impairs attention and waxes and wanes across the day. Management is guided by whether the steroid can be reduced, and where it cannot, as in sight threatening giant cell arteritis, the psychosis is treated concurrently with a low dose antipsychotic that is withdrawn as the steroid is tapered. Prior psychiatric history is a surprisingly weak predictor, so its absence offers no reassurance.
key_points: Risk rises steeply with dose, approaching one in five above 80 mg of prednisolone daily.
Onset is usually within the first two weeks of treatment.
Intact attention with a stable conscious state distinguishes steroid psychosis from delirium.
Where the steroid is sight saving it continues and the psychosis is treated concurrently.
Taper the antipsychotic as the steroid dose falls rather than continuing it indefinitely.
explanation.pearls: An absent psychiatric history gives no protection against steroid induced psychosis, and conversely a past episode does not reliably predict recurrence on a later course, so the practical safeguard is to warn every patient starting more than 40 mg of prednisolone daily and to ask a relative to report behavioural change in the first fortnight.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Giant cell arteritis

subtopic_detail: Registrar colleague smelling of alcohol while rostered to the ward with a slurred handover witnessed by two staff
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an evening shift. During handover a fellow registrar rostered to the ward until midnight smells strongly of alcohol, slurs several words and twice loses his place in the patient list. The nurse in charge quietly tells you she noticed the same thing last Friday.

When you speak to him privately he becomes upset, says he had two drinks at lunch because his marriage has broken down, insists he is fine to work and begs you not to say anything. He is due to review two involuntary patients tonight and holds the ward pager.

data_table.Examination: Slurred speech with an unsteady gait on walking to the office, alcohol on the breath, tearful and reactive affect, no suicidal ideation elicited on direct questioning, orientated with no gross cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Accept his reassurance, offer to review any complex patients with him tonight and encourage him to seek help from his general practitioner
options.rationale: Supervising a colleague who is intoxicated does not make the care safe, and his self assessment of fitness is itself impaired by the alcohol. Informal support is appropriate for a colleague who is struggling but sober and safe to practise. (Source: Ahpra: Mandatory notifications guidelines)

options.text: Advise him to complete this shift and then take personal leave, and agree that nothing needs to be reported if he starts treatment this week
options.rationale: Allowing him to complete a shift while intoxicated leaves patients exposed for the very hours in which the risk is highest, and a promise of confidentiality is one you cannot keep once the mandatory threshold is met. Supporting a colleague into treatment is a parallel obligation, not an alternative to protecting patients. (Source: Ahpra: Mandatory notifications guidelines)

options.text: Ask the nurse in charge to observe him for the remainder of the shift and document any further concerns for discussion at the next team meeting
options.rationale: Delegating observation to a nurse places the responsibility on a colleague with less authority to act and leaves the patients at risk during the observation period. Documentation and escalation at a later meeting is appropriate for a pattern of performance concerns, not for present intoxication. (Source: Ahpra: Mandatory notifications guidelines)

options.text: Remove him from clinical duties now by escalating to the on call consultant, arrange his safe transport home and make a mandatory notification
options.rationale: Practising while intoxicated by alcohol is one of the four categories of notifiable conduct under the national law, and the obligation arises from a reasonable belief rather than from proof, so the notification is mandatory and not discretionary. Removing him from duty and arranging safe transport protects both the patients and the colleague. (Source: Ahpra: Mandatory notifications guidelines)

options.text: Arrange an immediate breath alcohol test and take no further action if the reading falls below the legal limit for driving a motor vehicle
options.rationale: There is no legal blood alcohol threshold for clinical practice and the driving limit has no bearing on fitness to make clinical decisions. Objective testing may form part of a health program later, but it does not replace the judgement that a doctor is impaired now. (Source: Ahpra: Mandatory notifications guidelines)

explanation.summary: Under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law, registered practitioners must make a mandatory notification when they form a reasonable belief that another practitioner has engaged in notifiable conduct, which comprises practising while intoxicated by alcohol or drugs, engaging in sexual misconduct in connection with practice, placing the public at risk of substantial harm because of an impairment, or placing the public at risk because of a significant departure from accepted professional standards. The threshold is a reasonable belief rather than proof, and the obligation cannot be discharged by a promise of confidentiality or by agreeing to supervise the colleague. Immediate patient safety comes first, which means removing the practitioner from clinical duties through the on call consultant or hospital executive and arranging safe transport home rather than allowing them to drive. Compassion and regulation are not in conflict here, since notification opens access to structured health programs with monitored return to work pathways, and outcomes for doctors with substance use disorders who enter such programs are good. Western Australia has different arrangements for treating practitioners, and practitioners seeking their own treatment are protected in most jurisdictions to encourage help seeking.
key_points: Practising while intoxicated by alcohol is notifiable conduct under the national law.
The threshold is a reasonable belief, not proof, and the obligation is mandatory.
Immediate action is removal from clinical duties and arranging safe transport home.
A promise of confidentiality cannot override a mandatory notification obligation.
Notification opens access to health programs with good return to work outcomes.
explanation.pearls: Treating practitioners in most Australian jurisdictions are exempt from mandatory notification when a doctor patient seeks treatment for an impairment and is not currently placing the public at substantial risk, an exemption designed specifically so that unwell doctors present for care rather than concealing illness.

sources.label: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice code of conduct

subtopic_detail: Episodes labelled as panic attacks that bring pallor and severe hypertension and that worsened after an antidepressant was started
stem: A 42-year-old woman is referred with treatment resistant panic disorder. For eighteen months she has had twenty minute episodes of palpitations, headache and drenching sweats. Her husband says she goes chalk white during them. They come without warning, including from sleep, and she avoids nothing. Venlafaxine started eight weeks ago has made them worse. She has lost 6 kg in a year.

data_table.Examination: Pale with cool peripheries, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function normal, fasting glucose 6.9 mmol/L, left ventricular hypertrophy on electrocardiogram

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the venlafaxine and add a short benzodiazepine course
options.rationale: Serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors block noradrenaline reuptake and can provoke hypertensive crises where catecholamine secreting tumours are present, which is the most plausible explanation for her symptoms worsening after it was started. Dose escalation would be the correct response to a partial response in genuine panic disorder with a normal blood pressure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure plasma free metanephrines, withhold venlafaxine, refer to endocrinology
options.rationale: Paroxysmal headache, palpitations and sweating with pallor rather than flushing, unprovoked nocturnal attacks, sustained hypertension with end-organ change, weight loss and deterioration after a noradrenergic drug together point to a catecholamine secreting tumour rather than panic disorder. Plasma free metanephrines are the most sensitive screening test and the interfering drug should be withdrawn. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence a non selective beta blocker for the cardiovascular symptoms
options.rationale: Unopposed beta blockade in the presence of a catecholamine secreting tumour removes beta mediated vasodilation and leaves alpha mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. Beta blockade is added only after adequate alpha blockade has been established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer for further psychological therapy and add an antihypertensive
options.rationale: Treating the blood pressure as an incidental comorbidity and the episodes as psychological misses the single diagnosis that unifies both, and two failed adequate therapy trials should prompt review of the diagnosis rather than a third attempt. A further therapy course would be reasonable if the somatic workup were genuinely unremarkable. (Source: RANZCP: Anxiety disorders)

options.text: Arrange abdominal computed tomography before any biochemical testing
options.rationale: Imaging before biochemistry inverts the diagnostic sequence and risks finding an incidentaloma that is present in several per cent of adults and is unrelated to her symptoms. Imaging follows biochemical confirmation and is then directed at localising a tumour already proven to be secreting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma are rare but are disproportionately likely to be referred to psychiatry, because the paroxysmal adrenergic symptoms they produce are almost indistinguishable from panic attacks and patients are frequently labelled with an anxiety disorder for years. Several features separate them: attacks in panic disorder are typically situationally cued or arise in a context of anticipatory anxiety and avoidance, whereas catecholamine driven attacks are truly unprovoked, often wake the patient from sleep, and produce pallor rather than flushing. Sustained hypertension between attacks with evidence of end-organ damage, unexplained weight loss and impaired glucose tolerance from catecholamine mediated insulin suppression all point away from a primary anxiety disorder. Drugs that block noradrenaline reuptake, including serotonin noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors and tricyclics, can precipitate crises and also interfere with the assay, so they are withdrawn before testing where it is safe to do so. Plasma free metanephrines drawn supine after rest are the most sensitive screen, and imaging follows biochemical confirmation, with alpha blockade preceding any beta blockade and preceding surgery.
key_points: Truly unprovoked attacks that wake the patient from sleep argue against panic disorder.
Pallor during attacks rather than flushing is an important discriminating sign.
Sustained hypertension with end-organ change, weight loss and hyperglycaemia support a secreting tumour.
Noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors can precipitate crises and interfere with the assay.
Biochemistry precedes imaging, and alpha blockade always precedes beta blockade.
explanation.pearls: Around 40 per cent of phaeochromocytomas and paragangliomas carry a germline mutation, in genes including succinate dehydrogenase subunits, VHL, RET and NF1, so every confirmed case is referred for genetic counselling regardless of age or family history.

subtopic_detail: Adult requesting assessment for lifelong inattention with no documented childhood history
stem: A 27-year-old software tester describes losing track of tasks, missing deadlines and rereading paragraphs for as long as he can remember. A colleague taking stimulant medication suggested the diagnosis. He drinks alcohol at weekends only and sleeps seven hours.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative, frustrated but reactive affect, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Online self rating scale in the likely range; full blood count and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for neuropsychological testing to establish the diagnosis
options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing describes cognitive strengths and weaknesses but neither confirms nor excludes the condition, since many people with the disorder perform normally in a quiet one to one setting. It is useful when a learning disorder is suspected alongside. (Source: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline

options.text: Accept the rating scale, diagnose him today and refer for skills training
options.rationale: Rating scales have poor specificity in adults because anxiety, depression, sleep disorders and substance use all generate similar scores. Making the diagnosis on a screening instrument risks both mislabelling and missing the treatable condition actually present. (Source: RACGP: Adult ADHD assessment)

options.text: Treat as anxiety with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
options.rationale: There is no described anxiety syndrome here, and empirical antidepressant treatment would delay assessment while attributing symptoms to a disorder he has not been shown to have. Comorbid anxiety is common but is identified rather than assumed. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance)

options.text: Seek collateral evidence of childhood symptoms before diagnostic assessment
options.rationale: Diagnosis requires several symptoms to have been present before the age of twelve and to have caused impairment in more than one setting, so retrospective corroboration is a core part of the assessment rather than an optional extra. Adult recall alone is unreliable and self rating scales are screening tools. (Source: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline

options.text: Trial methylphenidate and use the response to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Stimulants improve attention in people without the disorder, so a symptomatic response has no diagnostic value. Prescribing is also restricted in Australian jurisdictions to authorised prescribers under state stimulant regulations. (Source: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is a valid and treatable diagnosis, but it is defined by symptoms beginning in childhood, so establishing the developmental history is central to assessment rather than a formality. Australian guidance expects several inattentive or hyperactive impulsive symptoms to have been present before the age of twelve, impairment in at least two settings, and exclusion of other explanations including sleep disorder, substance use, mood and anxiety disorders and thyroid disease. Self rating scales such as the adult self report scale are screening instruments with limited specificity, and neuropsychological testing cannot establish or exclude the diagnosis. Collateral information from school reports, parents or a long standing partner materially changes diagnostic accuracy and is the step most often skipped. Stimulant prescribing is regulated at state level in Australia, generally requiring an authorised prescriber, and driving advice depends on whether symptoms or treatment affect safe vehicle control rather than on the diagnostic label alone.
key_points: Symptoms must date from before the age of twelve and impair function in two or more settings.
Collateral history and school reports materially improve diagnostic accuracy.
Self rating scales screen rather than diagnose, with poor specificity in adults.
Neuropsychological testing cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis.
Stimulant prescribing in Australia is restricted to authorised prescribers under state regulation.
explanation.pearls: Screen deliberately for obstructive sleep apnoea and for stimulant misuse before referral, because untreated sleep fragmentation reproduces the entire inattentive symptom set, and a request framed around a specific drug or a colleague's prescription warrants the same careful history as any other controlled drug request.

sources.label: Australian ADHD Professionals Association: Clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Psychosis persisting for several weeks after the mood episode has resolved
stem: A 23-year-old woman was admitted six weeks ago elated, sleeping two hours nightly and convinced she had been chosen to reform banking. Mood and sleep settled within a fortnight. For the past four weeks, while euthymic, she has believed bank staff speak about her in code and has heard two voices commenting on her actions. She has had two similar admissions, living independently between them.

data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative on each admission

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Delusional disorder, given the systematised belief about bank staff
options.rationale: This diagnosis requires the absence of prominent hallucinations and excludes people who have had full manic episodes, and she has both. Functioning outside the delusional theme is also typically preserved, which does not describe her admissions. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Bipolar affective disorder in remission, with slowly resolving psychosis
options.rationale: Psychotic symptoms in this disorder occur only during mood episodes, so several weeks of active psychosis with a euthymic mood does not fit. The content described is also referential and third person rather than grandiose and mood congruent. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder, given psychosis persisting while mood is normal
options.rationale: The defining feature is a period of two weeks or more of delusions or hallucinations without prominent mood symptoms, in an illness where mood episodes occupy the majority of the total duration. That pattern is exactly what has emerged over the past four weeks. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Schizophrenia, with mood symptoms reactive to the psychotic experiences
options.rationale: Full manic episodes with reduced sleep, overspending and grandiosity are not secondary demoralisation, and her interepisode functioning has been preserved. Prominent mood episodes occupying much of the illness argue against this diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

options.text: Substance induced psychotic disorder from unreported stimulant use
options.rationale: Drug screening has been negative across three separate admissions and the symptoms have persisted far beyond any plausible period of intoxication or withdrawal. Screening cannot exclude every agent, but the longitudinal pattern is against it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder sits between bipolar disorder with psychotic features and schizophrenia, and it is defined longitudinally rather than cross sectionally. The two requirements are a period of at least two weeks of delusions or hallucinations in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, and mood episodes that are present for the majority of the total duration of the illness. If psychosis occurs only within mood episodes, the diagnosis is a mood disorder with psychotic features, while if mood episodes are brief and peripheral to a chronic psychotic illness, the diagnosis is schizophrenia. The distinction matters because it shapes maintenance treatment, with mood stabilisation and antipsychotic therapy usually both required, and because the prognosis lies between those of the two neighbouring diagnoses. Diagnosis often becomes clear only after the mood episode has been treated and the clinician looks at what remains, which is why the longitudinal course must be revisited rather than fixed at admission.
key_points: Two weeks or more of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms is the defining criterion.
Mood episodes must occupy the majority of the total illness duration.
Psychosis confined to mood episodes indicates a mood disorder with psychotic features.
Brief peripheral mood symptoms in chronic psychosis indicate schizophrenia.
The diagnosis is longitudinal and is often clarified after the mood episode resolves.
explanation.pearls: Chart the timeline of mood symptoms against psychotic symptoms on paper with the patient and family, because the diagnosis turns entirely on which symptoms were present when, and reconstructing that sequence from memory in a clinic interview is the commonest reason these three diagnoses are confused.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Return to driving three weeks after a first episode of psychosis while still symptomatic
stem: A 20-year-old apprentice is reviewed three weeks after discharge following a first psychotic episode, treated with risperidone. He has resumed driving to work. He still believes a particular car is following him and feels sedated in the mornings. He holds an unconditional private licence.

data_table.Examination: Alert but slowed, flat mood with reactive affect, persecutory delusion held with moderate conviction, mild bradykinesia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about driving?

options.text: Advise him not to drive now, document this and explain the reporting obligations
options.rationale: Active persecutory beliefs that direct his attention to other vehicles, together with sedation from recent treatment, mean he does not currently meet the medical criteria for an unconditional licence. Explaining the process honestly preserves the therapeutic relationship and supports later return to driving. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)

options.text: Allow private driving if he avoids night driving and long trips
options.rationale: The standards for private vehicles are less stringent than for commercial ones but still require that the condition does not impair the ability to drive safely. Restricting the hours of driving does not address a persecutory belief centred on another vehicle. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)

options.text: Notify the licensing authority immediately without telling him
options.rationale: The ordinary course is to advise the patient of the obligation to report and to document that advice, with direct notification reserved for continued unsafe driving despite counselling, and even then the patient is normally informed. Bypassing the conversation damages engagement in a service he needs. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)

options.text: Reduce the risperidone and let him drive once he feels alert
options.rationale: Sedation is only part of the problem and the persistent delusional belief remains, so dose adjustment alone does not restore fitness. Using his subjective alertness as the test devolves a medical judgement to a symptom he cannot assess objectively. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)

options.text: Tell him the diagnosis permanently disqualifies him from driving
options.rationale: The standards are functional rather than diagnostic, and most people whose symptoms remit and who remain adherent return to driving, often on a conditional licence with periodic review. A permanent disqualification misstates the guidance and removes any incentive to disclose symptoms. (Source: Austroads: Assessing fitness to drive)

explanation.summary: Australian fitness to drive standards are functional, asking whether the condition or its treatment impairs the ability to drive safely rather than turning on the diagnostic label. For psychotic illness the relevant features are active symptoms that could affect judgement or attention, such as persecutory beliefs involving traffic or vehicles, command hallucinations, and sedation or extrapyramidal effects from medication. The treating doctor advises the patient about fitness and about their legal obligation to report a long term condition to the licensing authority, and documents that advice. A conditional licence with periodic medical review is the usual pathway back once symptoms remit and treatment is stable, and most people with a treated psychotic illness do drive. Direct notification by the doctor is a fallback for the patient who continues to drive unsafely despite advice, and jurisdictions differ in whether that reporting is mandatory or discretionary, with the Northern Territory and South Australia having stricter provisions than other states.
key_points: The standards assess function and safety rather than diagnosis.
Active symptoms involving vehicles and treatment related sedation both impair fitness.
The doctor advises, documents and explains the patient's duty to report.
A conditional licence with review is the usual route back to driving.
Direct notification is reserved for continued unsafe driving despite advice.
explanation.pearls: Commercial vehicle standards are substantially stricter than private ones, so an apprentice who later moves into a driving role or acquires a heavy vehicle licence needs reassessment against the commercial criteria rather than carrying his private conditional licence across.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Purging several times weekly at normal body weight with dental erosion in a young adult
stem: A 20-year-old student has made herself vomit after eating for two years, three or four times a week, after episodes of eating far more than she intends. She weighs herself several times daily and judges herself almost entirely on her shape.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg/m2, palatal erosion of the upper incisors, mild parotid enlargement
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily
options.rationale: Lisdexamfetamine is registered for binge eating disorder, which does not involve compensatory purging, and stimulants can worsen restriction and weight preoccupation in this setting. The compensatory behaviour is what separates the two diagnoses. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Dietitian review with self help materials alone, deferring other treatment
options.rationale: Guided self help has a role as a first step in some services but withholding definitive treatment for months in an established two year illness allows the behaviour to entrench further. Dietetic input supports treatment rather than replacing it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and fluoxetine 60 mg daily
options.rationale: Structured psychological therapy targeting the binge and purge cycle is first line, and fluoxetine at this dose is the only antidepressant with established efficacy in reducing binge frequency in this disorder. The higher dose is specific to this indication rather than the usual antidepressant dose. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and sertraline 50 mg daily
options.rationale: Other selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors do not have the evidence base that exists for fluoxetine in this disorder, and a standard antidepressant dose has not been shown to reduce binge frequency. Choosing an alternative agent forfeits the one pharmacological option with good trial support. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

options.text: Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and bupropion 150 mg daily
options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in people who purge because of a markedly increased seizure risk in this population. That contraindication is absolute regardless of how attractive the drug's other properties appear. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Bulimia nervosa involves recurrent binge eating with compensatory behaviours and self evaluation dominated by shape and weight, and unlike anorexia nervosa the weight is usually in the healthy range, which is why the diagnosis is frequently missed for years. Physical clues include erosion of the palatal tooth surfaces, parotid enlargement, calluses on the knuckles and a hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from vomiting, and electrolyte disturbance is the main acute medical risk. Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy is the first line treatment and is available in Australia under an eating disorder treatment plan that funds a substantial number of psychological and dietetic sessions each year. Fluoxetine at sixty milligrams daily is the only medication with a clear evidence base, reducing binge and purge frequency, and the dose required is higher than the usual antidepressant dose. Dental review matters because erosion is irreversible, and patients are advised to rinse with water rather than brushing immediately after vomiting.
key_points: Weight is typically in the healthy range, so the diagnosis rests on behaviour and cognitions.
Vomiting produces hypokalaemia with metabolic alkalosis and irreversible dental erosion.
Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy is first line treatment.
Fluoxetine at sixty milligrams daily is the only well supported medication.
Bupropion is contraindicated because of seizure risk in people who purge.
explanation.pearls: Advise rinsing with water or a fluoride mouthwash rather than brushing after vomiting, because brushing enamel that has just been bathed in gastric acid accelerates the erosion, and arrange an eating disorder treatment plan to fund the sessions rather than a standard mental health plan, which provides too few.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for eating disorders

subtopic_detail: Escalating online gambling losses with borrowing and concealment over twelve months
stem: A 42-year-old man attends at his wife's insistence. Over the past year he has bet on sport through a phone application, staking more to recover losses. He has a loan she does not know about, is restless when he tries to stop and has lied about the money. He feels hopeless about the debt but denies intent to harm himself.

data_table.Examination: Mood low with reactive affect, no psychotic features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer to a financial counsellor and review him in three months
options.rationale: Financial counselling is a valuable component but relieving debt without treating the disorder commonly funds further gambling. The behaviour is not a rational response to money problems and does not resolve when they do. (Source: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling)
source_refs: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review the gambling later
options.rationale: Antidepressants have not been shown to reduce gambling behaviour, and mood symptoms here are closely tied to the losses and concealment. Treating them in isolation leaves the driver of the distress untouched. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance)

options.text: Advise blocking software and deposit limits, and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Access limiting measures help but are readily circumvented and are insufficient alone for a disorder of this severity with borrowing and concealment. Offering only self management also misses the elevated suicide risk. (Source: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling)
source_refs: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling

options.text: Refer for gambling focused cognitive behavioural therapy and assess suicide risk
options.rationale: Structured psychological therapy has the strongest evidence in this disorder, and formal risk assessment is essential because gambling disorder carries one of the highest suicide rates of any addictive disorder, driven by debt and shame. Financial counselling and self exclusion address the immediate access and harm. (Source: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling)
source_refs: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling

options.text: Start naltrexone, referring for psychological therapy only if it fails
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists have modest evidence as an adjunct, particularly with strong urges or comorbid alcohol problems, but they are not first line and do not address the cognitive distortions that drive the chasing of losses. Deferring therapy delays the intervention that works best. (Source: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling)
source_refs: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is classified with the substance related and addictive disorders and shows the same features of tolerance, withdrawal like restlessness, loss of control, chasing losses, concealment and continued use despite harm. Australia has the highest per capita gambling losses in the world and online sports betting has changed the demographic profile toward younger working men, with the phone providing continuous access. Cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the cognitive distortions of gambling, particularly the illusion of control and the belief that losses can be recovered, is the treatment with the best evidence, and free services are available nationally through the gambling help line and state services. Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive, with naltrexone the best studied agent for strong urges, particularly where alcohol problems coexist. Formal suicide risk assessment is mandatory at every review because the suicide rate in this disorder is among the highest in psychiatry, and the acute risk period often follows disclosure of debt to family.
key_points: The disorder is classified with addictive disorders and shows tolerance and loss of control.
Cognitive behavioural therapy targeting gambling specific cognitions is first line.
Naltrexone is an adjunct for strong urges rather than a first line treatment.
Financial counselling and self exclusion address access and harm but do not treat the disorder.
Suicide risk is high and must be assessed formally and repeatedly.
explanation.pearls: Ask directly about gambling in anyone presenting with unexplained debt, relationship breakdown or new low mood in a working age man, because patients almost never volunteer it, and screen the partner for distress too since family members of people with this disorder have markedly raised rates of depression and anxiety.

sources.label: Australian Guideline for Treatment of Problem Gambling

subtopic_detail: Obsessive compulsive symptoms unchanged after six weeks on a low dose serotonergic antidepressant
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 29-year-old teacher six weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg daily for obsessive compulsive disorder. She has intrusive thoughts about contamination and washes her hands until they crack, spending about three hours a day on rituals.

She has taken the tablet every day without missing a dose and reports no adverse effects beyond mild nausea in the first week. She has been on a waiting list for psychological therapy since the last visit and has not yet been seen. She estimates that nothing has changed and asks whether the medication is the wrong one for her.

data_table.Examination: Cracked and erythematous skin over both hands, mood mildly low with reactive affect, obsessions and compulsions described with good insight, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add a regular benzodiazepine to relieve the distress associated with the intrusive thoughts and review her when a therapy appointment becomes available
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not treat this disorder and regular use undermines exposure therapy by suppressing the anxiety that the treatment depends on the patient tolerating. Dependence in a young adult with a chronic disorder is a predictable harm. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose and continue for at least twelve weeks at the higher dose before judging whether this medication has failed her
options.rationale: This disorder responds to higher doses and over a longer period than depression, so six weeks at a starting dose is an incomplete trial rather than a failure. Escalating within the licensed range and waiting the full interval is what the evidence supports. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders

options.text: Switch to a different selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a starting dose and review the response after a further six weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Switching before the first agent has had an adequate dose and duration simply restarts the clock and risks cycling through several drugs at subtherapeutic doses. Switching is reasonable only after a genuinely adequate trial. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders

options.text: Add a low dose antipsychotic as an augmenting agent now and continue the current sertraline dose, reviewing the combination after a further six weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is reserved for people who remain symptomatic after an adequate trial of a serotonergic antidepressant at a high dose, usually with therapy as well. Using it early adds metabolic and movement risk without exhausting simpler options. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders

options.text: Stop the sertraline and rely on exposure and response prevention alone once a place becomes available, reviewing her again when therapy has commenced
options.rationale: Therapy is the treatment of choice and works well, but stopping an incompletely trialled medication while she waits leaves her without any active treatment at three hours of rituals a day. The two treatments are complementary rather than alternatives. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders

explanation.summary: Obsessive compulsive disorder differs from depression in both the dose and the duration of antidepressant treatment required, and this is the single commonest reason treatment is wrongly declared to have failed. Higher doses of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are typically needed, often at the upper end of the licensed range, and response builds over ten to twelve weeks rather than the four to six weeks expected in depression. Exposure and response prevention is the psychological treatment of choice and is at least as effective as medication, with the combination preferred for moderate to severe illness. When a genuinely adequate trial of one agent fails, options include switching to another serotonergic antidepressant, moving to clomipramine, or augmenting with a low dose antipsychotic such as aripiprazole or risperidone. Benzodiazepines have no role, both because they do not treat the disorder and because they blunt the anxiety that exposure therapy requires the patient to experience and tolerate.
key_points: Higher antidepressant doses are needed than for depression.
Allow ten to twelve weeks at an adequate dose before judging response.
Exposure and response prevention is the psychological treatment of choice.
Antipsychotic augmentation follows an adequate failed trial rather than preceding it.
Benzodiazepines do not treat the disorder and interfere with exposure therapy.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about mental compulsions such as silent counting, praying or reviewing, because patients who deny rituals often perform them entirely in their heads, and therapy that targets only the visible handwashing leaves the covert compulsions maintaining the disorder.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Mute immobile inpatient with waxy flexibility refusing food for two days
stem: A 24-year-old man admitted eight days ago with a relapse of schizophrenia had his olanzapine increased four days ago. For two days he has not spoken, sits in the same chair for hours and has eaten nothing. When staff raise his arm it stays where they leave it.

data_table.Examination: Mute with staring, posturing against gravity, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia, palpable bladder
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 U/L (40-320), WCC 8.2 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Stop olanzapine and start bromocriptine with dantrolene for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
options.rationale: He has no fever, no lead-pipe rigidity, no autonomic instability and a normal creatine kinase, so the malignant syndrome is not present. Treating it would expose him to dopaminergic and muscle relaxant effects he does not need. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give a parenteral lorazepam challenge and observe over the following hours
options.rationale: A benzodiazepine challenge is both the first line treatment and a diagnostic manoeuvre, with a substantial proportion of patients showing partial or complete response within hours. Response also guides the ongoing regimen while the underlying illness is treated. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia

options.text: Increase the olanzapine dose further to treat the underlying psychotic relapse
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen this state and raise the risk of progression to a malignant form, and the syndrome emerged after the last dose increase. Escalation is the intervention most likely to convert a treatable syndrome into a life threatening one. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy, withholding other psychotropic medication
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is highly effective and is escalated to when benzodiazepines fail or the malignant form develops, but organising it takes time that a simple challenge does not. Withholding the challenge delays a treatment that may work today. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia

options.text: Start intravenous fluids and nasogastric feeding with no medication change
options.rationale: Supportive care including hydration, prophylaxis against venous thromboembolism and bladder management is necessary but does not treat the syndrome itself. Waiting for spontaneous recovery risks dehydration, pressure injury and thrombosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome rather than a diagnosis and occurs across mood disorders, psychotic disorders and general medical conditions, with mood disorders being the commonest underlying cause overall. Recognition depends on the motor and behavioural signs, including mutism, stupor, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia, echopraxia and stereotypy, and structured instruments such as the Bush Francis scale improve detection. First line treatment is a benzodiazepine challenge, usually lorazepam given parenterally, which produces improvement within hours in a large proportion of cases and serves as a diagnostic test, and doses well above those used for anxiety are often needed without causing sedation. Electroconvulsive therapy is the definitive treatment when benzodiazepines fail or when the malignant form develops with fever and autonomic instability. Antipsychotics may worsen catatonia and can precipitate the malignant form, so continuing to escalate them is the central error to avoid, and supportive care covering hydration, nutrition, pressure areas and thromboprophylaxis runs alongside specific treatment.
key_points: Catatonia is a syndrome with many underlying causes, most often a mood disorder.
A parenteral benzodiazepine challenge is both first line treatment and a diagnostic test.
Doses higher than usual anxiolytic doses are frequently required without causing sedation.
Antipsychotic escalation may worsen the state and risks the malignant form.
Electroconvulsive therapy is definitive when benzodiazepines fail or malignant features appear.
explanation.pearls: Look for urinary retention, deep vein thrombosis and pressure injury at every review of an immobile catatonic patient, because these complications cause much of the mortality attributed to the syndrome and develop silently in someone who cannot report symptoms.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance on catatonia

subtopic_detail: Refusal of all food because of a delusion that it has been poisoned
stem: A 51-year-old man with schizophrenia stopped his depot antipsychotic six months ago. At a home visit he has eaten almost nothing for five days, certain that all food and water in the house is contaminated by a neighbour who wants him dead. He refuses hospital, saying nothing is wrong with him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 /min, BP 102/64 mmHg with a postural fall
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, weight down 6 kg in four months; oriented, no insight into the risk

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Assess his capacity and arrange involuntary assessment under the Mental Health Act
options.rationale: A belief that cannot be reasoned with prevents him from weighing the information relevant to the decision, so the refusal is not a capable one, and there is a serious risk to his health from the untreated mental illness. Involuntary assessment is the lawful pathway to treat that risk. (Source: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance

options.text: Accept his refusal and arrange community mental health follow up this week
options.rationale: Orientation and coherent speech are not the same as capacity, and he cannot use or weigh information because the delusion determines the conclusion. Deferring while he continues not to eat accepts a preventable deterioration. (Source: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance

options.text: Apply to the guardianship tribunal to consent to admission for him
options.rationale: Guardianship processes operate over days to weeks and are designed for enduring decisions rather than acute psychiatric emergencies. Mental health legislation exists precisely to allow timely assessment in this situation. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance)

options.text: Restart his depot antipsychotic today with his sister's consent
options.rationale: A relative cannot consent for an adult in this situation, and treating without lawful authority is an assault however well intentioned. Depot medication also takes weeks to act while he remains unable to eat. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidance)

options.text: Admit to a medical ward for rehydration, deferring psychiatric assessment
options.rationale: Physical stabilisation is needed but as part of the same admission rather than instead of psychiatric assessment, and a medical ward cannot lawfully detain him if he chooses to leave. The mental illness is what is driving the starvation. (Source: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance)
source_refs: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance

explanation.summary: Capacity is decision specific and is assessed against the ability to understand relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it in the decision and communicate a choice. A patient can be fully oriented and articulate while lacking capacity, because a fixed delusional belief removes the ability to weigh information that contradicts it, and this is the pattern in delusional food refusal. Australian mental health legislation differs in detail between states and territories but shares the core criteria of a mental illness, a serious risk to the health or safety of the person or others, and the absence of a less restrictive option that is reasonably available. Serious risk includes risk from self neglect and starvation, not only risk from self-harm or violence. The lawful pathway is assessment under the relevant act, arranged through the local mental health service or emergency department, with police or ambulance assistance for transport where required, and physical stabilisation proceeds alongside rather than instead of psychiatric care.
key_points: Capacity is decision specific and can be absent in an oriented, coherent patient.
A fixed delusion removes the ability to use and weigh relevant information.
Serious risk to health from self neglect satisfies the criteria for involuntary assessment.
Relatives cannot consent to treatment for an adult in this situation.
Guardianship processes are too slow for an acute psychiatric emergency.
explanation.pearls: Document the specific words the patient uses about the risk, because a record showing that he cannot weigh the consequences of not eating is what supports the lawfulness of the decision on later review, and a note that simply states that he lacks insight will not.

sources.label: NSW Health: Mental Health Act guidance
Australian Law Reform Commission: Equality, capacity and disability

subtopic_detail: Sodium of 121 in a man with schizophrenia who drinks water compulsively through the day
stem: A 46-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia has had a brief generalised seizure on the ward. Staff report he carries a two litre bottle everywhere and drinks from bathroom taps at night. He is drowsy but rousable.

data_table.Examination: No focal deficit, no oedema; weight 3.1 kg above yesterday
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 121 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 254 mosmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 84 mosmol/kg, urea 2.1 mmol/L, thyroid function and cortisol normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give hypertonic saline in boluses until the sodium rises by ten mmol/L
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or coma that are ongoing, given as a small bolus with a strict correction limit, and a rise of ten millimoles in this setting risks osmotic demyelination. His seizure has terminated and he is rousable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start demeclocycline and continue to allow free access to fluid
options.rationale: Inducing resistance to antidiuretic hormone treats the wrong mechanism when the hormone is already appropriately suppressed and the urine is maximally dilute. Continued free access to water is the problem that needs addressing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give normal saline with furosemide to remove excess free water
options.rationale: This combination is used for hypervolaemic hyponatraemia with oedema, which he does not have, and it risks rapid overcorrection when water diuresis is already about to occur. Sodium loading is not needed when the total body sodium is normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease the antipsychotic and observe the sodium over coming days
options.rationale: Drug induced inappropriate secretion produces concentrated urine rather than the maximally dilute urine seen here, so the biochemistry excludes it. Stopping the antipsychotic would also risk relapse of the illness driving the drinking. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Restrict fluid with supervision, monitor sodium and record daily weights
options.rationale: Dilute urine with a low serum osmolality shows that the kidney is appropriately excreting a water load that exceeds its capacity, so removing the excess intake is the treatment. Frequent sodium measurement is essential because water diuresis can correct the level dangerously fast once drinking stops. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Primary polydipsia occurs in up to a fifth of people with chronic psychotic illness and becomes dangerous when intake exceeds the renal capacity to excrete free water, which is roughly ten to fifteen litres a day in a healthy adult but is lower in those with impaired solute intake. The biochemical signature is hyponatraemia with a low serum osmolality and maximally dilute urine below one hundred milliosmoles per kilogram, which distinguishes it from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, where the urine is inappropriately concentrated. Rapid diurnal weight gain is the most useful bedside monitor and is more informative than intermittent sodium measurements. Management is supervised fluid restriction with frequent sodium monitoring, because once drinking stops the kidney excretes the water load quickly and the sodium can rise far faster than the safe limit of about eight to ten millimoles per litre in twenty four hours, risking osmotic demyelination. Hypertonic saline is reserved for ongoing seizures or coma and is given in small boluses with strict limits on the rise achieved.
key_points: Urine osmolality below one hundred milliosmoles per kilogram indicates appropriate suppression of antidiuretic hormone.
Inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion produces concentrated rather than dilute urine.
Daily and diurnal weights track water loading better than intermittent sodium levels.
Supervised fluid restriction is the treatment, with frequent sodium monitoring.
Overcorrection is a real risk once drinking stops because a water diuresis follows.
explanation.pearls: Measure the weight on waking and again in the late afternoon, since a diurnal gain above about five per cent of body weight identifies dangerous water loading before the sodium falls, and this simple ward measure prevents more seizures than any biochemical monitoring schedule.

subtopic_detail: Sedation and hypersalivation two weeks after a man stable on clozapine stopped smoking
stem: A 38-year-old man stable on clozapine for four years was admitted two weeks ago to a smoke free ward and has not smoked since, having previously smoked 30 a day. He was started on nicotine patches. His mother says he sleeps most of the day, is unsteady on his feet and soaks two pillowcases with saliva each night.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 /min, BP 108/66 mmHg with postural fall
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, pooling saliva, unsteady gait, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.8 x10^9/L, neutrophils 4.1 x10^9/L, troponin normal, QTc 428 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe an anticholinergic and a morning stimulant for the sedation
options.rationale: Treating two symptoms of drug toxicity while leaving the level raised risks seizures, myocarditis surveillance being missed and further deterioration. Symptomatic agents have a place only once the level itself is appropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and start another antipsychotic
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks cholinergic rebound and rapid psychotic relapse in a man who has been well for four years, and the problem is dose rather than drug. Ceasing for more than two days would also require retitration from the start. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise him to resume smoking at his previous level and review
options.rationale: Restoring a lethal exposure to manage a drug interaction is indefensible when dose adjustment achieves the same result. Cessation should be supported, with the dose adjusted to match. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Measure the plasma clozapine concentration and reduce the dose
options.rationale: Tobacco smoke induces the enzyme that clears this drug, so stopping smoking raises plasma levels substantially over one to two weeks and produces exactly this toxicity syndrome.
