source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital: Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents

explanation.summary: Gender dysphoria in adolescence is diagnosed on persistent incongruence between experienced gender and assigned sex causing clinically significant distress, and this young person meets that over four years. Australian standards of care direct referral to a specialist multidisciplinary gender service, where decisions about any medical intervention are made after comprehensive assessment involving the young person and the family. Coexisting mental health problems are common and are assessed and treated concurrently, not used as a precondition for referral or as an explanation that displaces the gender related distress. Family acceptance and the ability to live in the affirmed role are among the strongest protective factors against self-harm in this population.
key_points: Persistent, consistent and insistent incongruence with distress warrants specialist referral
Coexisting depression is treated in parallel, not before referral
Medical interventions are initiated only within a specialist multidisciplinary service
Reversing an established social transition is associated with worse mental health
Endocrine or genetic investigation is reserved for atypical physical findings
explanation.pearls: Ask directly about suicidal ideation and self-harm at every contact, because Australian survey data show that trans and gender diverse adolescents report self-harm and suicide attempts at several times the population rate, and family rejection is the largest modifiable risk factor. Use the young person's stated name and pronouns in the notes and in correspondence, since correspondence that reverts to the birth name is a common reason young people disengage from services entirely.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital: Australian Standards of Care for Trans and Gender Diverse Children and Adolescents
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Recognising and Addressing the Mental Health Needs of Trans and Gender Diverse People

subtopic_detail: weight to give a written advance care directive when a NSW patient is later detained and objects to one medication
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar admitting a 44-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder, detained in a NSW mental health facility with persecutory delusions and four nights without sleep. Eighteen months ago, while well, she wrote an advance care directive declining olanzapine because of weight gain and preferring aripiprazole, which has worked twice. She nominated her sister as designated carer. She now refuses oral medication and has thrown a chair.

data_table.Mental state: Persecutory delusions about staff, agitated, refusing oral medication
data_table.Investigations: Observations and physical examination normal, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: How should her directive influence your prescribing?

options.text: Disregard it, since detention overrides any previously recorded treatment preference
options.rationale: Detention authorises treatment without consent, but it does not make her recorded reasoning irrelevant. Reading the schedule as a blanket override is the commonest misunderstanding of the framework. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives

options.text: Disregard it, since a directive lapses twelve months after it is written
options.rationale: A NSW directive has no expiry: it stands until the person revokes or replaces it. What does lapse at twelve months is her nomination of a designated carer, which is worth checking on this admission. (Source: NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers)
source_refs: NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers

options.text: Follow it only if her designated carer agrees with the preference recorded
options.rationale: Her sister is entitled to information and to be involved, and may apply for her discharge, but the directive expresses the patient's own will and the carer neither validates nor vetoes it. (Source: NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers)
source_refs: NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers

options.text: Follow it only if she can explain and confirm the preference right now
options.rationale: Requiring present capacity defeats the purpose of a document written in advance for precisely this situation. It was made while she was well so that it could speak when she cannot. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives

options.text: Prescribe her preferred agent unless contraindicated, recording your reasoning
options.rationale: A NSW advance care directive cannot override treatment under the Mental Health Act 2007, but the treating team should take it into account, and there is no reason here not to. Aripiprazole has worked for her twice and nothing in the file contraindicates it, so following the directive is both lawful and good practice, and the reasoning belongs in the notes either way. (Source: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives

explanation.summary: NSW has no advance statement legislation. An advance care directive here is a common law document: it must be made with capacity, and it is followed for ordinary medical treatment, but it cannot prevent treatment given to an involuntary patient under the Mental Health Act 2007. That does not make it decorative. It records the patient's own reasoning about agents that have and have not worked, and where the preferred agent is appropriate and available there is no reason to depart from it. Compulsory status removes the need for consent, not the obligation to practise well, and the reasoning should be documented whichever way it goes.
key_points: A NSW directive does not expire; it stands until revoked or replaced.
A designated carer nomination does expire, twelve months after it is made.
The directive is taken into account but cannot override Mental Health Act treatment.
Present capacity is not a precondition for honouring a directive.
explanation.pearls: Check the date on the carer nomination every admission. The directive keeps its force indefinitely, but a nomination more than twelve months old has lapsed, and the default hierarchy of spouse, primary carer, then close relative or friend takes over.

sources.label: NSW Mental Health Rights Manual: advance care directives
NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers

subtopic_detail: disposition decision for a patient with repeated superficial self-harm presentations who requests admission during a crisis
stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with superficial forearm lacerations after an argument, now sutured. This is her fifth presentation in three months. She has borderline personality disorder and asks to be admitted because she cannot face going home.

data_table.Mental state: Settling, no current suicidal intent or plan, not intoxicated
data_table.History: Weekly dialectical behaviour therapy, two sessions missed; three previous admissions each followed by escalating self-harm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Structured safety plan and return to her therapy team this week
options.rationale: Australian guidance is that admission for this disorder should be brief and reserved for acute risk that cannot be managed otherwise, because longer stays reinforce crisis behaviour and disrupt the therapy that actually reduces self-harm. Collaborative safety planning with rapid re-engagement in the existing program is the intervention with evidence behind it. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Admission to an acute inpatient unit for containment and observation
options.rationale: Admission is appropriate for acute suicidal crisis with intent that cannot be managed in the community, and she has neither intent nor plan tonight. Her own history of escalating self-harm during each previous admission is the specific reason to avoid repeating it. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: A benzodiazepine for crisis use with clinic follow up next month
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are discouraged in this disorder because disinhibition increases impulsive self-harm and dependence develops readily. A month long gap also abandons her during the period when re-engagement matters most. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Start a mood stabiliser for affective instability and review in two weeks
options.rationale: Medication has at best a modest adjunctive role targeting specific comorbid symptoms and no drug is approved for the disorder itself in Australia. Starting one tonight frames the problem as pharmacological and competes with the psychological treatment that works. (Source: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.text: Discharge with advice to return only if suicidal intent develops
options.rationale: Discharging without a plan or follow up leaves her with the same crisis and teaches that presentation must escalate to be taken seriously. A structured discharge also sends her home, but with a written plan and a defined return to care. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Self-harm and Suicidal Behaviour)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Self-harm and Suicidal Behaviour

explanation.summary: Structured psychological therapy is the primary treatment for borderline personality disorder, and dialectical behaviour therapy has the strongest evidence for reducing self-harm. Australian guidance recommends that inpatient admission be brief and reserved for acute suicidal crises that cannot be managed in the community, because longer admissions can reinforce crisis presentations and interrupt the therapy program. This woman has no current intent or plan, has settled during assessment, and has a documented pattern of escalating self-harm during previous admissions. The intervention with the best evidence tonight is collaborative safety planning followed by rapid return to her existing team, which also treats the missed sessions as the clinical problem they represent.
key_points: Structured psychological therapy, not medication, is the primary treatment
Admission is brief and reserved for acute crisis that cannot be managed otherwise
Prolonged admission can reinforce crisis behaviour and interrupt therapy
Benzodiazepines increase impulsive self-harm through disinhibition
Discharge is structured with a written safety plan and defined follow up, never bare
explanation.pearls: Write the safety plan with the patient rather than for her, naming her own early warning signs, two distress tolerance skills she has already practised, and the specific number to call, because a generic plan handed over at discharge is not used. Treat the missed therapy sessions as the most important clinical finding of the presentation and contact the therapy team directly the next working day, since disengagement typically precedes escalating presentations by several weeks.

sources.label: NHMRC: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Self-harm and Suicidal Behaviour

subtopic_detail: collapse at a dance event with hyperthermia and a low sodium after a recreational stimulant and large volumes of water
stem: An 18-year-old woman is brought in from a music festival after a seizure lasting ninety seconds. Friends say she took two tablets sold as ecstasy four hours ago, danced continuously and drank large volumes of water. She is drowsy and confused.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 136 /min, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, temperature 40.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 12, flushed and diaphoretic
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), creatine kinase 3200 units/L (40-200)

lead_in: What are the two most urgent interventions?

options.text: Mannitol for cerebral oedema and phenytoin for seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Phenytoin is ineffective for toxic and metabolic seizures, where benzodiazepines are the agent of choice, and mannitol does not address the underlying sodium deficit that is generating the oedema. Neither touches the hyperthermia. (Source: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine: Toxicology Resources)
source_refs: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine: Toxicology Resources

options.text: Hypertonic saline for the sodium and active external cooling
options.rationale: Seizure with a sodium of 118 mmol/L is symptomatic hyponatraemia requiring hypertonic saline, and a core temperature above 39 degrees Celsius in this poisoning drives rhabdomyolysis, disseminated coagulopathy and death unless cooled rapidly. These two derangements kill first and both are correctable at the bedside within minutes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Isotonic saline for the sodium and active external cooling
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid is the right choice for the hypovolaemic hyponatraemic patient, but this woman is water loaded rather than depleted and isotonic saline corrects her sodium too slowly after a seizure. Volume loading also risks worsening the cerebral oedema that produced the seizure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Fluid restriction for the sodium and paracetamol for the fever
options.rationale: Restriction alone is far too slow when a seizure has already occurred, and antipyretics do not work because this hyperthermia is produced by muscle activity and impaired heat dissipation rather than by a raised hypothalamic set point. Both measures treat the numbers without changing the trajectory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Hypertonic saline for the sodium and dantrolene as first line
options.rationale: Dantrolene is reserved for severe hyperthermia that persists despite sedation and aggressive cooling, and relying on it first delays the physical cooling that does most of the work. The distinguishing relationship is that cooling removes heat directly while dantrolene only reduces its production. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: This presentation combines two separate life threatening problems produced by the same drug. The stimulant releases antidiuretic hormone and users are often advised to drink freely, so massive free water intake in the presence of impaired excretion produces acute hyponatraemia, cerebral oedema and seizures. Simultaneously, sustained exertion in a hot environment with impaired thermoregulation produces hyperthermia that leads to rhabdomyolysis, coagulopathy and multiorgan failure once the core temperature exceeds about 39 degrees Celsius. Symptomatic hyponatraemia after a seizure requires hypertonic saline, and hyperthermia requires immediate active cooling with benzodiazepines for agitation, with dantrolene held in reserve.
key_points: The drug stimulates antidiuretic hormone release, and advice to drink water compounds it
Seizure with a sodium of 118 mmol/L is symptomatic hyponatraemia requiring hypertonic saline
Hyperthermia here is from muscle activity, so antipyretics do not work
Benzodiazepines are first line for both agitation and toxic seizures
Dantrolene is reserved for hyperthermia refractory to sedation and active cooling
explanation.pearls: Correct the sodium by about 4 to 6 mmol/L acutely to stop the seizure, then respect the usual ceiling of 8 to 10 mmol/L over twenty four hours, since these young patients autocorrect briskly once the drug wears off and the antidiuretic effect ceases. Young women are disproportionately affected by the hyponatraemic presentation, and a normal or near normal sodium at triage does not exclude it because the level continues to fall for hours after the last drink.

sources.label: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine: Toxicology Resources

subtopic_detail: reframing a long history of anxiety and burnout in an adult woman whose difficulties are better explained by lifelong social camouflaging
stem: A 29-year-old woman has had generalised anxiety and recurrent depression since age 19, with partial response to two antidepressants and cognitive behavioural therapy. She rehearses conversations, copies colleagues' mannerisms and needs two days alone after a work social event. She has lifelong intense interests in timetables, finds seams and fluorescent lighting painful, and eats the same four meals.

data_table.History: School reports described her as quiet with no concerns; exhausted since a recent promotion
data_table.Mental state: No psychotic symptoms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add a low dose antipsychotic for her sensory symptoms and rigid eating
options.rationale: There is no indication for an antipsychotic here, and it would add metabolic risk without addressing sensory processing or routine. Medication in autism targets specific comorbidities rather than the core features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure her that her normal school reports exclude the diagnosis
options.rationale: Quiet and compliant school behaviour is precisely how autistic girls avoid detection, since the diagnostic threshold historically depended on disruption that they do not produce. Using the absence of childhood concerns to exclude the diagnosis perpetuates the delay. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Refer for a developmental history and neurodevelopmental assessment
options.rationale: Lifelong social effort with rehearsed interaction and imitation, intense circumscribed interests, sensory sensitivity and rigid routines, alongside anxiety that responds only partially to standard treatment, describes autism presenting late in an adult woman. The diagnosis rests on a structured developmental history with collateral rather than on current symptoms alone, so specialist assessment is the correct step. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

options.text: Switch to a third antidepressant from a different class
options.rationale: A further medication trial addresses the anxiety and depression as though they were the primary problem, when two adequate trials have produced the same partial pattern. It also leaves the exhausting social effort that is driving her presentation entirely unaddressed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for assessment of an emerging personality disorder
options.rationale: Personality disorder is a genuine differential and is frequently misapplied to autistic women, but her difficulties are with the mechanics of social processing rather than with unstable relationships, identity or affect regulation. The distinguishing relationship is that camouflaging is an effortful compensation, not an unstable sense of self. (Source: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia)
source_refs: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

explanation.summary: Autistic women are commonly identified late because camouflaging, meaning rehearsed conversation, imitation of others and suppression of self-regulatory behaviour, masks the features that diagnostic criteria were built around. The cost of that effort appears as anxiety, depression and exhaustion, which is why so many women accumulate mood and anxiety diagnoses first and respond only partially to treatment. The clues here are lifelong social effort rather than social fear, intense circumscribed interests, marked sensory sensitivity, rigid routines, and decompensation when social demand rises after a promotion. Diagnosis requires a structured developmental history with collateral information, which is why specialist assessment rather than another medication trial is the right step.
key_points: Camouflaging delays diagnosis in women and is effortful rather than automatic
Anxiety and depression are common consequences and often respond only partially
Quiet compliant school behaviour does not exclude the diagnosis
Sensory sensitivity and rigid routines are core features, not comorbid quirks
Diagnosis requires a structured developmental history, not a cross-sectional interview
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether social contact is frightening or merely exhausting, because social anxiety centres on fear of negative evaluation while autistic social fatigue reflects the processing cost of interaction itself, and the two call for different interventions. A late diagnosis remains worthwhile even when no service follows from it, since reframing a decade of perceived personal failure and adjusting workplace and sensory demands often achieves more than the third antidepressant would.

sources.label: Autism CRC: National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism in Australia

subtopic_detail: explaining a positive bedside inconsistency sign to a patient with sudden leg weakness and normal imaging
stem: A 41-year-old woman developed sudden right leg weakness five days ago and cannot weight bear. She has no psychiatric history and says she was told the scans were normal so nothing is wrong.

data_table.Examination: Give-way weakness of right hip flexion, right hip extends involuntarily on resisted left hip flexion, sensory loss ending abruptly at the inguinal crease
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance brain and whole spine, nerve conduction studies and inflammatory markers all normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Document suspected feigning and arrange covert observation
options.rationale: Inconsistency signs demonstrate that the movement pathway is intact but not under voluntary control, and they do not distinguish conscious feigning. The distinguishing relationship is that factitious disorder and malingering require evidence of intentional production, which these signs cannot supply. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder

options.text: Repeat the spinal imaging with contrast before explaining
options.rationale: Repeating adequate investigations reinforces the belief that an undiscovered structural lesion explains the symptoms, and each additional negative test makes the eventual explanation harder to accept. The diagnosis rests on positive signs already present rather than on further exclusion. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder

options.text: Start an antidepressant and review her mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants treat comorbid mood and anxiety disorders when they are present, and she has no psychiatric history or current depressive syndrome. Medication is not a treatment for the motor symptom itself. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Explain the positive bedside sign and refer for physiotherapy
options.rationale: Functional neurological disorder is diagnosed on positive signs of internal inconsistency, and involuntary hip extension during resisted contralateral hip flexion is exactly such a sign rather than evidence of feigning. Demonstrating it to the patient as proof that the pathway works, followed by physiotherapy that retrains automatic movement, is the treatment with the best evidence. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder

options.text: Explain that the investigations are normal and discharge her
options.rationale: A diagnosis of exclusion communicated as an absence leaves the patient with disabling symptoms and no explanation, which is what has already happened and left her distressed. Outcomes depend heavily on how the diagnosis is delivered, and a negative framing predicts poor recovery. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis resting on demonstrable internal inconsistency, not a label applied when investigations return normal. Hoover's sign, in which hip extension on the weak side returns involuntarily during resisted contralateral hip flexion, shows that the motor pathway is intact while voluntary access to it is not. A sensory level that stops precisely at an anatomical crease and give-way weakness are supporting features. Explaining the diagnosis positively, including demonstrating the sign to the patient, is itself therapeutic, and physiotherapy that retrains automatic rather than deliberate movement is the mainstay of treatment, with psychological therapy added where there are maintaining psychological factors.
key_points: The diagnosis is made on positive signs of inconsistency, not by exclusion alone
Hoover's sign demonstrates an intact pathway with impaired voluntary access
Inconsistency does not indicate feigning and cannot distinguish it
How the diagnosis is explained is a strong predictor of outcome
Physiotherapy retraining automatic movement is the primary treatment
explanation.pearls: Demonstrate the sign with the patient watching and explain it as a problem of the nervous system's software rather than its hardware, since patients who accept the diagnosis at the first explanation have substantially better outcomes than those referred on after months of further testing. Functional and structural disease coexist more often than not, so a previous injury such as her ankle fracture is frequently the physical trigger around which the functional pattern forms, and its presence does not argue against the diagnosis.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Functional Neurological Disorder

subtopic_detail: fever and tachycardia in the third week of an antipsychotic titration where the cardiac and neuroleptic explanations require different immediate actions
stem: A 27-year-old man on day 18 of a clozapine titration, now 250 mg at night, has two days of fever, lethargy and vomiting. He has treatment resistant schizophrenia.

data_table.Examination: Alert, normal tone with no rigidity or clonus, no focal infective source
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (<5), troponin I 640 nanograms/L (<20), creatine kinase 190 units/L (40-200)
data_table.Cardiac: Echocardiogram ejection fraction 44 per cent with global hypokinesis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease clozapine, start bromocriptine and dantrolene, and transfer to intensive care
options.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is the reflex answer to fever on an antipsychotic, but it requires rigidity, altered consciousness and a markedly raised creatine kinase, and his tone is normal with a creatine kinase of 190 units/L. The distinguishing relationship is that one syndrome damages muscle and the other damages myocardium, which is why the troponin and the creatine kinase separate here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue clozapine, attribute the fever to benign pyrexia and monitor daily
options.rationale: Benign transient fever is genuinely common in the first three weeks and would be a reasonable conclusion with normal cardiac markers, which is what makes this presentation dangerous. A troponin of 640 nanograms/L with new ventricular dysfunction removes that option entirely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease clozapine and start broad spectrum antibiotics for presumed sepsis
options.rationale: Culturing and covering for infection is a reasonable parallel action while results are pending, but attributing the picture to sepsis fails to explain the eosinophilia and the new global hypokinesis. Treating this as infection alone delays the cardiac care that determines outcome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Withhold two doses and resume at a lower dose with weekly troponin
options.rationale: A brief interruption followed by reintroduction treats this as a dose related intolerance rather than an immune mediated myocardial injury, and rechallenge after established myocarditis carries a high recurrence rate. Any interruption beyond 48 hours would in any case require full retitration. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Clozapine)

options.text: Cease clozapine permanently, transfer for cardiac monitoring and involve cardiology
options.rationale: Fever, tachycardia, eosinophilia, a raised C-reactive protein and a markedly raised troponin with new global hypokinesis in the third week of titration is clozapine induced myocarditis, which peaks between days 14 and 21. The drug is stopped permanently because rechallenge carries a high risk of recurrence and death, and cardiac monitoring with specialist input is arranged immediately. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Fever during a clozapine titration has three competing explanations that demand different actions, and separating them is the whole task. Benign transient pyrexia is common in the first three weeks and needs only observation, neuroleptic malignant syndrome produces rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness and a markedly raised creatine kinase, and myocarditis produces fever, tachycardia, eosinophilia, a rising C-reactive protein and a raised troponin with new ventricular dysfunction. Here the normal tone and normal creatine kinase exclude the neuroleptic syndrome, while the troponin of 640 nanograms/L with an ejection fraction of 44 per cent and global hypokinesis establishes myocarditis at its characteristic peak between days 14 and 21. The drug is ceased permanently, cardiac monitoring is arranged and cardiology is involved, because rechallenge carries a high risk of recurrent and sometimes fatal myocarditis.
key_points: Clozapine induced myocarditis peaks between days 14 and 21 of titration
Eosinophilia with a rising C-reactive protein and troponin is the characteristic signature
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requires rigidity and a markedly raised creatine kinase
Benign transient fever is common but never diagnosed in the presence of a raised troponin
Rechallenge after established myocarditis carries a high recurrence risk and is avoided
explanation.pearls: Monitor troponin and C-reactive protein at baseline and weekly for the first four weeks of every clozapine titration, since the diagnosis is made on a rising trend well before the echocardiogram changes, and a troponin above twice the upper reference limit warrants cessation pending assessment. When clozapine must be stopped, plan for cholinergic rebound with agitation, sweating and diarrhoea, and remember that any break of more than 48 hours mandates restarting the titration from a low dose because of the risk of severe hypotension.

subtopic_detail: choosing smoking cessation pharmacotherapy for a heavily dependent smoker with treated depression and a previous failed nicotine patch attempt
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 48-year-old man who wants to stop smoking. He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day since he was 17 and lights his first within five minutes of waking.

He made one attempt two years ago using a 21 mg nicotine patch alone and relapsed at day four with strong cravings, particularly in the evenings. He has major depressive disorder that has been stable for three years on sertraline 100 mg daily, with no hospital admissions and no self-harm. He drinks two standard drinks most nights and has no other substance use. He has no seizure history, no eating disorder, and his renal function is within normal limits. He is motivated and has set a quit date in three weeks' time, and he asks what will give him the best chance this time.

data_table.Smoking history: 25 cigarettes daily for 31 years, first cigarette within 5 minutes of waking, one previous attempt with patch monotherapy relapsing at day 4
data_table.Mental health: Major depressive disorder stable for 3 years on sertraline 100 mg daily, no admissions or self-harm
data_table.Investigations: Renal and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy would you recommend as first line for this quit attempt?

options.text: Varenicline commenced one week before the quit date and continued for twelve weeks
options.rationale: Varenicline is the single most effective agent for cessation and outperforms both patch monotherapy and bupropion in head to head trials, and the large randomised safety trial found no excess of neuropsychiatric events in people with stable treated psychiatric illness. His high dependence and previous patch failure both argue for the most effective option rather than a repeat of what did not work. (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: A 21 mg nicotine patch commenced on the quit date and continued for twelve weeks
options.rationale: Repeating patch monotherapy repeats the regimen that already failed him, and a patch alone does not address the acute evening cravings that broke the previous attempt. If nicotine replacement is chosen it should be combination therapy, patch plus a fast acting form. (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Bupropion commenced one week before the quit date and continued for twelve weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is an effective second line agent but is less effective than varenicline, lowers the seizure threshold, and carries a serotonergic interaction risk when added to an established selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. It would be a reasonable choice if varenicline were contraindicated or not tolerated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Nicotine lozenges used on demand for cravings without any scheduled background therapy
options.rationale: Oral nicotine used alone delivers erratic blood levels and does not suppress the background withdrawal that drives relapse in the first week, so it is used as the rapid acting partner to a patch rather than as monotherapy. In a smoker of this dependence it under-treats the problem. (Source: RACGP: Supporting Smoking Cessation)

options.text: Increasing the sertraline to 150 mg daily as antidepressants also assist smoking cessation
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have no cessation efficacy, and increasing a dose that is currently maintaining remission risks destabilising mood for no benefit. The antidepressant with a cessation indication is bupropion, which works through dopaminergic and noradrenergic mechanisms rather than serotonergic ones. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Smoking rates among people with mental illness remain roughly double those in the general population, and tobacco related disease accounts for a large share of the reduced life expectancy in this group, so cessation is one of the highest value interventions in psychiatric care. Concerns about neuropsychiatric harm from varenicline led to a black box warning that was later removed after a large randomised trial found no excess of serious neuropsychiatric events compared with patch or placebo, including in people with stable psychiatric disorders. Effectiveness ranks varenicline highest, followed by combination nicotine replacement, then bupropion or single form nicotine replacement. Every pharmacotherapy should be paired with behavioural support, since combining the two roughly doubles quit rates compared with either alone. Smoking induces the cytochrome P450 1A2 enzyme, so stopping raises levels of clozapine and olanzapine and these need dose review at cessation.
key_points: Varenicline is the most effective single agent and is started one to two weeks before the quit date.
Stable treated psychiatric illness is not a contraindication to varenicline.
Nicotine replacement works best as a combination of patch plus a rapid acting form.
Pair every pharmacotherapy with behavioural support such as the national quitline.
Time to first cigarette within 30 minutes of waking is the best single marker of high dependence.
explanation.pearls: Stopping smoking removes the cytochrome P450 1A2 induction that tobacco smoke produces, so clozapine levels can rise by 50 per cent or more within one to two weeks of quitting and the dose usually needs reducing with level monitoring.

subtopic_detail: responding to a rising thyroid stimulating hormone on long term lithium in a patient whose mood has been stable for years
stem: A 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium for nine years with no mood episode for seven years. Over four months she has felt the cold, gained 5 kg and become constipated.

data_table.Examination: Small diffuse non-tender goitre, dry skin, delayed ankle reflex relaxation
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.6 to 0.8), thyroid stimulating hormone 11.4 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free thyroxine 9.8 pmol/L (10 to 26)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for thyroid ultrasound and fine needle aspiration
options.rationale: A small diffuse non-tender goitre with biochemical hypothyroidism needs no imaging, and aspiration is reserved for a discrete nodule or features suspicious for malignancy. Imaging would delay replacement that is already clearly indicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Continue lithium and start thyroxine titrated to thyroid function
options.rationale: Lithium associated hypothyroidism is treated by adding thyroxine rather than by stopping a mood stabiliser that has kept her well for seven years, since the thyroid effect is fully correctable while the relapse risk on withdrawal is not. Her free thyroxine is below range with symptoms, which makes this overt rather than subclinical disease and removes any argument for observation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Cease lithium, switch to sodium valproate and recheck thyroid function
options.rationale: Stopping lithium after nine years of stability carries a substantial relapse risk, and abrupt discontinuation in particular is associated with rebound mania. Valproate is also a poor choice for a woman of reproductive age given its teratogenicity, and none of this is necessary for a treatable side effect. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Reduce the lithium dose to achieve a level near 0.4 mmol/L
options.rationale: The thyroid effect is not dose dependent in a way that a modest reduction reverses, and dropping below the therapeutic range trades a correctable hormone deficiency for a loss of prophylactic efficacy. Lithium induced hypothyroidism is treated with thyroxine replacement rather than by under-dosing lithium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Repeat thyroid function in three months before treating
options.rationale: Watchful repeat testing is the correct approach to an isolated mildly raised thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine and no symptoms. She has a free thyroxine below the reference range together with cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation and delayed reflex relaxation, which is overt hypothyroidism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Lithium remains the most effective long term prophylactic agent in bipolar disorder and is the only mood stabiliser with consistent evidence for reducing suicide, so preserving it through manageable side effects is usually the right trade. It interferes with thyroid hormone release from the gland and with iodine organification, producing goitre in up to 40 per cent of long term users and hypothyroidism in roughly one in five, with women over 45 and those with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies at highest risk. Standard monitoring is a lithium level with renal function, thyroid function and calcium every three to six months, with more frequent levels after any dose change or intercurrent illness. Lithium also causes hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and a slow decline in glomerular filtration rate over decades. Hypothyroidism is corrected with thyroxine while lithium continues, and the mood picture must be reviewed at the same time because hypothyroidism can itself mimic or precipitate a depressive episode.
key_points: Lithium causes hypothyroidism in roughly 20 per cent of long term users and goitre in up to 40 per cent.
Treat with thyroxine and continue lithium rather than stopping an effective mood stabiliser.
Monitor lithium level, renal function, thyroid function and calcium every three to six months.
Abrupt lithium discontinuation carries a particular risk of rebound mania.
Lithium associated hyperparathyroidism produces hypercalcaemia with an inappropriately normal or raised parathyroid hormone.
explanation.pearls: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and thiazide diuretics all reduce renal lithium clearance and can raise the level by 25 to 60 per cent within a week, so any new prescription in these classes warrants a level check at seven days.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: advising an adult newly started on a stimulant about driving obligations and dose timing for shift work
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27-year-old man four weeks after starting methylphenidate for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder diagnosed this year. He reports better focus at work, is sleeping adequately, and has had no appetite loss beyond a mild reduction at lunch.

He drives a courier van for a living on a commercial licence and works rotating shifts including a night shift block every third week. He asks whether he has to tell anyone about the medication, and says a workmate told him that being on a stimulant would cost him his licence. He has no history of substance misuse, no cardiac symptoms, and no family history of sudden cardiac death. His blood pressure today is 128/78 with a pulse of 82, unchanged from baseline, and his weight is stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No tremor, normal cardiovascular examination, weight unchanged from baseline
data_table.Treatment: Methylphenidate started 4 weeks ago with symptomatic improvement and adequate sleep
data_table.Occupation: Commercial licence courier driver on rotating shifts including night shift every third week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about his driving?

options.text: Notification is only required if he has a crash or receives an infringement while taking the medication
options.rationale: The duty to notify arises when the condition is diagnosed or the treatment begins, not retrospectively after an adverse event. Waiting for a crash inverts the purpose of the standards, which exist to prevent one. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: He should switch to atomoxetine, since non stimulant treatment removes any notification requirement
options.rationale: The notifiable matter is the underlying condition and its effect on driving, so changing drug class does not remove the obligation, and atomoxetine is less effective than a stimulant for most patients. Switching a treatment that is working would trade efficacy for a regulatory benefit that does not exist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: He must notify the driver licensing authority, and treated stable illness is generally compatible with driving
options.rationale: Australian fitness to drive standards place the obligation on the driver to notify the licensing authority of a condition likely to affect driving, and for a commercial licence the standards are stricter and require periodic review. Neither the diagnosis nor stimulant treatment disqualifies him, and treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder reduces rather than increases crash risk. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: No notification is required because stimulant medication is prescribed and lawfully obtained
options.rationale: Lawful prescription addresses the question of whether he is impaired by an illicit drug but does not remove the separate obligation to notify a condition relevant to driving. Drug driving law and fitness to drive standards are two different frameworks. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: He should stop driving commercially while taking any stimulant and change to a private licence
options.rationale: Blanket exclusion from commercial driving is not what the standards require, and it would impose a serious occupational penalty for a treatment that improves driving performance. Conditional licensing with periodic review is the mechanism the standards actually use. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

explanation.summary: Adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is increasingly recognised in Australia and stimulant prescribing is governed by state and territory authority requirements, with most jurisdictions requiring a specialist to initiate treatment. Untreated symptoms are associated with a measurably higher motor vehicle crash rate, and pharmacological treatment reduces it, so the safety argument generally favours treating rather than withholding. Fitness to drive is assessed under the national standards, which distinguish private from commercial licences and use conditional licences with review intervals rather than outright exclusion for most treated conditions. The legal duty to notify the licensing authority rests with the driver, while the doctor's duty is to advise clearly and document that advice, with a discretionary power to report directly where a patient continues to drive against advice. Shift work adds a separate consideration, since sleep deprivation impairs driving independently of any medication and stimulant timing must not be used to mask fatigue.
key_points: The driver holds the legal obligation to notify; the doctor's obligation is to advise and document.
Commercial licence standards are stricter and typically require periodic medical review.
Treated attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is associated with a lower crash risk than untreated illness.
Baseline and follow up blood pressure, pulse, weight and sleep are the core monitoring parameters on stimulants.
Sleep deprivation from shift work impairs driving independently of medication and must be addressed separately.
explanation.pearls: Immediate release methylphenidate has a duration of roughly three to four hours while modified release preparations last eight to twelve, so a late afternoon dose taken to cover a night shift will delay sleep onset well past the end of that shift and is the usual reason a shift worker reports insomnia on stimulants.

subtopic_detail: identifying the medication cause of a low sodium in an older adult started on an antidepressant three weeks earlier
stem: A 76-year-old woman started sertraline 50 mg daily three weeks ago for a first depressive episode. Her daughter reports three days of muddled thinking, unsteadiness and a fall. She also takes perindopril, unchanged for six years.

data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic, no postural drop, unsteady gait; abbreviated mental test score 6 out of 10, previously 9
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 119 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 468 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue sertraline, give intravenous sodium chloride and recheck the sodium
options.rationale: Isotonic saline in inappropriate antidiuresis can paradoxically lower the sodium further, because the kidney excretes the salt while retaining the water, and it leaves the causative drug in place. Volume expansion is the treatment for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, which her euvolaemia and high urine sodium exclude. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Switch to mirtazapine today and leave fluid intake unchanged
options.rationale: Mirtazapine is a reasonable later choice because it carries a lower risk of this complication, but starting it at the same visit confuses the picture and does nothing about the water retention already present. Correct the sodium first, then reintroduce an antidepressant with monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the head before changing medication
options.rationale: Imaging is warranted where a fall with head strike is accompanied by focal signs, anticoagulation or a reduced conscious level, and it may still be arranged here, but it does not explain a sodium of 119 mmol/L and delays treatment of a reversible cause. The confusion and unsteadiness are fully accounted for by the hyponatraemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease sertraline, restrict fluid and recheck the sodium in 48 hours
options.rationale: The biochemistry shows a euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, which is the pattern of inappropriate antidiuresis, and the temporal link to a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor started three weeks ago identifies the cause. Withdrawing the drug with fluid restriction corrects most cases within days, and close rechecking is needed because over rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue sertraline, cease perindopril and recheck the sodium in 48 hours
options.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors can contribute to low sodium, which makes this a genuine competing culprit, but she has taken perindopril unchanged for six years while the sertraline was introduced three weeks before the sodium fell. Temporal association points to the new agent rather than the long standing one. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are the commonest drug cause of hyponatraemia in older adults, with risk highest in the first four weeks of treatment and rising with age, female sex, low body weight, and concurrent diuretics or angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors. The mechanism is inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, producing a euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with urine that is inappropriately concentrated and a urine sodium above 30 mmol per litre. The presentation is easily misread as a worsening of the depression being treated, or as emerging dementia, because it produces confusion, unsteadiness, falls and lethargy rather than anything obviously biochemical. Management is withdrawal of the offending drug with fluid restriction for mild to moderate cases, reserving hypertonic saline for seizures or a markedly reduced conscious level. Correction should not exceed 8 to 10 mmol per litre in 24 hours because of the risk of osmotic demyelination, and the sodium should be rechecked within a fortnight whenever a serotonergic antidepressant is restarted in an older patient.
key_points: Risk is greatest in the first four weeks after starting a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.
Look for euvolaemia, serum osmolality below 275, urine osmolality above 100 and urine sodium above 30 mmol/L.
Exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency before attributing the picture to inappropriate antidiuresis.
Limit correction to 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Check sodium at baseline and around two weeks when starting these drugs in an older patient.
explanation.pearls: Mirtazapine and agomelatine carry the lowest reported risk of drug induced hyponatraemia among the antidepressants, which makes one of them the practical choice when depression still needs treating after a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor has caused it.

subtopic_detail: choosing between behavioural and pharmacological treatment for long standing sleep onset difficulty maintained by compensatory habits
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 39-year-old teacher who has had difficulty falling asleep for the past 14 months, most nights of the week. She takes about 90 minutes to get to sleep and feels unrefreshed and irritable during the day.

Her sleep diary shows she goes to bed at 9 pm to give herself the best chance, stays in bed reading on her phone until she feels sleepy, gets up at 6.30 am, and naps for 40 minutes most afternoons. She drinks one coffee at breakfast and none after midday. She has no snoring or witnessed apnoeas and her partner confirms this, no restless legs, and no low mood, anhedonia or anxiety on direct questioning. Her thyroid function and full blood count are within normal limits and she takes no regular medication. She asks for something to help her sleep.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24, Mallampati class 1, no goitre
data_table.Sleep diary: Bed at 9 pm, sleep onset latency about 90 minutes, rise at 6.30 am, afternoon nap of about 40 minutes most days, total sleep time about 6 hours in 9.5 hours in bed
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What would you recommend as first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe temazepam 10 mg at night for two weeks with a plan to review and taper
options.rationale: Short term hypnotics have a place for acute situational insomnia but do not address maintaining behaviours, and tolerance plus rebound insomnia commonly follow in chronic insomnia of 14 months duration. At 14 months her insomnia is chronic, where first line treatment is psychological rather than a hypnotic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe modified release melatonin 2 mg nightly for thirteen weeks with review at completion
options.rationale: Modified release melatonin is subsidised for primary insomnia in adults aged 55 and over, where age related decline in endogenous secretion is the rationale, and she is well below that age. Its effect size on sleep onset latency is modest even in the indicated population. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Hypnotics and Sedatives)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Hypnotics and Sedatives

options.text: Prescribe low dose amitriptyline 10 mg at night and review the response in four weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antidepressants are sometimes used off label for sleep but carry anticholinergic burden, daytime sedation and weight gain, with limited evidence in the absence of depression. She has no depressive symptoms on direct questioning, which removes the indication that would justify the class. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography before deciding on treatment for her sleep difficulty
options.rationale: Sleep studies are indicated when a specific sleep disorder such as obstructive sleep apnoea, periodic limb movement disorder or narcolepsy is suspected, and none of those features is present with a normal body mass index and no snoring. Routine polysomnography in uncomplicated insomnia changes neither the diagnosis nor the treatment. (Source: RACGP: Management of Chronic Insomnia)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia including stimulus control and sleep restriction
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia in every major guideline and produces benefits that persist after treatment ends, unlike hypnotics whose effect stops with the drug. Her diary shows the exact maintaining behaviours the therapy targets, namely excessive time in bed, using the bed for wakeful activity, and daytime napping that erodes sleep pressure. (Source: RACGP: Management of Chronic Insomnia)

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia is defined by difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep on at least three nights per week for at least three months with a daytime consequence, and it is best understood through a model in which a precipitating stressor is replaced over time by perpetuating behaviours that outlast it. Those behaviours are precisely the compensations that feel most sensible to the patient: going to bed earlier, staying in bed longer, napping, and using the bed as a place to wait for sleep. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia bundles stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive restructuring of sleep related beliefs, and relaxation, and it is delivered face to face, in groups, or through validated digital programs which have made access far more practical. Its effect is comparable to hypnotics in the short term and clearly superior beyond a few weeks, since the gains persist once treatment ends. Hypnotics retain a role for short term situational insomnia and as a bridge, but they are not the answer to a problem that has lasted more than a year.
key_points: Chronic insomnia requires symptoms on three or more nights weekly for three months with daytime impact.
Perpetuating behaviours include extended time in bed, napping and wakeful activity in bed.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and its benefit persists after treatment stops.
Sleep restriction works by consolidating sleep through increased homeostatic pressure, not by reducing total sleep.
Polysomnography is reserved for suspected apnoea, limb movement disorder or narcolepsy.
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction starts by setting time in bed to the average total sleep time from the diary, with a floor of five hours, and time in bed is extended by 15 minutes each week once sleep efficiency exceeds 85 per cent.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Hypnotics and Sedatives

subtopic_detail: distinguishing a persistent grief reaction from a depressive episode fourteen months after a bereavement
stem: A 58-year-old woman is referred 14 months after her adult son died in a workplace accident. She yearns for him daily, spends hours with his photographs, has kept his bedroom unchanged and avoids their mutual friends.

data_table.Symptoms: Yearning, preoccupation and identity disruption, present most days for 14 months
data_table.Negative findings: Appetite, sleep and enjoyment of gardening preserved; no guilt or suicidal ideation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for grief focused psychotherapy targeting the loss and avoidance
options.rationale: Persistent intense yearning with identity disruption, inability to accept the death and avoidance of reminders, present daily beyond 12 months and causing impairment, is prolonged grief disorder, and targeted grief focused psychotherapy is the treatment with the strongest evidence. It outperforms both generic supportive counselling and antidepressant monotherapy in randomised trials of this specific presentation. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Start an antidepressant and review the response in six weeks
options.rationale: Her sleep, appetite and capacity for enjoyment are preserved and there is no pervasive guilt, which means she does not meet criteria for a depressive episode, and antidepressant monotherapy does not reliably reduce grief severity in trials. Medication is added when a comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure her that this is normal grief and review in six months
options.rationale: Uncomplicated grief softens over the first year so that the person can hold the loss alongside ordinary life, whereas her yearning remains at daily intensity at 14 months with active avoidance narrowing her world. Normalising it withholds a treatment that works and risks a further six months of entrenchment. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Prescribe a short benzodiazepine course for distress at home
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not improve grief outcomes and there is evidence that early use after bereavement is associated with worse trajectories, partly because they blunt the emotional processing that recovery requires. They also reinforce the avoidance that is maintaining her symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing for the death
options.rationale: This is an established treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder, and it would be appropriate if she had intrusive re-experiencing, hyperarousal and nightmares of the event, which she does not describe. Her avoidance is of reminders of the person rather than of a witnessed traumatic scene, which is the feature separating the two conditions. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Prolonged grief disorder was added to the major diagnostic systems to name a presentation that is neither ordinary bereavement nor a depressive episode, and it affects roughly 7 to 10 per cent of bereaved adults, with higher rates after sudden, violent or unexpected deaths and after the loss of a child. The diagnosis requires persistent intense yearning or preoccupation with the deceased, together with symptoms such as identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, a sense that life is meaningless and difficulty re-engaging, present most days and causing impairment beyond 12 months in adults. Distinguishing it from major depression matters because the treatments differ: grief is oriented around the lost person with preserved capacity for pleasure elsewhere, while depression is pervasive with anhedonia, guilt and neurovegetative change. The evidence favours structured grief focused psychotherapy, which combines exposure to avoided reminders with work on restoring goals and relationships, over medication alone. Antidepressants are reserved for comorbid depression or anxiety rather than for the grief itself.
key_points: The adult time criterion is symptoms persisting beyond 12 months from the death.
Yearning and preoccupation centred on the deceased is the core feature, not pervasive low mood.
Preserved appetite, sleep and capacity for enjoyment argue against a comorbid depressive episode.
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms supportive counselling and antidepressant monotherapy.
Sudden, violent or unexpected deaths and the loss of a child carry the highest risk.
explanation.pearls: Avoidance is the treatment target that most reliably predicts response: keeping a room unchanged and avoiding shared friends prevents the repeated exposure through which the loss becomes tolerable, and grief focused therapy works largely by reversing exactly those two behaviours.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: recognising a motor syndrome mistaken for worsening psychosis when antipsychotic escalation has made it worse
stem: A 24-year-old man admitted eight days ago with relapsed schizophrenia had olanzapine increased from 10 mg to 20 mg daily four days ago. Over 48 hours he has stopped speaking and eats only when food is placed in his mouth.

data_table.Examination: Mute and immobile, holds a posture in which his arm is placed, resists passive movement with matching force, echolalia
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 U/L (60 to 220)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start nasogastric feeding and reassess the mental state afterwards
options.rationale: Attention to nutrition, hydration and thromboprophylaxis is genuinely part of supportive care in a patient who is not eating, but it addresses a complication rather than the syndrome. Treating the catatonia is usually what restores oral intake within a day or two. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Withhold the olanzapine and give a lorazepam challenge
options.rationale: Mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, gegenhalten and echolalia together make up a catatonic syndrome, and a parenteral lorazepam challenge is both the diagnostic test and the first line treatment, with a substantial response typically seen within minutes to hours. Antipsychotic exposure can precipitate and worsen catatonia and raises the risk of progression to the malignant form, so it is withheld while the benzodiazepine is trialled. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Increase the olanzapine to 30 mg daily for negative symptoms
options.rationale: Reading immobility and mutism as negative symptoms and escalating the antipsychotic is the main error to avoid in catatonia, and the deterioration that followed the last increase is the clue that it is already happening. Further dopamine blockade risks converting simple catatonia into the malignant form. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Guidance)

options.text: Start intravenous dantrolene and bromocriptine in a high dependency bed
options.rationale: This is the treatment for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, the main differential, but that diagnosis requires fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability and a markedly raised creatine kinase, none of which is present here. Waxy flexibility and gegenhalten are features of catatonia rather than of the rigidity of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange urgent brain imaging and lumbar puncture before treatment
options.rationale: Investigation for an organic cause including autoimmune encephalitis is appropriate in a first presentation or where there are neurological signs, fever or cognitive fluctuation, and it may still be pursued in parallel. It should not delay a lorazepam challenge that is low risk and may produce a diagnostic response within the hour. (Source: RANZCP: Catatonia Guidance)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a motor dysregulation syndrome that occurs across psychiatric and medical conditions, most commonly with mood disorders rather than schizophrenia despite its historical association, and also with autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic derangement and drug withdrawal. It is substantially underdiagnosed because its features are read as negative symptoms, depression or non compliance, and the Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale exists to make the examination systematic. Two or more of the recognised signs, including stupor, mutism, negativism, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia, echopraxia, stereotypy and automatic obedience, establish the diagnosis. Benzodiazepines are first line, with lorazepam producing a response in a majority of cases, and electroconvulsive therapy is the definitive treatment for those who do not respond and for malignant catatonia. Malignant catatonia adds fever and autonomic instability and overlaps clinically with neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with antipsychotics contraindicated in both.
key_points: Two or more catatonic signs establish the diagnosis; the Bush Francis scale structures the examination.
Mood disorders are the commonest psychiatric substrate, not schizophrenia.
A parenteral lorazepam challenge serves as both diagnostic test and first line treatment.
Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and risk progression to the malignant form.
Electroconvulsive therapy is definitive for benzodiazepine non response and for malignant catatonia.
explanation.pearls: A lorazepam challenge uses 1 to 2 mg parenterally with the catatonic signs re-scored at 5 to 10 minutes, and a partial response justifies proceeding to regular dosing that often reaches 8 to 16 mg daily without the sedation that those doses would cause in a non catatonic patient.

subtopic_detail: reviewing an established anticonvulsant mood stabiliser when a woman of reproductive age discloses she is no longer using contraception
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic reviewing a 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder. She has taken sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for four years and has had no mood episode in three years, having previously had two manic admissions.

Today she tells you she stopped her oral contraceptive three months ago because she and her partner would like to start a family within the year, and she has not told anyone at the service. She has had no mood symptoms, sleeps well and is working. She takes no other medication and no folate supplement. Her last menstrual period was two weeks ago and a urine pregnancy test in clinic today is negative. She asks whether she should just keep taking the valproate until she actually falls pregnant and then stop it.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychomotor change, insight preserved
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative today, full blood count and liver function within normal limits
data_table.Medication and history: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 4 years, no mood episode for 3 years, two previous manic admissions, contraception ceased 3 months ago, no folate supplement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue valproate and restart reliable contraception, deferring pregnancy until the illness is longer in remission
options.rationale: Requiring a longer remission before allowing a pregnancy substitutes the clinician's preference for the patient's reproductive decision when a safer alternative regimen exists. Reliable contraception is genuinely needed while she remains on valproate, but as a bridge during the switch rather than as the plan itself. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Cease valproate today and manage her without any mood stabiliser while she tries to conceive
options.rationale: Stopping a mood stabiliser without replacing it exposes a woman with two previous manic admissions to relapse during pregnancy and the postpartum, which is itself the period of highest risk in bipolar disorder. Untreated illness in pregnancy carries its own harms and is not the safe option it appears to be. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Plan a switch to a mood stabiliser suitable in pregnancy and start high dose folate now
options.rationale: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of any mood stabiliser, with major congenital malformation in roughly 10 per cent and neurodevelopmental impairment in around 30 to 40 per cent of exposed children, and the neural tube closes by day 28 when many pregnancies are not yet recognised. Switching must therefore be planned before conception rather than at a positive test, with high dose folate started in advance and the transition made slowly while she is euthymic. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Continue valproate and stop it as soon as a pregnancy test becomes positive, with folate then
options.rationale: This is the plan she proposes and it fails on timing, because neural tube closure is complete before a missed period is usually investigated and the damage is already done by the time a test turns positive. Abrupt cessation at that point also risks a manic relapse in the first trimester. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Continue valproate at a reduced dose of 500 mg daily with high dose folate supplementation
options.rationale: Teratogenic risk falls with dose but does not disappear below any safe threshold, and folate supplementation has not been shown to prevent valproate associated malformations in the way it prevents idiopathic neural tube defects. Halving the dose also risks losing the prophylaxis that has held her well for three years. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Valproate is effective in bipolar disorder but is the most teratogenic of the mood stabilisers, and regulatory authorities in Australia and internationally now require that it not be used in women of childbearing potential unless other options have failed and a pregnancy prevention framework is in place. Exposure in the first trimester produces neural tube defects, cardiac and craniofacial malformations, and limb defects, with an absolute major malformation rate around 10 per cent, and in utero exposure also lowers childhood cognitive scores and raises autism spectrum diagnosis rates. The practical problem is that roughly half of pregnancies are unplanned and the neural tube closes by day 28, so a plan that begins at a positive pregnancy test is always too late. Lithium is generally preferred for a woman with predominantly manic illness, with a small absolute increase in cardiac malformation risk that is far lower than valproate's, while lamotrigine suits predominantly depressive illness. Any switch is made while the patient is well, slowly, with contraception maintained until it is complete.
key_points: Valproate exposure in pregnancy causes major malformation in about 10 per cent and neurodevelopmental harm in 30 to 40 per cent.
The neural tube closes by day 28, before most pregnancies are recognised, so switching must precede conception.
Risk falls with dose but no safe threshold exists, and folate does not abolish the teratogenic effect.
Lithium suits predominantly manic illness in pregnancy; lamotrigine suits predominantly depressive illness.
Maintain contraception throughout the switch and complete it while the patient is euthymic.
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine clearance rises sharply through pregnancy because of oestrogen induced glucuronidation, so levels can fall by half by the third trimester and the dose must be raised during pregnancy and then reduced within days of birth to avoid toxicity.

subtopic_detail: selecting parenteral sedation for escalating aggression after verbal measures and oral medication have been refused
stem: A 32-year-old man brought in by police is pacing, shouting and has kicked a trolley across the corridor. Twenty minutes of de-escalation has failed and he has twice refused oral olanzapine. Police report three days of methamphetamine use. No electrocardiogram has been possible. He now advances on a nurse with a clenched fist.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122 /min, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dilated pupils, no focal signs or head injury
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 6.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management now?

options.text: Midazolam 10 mg intramuscularly, repeated every 10 minutes until sedated
options.rationale: Midazolam works quickly but produces more respiratory depression and more frequent need for airway intervention than droperidol, and an open ended repeat schedule compounds that risk. It is a reasonable adjunct where a single agent has failed rather than a first line choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Withhold sedation until an electrocardiogram excludes a prolonged QT interval
options.rationale: Waiting for a tracing that cannot be obtained in an actively assaultive patient leaves staff at risk and delays treatment indefinitely. Australian emergency data have shown that droperidol at these doses does not produce clinically significant QT related events, which is why a pre-sedation electrocardiogram is not a prerequisite in this setting. (Source: ACEM: Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline)

options.text: Ketamine 4 mg/kg intramuscularly with anaesthetic support on standby
options.rationale: Ketamine is reserved as a rescue agent for severe disturbance that has failed conventional sedation, because it carries higher rates of intubation, laryngospasm and emergence phenomena. Using it before a first line agent has been tried escalates risk without evidence of benefit. (Source: ACEM: Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline)

options.text: Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous monitoring after restraint
options.rationale: Droperidol given intramuscularly is the agent supported by the largest Australian emergency department trials for acute behavioural disturbance, achieving sedation faster and with fewer additional doses than benzodiazepine monotherapy, and its cardiac safety at these doses has been demonstrated prospectively. Continuous monitoring after administration is part of the intervention rather than an optional extra, because the main risks are over sedation and airway compromise. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Offer oral diazepam 10 mg with a further period of verbal de-escalation
options.rationale: Oral medication requires cooperation he has already twice declined, and diazepam has a slow and unpredictable onset by mouth, so this leaves a nurse exposed to imminent assault. Continued de-escalation is correct until the point of physical threat, which has now been crossed. (Source: ACEM: Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline)

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance is managed along a graded pathway that begins with environmental measures and verbal de-escalation, moves to offered oral medication, and reaches parenteral sedation with physical restraint only when there is an immediate risk to the patient or others. Australian emergency medicine research, particularly the work underpinning current practice, established droperidol as an effective and safe first line parenteral agent and overturned an earlier international withdrawal driven by concerns about QT prolongation.
