Sedation is a high risk intervention in its own right, so continuous observation with pulse oximetry, regular vital signs and airway readiness is mandatory afterwards, and the duration of any restraint must be the minimum necessary and fully documented. Every episode requires consideration of the medical differential, since hypoglycaemia, head injury, hypoxia, sepsis, delirium and drug intoxication or withdrawal all present with agitation. A debrief with the patient and with staff afterwards is part of the standard, as is review of whether the legal framework used was appropriate.
key_points: De-escalation and offered oral medication precede parenteral sedation wherever it is safe to attempt them.
Droperidol intramuscularly is the first line parenteral agent in Australian emergency practice.
Continuous monitoring after sedation is mandatory, with over sedation and airway compromise the main risks.
Exclude hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, head injury and sepsis as causes of agitation in every case.
Restraint must be for the shortest necessary period, documented, and followed by a debrief.
explanation.pearls: Check a blood glucose before or immediately alongside sedation in every agitated patient, since hypoglycaemia is the one cause of acute behavioural disturbance that sedation alone will convert from reversible into fatal.

subtopic_detail: selecting first line treatment for involuntary movements and vocalisations in an adolescent whose school is demanding they be stopped
stem: A 13-year-old boy's school asks that his shoulder shrugging, eye blinking and throat clearing be stopped because they disrupt the classroom. They began at age seven, different ones come and go over months, and they are worse when he is tired. He can hold them back briefly but the urge builds until he lets it out.

data_table.Examination: Movements observed, suppressible with rebound, no chorea, normal tone
data_table.Negative findings: No obsessions or compulsions, no academic or social impairment, only mild distress to him

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Commence risperidone and titrate against the frequency of the movements
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do reduce tic severity and are used when tics cause pain, injury or substantial impairment, but they bring weight gain, metabolic change and extrapyramidal effects to a boy whose tics bother his school more than they bother him. Tic treatment is guided by the patient's own impairment rather than by an external complaint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for compulsive behaviour
options.rationale: These agents treat the obsessive compulsive disorder that frequently coexists with tic disorders, but a compulsion is performed to neutralise an obsessional thought whereas his movements follow a physical premonitory urge. He has no obsessions on direct questioning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise suppression in class and reward successful suppression at home
options.rationale: Suppression without a substitute response is effortful and followed by a rebound increase, so a reward program built on it sets him up to fail and adds shame to the picture. Habit reversal differs precisely in that it supplies a competing movement to perform when the urge arrives. (Source: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

options.text: Arrange brain magnetic resonance imaging and an antistreptolysin O titre
options.rationale: Investigation is reserved for atypical features such as abrupt onset, a fixed rather than migrating pattern, or abnormal neurological signs, none of which he has after six years of a classical waxing and waning course. A raised streptococcal titre is common in healthy children and would generate uncertainty rather than resolve it. (Source: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

options.text: Refer for comprehensive behavioural intervention with habit reversal training
options.rationale: Behavioural therapy built around habit reversal is first line for tic disorders where the tics themselves cause limited impairment, and it teaches a competing response to the premonitory urge rather than attempting suppression. Psychoeducation directed at the school is an essential part of it, because demands to stop the tics increase anxiety and therefore tic frequency. (Source: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

explanation.summary: Tic disorders affect roughly 1 per cent of school-aged children, with Tourette syndrome requiring multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic present for more than a year with onset before age 18. The features that distinguish tics from other movement disorders are the premonitory urge, temporary suppressibility with rebound, a waxing and waning course over months, and variation with fatigue, excitement and anxiety. Severity typically peaks in early adolescence and improves substantially through the late teens in the majority, which is an important part of what families are told. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder coexist in a large proportion and frequently cause more functional impairment than the tics themselves, so both are screened for in every case. Treatment is stepped, beginning with education of the family and school and behavioural therapy, with medication reserved for tics causing pain, injury, or genuine impairment reported by the young person rather than by others.
key_points: A premonitory urge relieved by the movement distinguishes a tic from chorea, dystonia or a stereotypy.
Suppression is possible briefly but is effortful and followed by rebound.
Screen every child with tics for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder.
Severity usually peaks in early adolescence and improves through the late teens.
Treat the impairment the young person reports, not the disruption reported by others.
explanation.pearls: Habit reversal works by pairing awareness training with a competing response that is physically incompatible with the tic and held for about a minute until the urge subsides, which is why it succeeds where simple instruction to stop reliably fails.

sources.label: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

subtopic_detail: responding to new agitation in residential care when an antipsychotic is requested and a reversible precipitant has not been sought
stem:
You are the general practitioner attending a residential aged care facility. Staff ask you to prescribe risperidone for an 82-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer disease who has become agitated and resistive over the past five days, shouting during personal care and pushing a carer's hand away during showering.

He has lived there for two years with no previous behavioural concerns and no history of aggression. Staff say the behaviour happens almost entirely during showering and toileting and that he settles within minutes once left alone in his chair. They report he has been eating less and that his urine has smelled strong, although a dipstick two days ago showed leucocytes with no nitrites and he has no fever or dysuria. He started oxybutynin three weeks ago for urinary frequency, prescribed by a locum. His usual medications are donepezil, perindopril and atorvastatin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, blood pressure 126/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Calm when seated, distressed only during personal care, dry mouth, abdomen soft with a fullness suprapubically, no guarding
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick two days ago with leucocytes and no nitrites, no fever or dysuria
data_table.Medications: Donepezil, perindopril, atorvastatin, and oxybutynin started 3 weeks ago for urinary frequency

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Assess for a reversible precipitant including urinary retention and review the oxybutynin
options.rationale: New behaviour change in established dementia is treated as a symptom with a cause, and the timing after an anticholinergic was started, the dry mouth, the suprapubic fullness and the confinement of distress to toileting and showering all point to retention. Anticholinergics also worsen cognition directly and oppose the cholinesterase inhibitor he is already taking, so reviewing that drug addresses two problems at once. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Start trimethoprim 300 mg at night for seven days to treat a urinary tract infection
options.rationale: Leucocytes without nitrites in an afebrile resident with no dysuria most often represents asymptomatic bacteriuria or sample contamination rather than infection, and treating it drives resistance without improving behaviour. Strong smelling urine is not a diagnostic criterion for urinary tract infection at any age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start oxazepam 7.5 mg before showering to reduce distress during personal care episodes
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines in older people with dementia increase falls, fractures and confusion and can cause paradoxical disinhibition, and premedicating before care would entrench the problem rather than solve it. Timing sedation to a trigger also concedes that the trigger has not been examined. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the donepezil dose and arrange review by the dementia behaviour advisory service
options.rationale: Specialist behavioural advice is valuable and the service is a genuine Australian resource, but escalating the cholinesterase inhibitor does not treat acute agitation and the referral pathway takes time he does not need to spend in pain. The immediate task is to look for the reversible cause. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Start risperidone 0.25 mg at night and review the behaviour after two weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Antipsychotics in dementia raise the risk of stroke and of death and are indicated only after reversible causes are excluded and non-pharmacological measures have failed, usually where there is severe distress or risk of harm. Prescribing now would treat a behaviour whose trigger is identifiable and whose likely cause is sitting in his medication list. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are common but a sudden change in a resident who has been settled for years should be read as a new symptom with a cause rather than as disease progression. The standard approach examines pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, drug effects, sensory impairment, and the environmental and interpersonal triggers around care tasks, since resistance confined to showering or toileting almost always signals discomfort or a sense of threat during that activity. Anticholinergic drugs are a frequent and reversible contributor, worsening cognition, precipitating retention, and directly opposing cholinesterase inhibitors prescribed for the dementia itself. Antipsychotics carry an increased risk of cerebrovascular events and death in this population, are restricted under Australian aged care quality standards, require informed consent from the resident or substitute decision maker, and should be reviewed for cessation within twelve weeks when used. Non-pharmacological approaches, including changing who provides care, the time of day and the manner of approach, resolve a large proportion of these presentations.
key_points: A sudden behavioural change in stable dementia is a symptom with a cause until proven otherwise.
Screen for pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, new drugs and sensory deficits first.
Anticholinergics worsen cognition, cause retention and oppose cholinesterase inhibitors.
Antipsychotics in dementia increase stroke and mortality risk and require consent and time limited review.
Behaviour confined to personal care usually reflects discomfort or perceived threat during that task.
explanation.pearls: A bladder scan at the bedside takes two minutes and a residual volume above 300 mL identifies retention as the cause of agitation in a resident who cannot report it, which is a far higher yield first test than a urine dipstick in this setting.

subtopic_detail: deciding on inpatient medical admission for a young person with restrictive eating when the weight alone does not meet the usual threshold
stem: A 17-year-old woman has six months of food restriction and compulsive exercise. She weighs 52 kg at 168 cm (body mass index 18.4), down from 68 kg six months ago, and insists she is not underweight. She fainted once while running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38 /min sitting, blood pressure 98/56 sitting and 74/48 standing, temperature 35.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries, lanugo hair, cannot rise from a squat unaided
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), phosphate 0.71 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), corrected QT interval 468 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fluoxetine with psychiatric outpatient follow up in two weeks
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a role in bulimia nervosa and in comorbid depression once weight is restored, but it does not treat restrictive eating and is ineffective in the malnourished state. Starting it now would also delay the medical care that her observations demand. (Source: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Urgent medical admission for cardiac monitoring and refeeding
options.rationale: Admission criteria in eating disorders are driven by physiological instability rather than by body mass index, and she has bradycardia below 40, a postural systolic drop over 20 mmHg, hypothermia, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia and a prolonged corrected QT interval. The rate and magnitude of weight loss, 16 kg in six months, carries the physiological risk here even though the absolute weight sits in the population healthy range. (Source: ANZAED: Eating Disorder Treatment Principles)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Outpatient family based treatment with weekly weight and electrolytes
options.rationale: Family based treatment is the highest evidence outpatient treatment for adolescents and will be the right framework once she is medically stable, so this is the correct destination reached in the wrong order. Outpatient care assumes physiological stability, which her bradycardia and postural drop exclude. (Source: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Oral potassium replacement, stop running and review in one week
options.rationale: Correcting a single electrolyte while leaving her unmonitored ignores the bradycardia, the prolonged corrected QT interval and the hypophosphataemia, any of which can precipitate an arrhythmia. A week is a long interval for a patient who has already fainted. (Source: ANZAED: Eating Disorder Treatment Principles)

options.text: Reassurance that her body mass index is healthy, with dietitian review
options.rationale: Using body mass index alone as the gate for concern is the specific error this presentation tests, and it is the reasoning that produced the earlier reassurance she now quotes back. A person can be physiologically critical at a normal body weight if the loss has been rapid. (Source: ANZAED: Eating Disorder Treatment Principles)

explanation.summary: Decisions about admission in eating disorders rest on physiological parameters, the rate of weight loss and psychiatric risk, not on body mass index in isolation, and the group most often missed is those whose starting weight was high and who therefore remain in the population healthy range after losing a dangerous amount. Cardiovascular instability is the dominant acute risk, with bradycardia below 40 beats per minute, postural drops, hypotension, hypothermia and electrolyte disturbance all indicating a need for monitored inpatient care. Refeeding syndrome follows the reintroduction of carbohydrate to a depleted patient, as insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly and thiamine stores are consumed, producing arrhythmia, cardiac failure, delirium and seizures. A phosphate already below the reference range before feeding has begun marks a patient at particularly high risk. Australian practice uses supervised refeeding with daily electrolytes in the first week, thiamine before any carbohydrate load, and the recognition that starting too cautiously prolongs malnutrition and carries its own harm.
key_points: Admission decisions rest on physiological instability, not body mass index alone.
Rapid or large weight loss carries risk even when the absolute weight appears normal.
Bradycardia below 40, postural drop over 20 mmHg systolic and hypothermia are admission criteria.
A low phosphate before feeding starts identifies a patient at high risk of refeeding syndrome.
Give thiamine before any carbohydrate load and monitor phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily.
explanation.pearls: Bradycardia in anorexia nervosa is an adaptive energy conserving response, so a pulse that rises while the patient is still losing weight signals infection or another intercurrent illness rather than recovery, and it is a more worrying sign than the bradycardia itself.

sources.label: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: attributing persistent psychotic symptoms between mood episodes when a stimulant history offers a competing explanation
stem: A 29-year-old man has two years of case notes recording three episodes: two of elevated mood with reduced sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech lasting about a month each, and one depressive episode of ten weeks. He believed a government agency was inserting thoughts into his mind during all three. He used methamphetamine two to three times a week until fourteen months ago.

data_table.Course: Euthymic for four months with normal sleep, activity and speech, while thought insertion and a commenting voice have continued throughout
data_table.Substance history: Fortnightly supervised urine drug screens negative for fourteen months
data_table.Treatment: Quetiapine 400 mg at night throughout, no missed doses on pharmacy records

lead_in: Which diagnosis best accounts for this presentation?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
options.rationale: This cannot be correct because two discrete episodes of elevated mood with reduced sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech lasting a month each establish mania, which excludes a unipolar diagnosis entirely. Mood incongruent psychosis in unipolar depression does exist but requires that no manic episode has ever occurred. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features
options.rationale: This would be the diagnosis if every psychotic symptom appeared only alongside a mood episode and remitted with it, which was true of his first two years but is not true now. The four months of psychosis with euthymic mood ratings is the finding that breaks this option. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder of the bipolar type
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires an uninterrupted period of illness with a major mood episode concurrent with psychotic symptoms, plus delusions or hallucinations for two or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode, and mood episodes present for the majority of the total illness duration. His four months of psychosis with documented euthymia satisfies the second criterion, while three substantial mood episodes across two years satisfies the third. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Methamphetamine induced psychotic disorder
options.rationale: Stimulant induced psychosis usually resolves within a month of abstinence and a persisting form is described, which makes this a genuine competing explanation given his history. Fourteen months of supervised negative screens with symptoms continuing at full intensity, alongside three mood episodes, exceeds what the substance can account for. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Schizophrenia with a superimposed depressive episode
options.rationale: Schizophrenia is diagnosed when mood episodes are absent or brief relative to the total duration of illness, and his two manic and one depressive episodes occupy a substantial proportion of two years. The distinguishing quantity is the proportion of the illness during which a mood episode is present, which is the single criterion separating these two options. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder sits between the psychotic and mood disorders and is diagnosed longitudinally rather than cross sectionally, which is why a single interview can never establish it and a documented course is essential. The defining requirement is a period of two weeks or more of delusions or hallucinations without a prominent mood episode, occurring within an illness in which mood episodes are otherwise present for the majority of the time. If psychosis occurs only during mood episodes the diagnosis is a mood disorder with psychotic features, and if mood episodes are brief relative to the psychotic illness the diagnosis is schizophrenia. Substance induced psychosis must be excluded before either, and stimulant related psychosis is a particular problem in Australian practice because methamphetamine use is common, the symptoms are indistinguishable cross sectionally, and a persisting form exists. Diagnostic reasoning therefore rests on the timeline, namely how long the psychosis has outlasted abstinence and what proportion of the illness has been occupied by mood episodes, and the diagnosis is revisited as that picture develops.
key_points: The diagnosis requires two or more weeks of psychosis without a prominent mood episode.
Mood episodes must occupy the majority of the total duration of the illness.
Psychosis confined to mood episodes indicates a mood disorder with psychotic features instead.
Brief mood episodes relative to the psychotic illness indicate schizophrenia instead.
Stimulant induced psychosis usually resolves within a month of abstinence, so a persisting picture needs another explanation.
explanation.pearls: Methamphetamine associated psychosis recurs on re-exposure with far less drug and after a shorter interval than the original episode, a sensitisation effect that makes any return to use the single strongest predictor of relapse and which should shape relapse prevention planning more than adherence to antipsychotic alone.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Recognition and initial management of lithium toxicity precipitated by an NSAID interaction
stem: A 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has one week of tremor and drowsiness. She has taken lithium 900 mg nocte for six years, stable at 0.7 mmol/L. Two weeks ago she started ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, coarse tremor, 3 beats ankle clonus, ataxic gait, no rigidity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Whole bowel irrigation via nasogastric tube for 6 hours
options.rationale: Whole bowel irrigation is considered for acute massive ingestion of sustained-release lithium, not chronic toxicity with NSAID precipitant. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Reduce lithium to 450 mg nocte and stop the ibuprofen
options.rationale: Chronic toxicity at 1.6 mmol/L with neurological signs mandates cessation of lithium and admission; outpatient management is unsafe. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube, then observe
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind lithium; it is ineffective. Symptomatic management with saline and dialysis consult is required. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Stop lithium and ibuprofen, intravenous saline, nephrology review
options.rationale: Chronic lithium toxicity with neurological features and level >1.5 needs cessation, IV fluid and dialysis consult; NSAID must be stopped as the precipitant. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise the urine
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation does not enhance lithium clearance; normal saline volume expansion and dialysis (if severe) is appropriate. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Lithium is renally excreted; anything reducing renal function or sodium status raises lithium levels. Common precipitants of chronic toxicity: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, thiazide diuretics, dehydration, low-salt diet, acute kidney injury. Chronic toxicity typically presents at lower levels than acute (1.2 to 2.5 mmol/L) with neurological features (coarse tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, drowsiness). Severe toxicity (above 2.5 mmol/L or severe symptoms) causes seizures, coma, arrhythmia. Management: stop lithium and precipitant, intravenous normal saline for volume expansion (aiming for good urine output), monitor lithium 4 to 6 hourly and renal function. Haemodialysis is indicated for level above 4.0 mmol/L, above 2.5 with severe symptoms, or above 2.5 with renal failure. Activated charcoal is ineffective for lithium; whole bowel irrigation is for acute massive sustained-release ingestion.
key_points: Chronic lithium toxicity is precipitated by NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, thiazides, dehydration.
Neurological features (tremor, clonus, ataxia, confusion) at levels above 1.2 mmol/L.
Treat with cessation, IV saline; haemodialysis for level above 4.0 or severe symptoms.
explanation.pearls: Chronic lithium toxicity at 1.6 mmol/L with neurological signs after NSAID commencement: stop lithium and ibuprofen, IV saline 200 mL/h and nephrology consult for possible dialysis.

subtopic_detail: Recognition and immediate management of serotonin syndrome from an SSRI plus tramadol co-prescription
stem: A 38-year-old man taking sertraline 100 mg daily has two days of tremor, agitation and diarrhoea. Tramadol 50 mg four times daily was started four days ago.

data_table.Neurology: Agitated, diaphoretic, dilated pupils; spontaneous ankle clonus, hyperreflexia lower more than upper limbs, no rigidity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Intravenous methylene blue, with intensive care admission for monitoring
options.rationale: Methylene blue itself has serotonergic effects and would worsen the syndrome; it is contraindicated. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Intramuscular bromocriptine and dantrolene, then intubation for muscle rigidity
options.rationale: Bromocriptine and dantrolene are used for NMS not serotonin syndrome; distinguishing features are neuromuscular (clonus vs rigidity) and time course. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol for agitation, continuing both drugs at reduced dose
options.rationale: Continuing serotonergic agents perpetuates the syndrome; haloperidol adds anticholinergic burden without treating cause. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil for assumed benzodiazepine co-ingestion, pending drug screen
options.rationale: Flumazenil is not indicated (no benzodiazepine history); it can precipitate seizures. Serotonin syndrome does not need reversal - it needs cessation of the precipitants. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

options.text: Stop sertraline and tramadol, give diazepam, cool actively, consider cyproheptadine
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome (Hunter criteria met: clonus, hyperthermia, hyperreflexia) after tramadol added to SSRI needs cessation, benzodiazepine, cooling; cyproheptadine for refractory cases. (Source: TGA Poisons Information)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is a clinical diagnosis with the Hunter criteria: serotonergic agent plus one of: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; tremor and hyperreflexia; or hypertonia, temperature above 38 degC and ocular or inducible clonus. Common precipitants: SSRI plus tramadol, SSRI plus MAOI, SSRI plus linezolid, SSRI plus fentanyl or pethidine, SSRI plus St John wort, MDMA. Onset within hours to days. Distinguishing from NMS: serotonin syndrome features clonus and hyperreflexia predominantly in lower limbs, onset hours after precipitant; NMS features lead-pipe rigidity, onset over days after neuroleptic. Management: stop all serotonergic agents, benzodiazepines (diazepam 5-10 mg IV titrated) for agitation and tremor, active cooling for hyperthermia. Cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist, 12 mg orally then 2 mg every 2 hours) for moderate to severe cases. Muscle relaxation and intubation for severe hyperthermia (above 41 degC).
key_points: Hunter criteria: serotonergic agent plus clonus/hyperreflexia/temperature.
Clonus predominantly lower limbs distinguishes from NMS rigidity.
Treat: stop precipitants, benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine if severe.
explanation.pearls: SSRI plus tramadol with fever, agitation and lower-limb clonus is serotonin syndrome: stop both agents, give diazepam 5 mg IV titrated, cool actively, add cyproheptadine 12 mg for moderate to severe cases.

subtopic_detail: Interpretation of clozapine haematological monitoring and decision to continue or interrupt therapy
stem: A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg nocte for four years. He is well, with no fever or sore throat. Routine 4-weekly bloods were taken yesterday.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in clozapine management?

options.text: Empirical filgrastim daily for five days, continuing clozapine unchanged
options.rationale: Filgrastim is used in confirmed severe neutropenia (ANC below 0.5) or persistent moderate neutropenia; not indicated in amber range with a well patient. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)

options.text: Stop clozapine and admit for daily full blood counts and antibiotics
options.rationale: Immediate cessation and admission is for ANC below 0.5 x10^9/L (severe neutropenia); ANC 1.7 is amber not red. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)

options.text: Reduce clozapine to 300 mg nocte with monthly full blood counts
options.rationale: Dose reduction alone is not standard; weekly FBC is required in amber range and dose is unchanged unless further drop. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)

options.text: Continue clozapine, repeat the count in a week, screen for infection
options.rationale: ANC 1.5-2.0 x10^9/L is the amber (Watching) range: continue clozapine, repeat FBC weekly, monitor for infection. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)

options.text: Stop clozapine and switch to olanzapine 20 mg nocte the same day
options.rationale: Switching antipsychotic in a stable patient with amber-range neutropenia is not indicated and risks psychotic relapse. (Source: TGA Clozapine Monitoring Guideline)

explanation.summary: Clozapine can cause neutropenia and agranulocytosis (1 to 2 percent lifetime risk of agranulocytosis) requiring mandatory haematological monitoring. Australian monitoring (Clopine/Clozaril/Zaponex Patient Monitoring): weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then 4 weekly indefinitely. Traffic light system in Australia: Green (WCC >=3.5 and ANC >=2.0 x10^9/L) continue at current schedule; Amber (WCC 3.0-3.5 or ANC 1.5-2.0) continue with twice weekly FBC; Red (WCC below 3.0 or ANC below 1.5) stop clozapine and daily FBC (formal cut-offs vary by monitoring service - Clopine Red is WCC below 3.0 x10^9/L or ANC below 1.5 x10^9/L). ANC below 0.5 is severe agranulocytosis requiring reverse isolation and haematology involvement. Benign ethnic neutropenia (common in African, Middle Eastern, some Mediterranean descent) has separate lower thresholds under specialist supervision.
key_points: Clopine Red = WCC <3.0 or ANC <1.5 x10^9/L: stop clozapine, daily FBC.
ANC 1.5-2.0 (amber) = continue clozapine, weekly FBC, screen for infection.
ANC below 0.5 = severe agranulocytosis: haematology, reverse isolation.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine monitoring - ANC 1.7 x10^9/L in a well patient with no infection is in the amber range at RANZCP: continue clozapine, repeat FBC weekly and screen for occult infection - do not stop the drug.

subtopic_detail: Choice of benzodiazepine for alcohol withdrawal in the setting of established cirrhotic liver disease
stem: A 58-year-old man has drunk 15 standard drinks daily for 20 years and stopped 36 hours ago. He has alcoholic cirrhosis with a MELD of 14. He is agitated and diaphoretic with visual hallucinations of small animals.

data_table.Mental state: Alcohol Withdrawal Scale 14, coarse tremor, no seizures, no encephalopathy
data_table.Bloods: Platelets 82 x10^9/L, INR 1.4, albumin 28 g/L, bilirubin 40 micromol/L

lead_in: Which benzodiazepine regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam 5 mg two hourly
options.rationale: Midazolam is short-acting and unsuitable for withdrawal maintenance; intramuscular route has erratic absorption. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))

options.text: Oral diazepam 20 mg every two hours
options.rationale: Diazepam has active metabolites (nordiazepam) that accumulate in cirrhosis, risking prolonged sedation and precipitating hepatic encephalopathy. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))

options.text: Oral oxazepam 30 mg every four hours
options.rationale: Oxazepam has no active metabolites and non-hepatic metabolism (glucuronidation), making it safer than diazepam in cirrhosis. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))

options.text: Oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg every four hours
options.rationale: Chlordiazepoxide has active metabolites and hepatic metabolism, so it accumulates in cirrhosis; not preferred here. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))

options.text: Intravenous phenobarbital 130 mg two hourly
options.rationale: Phenobarbital is reserved for benzodiazepine-refractory delirium tremens; it is not first line and requires close monitoring. (Source: Australian Alcohol Guidelines (NHMRC))

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal severity is graded on the Alcohol Withdrawal Scale or CIWA-Ar. Mild withdrawal (score below 8): symptomatic care, no benzodiazepine needed. Moderate to severe (score 8 or above): benzodiazepine loading and symptom-triggered dosing. Diazepam 10 to 20 mg orally 2 hourly is first line in patients with normal liver function due to long half-life and active metabolites providing smooth wean. In cirrhosis, hepatic encephalopathy risk and metabolite accumulation make short-acting agents metabolised by glucuronidation (LOT: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) preferred; oxazepam 15 to 30 mg orally 4 hourly is the Australian standard in cirrhosis. Thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 3-5 days before any glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Delirium tremens (autonomic instability, hyperthermia, hallucinations) has mortality of 5-15 percent untreated; treat aggressively with high-dose benzodiazepines, IV fluid and monitoring. Phenobarbital is second line for benzodiazepine-refractory delirium tremens.
key_points: Diazepam is first line for alcohol withdrawal in normal liver function.
In cirrhosis, use LOT (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) - glucuronidation not oxidative metabolism.
Thiamine 300 mg IV daily 3-5 days before glucose to prevent Wernicke.
explanation.pearls: Alcohol withdrawal in cirrhosis at NHMRC uses oxazepam 15-30 mg orally 4 hourly (glucuronidated, no active metabolites) instead of diazepam - active nordiazepam metabolite of diazepam accumulates and can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.

subtopic_detail: First-line antidepressant selection and monitoring in a depressed adolescent with suicidal ideation but no intent
stem: A 15-year-old girl has eight weeks of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and 3 kg weight loss. She has passive thoughts of not wanting to wake up, with no plan or intent. Six weeks of weekly cognitive behavioural therapy has not helped. She has never taken psychotropic medication.

data_table.Mental state: Tearful, psychomotor slowing, hopelessness, no psychotic features
data_table.History: No family history of bipolar disorder

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral sertraline 25 mg daily titrated to 50 mg
options.rationale: Sertraline is used in adolescent MDD but has weaker adolescent evidence than fluoxetine; fluoxetine is first line in adolescents at RANZCP. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

options.text: Oral fluoxetine 10 mg daily titrated to 20 mg
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is the only SSRI with TGA and RANZCP recommendation for adolescent MDD after CBT failure; requires weekly review for suicidality first month. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

options.text: Oral venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily titrated to 75 mg
options.rationale: Venlafaxine has an FDA black box warning in adolescents with increased suicidality; not first line for adolescent MDD. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

options.text: Continue psychological therapy and defer pharmacotherapy
options.rationale: CBT for 6 weeks without improvement in moderate to severe adolescent MDD is trial failure; RANZCP recommends adding fluoxetine, not continuing psychotherapy alone. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

options.text: Admit to an adolescent inpatient psychiatric unit
options.rationale: Passive SI without plan or intent, with family support and no self-harm history, does not require inpatient admission; outpatient management with fluoxetine and safety planning is appropriate. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Depression)

explanation.summary: Adolescent major depression (age 12-17) is managed with a stepped approach. Mild MDD: psychoeducation, sleep hygiene, exercise, brief psychological intervention. Moderate to severe MDD or mild MDD failing brief intervention: cognitive behavioural therapy or interpersonal therapy for adolescents as first line for 6 to 8 weeks. If inadequate response or severe presentation, add pharmacotherapy. Fluoxetine 10 to 20 mg daily is the only SSRI with TGA and RANZCP endorsement as first-line pharmacotherapy in adolescents (based on TADS trial data). Sertraline is second line. Venlafaxine and paroxetine are avoided in adolescents due to increased suicidality risk. Weekly clinical review for the first four weeks of any antidepressant in adolescents is mandatory (increased short-term risk of suicidality in the first month). Safety planning should be documented and shared with parents/carers. Combination of CBT and fluoxetine is more effective than either alone (TADS trial).
key_points: Fluoxetine 10-20 mg is first-line adolescent SSRI (TADS trial, TGA and RANZCP endorsed).
Weekly review for 4 weeks after starting antidepressant in adolescents.
Avoid venlafaxine and paroxetine in adolescents (suicidality risk).
explanation.pearls: Adolescent MDD failing CBT: add fluoxetine 10 mg daily and review weekly for 4 weeks - fluoxetine is the only SSRI RANZCP endorses first line in adolescents, not sertraline.

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic choice in a first-episode psychosis in a young man with metabolic and adherence considerations
stem: A 21-year-old man has six weeks of paranoid delusions that his housemates are poisoning his food, third person auditory hallucinations and social withdrawal. He has smoked five to ten cones of cannabis daily for three years. He says he will not take a medication that causes weight gain.

data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4%, QTc 420 ms, urine cannabinoids only

lead_in: Which oral antipsychotic is most appropriate to commence?

options.text: Olanzapine 5 mg at night, increased to 10 mg after one week
options.rationale: Olanzapine has the highest weight gain and dyslipidaemia burden of second-generation antipsychotics and directly conflicts with this patient's stated preference and adherence risk. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

options.text: Aripiprazole 10 mg daily, increased to 15 mg after one week
options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the lowest weight-gain profile among second-generation antipsychotics and is preferred first-line for FEP where metabolic risk and adherence concern medication acceptance. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

options.text: Haloperidol 2 mg twice daily, increased to 5 mg twice daily
options.rationale: First-generation antipsychotics are not preferred first line in FEP due to higher extrapyramidal side-effect burden; second-generation agents are preferred. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

options.text: Risperidone 1 mg twice daily, increased to 3 mg twice daily
options.rationale: Risperidone has a dose-related risk of extrapyramidal side effects and prolactin elevation with reduced acceptability in a young man. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

options.text: Clozapine 12.5 mg daily, titrated upwards over two weeks
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of two adequate trials of other antipsychotics); not first line for FEP. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: First-episode psychosis is a critical intervention window where antipsychotic choice balances efficacy, tolerability, metabolic risk and patient preference to maximise adherence. RANZCP recommends second-generation antipsychotics as first line, matched to patient factors. Aripiprazole has the lowest weight-gain profile (partial dopamine agonist), no prolactin elevation and minimal QTc effect, making it preferred for young men with metabolic risk factors or concern about weight gain. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden. Risperidone has dose-related extrapyramidal and prolactin effects. Cannabis use is common in FEP and worsens the psychotic prodrome; concurrent referral to youth AOD services for brief intervention is standard. Depot antipsychotics can be considered early to support adherence. Metabolic monitoring at baseline, 6 weeks, 3 months, then annually is mandated (weight, BP, fasting glucose, lipids).
key_points: Second-generation antipsychotic first line in FEP, matched to patient factors.
Aripiprazole has the lowest weight-gain and prolactin profile; olanzapine the highest.
Refer to youth AOD service concurrently for cannabis brief intervention.
explanation.pearls: FEP in a young man with cannabis use and stated aversion to weight-gaining medications: aripiprazole 10 mg is preferred over olanzapine because aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic burden and best supports adherence.

subtopic_detail: Emergency department risk assessment and disposition for repeated self-harm in emotionally unstable personality disorder
stem: A 26-year-old woman with emotionally unstable personality disorder presents after superficial cutting of the forearm, her fifth presentation in three months, each after an interpersonal stressor. She attends weekly dialectical behaviour therapy, and her case manager agrees she is at her usual baseline.

data_table.Wound: Superficial, clean edges, no sutures needed
data_table.Mental state: Tearful, denies suicidal ideation, not intoxicated
data_table.Supports: Mother and partner at home overnight, safety plan in her bag

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with next-day case manager contact and safety plan review
options.rationale: Repeated superficial self-harm in EUPD without acute high-risk features is best managed in community per RANZCP; ED admission does not improve outcomes and can reinforce escalation. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

options.text: Admit involuntarily to an acute psychiatric unit for 72 hours
options.rationale: Involuntary admission is not indicated: she is at baseline, has supports and denies suicidality; inpatient admission worsens outcomes in EUPD. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

options.text: Admit to a short stay unit and start quetiapine 100 mg nocte
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not first line for EUPD and quetiapine sedation increases self-harm reinforcement; RANZCP recommends against routine pharmacotherapy. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

options.text: Admit voluntarily to a psychiatric intensive care unit for 48 hours
options.rationale: Intensive care admission is disproportionate and reinforces presentation escalation; DBT plus community support is the evidence-based pathway. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

options.text: Discharge with general practitioner review next week and no other contact
options.rationale: Discharge without case manager liaison or safety plan review misses the opportunity to reinforce structured support and update the crisis plan. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline BPD)

explanation.summary: Emotionally unstable personality disorder (EUPD, ICD-11) or borderline personality disorder is characterised by pervasive instability of affect, interpersonal relationships and self-image, with impulsivity and recurrent self-harm. Repeated brief emergency department presentations after interpersonal stressors are typical. RANZCP evidence-based guideline: psychotherapy (dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation based therapy) is first-line treatment. Pharmacotherapy is not routine and should be time-limited if used for a comorbid disorder. Hospital admission does not improve outcomes and can reinforce the pattern of self-harm as help-seeking; brief admission (24 to 72 hours) is reserved for objectively high risk of suicide (specific plan, means, escalation from usual pattern) or acute psychosocial crisis without other supports. In the ED, wound care, brief supportive assessment, validation of distress, safety plan review, and rapid linkage back to the community team is the recommended pathway. Family and case manager should be engaged.
key_points: DBT and MBT are first-line psychotherapies in EUPD; pharmacotherapy not routine.
Admission does not improve outcomes and can reinforce escalation of self-harm.
ED role: wound care, validation, safety plan review, community team linkage.
explanation.pearls: Recurrent superficial self-harm in EUPD at baseline: wound care, safety plan review, discharge to family with case manager next-day contact - admission reinforces the pattern and does not improve outcomes per RANZCP.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

subtopic_detail: Recognition and management of refeeding hypophosphataemia during nutritional rehabilitation of severe anorexia nervosa
stem: A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa was admitted 48 hours ago for nutritional rehabilitation at a body mass index of 12.8 kg/m2. Nasogastric feeding began at 20 kcal/kg/day. She reports new fatigue and leg weakness.

data_table.Bloods (48 h): Phosphate 0.42 mmol/L (0.75-1.5), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cease the feed and give intravenous dextrose with intravenous phosphate
options.rationale: Complete feed cessation loses accumulated nutritional gains; graded reduction with correction is preferred; dextrose stimulates insulin and worsens intracellular shift. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.text: Continue the feed at 20 kcal/kg/day and give oral phosphate three times daily
options.rationale: Continued full feed with symptomatic hypophosphataemia risks progression to cardiac and neurological failure; slow feed reduction and IV correction is needed. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.text: Increase the feed to 40 kcal/kg/day and give oral phosphate twice daily
options.rationale: Increasing feed will worsen refeeding syndrome; the pathophysiology is intracellular phosphate shift driven by insulin surge with feeding. (Source: RANZCOG Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.text: Reduce the feed to 10 kcal/kg/day and give intravenous phosphate, magnesium and potassium
options.rationale: Symptomatic refeeding syndrome with phosphate 0.42 mmol/L requires calorie reduction plus IV phosphate, magnesium and potassium replacement per RANZCP eating disorders guideline. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

options.text: Continue the feed and defer correction until phosphate falls below 0.3 mmol/L
options.rationale: Waiting for phosphate below 0.3 mmol/L or organ failure risks catastrophic outcome; refeeding syndrome is progressive and needs early correction. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is the metabolic response to reintroduction of nutrition in a malnourished patient, driven by insulin release causing intracellular shift of phosphate, magnesium and potassium and thiamine consumption. Risk factors: BMI below 16, 15 percent weight loss over 3 months, minimal nutrition intake over 10 days, low pre-refeed electrolytes. Diagnosis is a fall of at least 30 percent in serum phosphate from baseline or an absolute phosphate below 0.6 mmol/L. Australian practice starts refeeding at 20 kcal/kg/day in high-risk anorexia nervosa (previously as low as 10 kcal/kg/day, but current evidence supports 20 kcal/kg/day with intensive electrolyte monitoring and correction). Prevention and management: thiamine 300 mg IV daily for 5 days before or with feed commencement, daily electrolytes for the first week, prompt replacement of phosphate, magnesium and potassium. When refeeding syndrome develops: reduce feed rate to 10 kcal/kg/day, correct electrolytes intravenously if symptomatic or severe, then re-titrate feed upward as electrolytes normalise. Ongoing multidisciplinary eating disorders team involvement is essential.
key_points: Refeeding syndrome: intracellular shift of phosphate, magnesium, potassium with feeding.
Severe hypophosphataemia (below 0.6 mmol/L) or symptomatic: IV replacement, reduce feed.
Thiamine 300 mg IV daily 5 days precedes or accompanies refeeding.
explanation.pearls: Refeeding hypophosphataemia at 48 hours with phosphate 0.42 mmol/L in anorexia nervosa: reduce feed to 10 kcal/kg/day and give IV phosphate 30 mmol plus magnesium and potassium - do not increase or continue full feed rate.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines Eating Disorders

subtopic_detail: Second-generation antipsychotic metabolic monitoring schedule
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 29-year-old man 3 months after commencing olanzapine 15 mg orally each evening for a first episode of schizophrenia. He has stopped hearing voices and is looking for work. His weight has risen from 82 kg to 90 kg over the 3 months, his waist circumference is 102 cm, and he smokes 10 cigarettes daily. He has no personal or family history of diabetes and does not drink alcohol.

Baseline fasting glucose was 4.9 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4) and fasting lipids were within normal limits. Blood pressure today is 132/84 mmHg. He asks how often he now needs blood tests since he is feeling well and has commenced full-time TAFE study.

data_table.Weight trajectory: 82 kg baseline to 90 kg at 3 months; waist circumference 102 cm
data_table.Baseline metabolics: Fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4); fasting lipids within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate metabolic monitoring plan at this visit?

options.text: Repeat fasting glucose and lipids now, then every 3 months for the first year on treatment
options.rationale: RANZCP and eTG recommend fasting glucose and lipids at 12 weeks after starting a second-generation antipsychotic then quarterly during the first year, with weight and waist at every visit; olanzapine carries the highest metabolic burden and this patient's early weight gain and central adiposity make quarterly checks appropriate (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

options.text: Defer any fasting bloods until 12 months after commencement then repeat glucose and lipids
options.rationale: Waiting a full year misses the first-year risk window when metabolic derangement on olanzapine is most likely to emerge and be reversible with early switch or lifestyle input (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

options.text: Order an oral glucose tolerance test today and only recheck fasting bloods if the OGTT is impaired
options.rationale: OGTT is reserved for equivocal fasting glucose or high-risk patients with normal fasting values; the routine surveillance test is fasting glucose plus HbA1c, not baseline OGTT for every antipsychotic patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Rely on annual GP well person checks for metabolic surveillance while he remains on olanzapine
options.rationale: Annual only monitoring is inadequate for a high-metabolic-risk antipsychotic in the first year; delegating without a shared plan misses the point of shared care and lets weight and glycaemia drift (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

options.text: Measure only weight and blood pressure quarterly and skip fasting bloods while glucose remains normal
options.rationale: Weight and blood pressure alone underdetect dyslipidaemia and dysglycaemia on olanzapine; the first-year plan includes fasting glucose or HbA1c plus lipids at 12 weeks and quarterly thereafter (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidance).

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics, particularly olanzapine and clozapine, produce most of their metabolic harm in the first year. RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic set 12 week fasting bloods with quarterly repeat through year one, alongside weight and waist at every review. Early weight gain of 8 kg with a rising waist justifies rather than deferring the recommended schedule. Only after the first year does the interval extend to 6 to 12 months if metrics are stable. Skipping fasting glucose in favour of weight alone underdetects the dysglycaemia this drug class produces.
key_points: 12 week fasting glucose and lipids after starting a second-generation antipsychotic
Repeat quarterly during the first year, then 6 to 12 monthly if stable
Weight and waist every visit; blood pressure at each review
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine causes the largest early weight and lipid shift in its class; a rising waist at 12 weeks predicts future dysglycaemia and should trigger active lifestyle input, not a passive wait.

subtopic_detail: Ward monitoring for deterioration in treated catatonia
stem: A 41-year-old man with catatonia has improved partly on regular lorazepam and stays on the mental health unit. You are writing his monitoring plan for the coming days.

data_table.Observations: HR 92, BP 126/78, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate monitoring plan?

options.text: Four hourly temperature and pulse with a daily creatine kinase
options.rationale: Progression to malignant catatonia announces itself as fever, autonomic instability and a rising creatine kinase, so these are the observations that change management (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Daily weight, a fluid balance chart and a weekly full blood count
options.rationale: This schedule belongs to nutritional rehabilitation or clozapine haematological monitoring rather than to catatonia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Continuous cardiac monitoring with twelve hourly electrocardiograms
options.rationale: Cardiac monitoring is the answer when a drug that prolongs the QT interval is given or an arrhythmia is suspected (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Daily electroencephalography until the catatonic signs resolve
options.rationale: Electroencephalography is the answer when non convulsive status epilepticus is the working differential, not for routine monitoring (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard).

options.text: Twice weekly observations and a repeat computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Repeat imaging is prompted by a new focal neurological sign; twice weekly observations are too sparse for this risk (Source: ACSQHC Delirium Clinical Care Standard).

explanation.summary: Malignant catatonia is the complication that turns a treatable syndrome into an emergency. It presents as fever, autonomic instability with labile blood pressure and tachycardia, rigidity and a rising creatine kinase, and it overlaps clinically with neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Because it can develop over hours, the monitoring plan for any inpatient with catatonia is frequent vital signs and a regular creatine kinase, alongside daily review of hydration, oral intake and sedation. Early recognition moves the patient to a monitored bed and brings forward electroconvulsive therapy.
key_points: Fever and autonomic instability in catatonia signal malignant progression
A rising creatine kinase supports it and tracks severity
Frequent vital signs matter more than repeated imaging
Malignant catatonia needs a monitored bed and urgent specialist involvement
explanation.pearls: Any new fever in a catatonic patient is malignant catatonia until infection is proven, because the two are managed very differently. In context: catatonia is monitored like a medical illness because its dangerous complications are physiological, not behavioural (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

subtopic_detail: Managing a lapse after the quit date
stem: A 41-year-old woman stopped smoking five weeks ago on varenicline with Quitline support. At a party on Saturday she smoked three cigarettes and has not smoked since. She telephones, upset, asking whether to stop the medicine.

data_table.Treatment: Varenicline 1 mg twice daily, week 5 of 12
data_table.Since the lapse: No cigarettes for three days; cravings mild

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Continue varenicline to twelve weeks and review the triggers with her
options.rationale: A lapse is not relapse. Continuing the full course while problem-solving the situational trigger with behavioural support gives the best chance of sustained abstinence. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Stop varenicline and restart the whole course after a new quit date
options.rationale: A fresh course is for someone who has returned to regular smoking and is ready to try again later. Interrupting treatment in a woman abstinent for three days invites full relapse. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

options.text: Continue varenicline and add a 21 mg nicotine patch for cover
options.rationale: Adding replacement to varenicline is occasionally used for breakthrough craving despite full dosing, at the cost of more nausea. Her cravings are mild and controlled. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Stop varenicline and switch to bupropion for the remaining weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is an alternative when varenicline is contraindicated or not tolerated. Switching an effective, tolerated agent mid-course has no evidence behind it. (Source: AMH: Bupropion)

options.text: Continue varenicline and extend the course to twenty-four weeks from today
options.rationale: An extended course is offered at the end of 12 weeks to a patient who has quit and remains at high relapse risk, not decided in week five. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

explanation.summary: A lapse is a single episode of smoking after the quit date; relapse is a return to regular smoking. Most successful quitters lapse at least once, usually in a social or alcohol-related setting, and the evidence-based response is to normalise it, continue pharmacotherapy for the full course, and use the episode to identify and rehearse the trigger. Stopping the medicine at a lapse converts a recoverable slip into relapse, and the strongest predictors of relapse are alcohol, other smokers in the household and low mood. In context: nicotine dependence is a relapsing condition, so quit attempts are counted rather than graded, and each attempt supported by pharmacotherapy and behavioural support raises the probability of the next one succeeding.
key_points: Lapse is not relapse: continue the pharmacotherapy course
Use the lapse to identify the trigger and rehearse an alternative plan
Alcohol, other household smokers and low mood are the main relapse drivers
Extended pharmacotherapy is a decision for the end of the standard course
explanation.pearls: Framing a lapse as data rather than failure keeps the patient in treatment; the practical script is to ask what was happening in the ten minutes before the first cigarette.

subtopic_detail: Lithium chronic toxicity precipitants
stem: A 62-year-old woman on lithium carbonate 900 mg nightly for 24 years has three days of nausea, coarse tremor and unsteady gait, with confusion today. Her general practitioner added ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily 10 days ago. She has also been drinking cranberry juice.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, coarse tremor, truncal ataxia
data_table.Bloods: Lithium 2.4 mmol/L (was 0.7); urea 12.4 mmol/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (was 78)

lead_in: Which is the most likely precipitant of this toxicity?

options.text: Age related decline in glomerular filtration rate over 24 years of treatment
options.rationale: Age related eGFR decline is gradual and does not typically produce an acute doubling of creatinine over days; a specific precipitant is required to explain the acute rise (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory blockade of prostaglandins reducing renal lithium clearance
options.rationale: NSAIDs reduce afferent arteriolar prostaglandin dependent vasodilation, cutting GFR and lithium clearance; the temporal association with ibuprofen initiation 10 days ago and creatinine doubling identifies this as the primary precipitant (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH)).

options.text: Cranberry juice inducing hepatic cytochrome P450 3A4 metabolism of lithium
options.rationale: Lithium undergoes essentially no hepatic metabolism and is cleared unchanged by the kidneys; cranberry juice is not the mechanism here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook (AMH)).

options.text: Sodium depletion redistributing lithium from erythrocytes to the plasma
options.rationale: Volume depletion and low salt intake raise lithium levels through proximal tubular sodium and lithium reabsorption, but there is no reported gastrointestinal loss in this scenario; the mechanism described is inaccurate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Cumulative interstitial nephritis from decades of lithium causing tubular resistance
options.rationale: Chronic lithium nephropathy is a slow decline over decades and does not explain an acute doubling of creatinine and a lithium level rise over 10 days; it is a background risk, not the acute precipitant (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Any drug that reduces renal perfusion or afferent arteriolar prostaglandin activity raises lithium concentration acutely. NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and thiazide diuretics are the classical precipitants. Here ibuprofen at 400 mg three times daily started 10 days ago aligns with a doubling of creatinine and a lithium level of 2.4 mmol/L in a previously stable patient. Management is cessation of the offending agent, intravenous saline (avoiding hypotonic fluids), continuous cardiac monitoring, and haemodialysis when the level exceeds 4 mmol/L, when neurotoxicity persists, or renal function is severely impaired.
key_points: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides raise lithium acutely
Confusion plus level above 2.0 mmol/L is severe toxicity
Dialysis threshold: level above 4 mmol/L or refractory neurotoxicity
explanation.pearls: A level of 2.5 mmol/L with normal renal function may be managed with saline alone; the same level with rising creatinine or refractory neurology needs urgent renal replacement therapy.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnostic criteria and functional impairment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar assessing a 27-year-old graphic designer who describes lifelong difficulty finishing projects, chronic lateness, and losing wallets and keys weekly. She was described in Year 4 school reports as bright but not applying herself. She has been terminated from two jobs in the last 3 years for missed deadlines and now spends most weekend evenings catching up on work she was unable to complete on weekdays. She has never taken stimulant medication.

She scored 5 on the PHQ-9, 4 on the GAD-7, and 22 on the Adult ADHD Self Report Scale part A. Her collateral history from her mother confirms restlessness and inattention in primary school despite average academic ability. She uses no alcohol, cannabis, or stimulants. Thyroid function, ferritin, and full blood count are within normal limits. She asks whether she meets criteria for adult ADHD.

data_table.Onset history: Restlessness and inattention documented from Year 4 reports and by mother
data_table.Functional impairment: Two employment terminations in 3 years; weekend catch up work

lead_in: Which criterion is the most decisive in confirming DSM-5 adult ADHD in this presentation?

options.text: Symptoms present in more than one setting with clear functional impairment and childhood onset
options.rationale: DSM-5 adult ADHD requires several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms present before age 12, in two or more settings, with clear evidence of impairment; this scenario meets all three (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: A positive Adult ADHD Self Report Scale total score above 20 with contemporaneous PHQ-9 below 10
options.rationale: ASRS is a screening tool and mood exclusion does not by itself confirm ADHD; the DSM-5 diagnosis rests on symptoms, cross-situational impairment, and childhood onset (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: A positive short trial response to methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg twice daily over 2 weeks
options.rationale: Stimulant responsiveness is not diagnostic; healthy adults also experience cognitive enhancement, and empirical trials are not used to confirm the disorder (Source: RACGP Adult ADHD Guidance).

options.text: An informant confirmed history of restlessness during adolescence rather than primary school onset
options.rationale: DSM-5 requires onset of several symptoms before age 12, not before adolescence; an adolescent onset alone excludes the diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Neuropsychological testing showing global working memory in the low average range on formal measures
options.rationale: Neuropsychological test scores do not confirm or exclude adult ADHD; the disorder is a clinical diagnosis and cognitive testing is complementary rather than definitive (Source: RACGP Adult ADHD Guidance).

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD in DSM-5 requires five or more inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (rather than six for children), several present before age 12, symptoms in two or more settings, and clear evidence of interference with functioning. Symptoms must not be better explained by another mental disorder or substance effect. This patient has school reports, maternal collateral, cross-setting symptoms (work and home), and unambiguous functional loss. ASRS is a screen, not a diagnosis. Stimulant challenges are not diagnostic and neuropsychology is supportive rather than definitive.
key_points: DSM-5 requires several symptoms before age 12
Symptoms in two or more settings with functional impairment
Screening tools (ASRS) support but do not confirm the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about primary school reports and third party history; adults commonly reconstruct their childhood as unremarkable, but school reports and parental recall carry more diagnostic weight than adult recall alone.

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder first line treatment
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman on the second visit after her third emergency department presentation this year with self cutting. Her forearms show 20 or more parallel superficial cuts of varying age. She describes 5 years of unstable relationships, intense fear of abandonment, chronic emptiness, dissociative episodes lasting hours after arguments, and impulsive spending. She meets 7 of the 9 DSM-5 borderline personality disorder criteria.

Her mood is reactive rather than sustained: PHQ-9 12, GAD-7 14. She has no manic history and no psychotic symptoms. She uses alcohol only socially, no illicit substances. She has been prescribed quetiapine 100 mg nightly by her GP and sertraline 50 mg daily by a previous psychiatrist; she reports neither helped. She asks what treatment is actually going to help.

data_table.Presentations this year: Three ED attendances with self cutting
data_table.Current medications: Quetiapine 100 mg nocte; sertraline 50 mg daily (both unhelpful)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate primary treatment recommendation?

options.text: Add low dose olanzapine 5 mg nightly for mood instability and emptiness while continuing sertraline
options.rationale: NHMRC guidance and Cochrane reviews find no medication with meaningful benefit for the core features of borderline personality disorder; polypharmacy adds harm without benefit (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

options.text: Refer for structured, time limited psychotherapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy or mentalisation based therapy
options.rationale: The NHMRC guideline recommends a structured, evidence-based psychotherapy delivered by trained clinicians as the primary treatment for borderline personality disorder; DBT, MBT, transference focused psychotherapy, and schema therapy have the strongest evidence (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

options.text: Admit to the acute psychiatric inpatient unit for a planned 4 to 6 week stabilisation and behavioural monitoring
options.rationale: Prolonged inpatient admission for uncomplicated borderline personality disorder can reinforce dependence and self-harm without changing long term outcome; brief admission is reserved for imminent risk (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

options.text: Increase sertraline to 200 mg daily and reassess for reduction in cutting frequency in 6 weeks
options.rationale: SSRIs have very limited effect on borderline personality disorder core features and do not reliably reduce self-harm; escalation without a psychological plan is not recommended (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

options.text: Refer to a private hypnotherapist for weekly regression work on early attachment relationships
options.rationale: Hypnotic regression is not an evidence-based treatment for borderline personality disorder and is not recommended by the NHMRC guideline (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline).

explanation.summary: The 2013 NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder places structured evidence-based psychotherapy at the centre of treatment. Dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation based therapy, transference focused psychotherapy, and schema therapy have the most consistent evidence for reducing self-harm, emergency presentations, and improving function. Medication has no demonstrated benefit for the core features and should be used only for defined co-occurring conditions and time limited crisis management. Brief admission is reserved for imminent risk; prolonged admission can be iatrogenic. Care coordination, a written safety plan, and consistent multidisciplinary follow up are essential adjuncts.
key_points: Structured psychotherapy (DBT, MBT, TFP, schema) is the primary treatment
Medications have no evidence for core BPD features
Brief admission only for imminent risk
explanation.pearls: A written safety plan (early warning signs, coping strategies, contact numbers, means restriction) reduces subsequent self-harm and is standard of care after any BPD presentation.

subtopic_detail: Electroconvulsive therapy pre-anaesthesia considerations
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar planning a course of electroconvulsive therapy for a 68-year-old woman with severe treatment resistant depression (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale 32) who has stopped eating and lost 12 percent body weight over 2 months. She has failed sequential trials of sertraline, venlafaxine, mirtazapine and lithium augmentation. She has a history of atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily, hypertension on perindopril, and had a coronary artery bypass graft 5 years ago. Her most recent transthoracic echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 52 percent.

She had an anterior circulation ischaemic stroke 4 weeks ago with complete recovery of neurological function. Her partner has consented on her behalf under the Mental Health Act after a formal capacity assessment. Vital signs are pulse 78 regular, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C.

data_table.Depression severity: HDRS 32; 12 percent weight loss in 2 months; stopped eating
data_table.Cardiac history: AF on apixaban; CABG 5 years ago; EF 52 percent
data_table.Recent event: Anterior circulation ischaemic stroke 4 weeks ago, complete recovery
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 148/86, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, temp 36.8

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate action before proceeding with ECT?

options.text: Cancel the ECT course permanently because recent ischaemic stroke is an absolute contraindication
options.rationale: There are no absolute contraindications to ECT; recent stroke is a relative one that raises risk. Deferring rather than cancelling is the standard position when depression is severe (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

options.text: Continue apixaban unchanged as it does not increase risk during ECT and requires no perioperative planning
options.rationale: Apixaban is generally continued for ECT because the procedure is very low bleeding risk, but this ignores the more pressing recent stroke issue that dominates decision making here (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

options.text: Substitute intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg with sertraline 200 mg orally as an alternative treatment plan
options.rationale: She has failed the antidepressant sequence already and adding olanzapine does not address the severe depression with life threatening malnutrition; alternatives do not match ECT for severity of this magnitude (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

options.text: Proceed with ECT tomorrow because delaying more than 4 weeks after stroke removes the elevated risk
options.rationale: The recommended interval after a stroke is at least 4 to 6 weeks with cardiovascular and neurology review to define residual deficit and blood pressure control; going ahead the next day without that review is premature (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

options.text: Defer ECT until at least 4 to 6 weeks post stroke with cardiology and neurology review of risk
options.rationale: Recent ischaemic stroke is a relative contraindication; RANZCP recommends deferring at least 4 to 6 weeks and obtaining specialist assessment of stroke risk with strict perioperative blood pressure targets before proceeding (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement PS28).

explanation.summary: ECT has no absolute contraindications, but recent stroke, raised intracranial pressure, unstable coronary syndrome, aortic aneurysm, retinal detachment, phaeochromocytoma, and severe pulmonary disease are relative contraindications requiring risk assessment and modification. For an ischaemic stroke, RANZCP position statement PS28 recommends deferring ECT for at least 4 to 6 weeks and obtaining neurology and cardiology review with strict perioperative blood pressure control. Anticoagulants such as apixaban are usually continued because the procedure is very low bleeding risk. When severe depression demands ECT sooner, informed decision by treating team and patient (or substitute decision maker) is documented after formal risk balancing.
key_points: No absolute contraindications; recent stroke is relative
Defer at least 4 to 6 weeks after ischaemic stroke
Obtain neurology and cardiology review pre-anaesthesia
explanation.pearls: During ECT, systolic pressure can spike above 200 mmHg for seconds; premedication with a short-acting beta blocker such as esmolol blunts the surge in patients with cardiovascular disease.

subtopic_detail: Valproate teratogenicity and pregnancy prevention
stem:
You are the outpatient psychiatry registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder currently well on sodium valproate 1000 mg orally twice daily for 3 years, and lithium was previously stopped for polyuria. She has had no manic or depressive episodes for 26 months and is engaged to be married. She and her partner would like to start trying to conceive in the next 12 months. She has never previously discussed contraception with her psychiatrist. Her partner uses condoms inconsistently.

Her weight is 74 kg, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, and full blood count, electrolytes, and liver function tests are within normal limits. She has no personal or family history of neural tube defects. She is very concerned that any change in medication will trigger a relapse and asks what to do next.

data_table.Current medication: Sodium valproate 1000 mg twice daily for 3 years
data_table.Mood stability: No manic or depressive episodes for 26 months
data_table.Contraception: Condoms used inconsistently by partner only

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Refer urgently for perinatal psychiatry review to plan a switch to a safer mood stabiliser preconception
