options.rationale: Valproate causes major congenital malformation in 10 percent and neurodevelopmental impairment in 30 to 40 percent of exposed pregnancies; TGA guidance mandates a documented pregnancy prevention plan and specialist review for any woman of childbearing potential (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose and add high dose folate 5 mg daily until conception
options.rationale: Folate supplementation does not offset valproate teratogenicity and continuing valproate without discussion of alternatives fails the pregnancy prevention program (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

options.text: Cease valproate abruptly today and start lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated over the next 6 weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation risks acute relapse; switch should be gradual under specialist supervision with careful cross titration and monitoring (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Continue valproate but add long-acting reversible contraception until she stops planning pregnancy
options.rationale: LARC is essential during ongoing valproate therapy, but she plans to conceive within 12 months so the aim is a preconception switch, not indefinite contraception (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

options.text: Reduce valproate to 500 mg twice daily to lower teratogenic risk and continue at this dose during pregnancy
options.rationale: Teratogenic risk is dose related but even lower doses carry unacceptable risk versus alternatives; the plan is to switch off valproate preconception, not to reduce dose (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program).

explanation.summary: The TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program (2023) requires that any woman of childbearing potential prescribed valproate has documented understanding of teratogenic risk, effective contraception, an annual review, and a plan for pregnancy that involves an alternative mood stabiliser. Valproate carries a 10 percent risk of major congenital malformation (including neural tube defects) and a 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental impairment, well above lamotrigine (2 to 3 percent) or lithium (2 to 3 percent). The immediate step for a woman planning conception within 12 months is urgent specialist review to plan a gradual switch, not folate, dose reduction, or long term LARC on unchanged therapy.
key_points: Valproate MCM risk 10 percent; neurodevelopmental risk 30 to 40 percent
TGA program requires contraception plus annual review
Preconception switch to lamotrigine or lithium with specialist supervision
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine dose typically needs to be doubled by the third trimester because oestrogen induces UGT glucuronidation; drop back to preconception dose within 3 days postpartum.

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic discrimination among short duration psychoses
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 22-year-old university student 3 weeks after his acute admission for hearing derogatory voices, believing his housemates were poisoning his water, and 4 days of not sleeping. He had never before had psychiatric contact. On admission urine drug screen was negative and MRI brain was unremarkable. He was started on olanzapine 10 mg nightly and voices and delusions resolved within 8 days; sleep normalised.

He was discharged home after 12 days with complete symptom resolution. He remains well today with no residual positive or negative symptoms. Total duration of psychotic symptoms from onset to full resolution was 12 days. He has no family history of psychotic illness, no substance use in the last 6 months confirmed by hair testing at admission, and no recent bereavement or trauma. He asks what the diagnostic label is now.

data_table.Symptom duration: 12 days total from onset to resolution
data_table.Response: Complete resolution on olanzapine 10 mg within 8 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic label at this stage?

options.text: Schizophrenia with active phase symptoms controlled by second generation antipsychotic therapy
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires continuous signs for at least 6 months including active phase symptoms of at least 1 month; a 12 day episode does not meet criteria (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder with good prognostic features and complete symptom resolution on therapy
options.rationale: Schizophreniform disorder requires symptoms for at least 1 month but less than 6 months; a 12 day episode does not reach the 1 month threshold (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with symptom duration between 1 day and 1 month with return to prior functioning
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder in DSM-5 requires at least one of delusions, hallucinations or disorganised speech lasting at least 1 day but less than 1 month with eventual full return to premorbid functioning; a 12 day episode meets this criterion exactly (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Substance induced psychotic disorder related to unreported hallucinogen exposure prior to admission
options.rationale: A substance induced diagnosis requires temporal linkage to intoxication or withdrawal and evidence of substance exposure; UDS was negative and hair testing did not support recent use (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Delusional disorder with persecutory type since his beliefs about being poisoned were the dominant feature
options.rationale: Delusional disorder requires delusions for at least 1 month without prominent hallucinations, mood disturbance, or bizarre behaviour; hallucinations are prominent here and duration is under 1 month (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 discriminates short duration psychoses by two axes: symptom duration and functional recovery. Brief psychotic disorder requires 1 day to less than 1 month with full return to premorbid functioning. Schizophreniform disorder covers 1 month to less than 6 months. Schizophrenia requires 6 months of continuous disturbance including 1 month of active phase symptoms. Delusional disorder requires delusions of 1 month or more without prominent hallucinations, mood disturbance, or bizarre behaviour. Substance induced psychotic disorder requires temporal linkage and evidence of substance exposure. In this 12 day episode with full resolution, brief psychotic disorder is the correct provisional diagnosis; recurrence would trigger reclassification.
key_points: Brief psychotic disorder: 1 day to less than 1 month with full recovery
Schizophreniform: 1 to less than 6 months
Schizophrenia: 6 months continuous with 1 month active phase
explanation.pearls: About 50 percent of brief psychotic disorder episodes progress to another psychotic diagnosis over 5 years; longitudinal follow up rather than a definitive label is the safer position early on.

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural disturbance rapid tranquillisation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in the emergency department attending a 34-year-old woman brought in by police after threatening staff at a supermarket. She is known to services with schizoaffective disorder, currently on paliperidone long-acting injection given 5 weeks ago. She is pacing, shouting, and refusing all oral medications. Verbal de-escalation over 15 minutes has been unsuccessful. She has no known allergies, is not pregnant (bhCG negative from urine), has never had NMS, and is otherwise physically well.

Vital signs (obtained during a brief cooperative moment) are pulse 108, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Point-of-care glucose 6.2 mmol/L. Weight is estimated at 65 kg. Security officers and 4 nursing staff are present. There is no intravenous access.

data_table.Presentation: Agitated, pacing, verbally threatening; refuses oral medication
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 138/86, RR 22, SpO2 97% RA, temp 36.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial parenteral pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg alone as monotherapy without concurrent benzodiazepine at this time
options.rationale: The RANZCP and eTG rapid tranquillisation position places IM olanzapine 10 mg monotherapy as first line for acute behavioural disturbance in known psychosis; avoid concurrent IM benzodiazepine to reduce respiratory depression risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg concurrently with intramuscular midazolam 5 mg into the same deltoid muscle
options.rationale: Combined IM droperidol and IM midazolam increases risk of respiratory depression and hypotension and is not the first line combination; same site injection is also poor technique (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg with promethazine 50 mg in a single deltoid muscle injection
options.rationale: Haloperidol 10 mg carries higher extrapyramidal risk than lower doses; combined with promethazine 50 mg the anticholinergic burden and QT risk make this a second line rather than first choice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Intramuscular ziprasidone 20 mg pending intravenous access for potential propofol induction if needed
options.rationale: Ziprasidone is not widely available in Australia, and moving toward propofol induction without a trial of first line IM options is unnecessarily invasive (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Intramuscular ketamine 4 mg per kg as a single dose to achieve immediate dissociative sedation onset
options.rationale: Ketamine dissociative sedation is a prehospital or resistant restraint option; it is not the initial pharmacological choice in the emergency department with staff and safer options available (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Australian rapid tranquillisation guidance (Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP position) recommends verbal de-escalation and oral options first; when parenteral therapy is needed, intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg is a first line monotherapy for known psychosis, or intramuscular droperidol 10 mg. Concurrent IM benzodiazepines are avoided due to risk of respiratory depression. Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring with pulse oximetry for at least 1 hour follows any dose, plus glucose check within 30 minutes. If the initial dose is inadequate, repeat after 30 to 60 minutes rather than stacking multiple agents. Vital signs, glucose, ECG for QT, and search for reversible causes (hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, drug or alcohol intoxication) are essential adjuncts.
key_points: IM olanzapine 10 mg or IM droperidol 10 mg first line monotherapy
Avoid concurrent IM benzodiazepine (respiratory depression risk)
Monitor SpO2, pulse, BP, glucose after every dose
explanation.pearls: Do not repeat IM olanzapine within 2 hours; peak concentrations at 15 to 45 minutes mean early re-dosing risks cumulative sedation and hypotension.

subtopic_detail: Cannabis induced vs primary psychotic disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 19-year-old man 6 weeks after admission for auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions. On admission urine drug screen was positive for THC only, and hair testing at 3 cm covered the preceding 3 months and was positive for high potency cannabis (used 3 to 5 times daily). He was started on risperidone 2 mg twice daily and voices resolved by day 4.

He has been abstinent from cannabis since discharge (confirmed by weekly urine drug screens, all negative for 6 weeks) and remains on risperidone 2 mg twice daily. He still reports intermittent low grade suspiciousness and hears his name called once or twice weekly, though he is otherwise functioning at work and university. He has no family history of psychotic illness. Vital signs are within normal limits. Fasting glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4) and prolactin 780 mIU/L (60 to 620) are within normal limits and mildly elevated respectively.

data_table.Substance use: Abstinent 6 weeks (weekly UDS negative); prior heavy high potency use

lead_in: What does the persistence of these symptoms most strongly suggest?

options.text: Reasonable expectation of substance induced psychotic disorder that will resolve with more time abstinent
options.rationale: DSM-5 substance induced psychotic disorder should resolve within a month of cessation of the substance; persistence beyond a month suggests reclassification (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Primary psychotic disorder in the schizophrenia spectrum with cannabis acting as an environmental trigger
options.rationale: Positive symptoms persisting 6 weeks after cannabis cessation exceed the 1 month cut off for substance induced psychosis; DSM-5 and RANZCP guidance treat this as an emerging primary psychotic disorder with cannabis as a precipitant, not the diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Prolactinoma related psychosis given the modestly elevated prolactin of 780 mIU/L on risperidone therapy
options.rationale: Elevated prolactin on risperidone is a medication effect (D2 blockade); prolactinoma related psychosis is not a recognised entity and does not explain his symptoms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Ongoing covert cannabis use with false negative urine drug screens each week from insufficient sensitivity
options.rationale: Weekly UDS is highly reliable for detecting cannabis use over the preceding week in an abstinent user; sustained negatives over 6 weeks make continued use very unlikely (Source: RACP Chapter of Addiction Medicine Position).
source_refs: RACP Chapter of Addiction Medicine Position

options.text: Persistent hallucinogen perception disorder from previous LSD use rather than cannabis specific effects here
options.rationale: Persistent perception disorder is visual and follows classical hallucinogen use; auditory hallucinations after cannabis use do not fit this diagnosis (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 substance induced psychotic disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms arise during or soon after substance intoxication or withdrawal and resolve within a month of cessation. Symptoms lasting beyond this period despite confirmed abstinence should be reclassified as a primary psychotic disorder, most often schizophrenia spectrum, with cannabis acting as an important environmental trigger. Heavy high potency cannabis use in adolescence multiplies the risk of schizophrenia several fold. Ongoing antipsychotic therapy and specialist follow up are appropriate; prolactin elevation on risperidone is dose related and monitored, not diagnostic of a separate condition. Weekly urine cannabis screening is reliable for confirming abstinence over the preceding week in a previously heavy user.
key_points: Substance induced psychosis resolves within 1 month of cessation
Persistence beyond 1 month reclassifies to a primary psychotic disorder
Heavy adolescent cannabis use multiplies schizophrenia risk
explanation.pearls: Cannabis withdrawal alone can produce sleep disturbance and irritability for weeks but does not sustain positive psychotic symptoms; new hallucinations at 6 weeks abstinent point at a primary disorder.

sources.label: RACP Chapter of Addiction Medicine Position

subtopic_detail: Anorexia nervosa refeeding syndrome prevention
stem: A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa weighs 39 kg at 168 cm (BMI 13.8), having taken no more than 200 kcal daily for four weeks and lost 12 kg in six months. She is admitted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 42 supine, 68 standing; systolic blood pressure 96 falling to 78 mmHg on standing; temperature 35.6 degrees C
data_table.Bloods: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L, phosphate 0.72 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for the first 72 hours?

options.text: Full nutrition at 40 kcal/kg/day, replacing electrolytes only if deficits appear
options.rationale: Full calorie loading of a severely malnourished patient rapidly triggers refeeding syndrome; guidelines call for a cautious start with proactive electrolyte replacement (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Feed at 10 to 20 kcal/kg/day with thiamine and empirical phosphate, potassium and magnesium
options.rationale: MARSIPAN Australia and RANZCP guidance recommend cautious refeeding at 10 to 20 kcal per kg per day for the first 3 days, thiamine 200 mg daily before or with the first meal, and empirical phosphate, potassium, and magnesium supplementation with twice daily electrolyte checks (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Refuse admission and refer to a community dietitian for weekly weight review
options.rationale: BMI below 14 with bradycardia and hypokalaemia meets criteria for medical admission; community management alone would be unsafe (Source: MARSIPAN Australia Guidance).

options.text: Intravenous 10 per cent glucose for the first 24 hours before any feeding
options.rationale: Intravenous dextrose without thiamine and electrolyte replacement precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy and severe refeeding hypophosphataemia (Source: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline).
source_refs: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Nasogastric feeding at 60 mL per hour from admission, replacing electrolytes if abnormal
options.rationale: Rapid nasogastric feeding rates deliver too many calories on the first day of a severely malnourished patient; slow escalation with prophylactic electrolyte replacement is required (Source: MARSIPAN Australia Guidance).

explanation.summary: Severe anorexia nervosa with BMI below 14, bradycardia below 50, hypokalaemia, or postural hypotension is a medical admission per MARSIPAN Australia and RANZCP eating disorder guidance. Refeeding syndrome (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, fluid overload, cardiac failure, Wernicke encephalopathy) is prevented by starting calories at 10 to 20 kcal per kg per day for the first 3 days, giving thiamine 200 mg daily orally before feeds begin, and prescribing empirical replacement of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium. Electrolytes are checked twice daily for the first 5 days and calories are escalated as tolerated. Cardiac monitoring is required for QTc above 500 ms or pulse below 40.
key_points: Start at 10 to 20 kcal per kg per day for first 3 days
Thiamine 200 mg daily before feeds; empirical PO4, K+, Mg replacement
Twice daily electrolytes for 5 days; cardiac monitoring for severe bradycardia
explanation.pearls: The MEED Australian tool (medical emergencies in eating disorders) sets specific thresholds for cardiac monitoring: pulse below 40, systolic BP below 90, QTc above 500 ms, or postural drop above 20 mmHg.

sources.label: RANZCP Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Early intervention in psychosis family involvement
stem:
You are the early psychosis service registrar reviewing a 20-year-old university student 6 weeks after his first admission for schizophrenia. He is on aripiprazole 15 mg daily, positive symptoms have resolved, and he wants to return to living with his parents while he resumes engineering studies. His parents ask what they can do to reduce the chance of relapse. He consents to their involvement in his care.

He scores 4 on the PHQ-9, has no substance use, and family assessment shows warmth, but the father expresses high levels of criticism when his son does not respond immediately to requests. Mother is highly reassuring and takes over daily tasks he can manage. Both parents are anxious about future relapse and ask what to do at home. He agrees a family meeting would help. Vital signs and metabolic screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Recovery stage: 6 weeks post first admission; positive symptoms resolved
data_table.Family climate: Warmth present; father high critical comments; mother overinvolved

lead_in: Which family based intervention has the strongest evidence for reducing relapse in first episode psychosis?

options.text: Weekly individual supportive counselling for parents only, delivered separately from the patient
options.rationale: Individual parent counselling alone has less evidence than structured family intervention that includes the patient and addresses expressed emotion (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

options.text: A single family psychoeducation session at discharge covering illness basics and warning signs
options.rationale: One off sessions are insufficient; sustained multisession psychoeducation across 3 to 6 months is required to reduce relapse (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

options.text: Structured family intervention over 3 or more months addressing expressed emotion, problem solving, and psychoeducation
options.rationale: Meta analyses and RANZCP guidance find structured family intervention lasting 3 months or more, addressing expressed emotion (high criticism, hostility, emotional overinvolvement), problem solving skills, and psychoeducation reduces relapse by around 50 percent at 12 months (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

options.text: Referral of both parents to a chronic mental illness carer support group with peer led format only
options.rationale: Peer support groups are valuable adjuncts but have less evidence for relapse prevention than structured family intervention delivered by trained clinicians (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

options.text: Removing the patient from family home into a residential rehabilitation program for 12 months
options.rationale: Separation is not standard of care and disrupts a supportive attachment; structured family work addresses the specific expressed emotion pattern without separation (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).

explanation.summary: Structured family intervention (family psychoeducation, communication skills, problem solving, and modification of high expressed emotion) delivered over at least 3 months by trained clinicians reduces relapse in first episode psychosis by about 50 percent at 12 months. High expressed emotion (criticism, hostility, emotional overinvolvement) is the single most robust family predictor of relapse. Interventions include the patient wherever possible and combine group and individual family sessions. Single session psychoeducation, peer support, and separation from family are less effective when used alone. This intervention sits alongside medication adherence work, vocational recovery, and physical health monitoring.
key_points: Structured family intervention over 3 or more months
High expressed emotion is a major relapse predictor
Reduces relapse by around 50 percent at 12 months
explanation.pearls: Reducing criticism and emotional overinvolvement is more effective than raising warmth alone; simple weekly problem solving meetings taught to families can achieve this over 8 to 12 sessions.

sources.label: Orygen Australian Clinical Guidelines for Early Psychosis

subtopic_detail: Autism spectrum disorder in adult women
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman for assessment of what she wonders is autism. She reports lifelong difficulty in social groups (she can manage one to one but finds groups exhausting), intense special interests (marine biology since age 6, currently a competitive knitter with detailed knowledge of yarn weights), a need for predictable routines (rings her sister the same time every Thursday), and sensory overload in supermarkets that she manages with noise cancelling headphones.

She scored 32 on the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10 not shown), scored 42 on the Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale Revised, and describes exhaustion after long social days that she calls masking. Her school reports describe her as a well behaved bright student who kept to herself. She has no learning disability. Screening scores: PHQ-9 6, GAD-7 8. She uses no alcohol or illicit substances. She has never had a psychiatric diagnosis previously.

data_table.Core features: Social exhaustion; special interests; routines; sensory overload
data_table.Development: School reports describe reserved bright student

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step to make a confident DSM-5 diagnosis?

options.text: Prescribe an SSRI first line for probable social anxiety disorder and reassess autism features in 6 months
options.rationale: Attributing the presentation to social anxiety without full assessment risks missing autism spectrum disorder; the pattern here (early onset, special interests, sensory, routines) is not social anxiety (Source: NICE CG142 Adult Autism).

options.text: Advise she does not meet DSM-5 criteria because her school reports describe a well behaved child without concern
options.rationale: Autistic girls and women commonly present as well behaved in school reports because of masking; absence of behavioural concerns in childhood does not exclude the diagnosis (Source: Amaze Australia Autism in Women and Girls Position).
source_refs: Amaze Australia Autism in Women and Girls Position

options.text: Order genetic testing (chromosomal microarray) as the primary confirmatory diagnostic test in a well adult
options.rationale: Genetic testing is offered in children where a specific syndrome is suspected; in adults without intellectual disability it is not the diagnostic step (Source: NICE CG142 Adult Autism).

options.text: Refer for structured multidisciplinary assessment using DSM-5 criteria including collateral developmental history
options.rationale: NICE CG142 and Australian autism diagnostic guidelines recommend structured multidisciplinary assessment including a developmental history from a knowledgeable informant, DSM-5 criteria review, and validated tools such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule or interview (Source: NICE CG142 Adult Autism).

options.text: Prescribe methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg twice daily as a therapeutic trial for likely ADHD comorbidity
options.rationale: A stimulant trial is not a diagnostic test for autism spectrum disorder and would not clarify the presenting picture; formal ADHD assessment is separate and does not substitute (Source: RACGP Adult ADHD Guidance).

explanation.summary: Adult autism spectrum disorder in women is under recognised because of masking (learned social scripts, mimicking peers, camouflage). Presentation includes lifelong social exhaustion, restricted interests (often narrower topic focus that can be socially acceptable), routines, and sensory sensitivities. DSM-5 requires persistent deficits in social communication and interaction (across multiple settings), restricted or repetitive behaviours (at least two), symptoms present in early childhood (though masked), clinically significant impairment, and no better explanation. Diagnosis rests on structured multidisciplinary assessment including a developmental history from a knowledgeable informant (parent, older sibling, longstanding friend), review of school and childhood records, and use of validated tools (ADOS-2, ADI-R, DISCO). Screening tools like AQ and RAADS-R suggest but do not confirm the diagnosis.
key_points: Masking commonly hides autism in women and girls
DSM-5 requires early onset even if only apparent in retrospect
Diagnosis by structured multidisciplinary assessment with informant
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about school playground time (spent alone or with a single peer, watching from the edge, playing structured games only); adult recall of primary school playtime is often more diagnostic than academic performance.

sources.label: Amaze Australia Autism in Women and Girls Position

subtopic_detail: Conversion vs factitious vs malingering discrimination
stem: A 34-year-old teacher developed right leg weakness abruptly four days ago after witnessing a playground injury. She cannot weight bear. She wants to return to work and has no financial incentive.

data_table.Neurology: Right hip flexion and knee extension 0/5 on direct testing, but the leg moves spontaneously in bed; Hoover sign positive
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance brain and whole spine and nerve conduction studies normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate DSM-5 diagnosis and next step?

options.text: Malingering; discharge with a letter to her insurer and no further input
options.rationale: Malingering requires external incentive (compensation, avoiding duty, obtaining medication) which is absent here; her goal is return to work; symptoms are not consciously produced (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Factitious disorder; admit for behavioural observation to detect feigning
options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires intentional falsification of symptoms motivated by adopting the sick role; there is no evidence of intentional falsification and she is not seeking the sick role (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Functional neurological disorder; physiotherapy, psychology and a clear explanation
options.rationale: DSM-5 functional neurological (conversion) disorder requires positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency (Hoover sign, spontaneous movement out of keeping with formal testing); management is delivering a clear positive diagnosis, physiotherapy, and psychological therapy, not repeat imaging (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Somatic symptom disorder; start duloxetine and refer to a pain clinic
options.rationale: Somatic symptom disorder focuses on excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviours about somatic symptoms; conversion disorder is a distinct diagnosis with positive neurological signs of incongruity (Source: DSM-5-TR).

options.text: Occult demyelination; repeat imaging with gadolinium and lumbar puncture
options.rationale: Repeat neuroimaging without new clinical features reinforces illness behaviour and undermines the positive diagnosis; conversion disorder requires positive signs, not exclusion (Source: DSM-5-TR).

explanation.summary: DSM-5 renamed conversion disorder as functional neurological symptom disorder to emphasise that the diagnosis rests on positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency (Hoover sign for functional leg weakness, tremor entrainment, tubular visual fields) rather than an exclusion diagnosis. Management is delivering a clear positive explanation using neutral, non stigmatising language, engaging the patient in physiotherapy with a graded rehabilitation approach, and psychological therapy for common comorbid anxiety or trauma. Repeated imaging and specialist referrals reinforce illness behaviour and worsen outcome. Malingering (intentional falsification for external gain) and factitious disorder (intentional falsification to adopt the sick role) are separate diagnoses; both require intentional deception which is absent in conversion disorder.
key_points: Positive signs (Hoover, entrainment) confirm the diagnosis
Deliver a clear positive explanation early to aid recovery
Physiotherapy plus psychology; avoid repeat imaging
explanation.pearls: Websites like neurosymptoms.org (Jon Stone) are useful patient information adjuncts; sharing the positive diagnostic reasoning with the patient improves prognosis more than months of exclusion investigations.

subtopic_detail: Relapse prevention pharmacotherapy choice with hepatic impairment
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar seeing a 54-year-old man 10 days after completing a medically supervised inpatient alcohol withdrawal. His usual pattern before admission was 15 standard drinks daily for over a decade. He is highly motivated to stay abstinent and lives with his supportive wife. He is not on opioid pain relief and has no personal or family history of seizures.

Investigations from admission show ALT 96 U/L (under 40), AST 128 U/L (under 40), gamma-GT 320 U/L (under 60), bilirubin 26 micromol/L (under 20), albumin 34 g/L (33 to 47), INR 1.1, platelets 132 x 10^9/L (150 to 400), and a FibroScan reports significant liver fibrosis without established cirrhosis. eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73 m2. His BMI is 26 kg/m2 and there is no ascites or peripheral oedema. He has not previously tried any relapse prevention medication.

data_table.Alcohol history: 15 standard drinks daily for over a decade; 10 days abstinent post-withdrawal
data_table.LFTs: ALT 96; AST 128; gamma-GT 320; bilirubin 26; albumin 34; INR 1.1; platelets 132
data_table.Support: Living with supportive wife; not on opioids; no seizure history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate relapse prevention pharmacotherapy to commence?

options.text: Oral acamprosate 666 mg three times daily as first-line maintenance in significant liver fibrosis
options.rationale: Acamprosate is renally excreted and preferred over naltrexone when there is significant hepatic impairment; it is safe in liver disease as long as renal function is adequate and reduces relapse to heavy drinking (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Oral disulfiram 200 mg daily under supervised administration by his wife
options.rationale: Disulfiram is contraindicated in significant liver disease because of the risk of severe hepatotoxicity and requires strict abstinence; it is not first-line and is unsafe with these LFTs (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Oral gabapentin 300 mg three times daily titrated to 600 mg three times daily as sole therapy
options.rationale: Gabapentin has limited evidence for alcohol use disorder relapse prevention and is not a first-line agent in AU practice; acamprosate or naltrexone are the recommended options (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Oral naltrexone 50 mg daily starting today with LFT monitoring at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and carries a black box warning of hepatotoxicity in advanced liver disease; with AST double the upper reference range and significant fibrosis, acamprosate is safer (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

options.text: Continued oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily as chronic maintenance to prevent relapse
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines have no role in relapse prevention beyond the acute withdrawal window and expose him to cross-dependence and withdrawal reinstatement risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction).

explanation.summary: Relapse prevention pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder in AU practice centres on acamprosate and naltrexone with disulfiram as an adjunct in highly selected patients. Acamprosate is renally cleared and is preferred when there is significant liver disease; naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and contraindicated in acute hepatitis or advanced liver failure. Disulfiram is contraindicated in significant liver disease. Benzodiazepines have no role beyond acute withdrawal. Gabapentin has limited evidence and is not first-line.
key_points: Acamprosate preferred when significant hepatic impairment coexists with alcohol use disorder
Naltrexone contraindicated in acute hepatitis or advanced liver failure
Disulfiram is not first-line and requires excellent adherence and no hepatic risk
explanation.pearls: The renal versus hepatic clearance profile of acamprosate versus naltrexone decides the choice more often than efficacy; check eGFR and LFTs before either prescription.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners AOD Clinical Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Postnatal depression pharmacotherapy in a breastfeeding woman
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman at her 8 week postnatal check. She reports 6 weeks of persistent low mood, tearfulness, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps, and thoughts that her baby would be better off without her. She denies any active plans to harm herself or the baby. Her EPDS score is 21 and she is exclusively breastfeeding a healthy term infant. She had a similar depressive episode after her first child that responded to sertraline.

She has no other medical history and is on no regular medications. She is engaged with the maternal and child health nurse and her partner is supportive and home each evening. She would like to continue breastfeeding and asks whether medication is compatible.

data_table.Presentation: 6 weeks persistent low mood, tearfulness, poor sleep independent of baby
data_table.Passive suicidality: Thoughts baby would be better off without her; no active plan or intent
data_table.EPDS score: 21 with item 10 marked as denying active plans
data_table.Feeding: Exclusive breastfeeding of healthy term infant
data_table.History: Previous PND responded well to sertraline
data_table.Supports: Engaged with MCH nurse; supportive partner

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Cease breastfeeding and commence fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily as the primary antidepressant
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a longer half-life and higher relative infant dose than sertraline and is not first-line in breastfeeding; stopping breastfeeding is not needed when a compatible SSRI exists (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Arrange inpatient mother-baby unit admission today for severe postnatal depression
options.rationale: Inpatient admission is reserved for women with active suicidal or infanticidal intent, psychosis, or inability to care for the infant; this woman has passive ideation only and strong community supports and can be managed in the community with escalation criteria (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg orally daily uptitrated to 50 to 100 mg daily and continue breastfeeding
options.rationale: Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in breastfeeding women because of the lowest relative infant dose and best safety data, and her prior treatment response makes it the appropriate agent; breastfeeding does not need to be interrupted (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy alone without pharmacotherapy for the next 6 weeks
options.rationale: Moderate to severe postnatal depression (EPDS 21 with passive suicidal ideation) warrants pharmacotherapy with psychological therapy in parallel; therapy alone is inadequate at this severity (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Prescribe temazepam 10 mg at night to address the sleep disturbance and review in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not first-line for postnatal depression, sedate infants through breastmilk, and do not treat the underlying mood disorder (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Moderate to severe postnatal depression requires combined pharmacotherapy and psychological treatment. Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in breastfeeding because its relative infant dose is under 2 percent and the safety data is the largest of the class. A prior therapeutic response is a strong indication to use the same drug. Fluoxetine is second-line because of a longer half-life and higher relative infant dose. Inpatient mother-baby unit admission is reserved for active suicidality, infanticidal intent, psychosis, or inability to care for the infant; passive ideation with strong supports is managed in the community with a clear escalation plan.
key_points: Sertraline is the first-line SSRI in breastfeeding; do not interrupt breastfeeding
Combined SSRI plus psychological therapy for moderate to severe postnatal depression
Inpatient care reserved for active suicidality, infanticidal intent, or psychosis
explanation.pearls: EPDS item 10 (self-harm thoughts) is the trigger for direct safety enquiry; any positive answer needs a clear plan even when the total score is not extreme.

subtopic_detail: Clozapine initiation monitoring for neutropenia
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health team commencing clozapine on a 32-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who has failed adequate trials of risperidone and olanzapine. He is registered with a clozapine monitoring program. He lives independently with his mother and has weekly community mental health contact. He has no medical comorbidities and no family history of blood dyscrasias.

Baseline investigations before starting: white cell count 6.4 x 10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), absolute neutrophil count 3.8 x 10^9/L (2.0 to 7.5), haemoglobin 148 g/L (135 to 175), platelets 260 x 10^9/L (150 to 400), fasting glucose 4.6 mmol/L, ECG showing sinus rhythm with QTc 420 ms. He is not febrile and there are no signs of infection.

data_table.Diagnosis: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia after failed risperidone and olanzapine
data_table.Baseline FBC: WCC 6.4; ANC 3.8; Hb 148; platelets 260 (all within reference)
data_table.Metabolic and cardiac: Fasting glucose 4.6; ECG sinus with QTc 420 ms
data_table.Support and monitoring: Community mental health weekly; registered clozapine monitoring program

lead_in: What is the most appropriate schedule for full blood count monitoring in the first year of clozapine therapy?

options.text: Daily neutrophil count for the first 2 weeks then weekly for the remainder of the first year
options.rationale: Daily monitoring is disproportionate to the risk profile and imposes an impractical burden without changing detection of the true onset window of neutropenia which is weeks 6 to 18 (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.text: Full blood count only when clinical symptoms of infection develop during therapy
options.rationale: Symptom-triggered monitoring alone misses asymptomatic neutropenia and does not meet program requirements; clozapine dispensing requires the FBC to be checked on schedule (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.text: Weekly full blood count for 4 weeks then monthly thereafter for the duration of treatment
options.rationale: This underscreens for clozapine-induced neutropenia, which peaks in the 6 to 18 week window; the AU program requires weekly to 18 weeks (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.text: Weekly full blood count for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then monthly ongoing
options.rationale: The Australian clozapine monitoring program requires weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then monthly indefinitely; this reflects the temporal risk of clozapine-induced neutropenia (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

options.text: Fortnightly full blood count from the outset then monthly after 12 months of treatment
options.rationale: Fortnightly from the outset misses the highest risk window; weekly for 18 weeks is mandated at the start of therapy (Source: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

explanation.summary: Clozapine has a small but persistent risk of neutropenia and agranulocytosis, peaking in the 6 to 18 week window. The Australian clozapine monitoring program requires weekly FBC for the first 18 weeks, fortnightly to 52 weeks, and monthly indefinitely; dispensing is contingent on the FBC. Fever should also trigger an FBC regardless of schedule. Baseline metabolic and cardiac assessment is done before commencement and repeated at 3 to 6 months. The other main monitoring risks are cardiac (myocarditis in the first 3 months) and constipation-related ileus.
key_points: Clozapine monitoring: weekly FBC for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then monthly
Fever mandates an unscheduled FBC regardless of last check
Baseline and follow-up ECG, troponin, and metabolic parameters at 3 to 6 months
explanation.pearls: Clozapine dispensing in Australia is program-linked; the pharmacy cannot dispense unless the FBC has been submitted and cleared in the last week.

sources.label: Australian Clozapine Product Information and RANZCP Clozapine Prescribing Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Generalised anxiety disorder first-line pharmacotherapy in an older adult
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 74-year-old woman with 6 months of persistent worry about her adult children, restlessness, muscle tension, difficulty falling asleep, and irritability that has curtailed her activities. She lives alone and has hypertension well controlled on perindopril. She has osteopenia but no other medical comorbidities. Her creatinine clearance is 62 mL/min and her sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145). She is not on any regular psychotropic medication.

Her GAD-7 score is 15 and PHQ-9 is 6. She has never had suicidal thoughts. She is otherwise engaged, cognitively intact on brief bedside testing, and reports no falls in the last year. She has read patient information on cognitive behavioural therapy and is willing to try either medication or therapy, and can access both.

data_table.Presentation: 6 months of worry, restlessness, muscle tension, insomnia, irritability
data_table.Comorbidities: Hypertension on perindopril; osteopenia; no falls in past year
data_table.Function: Cognitively intact; lives alone; activities curtailed by worry

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line medication to consider?

options.text: Oral escitalopram 5 mg daily uptitrated to 10 mg with 2 week review and sodium check at 4 weeks
options.rationale: Escitalopram is first-line for generalised anxiety disorder in Australia with strong efficacy data; in older adults the starting dose is halved to 5 mg with a cap of 10 mg (QT and hyponatraemia risk), and sodium is checked at 4 weeks because SSRI hyponatraemia risk rises with age (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Oral amitriptyline 25 mg at night uptitrated as needed for anxiety and sleep
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants are anticholinergic and pro-arrhythmic and are on the Beers list to avoid in older adults; they are not first-line for GAD (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Oral pregabalin 75 mg twice daily titrated to 150 mg twice daily as monotherapy
options.rationale: Pregabalin is second-line for GAD in AU practice with dose adjustment needed in reduced eGFR and a growing recognition of dependence; SSRI is tried first (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Oral diazepam 5 mg twice daily as ongoing maintenance therapy for the anxiety symptoms
options.rationale: Chronic benzodiazepines in older adults are avoided per the Beers criteria because of falls, cognitive impairment, and dependence; short courses only during SSRI initiation are acceptable but not as maintenance (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Oral quetiapine 25 mg at night titrated to 100 mg for anxiolysis and sleep
options.rationale: Quetiapine is not first-line for GAD, carries metabolic and QT risks, and is associated with excess mortality in older adults when used for behavioural symptoms (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Generalised anxiety disorder in an older adult should be treated with combined SSRI and cognitive behavioural therapy when both are accessible. Escitalopram is first-line with the starting dose halved (5 mg) and a cap of 10 mg in over-65s because of QT prolongation and hyponatraemia risk; sodium is checked at 4 weeks and any symptom of hyponatraemia (headache, confusion, seizure) prompts immediate assessment. Chronic benzodiazepines and tricyclics are on the Beers list. Quetiapine has metabolic and mortality signals in older adults. Pregabalin is second-line.
key_points: SSRI (escitalopram) first-line for GAD across age groups
Older adult escitalopram cap 10 mg per PBS/TGA to reduce QT prolongation
Check sodium at 4 weeks after SSRI initiation in older adults
explanation.pearls: SSRI-induced hyponatraemia typically appears within the first month; older women with low body weight are the highest-risk group and warrant a scheduled sodium recheck.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine Position Statement on Prescribing

subtopic_detail: Explaining catatonia and its likely course to a family
stem: You have diagnosed catatonia in a 58-year-old woman with major depression and started regular lorazepam. Her husband asks what he should expect over the next few days.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: mute, immobile, catalepsy present; conscious state clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate information to give him?

options.text: Most patients improve markedly on benzodiazepines within days
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines produce substantial improvement in most people with catatonia, often within hours to days, which is honest and supports engagement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Improvement is unlikely without electroconvulsive therapy first
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy leads when catatonia is malignant or has failed an adequate benzodiazepine trial, not at the outset in a stable patient (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Catatonia settles by itself once the mood episode is treated
options.rationale: This holds only for brief, mild catatonia in someone still eating and drinking; sustained immobility causes thromboembolism, dehydration and pressure injury (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Antipsychotic medication is the mainstay and starts tomorrow
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are the mainstay of the psychotic illness that sometimes underlies catatonia, but they can deepen the catatonia itself (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Recovery usually needs several months of inpatient rehabilitation
options.rationale: A prolonged course is seen in treatment resistant illness; it is not the expected trajectory of newly treated catatonia (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Families watching a relative who cannot speak or move often assume the worst, and clear information changes how they engage with treatment. Catatonia carries one of the better short term prognoses in psychiatry: most patients improve substantially with benzodiazepines, frequently within hours to days, and electroconvulsive therapy is highly effective for those who do not. The honest message is that the syndrome usually responds quickly, that the underlying illness then needs its own treatment, and that nursing care during immobility prevents the serious complications.
key_points: Most people with catatonia respond well to benzodiazepines within days
Electroconvulsive therapy is effective for those who do not respond
The underlying mood, psychotic or medical illness still needs treatment
Complications of immobility are prevented by active nursing care
explanation.pearls: Telling the family that the patient can usually hear and remember what is said at the bedside changes how the whole team speaks in the room. In context: catatonia is among the more treatable syndromes in psychiatry, and saying so early is both accurate and therapeutic for the family (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose ECG interpretation and sodium bicarbonate threshold
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman brought in by ambulance 90 minutes after an intentional overdose of about 3 g of amitriptyline. She was found drowsy at home and gave the drug history en route. She has a background of major depressive disorder, and has recently been changed from sertraline to amitriptyline for chronic pain. She takes no other medication and drank no alcohol today.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable and orientated when awake. Vital signs: pulse 130/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96 percent, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 140 ms and a tall R wave in aVR of 5 mm. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34, PaCO2 32 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, glucose 5.8 mmol/L. Activated charcoal was declined at scene.

data_table.Ingestion: About 3 g amitriptyline 90 minutes ago; no coingestants; drowsy but rousable
data_table.Vitals: HR 130; BP 92/56; RR 20; SpO2 96 percent; T 36.8
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia; QRS duration 140 ms; R wave in aVR 5 mm
data_table.ABG: pH 7.34; PaCO2 32; HCO3 18; Na 138; K 3.8; lactate 3.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start intravenous amiodarone 300 mg for the tachycardia and to prevent ventricular arrhythmia
options.rationale: Class Ia and III antiarrhythmics prolong the QT and worsen sodium-channel blockade in TCA toxicity; sodium bicarbonate is the antiarrhythmic in this context, not amiodarone (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally as her level of consciousness permits
options.rationale: Activated charcoal at 90 minutes post-ingestion in a drowsy patient without a protected airway risks aspiration and provides little benefit; airway protection is not adequate for a drowsy woman and cardiotoxicity is the immediate threat (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.text: Give a 20 percent intralipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus as first-line therapy for the overdose
options.rationale: Intralipid is a rescue therapy for lipophilic drug cardiotoxicity when standard treatment fails; sodium bicarbonate is first-line for TCA overdose and intralipid is not initial therapy (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg for the reduced level of consciousness
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures in mixed TCA-benzodiazepine ingestion and does not reverse TCA toxicity (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg intravenously and titrate serum pH to 7.5
options.rationale: QRS 100 ms or more and R wave in aVR 3 mm or more predict TCA cardiotoxicity; sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus with pH target 7.45 to 7.55 reverses sodium-channel blockade and is the first-line treatment for TCA toxicity per AU toxicology guidance (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

explanation.summary: TCA overdose kills through sodium-channel blockade producing QRS widening, hypotension, seizures, and ventricular arrhythmia. ECG features that predict toxicity are a QRS of 100 ms or more, R wave in aVR of 3 mm or more, and an R/S ratio in aVR of 0.7 or more. Treatment is sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus with a pH target of 7.45 to 7.55, repeated as needed, plus intubation for airway protection, benzodiazepines for seizures, and fluid or vasopressors for hypotension. Class Ia, Ic, and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Intralipid is rescue therapy for refractory cardiotoxicity, not first-line.
key_points: QRS 100 ms or more or R wave in aVR 3 mm or more triggers sodium bicarbonate in TCA overdose
Target pH 7.45 to 7.55 with 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bicarbonate boluses
Avoid flumazenil and Class Ia/Ic/III antiarrhythmics; use intralipid only as rescue
explanation.pearls: The R wave in aVR is easier to measure than the QRS in an untidy trace; a tall R in aVR alone is a valid trigger to alkalinise.

sources.label: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Sodium valproate teratogenicity and pregnancy-prevention program
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder in remission on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily and quetiapine 100 mg nightly for 2 years. She reports 6 months of stable mood without hypomanic or depressive symptoms. She now tells you that her partner and she have started trying for a pregnancy 8 weeks ago and she does not want to change medications because 'nothing has ever worked as well'.

She has no other medical history. She is using no contraception. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago and a home pregnancy test today is negative. She has full capacity for the discussion, understands she is in remission, and has an existing psychiatric care plan and mental health team engagement. She is currently on the state sodium valproate pregnancy-prevention program.

data_table.Diagnosis and history: Bipolar I in remission 6 months; stable on valproate 1000 mg plus quetiapine 100 mg for 2 years
data_table.Reproductive intent: Actively trying to conceive; no contraception; LMP 2 weeks ago; pregnancy test negative today
data_table.Program status: Enrolled in state sodium valproate pregnancy-prevention program
data_table.Insight: Full capacity; aware of remission; declines medication change

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her care?

options.text: Recommend cross-titration off valproate to lithium or lamotrigine and effective contraception until switch is complete
options.rationale: Sodium valproate carries a 10 percent major congenital malformation rate and 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental disorders; RANZCP and TGA-mandated pregnancy prevention programs require withdrawal wherever safe, with a cross-titration to lithium or lamotrigine and continued contraception until the switch is complete (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Continue valproate at the same dose and add high-dose folate 5 mg daily as adequate teratogen prevention
options.rationale: Folate supplementation does not offset the intrinsic teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks of valproate; TGA and RANZCP mandate switching where possible in women who could become pregnant, not continuation with folate (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Stop valproate today without a substitute mood stabiliser and monitor mood clinically for the next 4 weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt discontinuation without a replacement mood stabiliser carries a high relapse risk in bipolar I disorder; cross-titration protects mood stability while removing teratogen exposure (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily as a lower teratogenic dose while she attempts to conceive
options.rationale: There is no safe teratogenic dose of valproate; reducing dose reduces but does not eliminate risk and is not an acceptable strategy when a switch is possible (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

options.text: Continue valproate and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy as the sole added support during conception
options.rationale: Psychological therapy does not neutralise valproate teratogenicity; continuing valproate while trying to conceive is not consistent with the program she is enrolled in (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate has the highest teratogenicity of the AU-available anticonvulsants and mood stabilisers, with a 10 percent major malformation rate (neural tube defects, cardiac, facial) and a 30 to 40 percent rate of impaired neurodevelopmental outcome. TGA mandates a pregnancy prevention program for all women of reproductive potential prescribed valproate. When conception is planned, cross-titration to lithium (with careful monitoring) or lamotrigine (with slow titration) is the standard, with effective contraception maintained until the switch is complete and the woman is stable on the new regimen for at least 3 months.
key_points: Valproate: 10 percent major malformation; 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risk
TGA pregnancy prevention program mandates alternative therapy in women who could conceive
Cross-titrate to lithium or lamotrigine with contraception until switch is complete
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine dose needs to be increased through pregnancy because glucuronidation clearance rises; lithium dose needs monitoring across trimesters because renal clearance rises then falls postpartum.

sources.label: TGA Sodium Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic selection in first episode psychosis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community early intervention team. A 19-year-old university student is referred by his general practitioner with a 6 week history of paranoid ideas that his housemates are recording him, hearing voices commenting on his actions, and social withdrawal. He is a rugby player who cares about his fitness. His mother has hypothyroidism.

On mental state examination he is guarded but cooperative, with thought disorder and second person auditory hallucinations. He has no suicidal ideation and no aggressive plans. His weight is 78 kg, height 182 cm, waist circumference 82 cm.

Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.2 percent (less than 5.7), total cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L, ECG QTc 402 ms. He is antipsychotic naive and consents to treatment. He asks specifically about medication that will not cause weight gain.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76/min; BP 122/76 mmHg; RR 14/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Weight 78 kg; height 182 cm; waist 82 cm; guarded; thought disorder; second person auditory hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.2%; total cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L; ECG QTc 402 ms
data_table.History: Antipsychotic naive; concerned about weight gain

lead_in: Which antipsychotic is the most appropriate first line choice?

options.text: Aripiprazole 10 mg orally in the morning, titrated according to symptomatic response
options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic burden among first line atypicals with minimal weight gain and prolactin elevation; the RANZCP schizophrenia guideline lists it among first line agents in first episode psychosis, and it aligns with the patient's expressed priority (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Olanzapine 5 mg orally at night, titrated according to symptomatic response
options.rationale: Olanzapine has efficacy in first episode psychosis but has the highest weight gain and metabolic burden of the atypicals and is generally avoided in a metabolically clean young man who has raised the concern (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Haloperidol 5 mg orally at night, titrated to symptomatic response
options.rationale: Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol are not first line in first episode psychosis because of higher extrapyramidal side effects that increase the risk of medication discontinuation (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

options.text: Clozapine 25 mg orally at night with a weekly full blood count for monitoring
options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia after two adequate trials of other antipsychotics due to its haematological and metabolic risks; it is not a first line choice in a treatment naive patient (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

options.text: Quetiapine 300 mg orally at night, titrated to symptomatic response
options.rationale: Quetiapine has moderate weight gain and sedation and is not as effective as other atypicals at doses under 400 mg per day; it is not the preferred first line agent for a metabolically conscious young man with first episode psychosis (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline).

explanation.summary: First episode psychosis is managed with an atypical antipsychotic chosen for its side effect profile rather than for a specific mechanism of action because the atypicals have similar efficacy in this setting. Aripiprazole is often chosen for young metabolically clean patients because it has the lowest weight gain and prolactin elevation among the first line agents. Olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden and is avoided when weight or diabetic risk is a concern. Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia after two adequate trials of other antipsychotics.
key_points: Aripiprazole: lowest weight gain and prolactin among first line atypicals.
Olanzapine has the highest metabolic burden.
Clozapine reserved for treatment resistant schizophrenia after 2 adequate trials.
explanation.pearls: In first episode psychosis the atypicals have equivalent efficacy but very different side effect profiles; matching the drug to the patient's own priorities (metabolic, sedation, sexual side effects) improves adherence and long term outcomes.

subtopic_detail: Long term lithium monitoring and renal decline
stem: A 58-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for 22 years, with levels of 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L. She is euthymic and has no polyuria or thirst. She takes occasional ibuprofen and recently started perindopril.

data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L; creatinine 118 micromol/L (was 92) (45-90); eGFR 48 (was 68) mL/min/1.73 m^2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step?

options.text: Stop lithium and switch to sodium valproate, with nephrology review
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium discontinuation risks relapse of bipolar illness within weeks and switching without discussion is inappropriate; renal decline is managed by review of contributing drugs and dose reduction with continued monitoring under specialist input (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Reduce the lithium dose, cease ibuprofen, review perindopril, refer to nephrology
options.rationale: The falling estimated glomerular filtration rate reflects contributions from long term lithium, ibuprofen and perindopril; the guideline recommends dose reduction to the lowest effective concentration, review of nephrotoxic co medication in collaboration with the general practitioner and nephrology referral once the eGFR is below 60 mL/min per 1.73 m squared (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Increase the lithium dose to target a level between 0.8 and 1.0 mmol/L
options.rationale: Higher lithium concentrations increase the risk of long term nephrotoxicity and thyroid dysfunction; in a euthymic patient the aim is to use the lowest effective concentration rather than the highest tolerated (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

options.text: Add hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily and repeat the level in a week
options.rationale: Thiazide diuretics reduce renal clearance of lithium and precipitate toxicity; they should not be added without careful review of the lithium dose (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline; TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Continue unchanged and repeat renal function in twelve months
options.rationale: A drop in eGFR of 20 mL/min per 1.73 m squared over 6 months is significant and requires active management; delayed review of 12 months risks irreversible renal decline (Source: RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

explanation.summary: Long term lithium therapy is associated with a progressive decline in glomerular filtration rate; the risk rises with duration, high concentrations, episodes of toxicity and concurrent nephrotoxic drugs. When the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below 60 mL/min per 1.73 m squared the RANZCP guidance is to reduce the dose to the lowest effective concentration, review co medication such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and thiazide diuretics, and consider nephrology referral. Thyroid dysfunction and hyperparathyroidism are also long term concerns and require targeted testing. Discontinuation is a specialist decision and requires slow tapering over months with alternative mood stabilisation planned.
key_points: eGFR below 60 mL/min per 1.73 m squared triggers dose review and specialist input.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and thiazides increase lithium levels.
Slow taper over months if discontinuation is required.
explanation.pearls: A creatinine rise of even 20 micromol/L in a stable lithium patient warrants review of nephrotoxic co medication because the combination of lithium plus non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug plus ACE inhibitor can accelerate irreversible renal decline within months.

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of SSRI discontinuation from depressive relapse
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 34-year-old woman who is 5 days into stopping paroxetine 20 mg daily after 14 months of treatment for a first episode of major depression. She stopped abruptly against advice when she felt too well to continue. She reports dizziness, brain zaps, and irritability over the last 3 days.

On assessment she has no anhedonia, her sleep is normal, appetite normal, energy has been high, and she has been enjoying her hobbies. There is no suicidal ideation and no hopelessness. She scores 4 on the PHQ-9.

Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. No focal neurological findings. She is worried that her illness is returning.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84/min; BP 122/76 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: No anhedonia; sleep normal; appetite normal; enjoying hobbies; no suicidal ideation; PHQ-9 score 4; no focal neurology
data_table.History: Stopped paroxetine 20 mg after 14 months, 5 days ago; dizziness, brain zaps, irritability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose depressive relapse, increase paroxetine to 40 mg daily and add cognitive behavioural therapy referral
options.rationale: Relapse presents with a return of core depressive symptoms over weeks, not with dizziness and brain zaps within days of stopping; the pattern here fits discontinuation syndrome and increasing to a higher dose is not warranted (Source: TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Reassure that the symptoms will resolve within a few days without any medication and review in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Untreated paroxetine discontinuation typically lasts 1 to 3 weeks and can be severe; simply waiting is unpleasant for the patient and misses the opportunity to teach appropriate tapering practice (Source: TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Switch immediately to fluoxetine 20 mg to bridge the discontinuation because of its long half life
options.rationale: Bridging with fluoxetine may be considered when a patient cannot tolerate re exposure to the original drug; it is not the first step when the pragmatic option of restarting the original drug and tapering is available (Source: TG Psychotropic).

options.text: Explain that these are discontinuation symptoms, restart paroxetine at the usual dose and taper over 6 to 8 weeks
options.rationale: The onset within days of stopping short half life SSRI, presence of dizziness and paraesthesia and absence of core depressive symptoms is classical SSRI discontinuation syndrome; restarting at the previous dose and tapering over 6 to 8 weeks resolves symptoms and avoids conflating them with relapse (Source: TG Psychotropic; RANZCP mood disorders guideline).

options.text: Refer urgently to psychiatry as the symptoms are likely a paroxetine hypersensitivity reaction
options.rationale: Discontinuation symptoms are the expected pharmacological response, not a hypersensitivity reaction; hypersensitivity would present with rash, angioedema or serotonin syndrome, none of which is present (Source: TG Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: SSRI discontinuation syndrome typically appears within 1 to 3 days of stopping a short half life SSRI such as paroxetine, includes dizziness, paraesthesia, brain zaps, irritability and flu like symptoms, and resolves within 1 to 3 weeks. It is distinguished from depressive relapse by the timing, absence of core depressive symptoms, and rapid response to restarting the drug. Restarting at the usual dose and tapering over 6 to 8 weeks is the standard approach. Fluoxetine bridging is an option if re exposure to the original drug is not tolerated.
key_points: Onset within days of stopping suggests discontinuation, not relapse.
Paroxetine and venlafaxine have the shortest half lives and cause the most severe discontinuation.
Taper over 6 to 8 weeks after restarting.
explanation.pearls: A PHQ-9 under 5 with dizziness, brain zaps and paraesthesia within a week of stopping paroxetine reads as discontinuation, not relapse; restart the drug and taper over 6 to 8 weeks rather than escalating dose.

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose triage
stem: A 32-year-old woman is brought in 90 minutes after taking about 3 g of amitriptyline. She is drowsy but rousable, warm and dry, with dilated pupils.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 /min, BP 96/58 mmHg, T 37.1 degrees C, GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, QRS 128 ms, terminal R wave in aVR 4 mm, QTc 468 ms; VBG pH 7.32, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L; glucose 5.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g orally with four hours of ward cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Activated charcoal is not routinely given beyond 1 to 2 hours of ingestion because gastric absorption is largely complete; more importantly the ECG changes require immediate sodium bicarbonate rather than delayed decontamination (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg, then reassess the airway and conscious state
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and has no role in tricyclic overdose; it may precipitate seizures in mixed overdoses and unmask sodium channel toxicity (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Gastric lavage and an intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion over 20 minutes
options.rationale: Gastric lavage is not standard care beyond the first hour and carries aspiration risk in a drowsy patient; magnesium is for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and not first line without arrhythmia (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading dose to prevent seizures
options.rationale: Phenytoin is contraindicated in tricyclic overdose because it shares sodium channel blockade and worsens cardiotoxicity; benzodiazepines are the anticonvulsant of choice (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4 per cent bolus with continuous telemetry
options.rationale: A QRS above 100 ms and terminal R wave in aVR indicate significant sodium channel blockade and predict cardiovascular collapse and seizures in tricyclic overdose; sodium bicarbonate at 1 to 2 mmol/kg (100 mL of 8.4 percent for a 70 kg adult) narrows the QRS and reduces arrhythmia risk (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre; TG Toxicology).

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose produces sodium channel blockade with QRS widening, terminal R wave in aVR and risk of cardiovascular collapse and seizures, plus anticholinergic effects. A QRS above 100 ms or a terminal R wave in aVR of at least 3 mm is an indication for a sodium bicarbonate bolus of 1 to 2 mmol/kg, repeated to keep the QRS narrow and to buffer acidosis. Benzodiazepines are used for seizures; phenytoin is contraindicated because it worsens the sodium channel blockade. Activated charcoal is only useful within 1 to 2 hours of ingestion and gastric lavage is not routine due to aspiration risk.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms or aVR terminal R at least 3 mm: give sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg.
Benzodiazepines for seizures; phenytoin is contraindicated.
Charcoal only within 1 to 2 hours; lavage is not routine.
explanation.pearls: A tricyclic overdose with QRS above 160 ms carries a 50 percent risk of ventricular arrhythmia, so give the first sodium bicarbonate bolus at the bedside as soon as the ECG is seen rather than waiting on blood gas results.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis and treatment considerations
stem: A 28-year-old accountant has lifelong difficulty concentrating, worse since starting a demanding role six months ago, with missed deadlines, restlessness and interrupting others. School reports at age 8 described him as fidgety and easily distracted.

data_table.Examination: No depressive or anxious cognitions, no history of mania
data_table.Investigations: Adult ADHD Self Report Scale Part A 5 of 6 positive; thyroid function and iron studies normal
data_table.Driving: Drives daily, no crashes in 3 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist for diagnostic assessment
options.rationale: The clinical picture is suggestive of adult ADHD with childhood onset symptoms and functional impairment; Australian practice is a formal assessment by a psychiatrist or paediatrician to confirm diagnosis, exclude co morbidity and initiate stimulant treatment under authority arrangements (Source: RANZCP ADHD guideline; Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD).
source_refs: Australian evidence based clinical practice guideline for ADHD

options.text: Start dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily, review in 2 weeks
options.rationale: In Australia stimulant medication for ADHD requires an authority from a psychiatrist or paediatrician; the general practitioner cannot initiate it and must refer for formal assessment (Source: RANZCP ADHD guideline; PBS authority conditions).

options.text: Diagnose generalised anxiety disorder and start sertraline
options.rationale: There are no core anxiety symptoms; treating a presumed anxiety disorder without evidence risks missing the underlying ADHD and delays appropriate care (Source: RANZCP ADHD guideline).

options.text: Advise him to stop driving until treatment starts
options.rationale: Australian fitness to drive standards do not require driving cessation while awaiting ADHD assessment in a patient with no crashes and no significant impairment behind the wheel (Source: Austroads assessing fitness to drive).
