options.rationale: This masks the amenorrhoea without lowering prolactin and leaves the galactorrhoea and the underlying oestrogen deficiency untreated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Cease risperidone entirely and monitor her mental state closely over the next month
options.rationale: Stopping antipsychotic cover eight months into remission from a psychotic illness carries a high relapse risk when a prolactin sparing alternative is available (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride cause the highest rates of hyperprolactinaemia among antipsychotics because they block tuberoinfundibular dopamine receptors and lift the tonic inhibition of prolactin release. Symptoms include amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction and, over years, reduced bone mineral density from oestrogen deficiency, which is why the problem is treated rather than tolerated. Drug induced levels usually sit below about 2000 to 3000 mIU/L, and a level substantially above that or any headache or visual field defect should redirect towards pituitary imaging. Aripiprazole is the standard destination because partial dopamine agonism preserves antipsychotic effect while releasing prolactin inhibition.
key_points: Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride carry the highest prolactin liability
Drug induced elevation is usually below about 2000 to 3000 mIU/L
Imaging is triggered by disproportionate levels, headache or visual field defect
Untreated hyperprolactinaemia reduces bone mineral density through oestrogen deficiency
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole added at low dose alongside the existing antipsychotic will also lower prolactin, which is the workaround when a patient has responded only to risperidone and a full switch is judged too risky.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant selection with a cytochrome P450 2D6 interaction
stem:
You are the consultation liaison registrar asked to advise on a 52-year-old woman attending the breast clinic. She completed treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer 10 months ago and takes tamoxifen 20 mg daily, which is planned to continue for five years.

Over the past three months she has had persistent low mood, loss of interest, poor concentration and early morning waking, and she scores in the moderate range on a depression rating scale. She has never taken an antidepressant. She has no history of mania, takes no other regular medicines, and her renal function, liver function, sodium and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Medications: Tamoxifen 20 mg daily
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145); renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate first choice?

options.text: Paroxetine 20 mg daily, increasing to 40 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
options.rationale: Paroxetine is the strongest cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor among the antidepressants and has been associated with increased breast cancer mortality in women taking tamoxifen (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg daily, increasing to 40 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is also a potent cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor and its long half life means the interaction persists for weeks after any dose change (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily, increasing to 300 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
options.rationale: Bupropion is a moderate to strong cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor and is not registered as an antidepressant in Australia, so it fails on both interaction and availability grounds (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Duloxetine 30 mg daily, increasing to 60 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
options.rationale: Duloxetine is a moderate cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor, so it is a less clean choice than an agent with negligible effect on that enzyme (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Escitalopram 10 mg daily, increasing to 20 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
options.rationale: Escitalopram has negligible cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibition and so does not impair the conversion of tamoxifen to its active metabolite endoxifen, making it the standard first choice in this setting (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; eviQ Cancer Treatments Online).

explanation.summary: Tamoxifen is a prodrug that requires cytochrome P450 2D6 to be converted to endoxifen, the metabolite responsible for most of its antioestrogen activity. Strong inhibitors of that enzyme reduce endoxifen concentrations substantially, and observational data link paroxetine co prescription with increased breast cancer mortality. Depression is common after breast cancer treatment and undertreating it is not the answer, so the task is agent selection rather than avoidance of antidepressants. Escitalopram, citalopram and venlafaxine all have minimal effect on the enzyme, and venlafaxine has the added advantage of evidence for tamoxifen related hot flushes.
key_points: Tamoxifen is a prodrug activated by cytochrome P450 2D6 to endoxifen
Paroxetine and fluoxetine are strong inhibitors and are avoided with tamoxifen
Escitalopram, citalopram and venlafaxine have minimal effect on the enzyme
Depression after breast cancer treatment is treated, not avoided, with careful agent choice
explanation.pearls: Venlafaxine is the preferred choice when the same patient also needs treatment for tamoxifen induced hot flushes, since it spares cytochrome P450 2D6 and reduces flush frequency, whereas paroxetine would treat the flushes while undermining the tamoxifen.

subtopic_detail: Long term benzodiazepine deprescribing in an older patient
stem:
You are the registrar in a general practice clinic seeing a 71-year-old woman who has taken temazepam 20 mg nightly for six years, originally prescribed after a bereavement.

She has fallen twice in the past three months, both times when getting up overnight, and sustained a wrist fracture on the second occasion. She says the tablets no longer help her sleep but that she cannot manage without them and becomes anxious if she misses a dose. Her cognition is normal on formal testing, her postural blood pressure drop is 6 mmHg, and her vision, vitamin D and renal function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Gait steady in daylight, no peripheral neuropathy, cognitive screening normal
data_table.Investigations: Renal function, liver function, full blood count and vitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her temazepam?

options.text: Continue temazepam at the current dose and install home rails and night lighting
options.rationale: Environmental modification helps but leaves the single most modifiable falls risk factor in place, and she herself reports the drug no longer produces the intended effect (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Substitute an equivalent diazepam dose and reduce it gradually over several months
options.rationale: Switching to a long-acting agent smooths the interdose fall in concentration that drives rebound anxiety, and a slow staged reduction over months is what makes withdrawal tolerable in long term use (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Cease temazepam tonight and prescribe temazepam 10 mg for occasional rescue use
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after six years risks a withdrawal syndrome including seizures, and intermittent rescue dosing perpetuates the dependence it is meant to end (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Replace temazepam with nightly quetiapine 25 mg and review her sleep in one month
options.rationale: Substituting an antipsychotic exchanges one falls risk for another and adds metabolic and extrapyramidal harm, and quetiapine is not indicated for insomnia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Replace temazepam with nightly melatonin and give her written sleep hygiene advice
options.rationale: Melatonin and sleep hygiene are useful adjuncts during a taper but cannot cover an abrupt substitution after six years of physiological dependence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Benzodiazepine use in older people roughly doubles the risk of falls and hip fracture, and tolerance to the hypnotic effect develops within weeks while the falls risk persists indefinitely. Deprescribing is therefore a positive intervention rather than the withdrawal of a comfort, but it fails when it is done abruptly or on a timescale set by the clinician rather than the patient. Substituting a long-acting agent such as diazepam is standard when interdose rebound anxiety is prominent, as it is when a short-acting hypnotic has been taken nightly for years. Reductions of around 10 to 25 per cent of the dose every one to two weeks, slowing further as the dose falls, are typical, and cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the definitive treatment for the underlying sleep complaint.
key_points: Benzodiazepines roughly double falls and hip fracture risk in older people
Hypnotic tolerance develops within weeks while falls risk does not diminish
Long-acting substitution reduces interdose rebound during a taper
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the definitive treatment for the sleep complaint
explanation.pearls: Reduce by about 10 to 25 per cent of the dose every one to two weeks and slow the rate as the total dose falls, because the final 5 mg of diazepam equivalent is reliably harder than the first 20 mg.

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant continuation during breastfeeding
stem:
You are the registrar in a perinatal mental health clinic seeing a 30-year-old woman who is six weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding a healthy term infant.

She has recurrent major depressive disorder with three previous episodes, one of which required admission. She has taken fluoxetine 20 mg daily for four years, remained on it through pregnancy, and has stayed well throughout including the past six weeks. Her infant is feeding well, is gaining weight along the fiftieth centile and is neurologically normal at the six week check. She asks whether she should stop or change her medication now that she is feeding.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no suicidal ideation, mother and infant interaction warm and responsive
data_table.Investigations: Edinburgh postnatal depression scale score 4; full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her medication?

options.text: Stop fluoxetine now and restart it promptly if any depressive symptoms return
options.rationale: Discontinuation in the first postpartum year in recurrent depression carries a high relapse risk, and waiting for symptoms means intervening after the illness has already returned (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Switch to sertraline because it produces the lowest relative infant dose available
options.rationale: Sertraline is the usual first choice when starting an antidepressant during lactation, but switching an agent that has already kept her well through pregnancy risks relapse for a marginal pharmacokinetic gain (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Halve the dose to 10 mg daily to reduce the total quantity reaching her infant
options.rationale: A subtherapeutic dose exposes the infant to the drug anyway while withdrawing the protection the mother needs, which is the worst of both positions (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Continue fluoxetine unchanged and support her to keep breastfeeding as she wishes
options.rationale: The relative infant dose of fluoxetine sits within the range generally regarded as acceptable, the infant is thriving and neurologically normal, and continuing an agent that has maintained remission through pregnancy is the lowest risk option for both (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

options.text: Continue fluoxetine and advise her to change to formula feeding to avoid exposure
options.rationale: Ceasing breastfeeding forfeits its established maternal and infant benefits to avoid an exposure that is already within accepted limits in a thriving infant (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: Almost all antidepressants pass into breast milk in small quantities, and the relative infant dose, meaning the infant dose expressed as a percentage of the maternal weight adjusted dose, is the standard measure of that exposure. A relative infant dose below 10 per cent is generally regarded as acceptable, and the commonly used antidepressants sit well below that. Sertraline and paroxetine have the lowest relative infant doses and are usual first choices when initiating during lactation, while fluoxetine's longer half life gives it a slightly higher figure that is still within accepted limits. The dominant risk in this scenario is not drug exposure but maternal relapse, which carries measurable harm to infant attachment and development.
key_points: Relative infant dose below 10 per cent is generally regarded as acceptable in lactation
Sertraline has the lowest relative infant dose and is a usual first choice when starting new treatment
An agent already maintaining remission is generally continued rather than switched
Maternal relapse carries its own substantial risk to infant attachment and development
explanation.pearls: Watch a breastfed infant of a mother on fluoxetine for irritability, poor feeding or excess drowsiness rather than for any specific syndrome, since the long half life of norfluoxetine means any effect accumulates over the first weeks rather than appearing immediately.

sources.label: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

subtopic_detail: Delusional disorder versus schizophreniform and brief psychotic disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 46-year-old electrician brought in by his wife. For eight months he has been certain she is having an affair with a neighbour, and he checks her phone, odometer and laundry daily and has begun following her car.

He has continued to run his business without difficulty, meets his contract deadlines and is described by his employees as unchanged in every other respect. He has no hallucinations, his speech is organised, his self care is intact and his mood is not elevated or depressed. His wife confirms the accusations have no basis and that nothing else about him has altered. His urine drug screen is negative and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain is unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Speech organised and goal directed, affect reactive, no hallucinations, no negative symptoms, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; magnetic resonance imaging of the brain unremarkable; full blood count, renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Delusional disorder, jealous type, with function preserved outside the belief itself
options.rationale: A non bizarre delusion of at least one month with no other psychotic symptoms and function not obviously impaired apart from behaviour flowing directly from the belief is the defining pattern (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Schizophreniform disorder, given the eight month duration of psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: Schizophreniform disorder is defined by a duration of one to six months and requires the broader symptom criteria of schizophrenia, neither of which is satisfied at eight months with an isolated delusion (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder, given the abrupt onset of a clearly circumscribed belief
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires full remission within one month, so eight months of continuous symptoms excludes it regardless of how circumscribed the content is (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Paranoid personality disorder with pervasive suspiciousness of his wife and others
options.rationale: Personality disorder requires a pervasive lifelong pattern across relationships, whereas this is a discrete belief that began eight months ago in a man previously described as unchanged (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Obsessive compulsive disorder with poor insight driving his repeated checking rituals
options.rationale: Obsessional checking is driven by doubt and is experienced as unwanted and intrusive, whereas he holds the belief with full conviction and checks to confirm rather than to relieve anxiety (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

explanation.summary: Delusional disorder is easily missed because functioning outside the delusional system is preserved, so patients present late and usually at the instigation of a family member rather than themselves. The three psychotic disorder diagnoses that turn on duration are worth holding as a set: brief psychotic disorder resolves within one month, schizophreniform disorder runs one to six months, and schizophrenia requires six months of disturbance including one month of active symptoms. Delusional disorder sits outside that sequence, requiring one month or more of delusions without the other criteria for schizophrenia. The jealous subtype carries a specific and serious risk of violence towards the accused partner, so a risk assessment that includes the wife's safety is part of the initial management rather than an afterthought.
key_points: Brief psychotic disorder resolves within one month and schizophreniform runs one to six months
Delusional disorder requires one month or more of delusions without other schizophrenia criteria
Function outside the delusional system is characteristically preserved
The jealous subtype carries a specific risk of violence towards the accused partner
explanation.pearls: In delusional jealousy, ask the partner separately about stalking, threats and access to weapons, because the risk assessment that matters concerns a person who is not your patient and who will not be in the room if you do not ask for it.

sources.label: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Gamma hydroxybutyrate withdrawal
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man brought in by friends with agitation and tremor. He has been using a clear liquid he buys in a small bottle and doses every two to three hours around the clock, including overnight, for the past eight months.

His last dose was three hours ago, taken because he woke with the same symptoms. He is sweating, tremulous and repeatedly tries to get off the trolley. He has already received diazepam 20 mg orally in divided doses over the past hour with no discernible change. His breath has no alcoholic smell, his blood alcohol is not detected, and his blood glucose is 5.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 168/96, RR 24, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, diaphoresis, disoriented to time and place, visual hallucinations of insects
data_table.Investigations: Blood alcohol not detected; blood glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.0-7.7); sodium, potassium and creatinine within normal limits; creatine kinase 340 U/L (30-190)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give oral thiamine and manage him with hourly observation in the short stay unit
options.rationale: Thiamine is appropriate supportive care but oral dosing and ward level observation badly underestimate a withdrawal syndrome that can progress to rhabdomyolysis and death within hours (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Give intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg and repeat once after 30 minutes if required
options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not act on the receptor system driving this withdrawal, so they are adjuncts at most and never the primary agent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Escalate to high dose intravenous diazepam titrated in a monitored critical care area
options.rationale: Gamma hydroxybutyrate withdrawal is benzodiazepine responsive but characteristically requires very large and rapidly escalating doses given intravenously, and the failure of 20 mg orally is the expected pattern rather than evidence against the diagnosis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine; Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).

options.text: Commence an intravenous fluid infusion and reassess his agitation in two hours
options.rationale: Fluids address the rhabdomyolysis risk but leave the withdrawal itself untreated, and a two hour reassessment interval is far too long for a syndrome that deteriorates this quickly (Source: Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).

options.text: Commence a buprenorphine and naloxone film and observe for symptom improvement
options.rationale: Opioid substitution treats opioid withdrawal, which does not produce this degree of hyperthermia, hypertension and delirium and is not suggested by the described use pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

explanation.summary: Gamma hydroxybutyrate has a half life of under an hour, so dependent users must dose every two to three hours around the clock and withdrawal begins within hours rather than days of the last dose. The syndrome resembles severe alcohol withdrawal but is faster in onset, more likely to progress to delirium, and notoriously refractory, with reported total diazepam requirements running into hundreds of milligrams. Barbiturates and, in some centres, baclofen are used as adjuncts when benzodiazepine escalation alone is insufficient. Mortality arises from hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, arrhythmia and aspiration, so management belongs in a critical care environment from the outset.
key_points: Overnight dosing every two to three hours is the historical signature of dependence
Withdrawal begins within hours of the last dose, not days
Benzodiazepine requirements are large, escalate rapidly and are given intravenously
Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and are adjuncts at most
explanation.pearls: A patient who sets an alarm to dose overnight has a substance with a half life under about two hours, which points at gamma hydroxybutyrate rather than alcohol or benzodiazepines before any test result is available.

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural disturbance in Parkinson disease
stem:
You are the medical registrar on call. A 74-year-old man admitted two days ago with a urinary tract infection has become acutely agitated overnight. He is pulling at his intravenous line, has struck out at a nurse and cannot be redirected by verbal reassurance or by his wife.

He has Parkinson disease treated with levodopa and carbidopa, and his mobility depends on it. He is disoriented to place and time, and his attention fluctuates markedly over minutes. Reorientation, dimmed lighting and the removal of unnecessary lines have already been tried without effect, and he now poses an immediate risk to himself and to staff. His oxygen saturation, blood glucose, sodium and calcium are within normal limits and he is not in urinary retention.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 142/84, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Examination: Fluctuating attention, disoriented, resting tremor and rigidity, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Sodium, potassium, calcium, blood glucose and liver function within normal limits; bladder scan 40 mL

lead_in: Which medication is the most appropriate choice for immediate sedation?

options.text: Haloperidol 0.5 mg intramuscularly, repeated once after 30 minutes if required
options.rationale: Haloperidol is the usual first choice in hyperactive delirium but its potent dopamine blockade can precipitate a severe and prolonged deterioration in parkinsonian motor function (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Olanzapine 5 mg intramuscularly, repeated once after 30 minutes if required
options.rationale: Olanzapine has less extrapyramidal liability than haloperidol but still worsens motor function in Parkinson disease and is not one of the two agents considered safe in this population (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Risperidone 0.5 mg orally, repeated once after 30 minutes if he remains agitated
options.rationale: Risperidone has the highest extrapyramidal liability of the second generation agents at any effective dose, which makes it a poor choice when nigrostriatal dopamine is already depleted (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg orally, repeated once after 30 minutes if he remains agitated
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines prolong and deepen delirium in older patients and are reserved for alcohol or sedative withdrawal or for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Quetiapine 25 mg orally, repeated once after 30 minutes if he remains agitated
options.rationale: Quetiapine and clozapine are the only antipsychotics with sufficiently loose striatal dopamine binding to be used in Parkinson disease, and quetiapine is the practical choice since clozapine requires haematological monitoring and titration (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Delirium is managed first by treating the precipitant and by non-pharmacological measures, and medication is reserved for distress or risk that persists after those have failed, as described here. The default agent in hyperactive delirium is low dose haloperidol, but Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies invert that default because dopamine blockade can produce catastrophic and long lasting motor deterioration or neuroleptic sensitivity reactions. Quetiapine and clozapine dissociate rapidly from the striatal dopamine receptor and are the accepted exceptions. Withdrawing or reducing levodopa to control the agitation is a common error that trades confusion for immobility and risks a parkinsonism hyperpyrexia syndrome.
key_points: Treat the precipitant and use non-pharmacological measures before any sedating medication
Haloperidol is the usual first choice in hyperactive delirium but not in Parkinson disease
Quetiapine and clozapine are the antipsychotics tolerated in parkinsonian patients
Benzodiazepines deepen delirium except in withdrawal states or neuroleptic malignant syndrome
explanation.pearls: Never abruptly stop levodopa to settle agitation in Parkinson disease, because withdrawal can precipitate a parkinsonism hyperpyrexia syndrome that is clinically indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy with a psychiatric history
stem:
You are the registrar in a general practice clinic seeing a 44-year-old woman who smokes 30 cigarettes a day and has done so since she was 17. She wakes at night to smoke and lights her first cigarette within five minutes of waking.

She has tried nicotine patches alone twice and relapsed within a fortnight on both occasions. She has a history of a single depressive episode eight years ago, treated with sertraline and in full remission for seven years off all medication. She has no history of seizures, no eating disorder and no current depressive symptoms. Her renal function and liver function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 130/82, RR 15, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no suicidal ideation, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Renal function, liver function, full blood count and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is the most appropriate first choice?

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg daily used alone for 12 weeks with behavioural support
options.rationale: Single form nicotine replacement has already failed twice in a heavily dependent smoker, so repeating it without escalation is unlikely to succeed a third time (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation guideline).

options.text: Bupropion 150 mg daily for three days then twice daily for nine further weeks
options.rationale: Bupropion is less effective than varenicline in head to head comparison and lowers the seizure threshold, so it sits behind varenicline rather than ahead of it (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation guideline; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Varenicline titrated over the first week and continued for 12 weeks after quitting
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation, and a large randomised safety trial found no excess neuropsychiatric events in people with treated and stable psychiatric illness (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation guideline; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Nicotine lozenges used as required alone for 12 weeks with behavioural support
options.rationale: Oral nicotine alone provides less consistent coverage of background craving than a patch, so it is weaker rather than stronger than the strategy that has already failed (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation guideline).

options.text: Behavioural counselling and quitline referral alone with no pharmacotherapy offered
options.rationale: Behavioural support roughly doubles quit rates but withholding pharmacotherapy from a heavily dependent smoker forfeits the larger part of the achievable benefit (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation guideline).

explanation.summary: Time to first cigarette under 30 minutes and waking overnight to smoke are the two most useful bedside markers of heavy nicotine dependence and both predict that monotherapy with a patch will fail. Varenicline is the most effective single pharmacotherapy, with combination nicotine replacement using a patch plus an oral form as the closest alternative. Historical concerns about varenicline causing neuropsychiatric harm were largely resolved by a large randomised trial that found no excess of such events in people with stable psychiatric illness, and a boxed warning was subsequently removed in several jurisdictions. Remitted depression is therefore not a reason to avoid varenicline, though monitoring mood during a quit attempt remains sensible because nicotine withdrawal itself lowers mood.
key_points: Smoking within 30 minutes of waking and overnight smoking mark heavy dependence
Varenicline is the most effective single agent and combination nicotine replacement is the closest alternative
Randomised safety data found no excess neuropsychiatric events in stable psychiatric illness
Behavioural support roughly doubles quit rates and is combined with, not substituted for, pharmacotherapy
explanation.pearls: Start varenicline one to two weeks before the nominated quit date and keep smoking during the titration, because the quit date is set after steady state is reached rather than on the first day of treatment.

subtopic_detail: Alcohol use disorder pharmacotherapy with hepatic impairment
stem:
You are the registrar in a hospital drug and alcohol service reviewing a 55-year-old man three days after an admission for decompensated alcohol related liver disease. He has completed uncomplicated withdrawal management and is now medically stable.

He has been drinking about 20 standard drinks daily for 15 years and states that his goal is complete abstinence. His most recent imaging and bloods confirm established cirrhosis with a bilirubin of 46 micromol/L, an albumin of 29 g/L and an international normalised ratio of 1.6. He takes no opioids and has no renal impairment. He has never taken pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 118/70, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Palmar erythema, spider naevi, no asterixis, no ascites on examination
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 46 micromol/L (less than 20); albumin 29 g/L (35-50); international normalised ratio 1.6 (0.9-1.3); creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is the most appropriate choice to support abstinence?

options.text: Naltrexone 50 mg daily commenced now and continued for at least six months
options.rationale: Naltrexone undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism and is avoided in acute hepatitis and decompensated liver disease, which is the situation here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Disulfiram 200 mg daily commenced now and continued with supervised dosing
options.rationale: Disulfiram is hepatotoxic in its own right and is contraindicated in significant hepatic impairment, so it is the least safe option in a decompensated patient (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg twice daily continued as maintenance to reduce his craving for alcohol
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines have no role beyond managing withdrawal, and ongoing use risks dependence and precipitates encephalopathy in cirrhosis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Topiramate titrated slowly to 100 mg twice daily as first line relapse prevention
options.rationale: Topiramate has supportive evidence but is used off label in Australia and sits behind the registered agents when one of them is safe to give (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

options.text: Acamprosate 666 mg three times daily commenced now that withdrawal has resolved
options.rationale: Acamprosate is renally rather than hepatically cleared, which makes it the preferred agent in significant liver disease, and it supports maintenance of abstinence in a patient whose stated goal is complete abstinence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine; Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Naltrexone and acamprosate are the two first line registered pharmacotherapies for alcohol use disorder in Australia, and the choice between them turns on organ function and on the patient's treatment goal. Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and is preferred when the goal is reduced drinking rather than abstinence, since it blunts the reinforcing effect of alcohol that is drunk. Acamprosate is renally cleared and helps maintain abstinence once it has been achieved, which makes it the better fit for both the hepatic picture and the stated goal here. Both agents work best alongside psychosocial treatment, and neither is a substitute for it.
key_points: Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and acamprosate is renally cleared
Acamprosate maintains abstinence once achieved, naltrexone reduces heavy drinking
Disulfiram is hepatotoxic and contraindicated in significant liver disease
Benzodiazepines have no maintenance role and precipitate encephalopathy in cirrhosis
explanation.pearls: Acamprosate needs a dose reduction once the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below 60 mL/min and is contraindicated below 30, which is the mirror image of the hepatic limits that rule out naltrexone.

subtopic_detail: Substance induced depressive disorder versus independent major depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 39-year-old man in the outpatient clinic, four weeks after an inpatient admission for alcohol withdrawal.

On admission he described eight months of low mood, hopelessness, poor sleep and thoughts that his family would be better off without him. Those eight months coincided exactly with an escalation from 10 to 30 standard drinks daily after he lost his job. He has now been continuously abstinent for four weeks, verified by carbohydrate deficient transferrin, and has taken no antidepressant at any stage. Today he reports that his mood, sleep, appetite and outlook have all returned to normal and he denies any suicidal thoughts. He had no depressive symptoms during a previous two year period of abstinence in his twenties.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic with reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Carbohydrate deficient transferrin within the abstinent range; liver function improving; thyroid function, full blood count and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder in early remission following his recent hospital admission
options.rationale: Independent major depression does not reliably remit within four weeks of abstinence alone and without any antidepressant, and his previous abstinent period was symptom free (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Alcohol induced depressive disorder that has resolved with sustained abstinence
options.rationale: The symptoms began with the escalation in drinking, were absent during a previous prolonged abstinent period, and remitted within four weeks of abstinence without antidepressant treatment, which is the defining temporal signature (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Adjustment disorder with depressed mood precipitated by the loss of his employment
options.rationale: Adjustment disorder requires symptoms to resolve within six months of the stressor ending and does not accommodate eight months of symptoms of this severity including suicidal thinking (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Persistent depressive disorder with a superimposed alcohol use disorder developing
options.rationale: Persistent depressive disorder requires depressed mood for at least two years, whereas his symptoms lasted eight months and he was well through an earlier abstinent period (Source: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision).
source_refs: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

options.text: Protracted alcohol withdrawal syndrome producing his ongoing affective disturbance
options.rationale: Protracted withdrawal would explain persisting symptoms rather than their complete resolution, and he is now entirely asymptomatic at four weeks (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine).

explanation.summary: Roughly 30 to 40 per cent of people presenting with depression and heavy alcohol use have a substance induced disorder rather than an independent one, and the distinction cannot be made at the first interview because the cross sectional picture is identical. Three pieces of longitudinal evidence separate them: whether symptoms preceded the substance use, whether they persisted during previous prolonged abstinence, and whether they remit with abstinence alone. Most substance induced depressive symptoms resolve within two to four weeks of abstinence, which is why a period of observation before committing to an antidepressant is standard rather than negligent. Persistence beyond about four weeks of verified abstinence redirects the diagnosis to an independent depressive disorder and prompts antidepressant treatment.
key_points: Substance induced depression is identical to independent depression cross sectionally
The separators are onset relative to use, symptoms during prior abstinence, and remission with abstinence
Most substance induced symptoms resolve within two to four weeks of abstinence
Persistence beyond four weeks of verified abstinence points to an independent disorder
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about mood during any previous period of sustained abstinence, because a symptom-free abstinent interval of months or years is the single most discriminating piece of history and is almost never volunteered.

sources.label: American Psychiatric Association Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition Text Revision

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome during inpatient nutritional rehabilitation
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 19-year-old woman admitted three days ago for nutritional rehabilitation. Her body mass index is 13.4 kg/m2 and she had eaten almost nothing for the preceding two weeks.

Nasogastric feeding was commenced on admission and she is now receiving 1400 kilocalories a day. She has taken thiamine and a multivitamin since admission. This morning she reports calf cramps and feels short of breath climbing one flight of stairs. Her chest is clear on auscultation, her jugular venous pressure is not elevated and there are no peripheral oedema or crackles. Her electrocardiogram shows a corrected QT interval of 470 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 52, BP 96/60, RR 20, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.2
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no oedema, proximal weakness on standing from a chair
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.38 mmol/L (0.75-1.50); potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); magnesium 0.58 mmol/L (0.70-1.10); corrected QT interval 470 ms; creatinine and glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Stop nasogastric feeding entirely and resume it once her electrolytes have normalised
options.rationale: Stopping nutrition in a severely malnourished patient causes further deterioration and prolongs the period of risk, and it is not what current guidance recommends for a correctable biochemical abnormality (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.text: Increase her caloric intake as planned and repeat the electrolyte panel tomorrow
options.rationale: Escalating the caloric load drives further intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium, and a 24 hour interval is far too long once the phosphate has already fallen this low (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.text: Commence intravenous fluid resuscitation with normal saline and monitor her hourly
options.rationale: Sodium and volume loading risks precipitating cardiac failure in a myocardium that is atrophied and poorly compliant, and it does nothing about the electrolyte deficits driving her symptoms (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.text: Continue feeding at a reduced rate and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium
options.rationale: Refeeding syndrome is managed by slowing rather than ceasing nutrition while aggressively correcting the three electrolytes that shift intracellularly, with continuous cardiac monitoring given the prolonged corrected QT interval (Source: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).
source_refs: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

options.text: Replace phosphate alone and continue the current feeding rate without other changes
options.rationale: Correcting phosphate while leaving hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia untreated leaves the arrhythmia risk in place, and magnesium repletion is required before potassium will correct at all (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome arises when carbohydrate delivery to a starved patient triggers an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, on top of total body stores that are already depleted. Phosphate depletion impairs adenosine triphosphate generation and red cell oxygen delivery, producing the weakness, breathlessness and cardiac dysfunction seen here. The historical response of stopping feeding has been superseded, because starvation itself is what the patient is being treated for, and current practice slows the rate while replacing electrolytes and continuing thiamine. Highest risk features include a body mass index below 14, negligible intake for more than five days, and low baseline electrolytes, all of which mandate cardiac monitoring and at least daily biochemistry during the first week.
key_points: Insulin driven intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium is the mechanism
Slow the rate of feeding rather than stopping it and replace the electrolytes
Magnesium must be corrected before hypokalaemia will respond to potassium replacement
Thiamine is given before and throughout refeeding to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy
explanation.pearls: Check phosphate, potassium and magnesium at least daily for the first week of refeeding in anyone with a body mass index under 14, because the nadir typically falls on days two to four rather than on the day feeding starts.

sources.label: ANZAED and RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Eating Disorders

subtopic_detail: Lithium continuation in early pregnancy
stem:
You are the registrar in a perinatal mental health clinic seeing a 32-year-old woman who has just discovered she is seven weeks pregnant. The pregnancy is wanted and she intends to continue it.

She has bipolar I disorder with four previous manic episodes, two of which required involuntary admission and one of which followed an abrupt cessation of treatment. She has been well for five years on lithium carbonate 900 mg nightly and has never responded to any other agent. Her lithium level is 0.72 mmol/L, her renal and thyroid function are within normal limits, and she has no other medical history. She asks whether she should stop the lithium immediately.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, insight intact, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.6-0.8); creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate and thyroid function within normal limits; dating ultrasound consistent with seven weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her lithium?

options.text: Continue lithium with more frequent level monitoring and arrange a detailed cardiac scan
options.rationale: The absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly is roughly 1 in 1000 with first trimester lithium, which is far outweighed by a relapse risk above 50 per cent after cessation in a woman with four manic episodes and no alternative that has worked (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health; RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Cease lithium immediately and monitor her mental state weekly through the pregnancy
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation carries the highest relapse risk of any option and has already precipitated one manic episode in her history, and organogenesis is in any case well advanced by seven weeks (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Cross taper lithium to sodium valproate over four weeks and monitor her levels
options.rationale: Valproate is the most teratogenic of all the mood stabilisers and swapping to it in pregnancy exchanges a small cardiac risk for a much larger malformation and neurodevelopmental risk (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Cross taper lithium to lamotrigine over four weeks and continue it through delivery
options.rationale: Lamotrigine protects mainly against depressive relapse and has weak evidence for mania prevention, so it is a poor substitute in an illness that has been consistently manic (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.text: Halve the lithium dose for the first trimester and restore the full dose afterwards
options.rationale: A subtherapeutic level leaves her exposed to the drug while removing its prophylactic effect, and the teratogenic association is with exposure rather than being reliably dose avoidable (Source: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health).
source_refs: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: The absolute teratogenic risk of first trimester lithium has been revised sharply downward from early registry estimates, with the risk of Ebstein anomaly now put at roughly 1 in 1000 against a background population rate of about 1 in 20000. That has to be weighed against relapse rates above 50 per cent when lithium is stopped in pregnancy, rising further with abrupt cessation, and against the consequences of mania in pregnancy for both mother and fetus. By seven weeks the cardiac outflow tract has already formed, so stopping now removes future protection without undoing past exposure. Practical management involves more frequent level monitoring as renal clearance rises through pregnancy, a fetal echocardiogram at around 18 to 20 weeks, and a plan to withhold or reduce the dose around labour when volume shifts make toxicity likely.
key_points: Ebstein anomaly risk with first trimester lithium is about 1 in 1000
Relapse risk after stopping lithium in pregnancy exceeds 50 per cent and rises with abrupt cessation
Cardiac organogenesis is complete by seven weeks, so stopping does not undo exposure
Renal clearance rises through pregnancy so levels need checking more often
explanation.pearls: Lithium clearance falls abruptly at delivery as plasma volume contracts, so withhold the dose at the onset of labour and recheck the level within 24 hours postpartum before restarting the pre-pregnancy dose.

sources.label: COPE Australian Clinical Practice Guideline for Perinatal Mental Health
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

subtopic_detail: Serotonin toxicity after an antidepressant switch
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman brought in by her partner with agitation and shaking that began six hours ago.

Her general practitioner stopped fluoxetine 40 mg daily last week and started tranylcypromine four days ago. She takes no other regular medication and no illicit substances. On examination her jaw is not rigid, her limbs move freely against gravity, and inducible clonus is present at both ankles with ocular clonus also seen. Her lower limb tone is markedly greater than her upper limb tone. Her creatine kinase is 620 U/L and she has had no recent antipsychotic exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126, BP 158/94, RR 26, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Inducible ankle clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, lower limb tone greater than upper limb, diaphoresis, mydriasis
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 620 U/L (30-190); sodium, potassium, creatinine and blood glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give dantrolene and bromocriptine and admit her to a critical care bed for cooling
options.rationale: These agents treat neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which is excluded by the absence of any antipsychotic exposure and by clonus and hyperreflexia rather than lead-pipe rigidity and bradykinesia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Restart fluoxetine at a lower dose and continue tranylcypromine under observation
options.rationale: Reintroducing a serotonin reuptake inhibitor alongside a monoamine oxidase inhibitor is the interaction that caused this presentation and would make it substantially worse (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Cease both antidepressants, give benzodiazepines and add oral cyproheptadine
options.rationale: Withdrawal of the serotonergic agents with benzodiazepine sedation is the foundation of treatment, and cyproheptadine is the serotonin antagonist added when features are moderate to severe as they are with hyperthermia and clonus (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology; Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).

options.text: Give a single dose of intravenous haloperidol and observe her for two hours
options.rationale: Antipsychotics with dopamine blockade do not treat serotonin toxicity, impair heat dissipation and can convert the presentation into a mixed and more dangerous syndrome (Source: Austin Health Toxicology Handbook).

options.text: Give paracetamol for the fever and observe her overnight on the short stay unit
options.rationale: Hyperthermia here is generated by muscular hyperactivity rather than by a raised hypothalamic set point, so antipyretics are ineffective and ward observation underestimates the risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity is a clinical diagnosis made on the triad of neuromuscular excitation, autonomic instability and altered mental state, with the Hunter criteria resting heavily on clonus. It is separated from neuroleptic malignant syndrome by tempo and by the character of the motor findings, since serotonin toxicity develops within hours and produces clonus and hyperreflexia that are greater in the legs, while neuroleptic malignant syndrome evolves over days with generalised lead-pipe rigidity and bradykinesia. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors combined with any serotonergic drug produce the most severe form, and fluoxetine's long half life means a washout of about five weeks is required before starting one. Treatment is withdrawal of the offending agents, benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity, active cooling, and cyproheptadine for moderate to severe cases, with paralysis and intubation if hyperthermia exceeds 39 degrees.
key_points: Clonus, hyperreflexia and lower limb predominant hypertonia define serotonin toxicity
Onset within hours contrasts with the days long evolution of neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Fluoxetine requires about five weeks of washout before a monoamine oxidase inhibitor
Antipyretics do not work because the heat is generated by muscular activity
explanation.pearls: A temperature above 39 degrees in serotonin toxicity is an indication for immediate paralysis, intubation and active cooling rather than escalating drug therapy, because the hyperthermia itself causes rhabdomyolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation within hours.

subtopic_detail: Clozapine induced myocarditis in the initiation window
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 25-year-old man on day 18 of a clozapine titration for treatment resistant schizophrenia. He is now taking 250 mg daily and his psychotic symptoms have improved.

Over the past two days he has felt increasingly tired and short of breath walking to the dining room, which he could do comfortably last week. He has no cough, no pleuritic pain and no calf swelling. His neutrophil count has remained normal throughout and his chest radiograph shows no consolidation. His troponin and C reactive protein were both normal at baseline before clozapine was started.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 104/64, RR 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.8
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation, no murmur, no calf tenderness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 340 ng/L (less than 16); C reactive protein 78 mg/L (less than 5); neutrophils 4.6 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (less than 0.5); chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose and repeat the troponin again in 48 hours
options.rationale: Continuing the drug in the face of a rising troponin and C reactive protein risks progression to fulminant myocarditis and death, and a 48 hour delay is not a safe observation interval (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Halve the clozapine dose and arrange an outpatient echocardiogram within two weeks
options.rationale: Myocarditis is a hypersensitivity reaction that is not dose dependent, so halving the dose provides no protection and defers the investigation that decides management (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Withhold clozapine tonight and recommence the titration if he improves by morning
options.rationale: A single withheld dose followed by rechallenge exposes him again to the agent causing the reaction, and rechallenge after confirmed myocarditis is undertaken only in highly specialised settings (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous antibiotics and continue the clozapine titration
options.rationale: The clear chest radiograph, normal neutrophil count and absence of a septic focus make bacterial infection unlikely, and treating it does not address the cardiac injury (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and arrange an urgent echocardiogram and cardiology review
options.rationale: Tachycardia, breathlessness and fever with a rising troponin, C reactive protein and eosinophil count between days 14 and 21 of titration is clozapine induced myocarditis until proven otherwise, and immediate cessation with urgent cardiac assessment is the standard response (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Clozapine induced myocarditis occurs in roughly 1 to 3 per cent of Australian patients and clusters tightly in the second and third weeks of titration, which is why many local protocols include baseline and weekly troponin and C reactive protein for the first four weeks. It is a hypersensitivity reaction rather than a dose-dependent toxicity, and eosinophilia is a supportive feature. The early symptoms of fatigue, breathlessness, tachycardia and low grade fever are easily attributed to clozapine's known sedation or to an incidental viral illness, and that misattribution is the main cause of death. Neutrophil monitoring, which is mandatory and familiar, gives no protection against this complication at all, so a normal neutrophil count is falsely reassuring.
key_points: Myocarditis clusters between days 14 and 21 of clozapine titration
Baseline and weekly troponin and C reactive protein for the first four weeks are standard in Australia
It is a hypersensitivity reaction and is not dose dependent
A normal neutrophil count offers no reassurance about myocarditis
explanation.pearls: A persistent resting tachycardia above 120 beats per minute in the third week of clozapine titration warrants a troponin and C reactive protein the same day, even when the patient attributes the breathlessness to being unfit.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Chronic insomnia first line treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 44-year-old accountant who has had trouble getting to sleep and staying asleep on five nights a week for nine months. She lies awake for up to two hours and then watches the clock, and she is irritable and unproductive at work.

She drinks one coffee before midday and uses no alcohol or other substances. She has no depressive or anxiety disorder on structured assessment, her thyroid function is within normal limits, and her partner has never heard her snore or stop breathing. A sleep diary shows eight and a half hours in bed for about five and a half hours of sleep, and she has already removed her phone from the bedroom without benefit.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, no goitre, mental state examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, full blood count and ferritin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia including sleep restriction
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line for chronic insomnia disorder, and the excessive time in bed with poor sleep efficiency is precisely what its sleep restriction component targets (Source: RACGP: Management of Chronic Insomnia; Sleep Health Foundation Australia).

options.text: Prescribe temazepam at night for four weeks and review her sleep diary after that
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are for short term situational insomnia only, and starting one in a nine month problem sets up tolerance and rebound insomnia on withdrawal (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Prescribe low dose amitriptyline at night and review her symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Sedating antidepressants are prescribed off label for sleep but have anticholinergic effects and no evidence base as first line in primary insomnia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Prescribe melatonin modified release nightly and review her symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Modified release melatonin is approved for people aged 55 and over and has modest effects on sleep onset, so it does not displace structured therapy here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Provide written sleep hygiene advice alone and review her sleep diary in six weeks
options.rationale: Sleep hygiene as a standalone intervention performs poorly in trials and is the weakest component of the therapy package rather than a substitute for it (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia).

explanation.summary: Chronic insomnia disorder requires difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep at least three nights a week for at least three months, with daytime consequences, in the presence of adequate opportunity to sleep. Assessment excludes contributors such as obstructive sleep apnoea, restless legs, shift work, substances, pain and untreated mood or anxiety disorder. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia combines stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive restructuring and relaxation, and it outperforms hypnotics at follow up because its gains persist after treatment ends. Australian access has broadened through digital programs and psychologists trained in the model, which matters where face to face therapy is limited.
key_points: Diagnosis requires three nights weekly for three months with daytime impairment
Exclude sleep apnoea, restless legs, substances and untreated mood or anxiety disorder
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is first line and its gains persist after treatment
Sleep restriction targets low sleep efficiency and is the most active ingredient
Hypnotics are short term adjuncts, not maintenance therapy
explanation.pearls: Sleep restriction sets time in bed to the average total sleep time from the diary, never below five hours, then extends it by fifteen minutes each week once sleep efficiency exceeds 85 per cent.

subtopic_detail: Gambling disorder identification and initial management
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 38-year-old man referred after presenting to his general practitioner with insomnia and low mood. On questioning he describes betting on sport through a phone application most evenings, increasing his stakes over two years to chase losses.

He has hidden a personal loan from his partner and has twice tried to stop for a month without success. He drinks two standard drinks a week and uses no other substances. He denies current suicidal intent but says he has thought that his family would be better off without him, and his mood improves on days when he does not bet.

data_table.Examination: Mildly anxious, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence an antidepressant for the depressive symptoms and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants do not treat the disorder itself and his mood tracks his betting, so treating mood alone leaves the driver of the presentation untouched (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence naltrexone and arrange psychiatric review of his mood in four weeks
options.rationale: Opioid antagonists show benefit in some trials but are an adjunct after psychological therapy has been organised, not the opening intervention (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Refer for structured psychological therapy with safety assessment and self-exclusion advice
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy is the best evidenced treatment, and it is paired with a suicide risk assessment and practical harm reduction such as national self-exclusion registration and financial safeguards (Source: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register

options.text: Advise him to disclose the debt to his partner and review his progress in six weeks
options.rationale: Disclosure is often part of recovery but is his decision to time, and advice alone provides no treatment for a disorder with a high relapse rate (Source: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register).
source_refs: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register

options.text: Admit to an inpatient unit for supervised withdrawal from gambling behaviours
options.rationale: There is no physiological withdrawal syndrome requiring admission, and inpatient care is reserved for acute suicide risk or severe comorbidity (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

explanation.summary: Gambling disorder is classified with the substance related and addictive disorders because of shared features of tolerance, withdrawal-like irritability, loss of control and chasing losses. It is strongly associated with depression, anxiety, alcohol use disorder and suicide, with suicide risk several times that of the general population, so risk assessment is part of every consultation. Cognitive behavioural therapy has the strongest evidence, delivered face to face, by telephone or online, alongside financial counselling and practical barriers such as the national self-exclusion register and bank gambling blocks. Comorbid depression is treated in its own right when it does not remit as gambling reduces.
key_points: Classified with addictive disorders and shares tolerance and loss of control features
Suicide risk is markedly elevated and is assessed at every contact
Cognitive behavioural therapy is the best evidenced treatment
Self-exclusion registration, bank blocks and financial counselling are practical adjuncts
Treat comorbid depression separately if it persists as gambling reduces
explanation.pearls: The national self-exclusion register blocks a person from all licensed Australian online and telephone wagering operators for a chosen period of at least three months, and registration is a concrete first session task rather than general advice.

sources.label: Gambling Help Australia and BetStop National Self-Exclusion Register

subtopic_detail: Initial approach to an adult seeking gender affirming care
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 24-year-old trans woman referred by her general practitioner for an opinion before starting feminising hormone therapy. She has identified as female since her mid teens, has socially transitioned for two years and uses her chosen name at work.

She describes persistent low mood and social anxiety that she attributes to family rejection and to workplace misgendering, with no self-harm and no psychotic symptoms. She has capacity, is not intoxicated and has read reputable material about the effects and limits of hormone therapy. Her general practitioner has asked whether her mood symptoms mean treatment should be deferred.

data_table.Examination: Mood mildly low with reactive affect, no thought disorder, no suicidal intent, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function, renal function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Defer hormone therapy until her depressive and anxiety symptoms have fully remitted
options.rationale: Requiring full remission before affirming care sets a threshold not applied to other treatments and delays an intervention that itself improves mood (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care; RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity

options.text: Request a two year documented real life experience before supporting hormone therapy
options.rationale: Mandatory real life experience requirements have been removed from contemporary standards as a barrier without evidence of benefit (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care).

options.text: Commence a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review the gender question in six months
options.rationale: Medicating distress that arises largely from rejection and misgendering, while postponing the affirming intervention, treats the symptom and not the situation (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity

options.text: Advise that psychiatric assessment is mandatory before any hormone can be prescribed
options.rationale: Australian standards support an informed consent model delivered by experienced prescribers, with mental health input available rather than compulsory (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care).

options.text: Support hormone therapy now and treat her mood symptoms alongside it
options.rationale: Coexisting mood or anxiety symptoms are not a barrier to affirming care when capacity is intact, and gender affirming hormone therapy is associated with improved psychological outcomes while the mood symptoms are treated concurrently (Source: AusPATH Standards of Care; RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity).
source_refs: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity

explanation.summary: Contemporary Australian standards for adult gender affirming care use an informed consent model in which capacity, understanding of the effects and limits of treatment, and management of relevant medical risks are what matter, rather than psychiatric gatekeeping. Mental health problems are common in trans and gender diverse populations and largely reflect minority stress, family rejection and discrimination, so they are treated alongside affirming care rather than as a precondition for it. Psychiatric input is valuable where diagnostic uncertainty, significant mental illness affecting capacity, or complex comorbidity exists. Cohort data consistently show improvement in depression, anxiety and quality of life after commencing affirming hormone therapy.
key_points: Adult care follows an informed consent model, not compulsory psychiatric approval
Real life experience requirements have been removed from current standards
Coexisting mood and anxiety symptoms are treated alongside affirming care
Minority stress explains much of the psychological distress in this population
Psychiatric input is for capacity concerns, diagnostic uncertainty or complex comorbidity
explanation.pearls: Feminising hormone therapy produces breast development and body fat redistribution over one to two years but does not change voice pitch, which is why speech pathology referral is discussed at the same visit rather than after treatment disappoints.

sources.label: RANZCP Position Statement on Gender Diversity

subtopic_detail: Family intervention where relapse follows household conflict
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 23-year-old man with schizophrenia three weeks after discharge following his second admission in a year. He lives with his parents and takes paliperidone by monthly depot injection, with confirmed administration of every dose.

He has no positive symptoms currently and his negative symptoms are stable. His mother describes daily arguments in which she tells him he is lazy and should try harder, and both parents say they are exhausted and do not understand the illness. He uses no substances, urine drug screening is negative, and his admissions both followed periods of escalating conflict at home.

data_table.Examination: No hallucinations or delusions elicited, affect blunted, insight partial, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; full blood count, renal function and metabolic panel within normal limits

lead_in: What intervention is most likely to reduce his risk of relapse?

options.text: Increase the depot dose and review his mental state again in four weeks
options.rationale: Dose escalation targets breakthrough symptoms or non-adherence, and he has neither, so it adds adverse effect burden without addressing the pattern (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Add an oral antipsychotic alongside the depot to broaden his relapse protection
options.rationale: Antipsychotic polypharmacy increases adverse effects without consistent efficacy gains and is discouraged outside treatment resistance (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Arrange supported independent accommodation to remove him from the household
options.rationale: Moving out may eventually suit him, but separating a young person from his main supports is a large step before the family has been offered treatment (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Refer him for individual cognitive behavioural therapy for his negative symptoms
options.rationale: Individual therapy helps residual symptoms and distress, but it does not modify the household environment that has preceded both relapses (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.text: Offer structured family intervention with psychoeducation over at least ten sessions
options.rationale: Family intervention including psychoeducation, communication training and problem solving reduces relapse and readmission where household criticism is high, and it is the highest yield addition when medication is already effective and taken (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Relapse prevention in schizophrenia rests on effective antipsychotic treatment that is actually taken, on avoiding substances, and on the psychosocial environment. High expressed emotion in the household, meaning criticism, hostility or emotional over-involvement, is one of the most consistent predictors of relapse and is modifiable. Structured family intervention delivered over at least ten sessions reduces relapse and readmission by roughly half in the year after treatment and also reduces carer burden. Attributing negative symptoms to laziness is a common and correctable misunderstanding that psychoeducation directly targets.
key_points: High expressed emotion in the household predicts relapse and is modifiable
Family intervention needs at least ten sessions to show benefit
It reduces relapse and readmission and lowers carer burden
Negative symptoms misread as laziness drive household criticism
Polypharmacy and dose escalation do not address environmental relapse drivers
explanation.pearls: Family intervention reduces twelve month relapse from around 50 per cent to around 25 per cent in high expressed emotion households, an effect size comparable to that of maintenance antipsychotic treatment itself.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia
Cochrane Review: Family Intervention for Schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Choosing the NSW instrument for recording preferences and carer involvement
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 35-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, well and working three months after a manic episode that required involuntary admission in NSW. Olanzapine was intolerably sedating during that admission and another agent suited her. She wants her objection to olanzapine known if she relapses, and her sister rather than her estranged father contacted. She has capacity and asks what she can put in place now.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychotic features, insight good, cognition intact
